Monday morning
8:00 Your numbers Salesforce is full of data and the dashboard still can't say what the mail bought. Best guess: “I think it's working.” Your five Monday numbers are in your inbox: cost per contract by channel, last month's mail included.
8:15 Weekend calls A seller called the mailer number Friday at 6:40pm. Voicemail, and nothing in Salesforce. Nobody heard it. Friday's 6:40pm call set off an alert and a callback task. A rep called back that night.
8:40 Offers An offer went out last week and went quiet. Salesforce shows it open, with no task and no owner. Offers with no activity are on one list, each with an owner and a due date.
9:00 Texts A seller who replied on Saturday still gets this morning's follow-up text. The cadence never stopped. Cadences stopped when sellers replied. Nobody texts a seller who already answered.
9:20 Automations A Flow or a Zap stopped firing two weeks ago. You hear about it today, from a rep. The automations are native Flows with failure alerts. If one stops firing, you know within a day.
9:45 A change You need a new lead source set up. It's a developer ticket and a week, and nobody is sure what is safe to change. The new lead source goes live this week. Ops turned on its alerts, no developer.
10am: money spent, sellers missed, and nobody sure why.
10am: you know what the mail bought, and every seller has an owner.

Watch
Two Mondays where Salesforce leaks, in two short videos
The 6:40pm call 43 seconds
The 5 leaks 1 minute 45 seconds
Read both videos as text
The 6:40pm call
On-screen text and sound effects, no voice. A normal Tuesday. A seller calls at 6:40pm and nobody answers. Then what usually happens: at 6:41pm the voicemail lands in a shared inbox. The next day someone calls back at 10am and gets no answer. From day 2 to day 7 the status still says “new”. By then he called someone else. No one's fault: there's no system.
The fix is two rules. When a call is missed, a callback task is created and the seller gets a text. When a lead sits untouched for an hour, someone gets pinged. Nobody has to remember. How many did you miss last week? See what they cost you with the missed-call cost calculator .
The 5 leaks
On-screen text and sound effects, no voice. You don't have a lead problem. You have a leak problem, and there are 5 of them: 5 places money leaks out between the marketing dollar and the kept deal.
Spend. The lead source report tracks leads by source, but contracts by source and cost per deal are question marks. Nobody knows. The fix: the lead source follows the deal all the way to closing.
Answer. Two missed seller calls, at 6:42pm and 7:15pm. A callback task due in 5 minutes is created and assigned to the next rep. Replying within an hour makes you about 7 times likelier to qualify the lead (Harvard Business Review, 2011).
Follow-up. Of five open leads, only two have a next step: a call on Tuesday and an offer on Friday. How many of yours have none? The fix: no open lead without a next task.
Offer. Three reps offer $118k, $131k and $142k on the same house. On the example deal, ARV $250,000 × 70% is $175,000, minus $40,000 of repairs and a $10,000 fee, so the max offer is $125,000 and two of the three offers are over it. The fix: MAO lives on the deal as a formula, not in someone's head.
Keep. Ten contracts signed this month and three fell out, so you kept 7, not 10, and ROI is overstated by 43%. The fix: ROI counts kept deals only.
Which one is yours? Score yours in 30 seconds, free, with the kept-deal map .

Questions
Before you book
Working with me
We're about to hire a full-time Salesforce admin. Should we?
Maybe later. At a team of 10 to 50, most of the work is small changes every week: a new lead source, a new hire, an alert that broke. A retainer covers that for less than a salary, and the audit shows how much work there really is. Hire an admin or use a retainer compares the two. If you do hire, here's how to hire a Salesforce admin , with interview questions and a paid test.
We're adding reps or opening a new market. Should we fix the CRM first?
If you can, yes. More leads through the same leaks means more money lost the same way. The audit tells you what to fix before you scale, in the order I'd fix it. For the setup itself, use the checklists for adding acquisitions reps and opening a new market .
We're on Podio, REsimpli or GoHighLevel. Can you audit that?
No. The audit is built for Salesforce. If you're outgrowing another CRM or spreadsheets, the right first step is a move to Salesforce: I map what you track today, move your data and build around how your team works. See how a move to Salesforce works , or plan it on a free call.
What does it cost?
The CRM Revenue Audit is $1,500, fixed, and the full fee comes off the build if you go ahead within 30 days. A full implementation is quoted as a project after a free call. Ongoing support is a monthly retainer with no long-term contract. Salesforce licenses are billed by Salesforce, so ask your account manager for a quote for your team size; teams can often get a discount.
You're in Cairo. How does that work?
I work US hours, 9am to 6pm Eastern, Monday to Friday, and reply within one business day. That's how I've worked with a home-buying company in Ohio for two years. Calls are booked at a time that suits you.
You're one person. Why not an agency?
With an agency, your project often goes through a project manager to a consultant who may never have worked in real estate. With me, the person who answers your message is the person who builds it. The honest trade-off: I'm one specialist, not a ten-person team, so I take on a small number of clients at a time. Everything I build lives in your org and belongs to you, and I write down how each piece works so another admin could take it over.
What access do you need, and is our data safe?
For the audit, a read-only Salesforce user covers most of the review. You create the user, so you can see what it does and switch it off at any time. It does use one of your Salesforce licenses; if none is spare, we can free one or do the review on screen shares instead. Nothing in your org changes without your OK, and each quick fix (up to 3) is agreed with you first. Your data stays in your org, and I'm happy to sign your NDA before I log in.
What have you actually built?
For two years I've run the Salesforce for a two-market home-buying company in Ohio: campaign ROI by market checked against the books, missed-call alerts on every marketing number, follow-up that stops when a seller replies, a Transactions Board for every file under contract, and settings ops can change without a developer. At Pezon Properties in Pennsylvania I delivered 50+ requests, including a campaign ROI dashboard with 25 funnel metrics and a rebuilt transaction coordination app.
Do you work with teams outside the US?
Yes. Investors in Canada, the UK and Europe get the same offer and the same terms, and their working hours overlap with mine. See Salesforce for Canadian investors and Salesforce for UK property investors .
Do you train the team too?
Yes. Before Salesforce I spent eight years as an Adobe Certified Instructor and taught 8,000+ students, rated 4.9/5. Every build comes with training built around your team's daily work.
About Salesforce
Is Salesforce worth it for a wholesaling or home-buying team?
It depends on your size and how custom your process is. Investor CRMs are faster to start with. Salesforce makes sense when you need your own pipeline, reports leadership trusts, or more integrations than an investor CRM allows. I wrote the honest version, including when Salesforce is overkill: Salesforce vs investor CRMs .
How do you set up speed to lead in Salesforce?
A Flow runs the moment a lead is created: it assigns the lead to the right rep or queue, creates a callback task and sends an alert. Missed calls on marketing numbers create their own callback tasks, and a report shows how long sellers really wait. The full setup is in the speed to lead guide .
How long does a Salesforce implementation take?
Most focused builds take 6 to 12 weeks, scoped up front: the design first, then the core build (lead routing, pipeline, automations and integrations), then reports and training. Bigger builds take longer and are scoped before they start.

## Acquisitions Team Capacity Calculator for Wholesalers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/acquisitions-team-capacity-calculator.html

How many acquisition reps do you need?
Add up the hours your seller leads actually need each month (first calls, follow-up and offers) and compare them with what your team can cover. When the hours needed are higher than the hours available, leads go uncalled, whatever your CRM says.
The formula
Hours needed = (leads × first-conversation rate × minutes per first conversation
 + leads × follow-up touches × minutes per touch
 + offers × minutes per offer) ÷ 60
Hours per rep = productive hours per day × working days
Reps needed = hours needed ÷ hours per rep
Worked example
300 new leads a month at 15 minutes for the first conversation, 4 follow-up touches of 4 minutes each, and 40 offers at 45 minutes need about 185 hours a month. A rep with 5 productive hours over 21 days covers 105 hours, so this volume needs about 1.8 reps.
Questions
How many leads can one acquisition rep handle?
It depends on how much time each lead takes. A rep with 5 productive hours a day over 21 working days has about 105 hours a month. Divide that by the minutes each lead needs across first contact, follow-up and offers. Use the calculator with your own minutes.
Why count follow-up touches?
Follow-up is the work that gets dropped first when a team is over capacity, and it is often where the deals are. Counting it shows the real load, and shows how many hours automated reminders and texts could give back.
What are productive hours?
Time a rep spends talking to sellers or working leads, not total hours at work. Meetings, admin and breaks come out. Most teams overestimate this number, so measure it from call logs if you can.
Can a CRM reduce the hours needed?
It can remove the hours that do not need a person: logging calls, creating next tasks, sending scheduled texts and reminders, and routing missed calls. It cannot replace the conversations themselves.
How do I measure the inputs from my own data?
Pull talk time per call and touches per lead from your phone system and CRM for the last 30 days. If those numbers are not available, that gap is the first thing to fix.
Related free tools
Adding acquisitions reps: setup checklist · Wholesaling team roles · Salesforce access for VAs · Cold caller handoff checklist · Missed seller call cost · Deal Leak Score · The Monday 5 · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.

## Adding Acquisitions Reps: What to Set Up in Salesforce First
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/add-acquisitions-reps-crm.html

Adding acquisitions reps? Set this up in Salesforce before their first call
Adding a rep usually goes like this: a login, a dialer seat, a couple of days listening to calls, and then leads. The first weeks are when leads slip the most, and nobody notices until the owner asks about a seller who never got a callback. This checklist is for owners and acquisitions managers on Salesforce who are about to hire. It's what I'd want in place before a new rep's first call, plus two short check-ins after.
Before day one, give the rep their own user with a sales profile and a permission set, under their manager in the role hierarchy. Connect their phone, texting and email to that user, add them to lead assignment only from their first calling day, and give them three list views and approved templates. In the first week, add a speed-to-lead alert and required fields by stage, and read their leads on day three. After two weeks, compare them with the team on a ramp report, and have a plan ready for the day a rep leaves.
Still deciding whether you need another rep? The acquisitions capacity calculator works out how many leads your current reps can handle. If the answer is yes, hand this page to whoever runs your Salesforce. Go through the first five steps before the rep's first day, and book 20 minutes at the end of week two for the last three.
Before day one
Set up | Why it matters | How to check it works
1. User, profile and role. A sales profile plus a permission set, not admin rights, placed under their manager in the role hierarchy. | The manager sees every lead the rep owns, and the rep can't change automations by accident. | Log in as the rep and open one lead and one report.
2. Phone, texting and email under their own user. Connect the dialer, texting tool and inbox to the rep's user, not a shared login. | Every call, text and email lands on the seller record, so nothing lives only in their phone. | Make a test call and send a test text. Both show on the lead within a minute.
3. Lead assignment with a start date. Add them to round robin or the assignment rules only from the day they take calls, and decide what happens after hours. | New leads don't sit with someone who isn't ready yet. | Create a test lead and see who gets it.
4. Three list views. "My new leads" (newest first), "No activity in 48 hours" and "Follow-ups due today". | The rep starts every day from the same lists instead of memory. | The rep finds all three in one click.
5. Approved templates. First contact, no answer, after the offer, and "call me later". | A new rep sounds like the rest of the team from day one. | The templates show up in the dialer and the email composer.
Three things people forget in this part:
A license. Every rep needs their own Salesforce user license. If someone has left, deactivating their user frees that license. Freezing them doesn't.
Multi-factor authentication. Salesforce enforces MFA for all employee logins, so set it up with the rep before their first calling day, not at 8 a.m. on it.
The round robin itself. If yours is a formula, such as MOD(VALUE(Lead_Number__c), 3) for three reps, a fourth rep means changing the 3 to a 4 and adding a rule for the new value. Do it on the rep's first calling day, and create a test lead afterwards. More options in lead and call routing .
If the new person is a VA or a cold caller rather than an acquisitions rep, they need a narrower setup. See VA access in Salesforce .
First week
Set up | Why it matters | How to check it works
6. Speed-to-lead alert. If a new lead gets no call or text within a set number of minutes, alert the rep, then the manager. | The first weeks are when leads slip the most. | Leave a test lead untouched and watch the alert fire.
7. Required fields by stage. Motivation, timeline and asking price before "Offer made". A reason before "Dead". | Notes stay useful when someone else picks up the lead. | Try to skip a stage. Salesforce should stop you.
8. Day-three spot check. The manager opens a few of the rep's leads and reads the notes and next steps. | Bad habits get fixed before they spread. | Every open lead has a next task with a date.
Some teams start a new rep on a smaller share of new leads, or on one lead source, and widen it once the first numbers look right. That's easier to do if your routing supports weights, and it's one more reason to keep routing rules where ops can change them without a developer.
If your team has a lead manager or cold callers passing sellers to acquisitions, the new rep should know exactly what a qualified handoff looks like. The cold caller handoff checklist lists the fields.
After two weeks
Set up | Why it matters | How to check it works
9. Ramp report. Leads assigned, contacted, appointments and offers for each rep, next to the team average. | You see who's ramping and who needs help without asking around. | It runs for any rep and any date range.
10. Leads with no next step. A report of open leads that have no future task. | These are the leads that quietly die. | The list is short and gets shorter each week.
Compare a new rep with your own team over the same number of weeks, not with a benchmark from the internet. Lead flow, sources and markets differ too much between teams for an outside number to mean much. What you're looking for is the trend. Activity numbers, like contacts and next steps, are the ones a new rep controls, so they should catch up with the team first. Offers and contracts take longer.
If the rep's leads keep showing up on the "no next step" report, that's a coaching conversation, not a Salesforce problem. If everyone's leads show up there, it's the follow-up process. See the follow-up cadence builder .
When a rep leaves
Step 11 on the checklist is a plan for the day a rep leaves, written before you need it. Reps leave, and the leads they owned still belong to you. In order:
Reassign their open leads, deals and tasks the same day. Every seller history stays on the record, so the next rep can read it before calling.
Take them out of everything that sends them work: round robin, assignment rules, queues, alert recipients, scheduled reports and any dashboard that runs as them.
Freeze the user , so they can't log in while you finish the cleanup. Freezing doesn't free the license.
Deactivate the user once nothing depends on them. If Salesforce won't let you, something still points at them, such as a default lead owner setting or an automation. That's useful to know, and worth fixing.
Close the side doors: their dialer, texting and email seats, and any phone number sellers know them by. If that number stays live, point it at someone who can answer.
Practice this once on a test user, so the first time isn't the day someone leaves. To limit what a rep can take with them in the first place, see stopping reps from exporting your seller list . If the person leaving is the one who runs Salesforce, it's a bigger job. See what to do when your Salesforce admin leaves .
Where a new rep's leads usually slip
A shared login "until the license comes through". Nothing they do is tracked to them, and every report on that user is wrong for weeks.
Texting sellers from a personal cell. The conversation never reaches Salesforce, and it leaves with the rep. Every text should go through your texting tool. More in texting in Salesforce .
Admin rights "to save time". One wrong click edits an automation for the whole team.
Leads before the phone works. The first leads wait while someone fixes the dialer connection.
No manager above them in the role hierarchy , so the person accountable for the rep can't see the rep's leads.
Missed calls with nowhere to go. If the rep owns a seller who calls back while they're on another call, a missed-call alert should reach them, or a queue. See missed-call alerts in Salesforce .
Questions
What should I set up in Salesforce before a new acquisitions rep starts?
Their own user with a sales profile and permission set under their manager, MFA, phone, texting and email connected to their user, lead assignment starting on their first calling day, three list views (new leads, no activity in 48 hours, follow-ups due today) and approved templates.
Should a new acquisitions rep get leads on their first day?
Only once their phone, texting and email are connected and tested, and they know the follow-up process. Add them to lead assignment from the day they start taking calls, not the day their user is created. Some teams start a new rep on a smaller share of leads and widen it later.
Can two reps share one Salesforce login?
They shouldn't. Each Salesforce license is for one named user, nothing either rep does can be told apart in reports, and with MFA enforced, sharing a login means sharing one person's phone or authenticator app. Give each rep their own user from day one.
Do I need a new Salesforce license for every rep?
Yes, each user needs their own license. If a former rep's user is still active, deactivating it frees that license for the new rep. Freezing a user blocks their login but doesn't free the license.
What permissions should an acquisitions rep have in Salesforce?
A sales profile plus a permission set with what the job needs: their leads and deals, the dialer and texting tools, and their reports. No admin rights, no export and no delete. Their manager should sit above them in the role hierarchy so the manager sees their records.
How do I know if a new rep is ramping well?
Run a ramp report with leads assigned, contacted, appointments and offers for each rep, next to the team average over the same weeks. Watch the trend and the list of their open leads with no next step, rather than comparing them with a number from outside your team.
What happens to a rep's leads when they leave?
Reassign their open leads, deals and tasks the same day, take them out of round robin, queues and alerts, freeze their user, then deactivate it once nothing depends on it. The seller history stays on each record for the next rep to read.

## AI for Wholesalers: Lead Follow-Up Jobs to Automate First
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/ai-for-wholesalers-lead-follow-up.html

AI for wholesalers: the follow-up jobs to automate first, and the ones to leave alone
Every vendor now promises an AI that answers calls, qualifies sellers and follows up for you. Some of it works. The part nobody mentions is that AI is only as good as the system underneath it: if your CRM has duplicate sellers, no stage rules and no consent flags, an AI will follow up on the wrong people, in the wrong order, at the wrong time, faster than a person could. This guide ranks the follow-up jobs by how much they give back and how much they can go wrong, covers the rules for AI calls and texts, and gives a 30-day plan. It's written from a systems view, not a product view: I'm not selling an AI tool, so there is no ranking of brands here.
Start with the jobs where AI helps a person: summarizing calls into the record, drafting follow-up for a person to send, and ranking leads for a person to call. Then rule-based automation for the basics (missed-call text-back, follow-up tasks). Leave AI that talks to sellers on its own until last. The FCC ruled in February 2024 that AI-generated voices are "artificial" under the TCPA, which means prior express consent is required before an AI voice call, and prior express written consent when it's telemarketing. Fix your data first: one record per seller, defined stages, a consent field and a source on every lead.
What does AI need from your CRM before it helps?
Whatever tool you pick, it will read your records and write back to them. Five things have to be true first:
One record per seller. Otherwise the AI works the same person twice. See duplicate seller leads .
Stages with rules. An AI can't know what "qualified" means unless you've defined it. See pipeline stages with entry and exit rules .
A consent field and an opt-out flag that every tool respects. One source of truth for who can be texted or called.
A source on every lead. So you can tell later whether AI follow-up helped on mailers, PPC or cold lists.
A named human owner for every record. The AI hands off to someone.
If two of those five are missing, fix them before you buy anything. They improve a human team's results too.
Which follow-up jobs should you hand to AI first?
I rank these by two questions: how much time do they give back, and what's the worst that happens if the AI gets it wrong?
# | Job | Who stays in control | Risk if wrong
1 | Summarize calls into the record : reason for selling, timeline, condition, next step as fields, not a wall of notes | The rep reviews and saves | Low: a bad summary is caught by a person
2 | Draft the follow-up text or email using what the seller said | A person edits and sends | Low
3 | Rank leads to call next from source, timing, motivation and last contact | The rep decides who to call | Low to medium
4 | Missed-call text-back and follow-up tasks (plain rules, no AI needed) | Rules you wrote | Medium: depends on consent
5 | Reactivate old leads in segments a person approved | A person approves each segment and message | Medium: compliance and tone
6 | Answer inbound calls and book the appointment | Hand-off to a person on any complication | Medium to high: seller trust
7 | Call or text sellers on its own, outbound | Nobody in the moment | High: consent, opt-outs, reputation
Jobs 1 to 3 can start this month with little risk and often give the biggest return, because they remove the typing that reps skip. Job 4 isn't AI, but it's worth doing first because it catches the leads you're already losing; see missed-call alerts and speed to lead . Jobs 6 and 7 are where vendors sell hardest and where mistakes cost the most, so they belong after the basics.
What rules apply to AI calls and texts?
This is a summary, not legal advice. Talk to a lawyer who knows the TCPA and your states before you launch anything that contacts sellers on its own.
AI voices count as artificial voices. In a February 2024 declaratory ruling (FCC 24-17), the FCC said AI technologies that resemble human voices are "artificial" under the TCPA. Calls using them need the called party's prior express consent, and when the call includes an advertisement or telemarketing, prior express written consent.
Opt-outs must be honored fast. Since April 11, 2025, callers must process opt-out requests within a reasonable time not to exceed 10 business days, and honor keywords such as STOP, QUIT, END, REVOKE, OPT OUT, CANCEL and UNSUBSCRIBE, plus other reasonable requests.
A broader rule is coming. The FCC's "global revocation" rule, under which one opt-out applies to all unrelated robocalls and robotexts from that caller, now takes effect January 31, 2027, after earlier delays, and the FCC may still change it. Build for it now.
Texting has its own gatekeepers. Carriers require registration of your messaging campaign (10DLC) and expect consent and opt-out handling. See texting sellers .
Whether a person or an AI wrote the text, the consent rules are the same. The AI doesn't change who you're allowed to contact.
State rules can be stricter. Several states have their own telemarketing and texting laws, including time-of-day limits, so check each state you market in.
What guardrails should every AI follow-up setup have?
It reads the consent and opt-out fields before every message or call, and writes opt-outs back immediately.
Quiet hours by the seller's time zone, not yours.
A clear hand-off to a person: a trigger word, a question it can't answer, or any mention of a lawyer, an agent or a complaint.
Every AI action logged on the seller's record: what it sent, when, and what the seller said.
A kill switch one person can use in a minute.
No promises about price, timing or terms in anything the AI writes.
A weekly sample: someone reads ten real conversations. This catches tone problems no dashboard shows.
A cost cap. AI and messaging are often billed by use, so set an alert before a loop sends something thousands of times. Ask every vendor exactly what is metered.
What does a 30-day rollout look like?
Week 1: clean the base. Add the consent field, deduplicate open leads, write down stage rules.
Week 2: jobs 1 and 2. Call summaries into fields and drafted follow-up, for one rep or a small group. Measure how many leads have a next step set.
Week 3: job 3 plus the rule-based basics. Lead ranking, missed-call text-back where you have consent, follow-up tasks.
Week 4: review. Compare response time, tasks completed on time and appointments set against the month before. Decide whether to go further, based on those numbers.
Where Salesforce fits: it can hold the rules, the consent and the history, and its own AI features (Agentforce, Einstein) are covered in AI agents for home buyers . Whatever platform you use, the order is the same.
Where does AI follow-up go wrong?
It trusts dirty data. Two records, two sequences, one confused seller.
It reactivates the wrong people. Sellers who said stop on another record, or who already sold to someone else.
It sounds like a script. Sellers in a hard situation can tell. Keep wording plain and short, and let a person take over early.
Nobody owns it. If no one reads the logs, small errors repeat for weeks.
It's measured by activity. More messages sent isn't the goal. Appointments set and contracts signed are.
Questions
What is the best AI for real estate wholesalers?
The best one is the one that reads and writes to your CRM, respects your consent and opt-out fields, and hands off to a person cleanly. I don't rank brands, because the right fit depends on your CRM, your lead sources and your states. Check how it handles opt-outs and what it bills by use.
Can AI call sellers for me?
It can, but the FCC ruled in February 2024 that AI-generated voices are artificial voices under the TCPA, so you need the seller's prior express consent, and prior express written consent for telemarketing. Because this is the riskiest job, I'd put it after the basics and get legal advice first.
Is AI cold calling legal in real estate?
Not as a blanket yes or no. AI voice calls need consent under the TCPA, which people you've never spoken to haven't given, and states add their own rules. This is not legal advice: check with a lawyer before any AI voice outreach to people who haven't agreed to it.
Can AI follow up with old leads automatically?
Yes, but start with segments a person approves, check consent and opt-outs across every duplicate record first, and have a human take over when a seller replies. See the reactivation guide for how to segment.
Do I need a CRM before using AI for lead follow-up?
Yes, or at least a single clean record of each seller. AI tools read your lead data, stages and consent. Without one source of truth they follow up on duplicates, skip people who need a call and contact people who opted out.
How do I stop AI from texting someone who opted out?
Keep one consent and opt-out field that every tool reads before sending, copy an opt-out to every duplicate record, and write opt-outs back from your texting tool in real time. Since April 2025 opt-outs must be processed within 10 business days at most, so faster is safer.
Will AI replace my cold callers?
I wouldn't plan on it. In the setups I see working, AI takes the typing and the sorting, such as call notes, drafts and who to call first, and people keep the conversations that win deals. Measure it against your own numbers before changing headcount.
What does AI follow-up cost?
It varies and is often metered, billed by messages, minutes or actions, on top of a platform fee. Ask each vendor what is metered, what the cap is and what happens at the cap. Set an alert so a loop can't run up a bill unnoticed.
Related guides
Sources
Rules were checked in October 2026 and can change. This page is information, not legal advice.

## Assignment vs Double Close Calculator for Wholesalers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/assignment-vs-double-close-calculator.html

Assignment vs double close calculator.
Should you assign the contract or double close? Enter your contract price, the end buyer's price and your costs for each route to see what you actually keep, and how big the spread has to be before a double close is worth it.
The formula
Spread = end buyer's price − your contract price
Assignment: you keep = spread − assignment costs
Double close: you keep = spread − purchase closing costs − resale closing costs − transactional funding
Break-even: a double close only pays off when you could not assign, or when assigning would cost you the deal
Worked example
You have a house under contract at $120,000 and a buyer at $140,000: a $20,000 spread. Assigning costs $500, so you keep $19,500. A double close adds $2,500 and $2,500 of closing costs plus 1.5% transactional funding ($1,800), so you keep $13,200, which is $6,300 less.
Questions
What is the difference between an assignment and a double close?
With an assignment you sell your rights in the purchase contract to the end buyer for a fee, and there is one closing. With a double close you actually buy the property and resell it, usually the same day, so there are two closings and two sets of costs.
When is a double close better?
When the contract cannot be assigned, when the seller or buyer would object to the size of the fee, or when a lender or the end buyer's financing does not allow assignments. It costs more, so it is a tool for protecting the deal, not for raising the profit.
What is transactional funding?
A short-term loan that funds your purchase in a double close and is repaid from the end buyer's funds the same day. Lenders usually charge a percentage of the purchase price, sometimes with a minimum fee. Get a quote before you count on it.
Is wholesaling by assignment legal everywhere?
Rules differ by US state and change over time. Several states now require disclosure, a license or registration for certain wholesaling activity. Check the current rules in your state, and in Canada check your provincial regulator, before you assign a contract.
How do I track fees by exit route?
Record the exit type (assignment or double close), the spread and every cost on the deal record in your CRM. Then you can report net fee per deal by exit route and by lead source, not just the headline number.
Related free tools
Wholesale deal analyzer · Cost per deal by lead source · Deal Leak Score · Assignment fee guide · Double closing costs · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.
Add this calculator to your site
Free to embed on your blog or investor site. Copy the code below.

## Best CRM for Wholesalers (2026): 11 Options Compared
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/best-crm-for-wholesalers.html

Best CRM for wholesalers in 2026.
There isn’t one best CRM for wholesalers. There’s a best one for your team size and the tools you already use. Below are 11 options compared on the things that matter for wholesaling, with every feature and price linked to the vendor’s own site.
Want calling, texting, lists, skip tracing and buyer sites in one login? Look at the all-in-one investor CRMs: REsimpli , FreedomSoft , REI BlackBook .
Already have a dialer and data, and want strict follow-up workflows? InvestorFuse / CarrotCRM .
Want to build your own process as you grow past a few reps or markets? Salesforce , with setup help.
BatchLeads and DealMachine are data tools, not pipeline CRMs. Follow Up Boss and HubSpot aren’t built for investors.
Disclosure: I build Salesforce CRMs for investors, so I have a bias. To keep it in check, every feature and price below comes from the vendor’s own site, linked in the row. I don’t list Salesforce prices: most businesses get a discount from a Salesforce account executive based on the business and number of users.

Starting small? Read what free CRMs give you and where they stop . Running a home-buying company? See the seven jobs your CRM has to do .
How to choose in 15 minutes
Count the logins. One to three people: an all-in-one is usually enough. Five or more reps, VAs or markets: look harder at reporting, permissions and custom records.
List the tools you’ll keep. If you love your dialer and data provider, you don’t need them bundled.
Price the usage, not the plan. Texts, minutes, skip tracing and AI are billed on top for most of these.
Ask how you get your data out. Export, API or Zapier. You’ll care the day you switch.
Test one deal end to end in the trial. Lead in, call, offer, contract, buyer, assignment. Where you hit copy-paste is your answer.
Not sure where your current CRM leaks deals? Take the Deal Leak Score (10 yes/no questions).
Questions
What is the best CRM for wholesalers in 2026?
It depends on team size and what you already use. All-in-one investor CRMs like REsimpli, FreedomSoft and REI BlackBook bundle calling, texting and lists. InvestorFuse focuses on follow-up workflows. Salesforce fits teams that want their own process and deeper reporting and are willing to set it up.
What is the cheapest CRM for wholesaling?
Podio has a free plan and paid plans from $11.20 per user a month on annual billing, but you build everything yourself. REI BlackBook starts at $97 a month with a 500-contact cap. These are published prices from October 2026.
Is GoHighLevel good for wholesaling?
It handles funnels, texting and workflows well, but skip tracing, list stacking and cash buyer search aren’t built in, and calls and texts are billed by usage. Its real estate page targets agents and brokerages.
Is Salesforce too much for a small wholesaler?
Often, yes. A solo wholesaler closing a few deals a month is usually fine on an investor CRM. Salesforce starts making sense with several reps, markets or entities, or when you need reports your current CRM can’t do.
Is BatchLeads a CRM?
Not really. BatchLeads is a data and outreach tool with list stacking, enrichment and click-to-dial. It has no deal pipeline, so most teams connect it to a CRM.
How much does Salesforce cost for a wholesaler?
I don’t quote list prices. Most businesses get a discount from a Salesforce account executive based on the business and number of users. Use the edition picker to work out which edition to ask about.

## Zapier to Salesforce Flow: What to Move First
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-migrate-zapier-to-salesforce-real-estate.html

How I moved a home-buying team’s Zapier automations to native Salesforce
Zapier is the right tool when you're connecting two systems that don't have a native integration. But when your Salesforce org has matured and you're using Zapier primarily to send Slack messages from Salesforce, create tasks, or trigger emails — you're paying for a middleman you don't need.
At Central City Solutions, Zapier API limits were being hit every month. The team was getting "Zap limit exceeded" errors at critical moments — when new leads came in, when deals moved to under contract. I was asked to investigate, and what I found was that most of their Zaps were doing things that Salesforce could do natively, better, and for free.
What Zapier Was Being Used For
When I audited the Zaps, they fell into clear categories:
Slack notifications — Zapier was watching Salesforce for record changes and sending Slack messages. Salesforce's direct Slack integration does this natively.
Task creation — Zapier was creating Salesforce Tasks based on other Salesforce record changes. Salesforce Flow does this in milliseconds with no middleman.
Field updates — Zapier was updating fields on Salesforce records when other fields changed. Again: native Flow territory.
Email alerts — Zapier was sending emails when Salesforce records updated. Salesforce Email Alerts handle this out of the box.
Only a fraction of the Zaps were doing what Zapier is actually designed for: connecting Salesforce to external systems that don't have a Salesforce integration (Facebook Lead Ads, external forms, Google Sheets).
The rule I now apply: if both the trigger AND the action are in Salesforce, or if the action is in a system with a Salesforce-native connector, Zapier is unnecessary. Zapier earns its place when connecting to external systems without native Salesforce integrations.
I migrated their Zaps to native Flows at Central City Solutions — the founder called the work “drastic improvements” in a written referral. See the full case study →
The Migration Process
Step 1: Audit every Zap
Export a list of all active Zaps and categorize by: trigger system, action system, and whether Salesforce is on both ends. In this case, most of the Zaps had Salesforce on both sides. Those were all migration candidates.
Step 2: Map Zap logic to Salesforce objects
For each Zap being migrated, document the trigger condition, any filters, and the exact action. A Zap that says "When Opportunity Stage = Under Contract → Send Slack to #transactions-channel with message: 'New contract at {Property Address}'" maps directly to a Record-Triggered Flow on Opportunity.
Step 3: Set up the Salesforce-Slack direct integration
Central City Solutions had been using Zapier as the Slack bridge for years. Setting up Salesforce's native Slack integration (available in AppExchange or via the Salesforce for Slack app) was a one-time configuration that unlocked direct Slack messaging from any Flow — with no Zap usage, no delay, no API limits.
Step 4: Build the Flows
Each migrated Zap became a Record-Triggered Flow. The advantage over Zapier: Salesforce Flows run in real time (not on Zapier's polling interval, which can be 2-15 minutes). A lead coming in from Facebook now triggered a Slack notification in seconds instead of minutes.
Step 5: Test in parallel, then deactivate Zaps
Run both the Zap and the Flow simultaneously for one week. Verify the Flow output matches. Then deactivate the Zap. Never delete Zaps immediately — keep them paused for 30 days in case anything was missed.
What Stayed in Zapier
After the migration, Zapier still had an important role — but a much smaller one:
Facebook Lead Ads → Salesforce — no native integration, Zapier handles it
Website forms → Salesforce — form platforms without a Salesforce connector
Google Drive folder creation — on new transactions, automatically creating a structured Drive folder
SmrtPhone lead creation edge cases — handling specific SmrtPhone scenarios that the native integration didn't cover
The Reliability Improvement
The API limit errors stopped immediately. But the more significant improvement was reliability. Zapier has an inherent delay (polling interval) and can fail silently when Zap limits are hit. Native Salesforce Flows run synchronously or asynchronously but always fire when the trigger fires — there's no polling, no delay, no external API dependency.
For a real estate company where speed-to-lead is critical, the difference between a 15-minute Zapier delay and an instant Salesforce notification is meaningful. A lead that sat in a Zap queue for 12 minutes is a lead that didn't get called fast enough.
When to Keep Zapier
Zapier is still the right tool for connecting Salesforce to external platforms that don't have native connectors. If you're connecting to Zillow, Facebook Lead Ads, custom forms, or niche real estate software — Zapier is the fastest and most reliable bridge. The goal isn't to eliminate Zapier. It's to use it only where it's irreplaceable.

## RingCentral to Salesforce Call Sync with Apex
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-ringcentral-salesforce-integration-real-estate.html

How to Build a RingCentral–Salesforce Daily Call Sync with Apex (Real Estate Case Study)
A real estate acquisition team makes dozens of calls per day — to motivated sellers, to follow up on leads, to check in on contracts. Logging all of those calls manually in Salesforce is hours of administrative work that takes agents away from their actual job. And if calls aren't logged, reports are wrong, accountability breaks down, and management can't see what's actually happening.
At Central City Solutions, the team was using RingCentral as their phone system. Calls were being made but not consistently logged in Salesforce. The solution was a custom Apex integration that automatically pulls yesterday's call logs from RingCentral's API and creates Salesforce Task records — every day, at 2 AM, without any human involvement.
The Architecture
The solution has two Apex classes working together:
RCDailyCallLogSync.cls — Schedulable class that runs at 2 AM daily, authenticates with RingCentral's API, fetches yesterday's call logs, and creates Task records in Salesforce
RCNextUserScheduler.cls — Queueable class that chains user processing with a 2-minute delay between users, preventing API governor limit violations
Why Chained Processing?
RingCentral rate-limits API requests. If you try to sync 15 users' call logs simultaneously, you'll hit rate limits. The solution: process one user at a time, with a 2-minute delay between users via chained Queueable jobs. Each job processes one user's calls, then enqueues the next user's job with a delay.
This Apex sync runs in production at Central City Solutions today — it eliminated all manual call logging for the team. See the full case study →
Authenticating with RingCentral
RingCentral uses OAuth 2.0. The integration stores the access token in Salesforce Custom Settings or Named Credentials and refreshes it as needed. Each API call fetches call logs for a specific extension (stored as a custom field on the Salesforce User record) for the previous day:
Creating Salesforce Tasks from Call Logs
For each call log record returned by the API, the class creates a Salesforce Task. The key logic:
Recording filter — only create Tasks for calls that have a recording attached (calls under 30 seconds are typically not useful)
Contact matching — match the caller's phone number to an existing Lead or Contact in Salesforce and link the Task to that record
Duration and direction — store call duration, inbound/outbound direction, and the recording URL in the Task description
Bulk safety — process in batches of 250 calls per user to stay within Salesforce governor limits
Handling Errors Gracefully
The integration has built-in error handling for the most common failure scenarios:
API timeout — if RingCentral doesn't respond within 120 seconds, log the error and skip to the next user
User without extension — skip users whose RingCentral_Extension__c field is empty
API authentication failure — catch HTTP 401 responses, refresh the token, and retry once
Empty response — handle gracefully when a user had no calls the previous day
Scheduling and Monitoring
Schedule with a cron expression that runs at 2 AM daily:
After deployment, monitor via Setup → Scheduled Jobs. Check that Tasks are being created by running a Salesforce report filtered to Tasks created by the integration user with yesterday's date.
The Business Impact
Before this integration, call logging at Central City Solutions was inconsistent. Reports showed whatever agents remembered to log. After deployment: every call over 30 seconds was automatically logged, linked to the correct record, and searchable in Salesforce the next morning. Management could finally see actual call activity, not self-reported activity. The accuracy of acquisition performance reports improved immediately.
One unexpected benefit: because call recordings were now attached to the Salesforce Task and linked to the relevant Lead or Transaction record, the transaction coordination team could review seller conversations without asking agents to track down recordings manually.
What You Need to Implement This
To replicate this in your Salesforce org, you'll need: a RingCentral account with API access enabled (Platform plan or higher), RingCentral extension IDs mapped to Salesforce User records, Salesforce API access enabled for the integration user, and a Named Credential or Custom Setting to store the OAuth tokens securely. The Apex classes themselves need to be deployed to your org and the scheduled job activated.

## Why Your Team Isn't Using Salesforce (and the Fix)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-adoption-real-estate.html

Why Your Real Estate Agents Aren't Using Salesforce (And How to Fix It)
Here is the uncomfortable truth about Salesforce adoption in real estate: the system is not the problem. In almost every case, agents are not using Salesforce because using it is harder than not using it. That is a configuration problem, not a people problem.
Failure Mode 1: Too Many Fields, Too Many Steps
The most common reason agents abandon Salesforce: logging a simple contact takes 12 fields and 4 clicks. So they use their notes app instead. The fix: audit every required field on Lead and Opportunity objects. Remove anything not genuinely needed at point of entry. Use dynamic forms so agents only see fields relevant to their current stage. Logging a contact should take under 30 seconds.
I use these frameworks at a home-buying client in Ohio, where the team runs the business from Salesforce, not spreadsheets. See the full case study →
Failure Mode 2: The System Does Not Match How Agents Actually Work
If your Salesforce process was designed without deeply understanding the real estate sales workflow, agents will naturally work around it.
Before configuring anything, I spend time understanding how the team actually works: how they track leads, what information they need at each stage, how they hand off between departments. The CRM should mirror reality — not force a new reality onto the team.
Failure Mode 3: No One Reinforced the Habit
Sending agents to a 2-hour training session and expecting consistent logging is wishful thinking. Habits form from repetition with immediate consequences — not from training alone.
Make the dashboard the source of truth — leadership only discusses deals that exist in Salesforce. If it is not in the system, it does not exist in the pipeline review.
Give agents a personal benefit — automated follow-up reminders, their own performance dashboard, instant lead notifications. Salesforce should make their job easier.
Manager reinforcement — the team leader checks Salesforce before every one-on-one. Agents update Salesforce because their manager references it.
Failure Mode 4: One-Size-Fits-All Training
Your buyer's agent, acquisitions manager, and transaction coordinator all use Salesforce differently. A single generic session serves none of them well. Role-based training teaches each persona exactly what they need — nothing more, nothing less.
The Metric That Tells You If It Is Working
Do not measure adoption by login frequency. Measure data completeness: what percentage of leads have a next activity date set, and what percentage of deals have been updated in the last 7 days. These numbers tell you whether Salesforce is being used as a working tool — or just occasionally checked.

## Manage Salesforce Automations Without a Developer
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-configuration-object-real-estate.html

The Salesforce Configuration Object: How to Manage Automations Without Touching Code
By the time a real estate company's Salesforce has been live for a year, it has accumulated dozens of automation rules — tasks triggered on status changes, Slack notifications for new leads, email alerts when contracts are signed, SMS messages for follow-ups. Every time a business rule changes, someone has to open Flow Builder and modify code.
At Central City Solutions, this became unsustainable. Multiple stakeholders requesting changes weekly. A bottleneck every time a notification needed to be updated, a task reassigned, or a new trigger added.
The solution was a Configuration Object — a custom Salesforce object that acts as the control panel for all automations. Non-technical users can add, edit, enable, and disable any notification without touching a single flow.
What the Configuration Object Is
The Configuration Object is a custom Salesforce object where each record represents one automation rule. Instead of building a separate Flow for every notification, you have one master Flow that reads from the Configuration Object and executes the right action based on the record's settings.
A single Configuration record might say: "When Transaction status changes to Under Contract, send a Slack message to #transactions-channel, and create a task for the TC Rep saying 'Reach out to seller' due same day." Non-technical users can modify that record directly — no Flow Builder, no Salesforce setup, no developer needed.
This is the exact system I built at Central City Solutions (Ohio), where ops changes the rules with no developer. See the full case study →
The Object Fields
The Configuration Object has fields that define what the automation does:
Trigger Object — which Salesforce object triggers the action (Lead, Opportunity, Transaction, Project)
Trigger Condition — the field and value that fires the automation (e.g., Status = "Under Contract")
Notification Type — picklist: Task, Slack, Email, SMS (via SmrtPhone integration)
Assignee / Recipient — lookup to User or Queue, or a formula-based dynamic field
Message Template — rich text field using merge field syntax (e.g., {{Transaction.Property_Address__c}} → replaced at runtime)
Delay — number field for time-delayed triggers (e.g., 24 hours after status change)
Active — checkbox toggle: turn any automation on or off in one click
The Active checkbox was one of the most requested features. When SmrtPhone had an integration issue causing false missed-call notifications, we turned off that specific automation in 30 seconds — without touching any Flow or requiring a developer.
The MergeFieldReplacer Apex Class
The Configuration Object's real power comes from dynamic message templates. A message might say: "14 days out from closing {Transaction.Property_Address__c}. Do we have a buyer?" At runtime, {Transaction.Property_Address__c} needs to be replaced with the actual address.
I built MergeFieldReplacer — an Apex class that takes a text template and a record ID, then replaces all merge field tokens with live Salesforce data:
The class supports:
Standard and custom fields — {{!Transaction__c.Property_Address__c}}
Cross-object relationships — {{!Transaction__c.Opportunity__r.Owner.Name}}
Date arithmetic — {{!Opportunity__c.CloseDate__c-14d}} computes a date 14 days before close
Current user — {{!$User.Name}}
System dates — {{!$Flow.CurrentDate+1d}}
How the Master Flow Works
A single Record-Triggered Flow on each object queries the Configuration Object for active records matching the current trigger condition. For each matching Configuration record, it calls the appropriate action: creates a Task, sends a Slack message via Salesforce's native Slack integration, sends an email via Email Alert, or fires an SMS via SmrtPhone's API.
Adding a new automation means adding one record to the Configuration Object. That's it. No Flow Builder, no deployment, no sandbox testing cycle.
The Business Impact
After deploying the Configuration Object at Central City Solutions, the Salesforce admin bottleneck essentially disappeared. Business users could add notification rules themselves. When a new team member joined, their task triggers were added by their manager in under a minute. When business rules changed — a new task for a new role, a Slack message redirected to a different channel — it happened in real time.
The Configuration Object became the single most referenced system at Central City Solutions. Every new automation request — from transaction coordinators, from acquisitions, from dispositions — was handled by adding or modifying Configuration records rather than building new Flows.
When to Build a Configuration Object
This pattern is worth building when your Salesforce org has more than 15-20 distinct automation rules that business users want to control, when you're receiving frequent requests to modify notification text or recipients, or when the same automation logic repeats across multiple triggers with slightly different parameters. If those conditions don't apply yet, a direct Flow approach is simpler. But if your org is growing and your automation library is expanding, a Configuration Object pays for itself within weeks.

## Track Deal Profit and Campaign ROI in Salesforce
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-financial-analytics-real-estate.html

How to Track Real Estate Deal Profitability, Cost Per Lead, and Campaign ROI in Salesforce
Real estate companies track leads and deals in Salesforce. Their marketing spend — on direct mail, dialers, PPC, TV, and referral programs — lives in spreadsheets. At the end of the month, someone manually calculates which campaigns made money and which didn't.
This is the gap that costs the most: when you don't know your true cost-per-closed-deal by campaign, you can't allocate your marketing budget with any precision. You invest based on volume — which campaigns generate the most leads — instead of profitability — which campaigns generate leads that actually close at a profit.
Building this analysis directly inside Salesforce, connected to your actual deal data, solves that problem permanently.
The Four Financial Metrics That Matter
Before building anything, define exactly what you're measuring. For real estate acquisition companies, the four metrics that drive budget decisions are:
Cost Per Lead (CPL)
Total marketing spend on a campaign divided by the number of leads generated from that campaign. Tells you how expensive it is to fill the top of your funnel from each source.
Cost Per Opportunity (CPO)
Total campaign spend divided by qualified opportunities. More meaningful than CPL because it filters out leads that never progressed — showing which sources bring genuinely interested sellers.
Cost Per Closed Deal (CPCD)
Total campaign spend divided by closed transactions. The number that actually tells you whether a marketing channel is worth the investment.
Net Profit Per Deal
Sale price minus acquisition cost, holding costs, renovation costs, and closing costs. The actual P&L on each deal — broken by lead source to show which channels generate the most profitable deals, not just the most.
I built this exact financial analytics system at Pezon Properties (Pennsylvania) — real-time net profit per deal. See the full case study →
The Salesforce Object Model
To calculate these metrics inside Salesforce, you need financial data to live in the right places. The key principle: marketing spend belongs on the Campaign object , and deal financials belong on the Transaction or Opportunity object. The Campaign field on each Lead, Opportunity, and Transaction is the thread that connects them.
Campaign Object — Marketing Spend Fields
Add these custom fields to the Campaign object to capture your marketing investment:
Monthly Spend — currency field for total spend this month on this campaign
Spend to Date — cumulative spend since campaign launch
Cost Per Mail Piece (for direct mail) — unit cost for calculations
Total Pieces Sent — for calculating actual spend from unit cost
Transaction / Opportunity Object — Deal Financial Fields
Deal financials should live here, not in a spreadsheet:
Contract Purchase Price — what you agreed to pay the seller
Acquisition Closing Costs — title fees, legal, transfer taxes
Renovation Budget / Actual Cost — for flips and wholetails
Holding Costs — insurance, taxes, utilities during hold period
Sale Price — what you sold the property for
Selling Closing Costs — agent commission, title, other costs at sale
Net Profit — formula field (see below)
The Net Profit Formula
A Salesforce formula field on the Transaction object calculates net profit automatically the moment fields are updated:
This formula runs in real time. The moment your transaction coordinator updates the sale price or enters final renovation costs, the net profit figure updates everywhere — in the record, in reports, and in dashboards.
Once this formula is in place, your leadership dashboard can show total net profit for the month alongside closed deal count — not just "we closed 8 deals" but "we closed 8 deals and made $312,000 net."
Cost Per Lead by Campaign — The Report Structure
To calculate cost per lead by campaign, you need a report that joins Campaign spend data with Lead counts. In Salesforce, this is a Cross-Object Summary Report:
Report type: Campaigns with Leads
Grouping: Campaign Name
Columns: Campaign Spend to Date, Lead Count (record count), and a formula column: Spend_to_Date__c / LEAD_COUNT
Filter: Campaign Status = Active, Lead Created Date = this quarter
The result: a single table showing every active campaign, how many leads it generated, what it cost, and the cost per lead — updated every time the report is run.
Campaign ROI — Connecting Spend to Closed Deals
The most valuable report connects marketing spend all the way through to closed revenue and net profit. This requires Leads, Opportunities, and Transactions to all have the Campaign field correctly populated — which is exactly why lead source and campaign management automation is worth investing in early.
Campaign attribution only works if the Campaign field follows the record through its lifecycle — from Lead to Opportunity to Transaction. Building Flow automation to copy and preserve the original lead source campaign is the foundational requirement for any financial analytics layer.
With that in place, a Cross-Object Summary Report across Campaigns → Leads → Opportunities → Transactions gives you a complete attribution chain: this campaign generated X leads at $Y CPL, produced Z opportunities at $A CPO, closed B deals at $C net profit each, and delivered a total ROI of D% on marketing spend.
The Dashboard View
With the reports built, the dashboard that leadership actually uses shows four components side by side:
Cost Per Lead by Campaign — bar chart sorted high to low, showing which campaigns are expensive to generate leads from
Cost Per Closed Deal by Campaign — the number that matters for budget allocation
Net Profit by Lead Source — which sources generate the most profitable deals, not just the most deals
Campaign Spend vs Revenue This Month — rolling 30-day view of marketing investment versus closed revenue
This dashboard answers the question leadership asks every month: "Where should we put next month's marketing budget?" Instead of answering from gut feel or volume metrics, you answer with data: the campaign that generates the highest net profit per dollar of marketing spend gets the budget increase.
What to Build First
If your Salesforce doesn't have any of this today, the priority order is:
Step 1 — Add Campaign field to Transactions and build automation to populate it from the linked Lead/Opportunity
Step 2 — Add financial fields to the Transaction object (purchase price, costs, sale price)
Step 3 — Build the Net Profit formula field
Step 4 — Add marketing spend fields to Campaigns and start populating them monthly
Step 5 — Build the reports and dashboard once you have 30-60 days of data
The whole system can be live in 2-4 weeks. After that, every closed deal automatically feeds the financial analytics — no spreadsheets, no manual data pulls, no end-of-month scramble.
Want this built for your real estate company?

## Real Estate Investor KPIs: What to Track in Salesforce
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-kpis-real-estate.html

Real estate investor KPIs: what each role should track, and how to build it in Salesforce
Not everything you can measure in Salesforce is worth measuring. Teams that track everything end up with dashboards nobody opens and reports that don't change a decision. This guide is for owners and ops leads at home-buying and wholesaling companies who want a short list instead: the numbers each role should be judged on, how each one is defined, and how to build it so the numbers can be trusted.
Give each role one or two numbers it can move. Marketing: cost per appointment and cost per contract by campaign. Lead manager: time to first contact and qualified leads passed. Acquisitions: appointments, offers and contracts, plus open leads with no next step. Dispositions: days to assign and actual against projected fee. Transaction coordinator: on-time closings and cancellations with reasons. The owner watches profit on deals that actually closed, by campaign and market. Write each definition down, build it from fields the system fills in, and check the money against your books every month.
What makes a KPI worth tracking?
Someone can move it. Every number belongs to one role. If nobody on the team can change it this week, it's a fact, not a KPI.
It's defined in writing. What counts, which date it counts by, which records are in and out. Two people pulling the same number should get the same answer.
The system fills in the data. Sources come from tracking numbers and forms, dates are stamped by automation. A KPI that depends on reps remembering to update a field is a guess.
It leads to a decision. If nobody would do anything differently when it moves, drop it.
It counts what you keep. Closed deals, not signed contracts. Contracts that fall apart shouldn't make a campaign look good.
The rest of this page is laid out by role. For who does what on a typical team, see wholesaling team roles .
Marketing KPIs
KPI | Definition | In Salesforce
Spend by campaign | Money spent on each campaign each month, from the books | Cost fields on the campaign, filled monthly and checked against accounting
Cost per lead | Spend ÷ new leads, by campaign | Campaign report with a summary formula
Cost per appointment | Spend ÷ appointments set from that campaign's leads | Appointments counted by original source and campaign
Cost per contract | Spend ÷ contracts signed from that campaign | Source copied from the lead to the deal and locked
Cost per closed deal | Spend ÷ deals that actually closed, cancellations left out | Closed deals by original campaign
ROI on kept deals | (Profit from closed deals + equity in houses you kept − spend) ÷ spend | Final profit on each closed deal, and a kept flag with an equity value (after-repair value minus all-in cost)
Cost per lead is the most quoted and the least useful on its own. A cheap lead that never answers costs more than an expensive one that signs. Judge channels on cost per appointment and cost per contract, and settle budgets on ROI. Which campaign gets credit when a seller responds to several is its own question, covered in lead attribution for investors .
First contact: lead manager and cold callers
KPI | Definition | In Salesforce
Time to first contact | Minutes from the lead arriving to the first call or text, during business hours | A first-contact time stamped by Flow when the first call or text is logged, and a formula for the minutes
Contact rate | Leads reached ÷ leads attempted, by list or source | Call outcomes as a picklist, so "reached" means the same thing for everyone
Missed calls without a callback | Missed seller calls with no callback inside your time limit | Missed calls logged by the phone system, with a callback task; target zero
Qualified leads passed | Handoffs to acquisitions with every required field filled | Required fields on the handoff stage
Leads that arrive at night make time to first contact look worse than the team's real performance. Flag them and measure them from the start of the next business morning. The org I run tracks time until contacted, and flags leads that arrive overnight. Set the target with your team; the research on response times is in my lead response statistics , and the setup is in speed to lead for investors .
Acquisitions KPIs
KPI | Definition | In Salesforce
Appointments set and completed | By rep, by week | Appointment date and status on the deal or an event
Offers made | Offers sent to sellers, by rep, with amount and date | An offer record or offer fields on the deal
Offer to contract rate | Contracts signed ÷ offers made, by rep | Offers and deals in one custom report type
Contracts signed | By rep, by week and month | A contract date stamped when the stage changes
Open leads with no next step | Open leads without a future task | A cross filter: leads without open activities
Overdue follow-ups | Follow-up tasks past their due date, by rep | Task report, due date before today, not completed
Dials and talk time help when you're coaching a new rep. Judge experienced reps on what turns into money: appointments, offers and contracts, and on not letting leads go quiet. For the fields and tasks behind two of these, see appointment no-shows and offer follow-up . If you're about to add reps, see what to set up before a new rep starts , including a ramp report.
Dispositions KPIs
KPI | Definition | In Salesforce
Days to assign | Days from signed contract to an assigned buyer | Contract and assignment dates stamped on the deal
Projected against actual fee | The fee expected at contract next to the fee actually collected | Projected fee locked at contract, actual fee at closing
Deals with no buyer after a set number of days | Deals under contract with no buyer past your limit | A report filtered on days since contract and no buyer
Repeat buyers | Buyers who closed more than one deal with you in the last 12 months | Buyers and deals in one custom report type
More on the buyer side in dispositions in Salesforce .
Transaction coordination KPIs
KPI | Definition | In Salesforce
Contract to first seller call | Hours between "under contract" and the first logged call to the seller | A date stamp at contract and the first call logged after it
Days to close | Days from signed contract to closing | Contract and closing dates
On-time closings | Deals that closed on or before the original closing date | The original closing date locked at contract
Cancellations, with reasons | Contracts that fell apart, by reason and by source | A required cancellation reason from a fixed list
Files missing a key date | Deals under contract without an inspection deadline, closing date or title company | A report; target zero
Cancellation reasons by source are worth a look every quarter. A campaign that produces contracts which keep falling apart is more expensive than its cost per contract says.
Owner and finance KPIs
Profit on closed deals , by campaign and by market.
Booked revenue against forecast: the profit expected when each deal went under contract, next to the profit actually kept at closing. A gap that grows means underwriting or renegotiation needs attention.
Deals closed per month , by market.
Profit per acquisitions rep , over a quarter rather than a week.
For the Monday meeting, the short version is the Monday 5 : cost per appointment by campaign, contracts per campaign, contract to first seller call, booked vs. kept profit, and campaign ROI that includes the houses you keep.
How do you tie KPIs to your accounting?
Salesforce isn't accounting software, and it shouldn't try to be. The CRM should know what each deal was expected to make and what it actually made. The books hold the money. Two connections keep the KPIs honest:
Spend by campaign, every month , entered from the books or synced from them.
The final fee or profit on every closed deal , matching what accounting recorded.
Some teams type both in once a month. Others connect QuickBooks Online through a connector, which is covered in QuickBooks and Salesforce for investors . Either way, reconcile once a month, because ROI built on spend that doesn't match the books is wrong however good the rest is. Campaign ROI by market and source, checked against the books, is one of the things I built for a two-market home-buying company in Ohio.
How do you build KPIs people trust?
Stamp the dates. A record-triggered Flow writes the date and time of first contact, appointment, offer, contract and closing as each happens.
Use picklists for source, stage, call outcome, dead reason and cancellation reason. Free text can't be counted.
Lock the original source once it's set, and copy it to the deal.
Require fields by stage , so a deal can't reach "under contract" without a closing date or "closed" without the final fee.
Save the history. Reporting snapshots store a report's results on a schedule, so you can chart trends week by week.
The reports behind most of these are in my 20 Salesforce report recipes . How to lay them out for each role is in the pipeline dashboard guide , and if a number looks off, start with why Salesforce numbers don't match .
Questions
What KPIs should a real estate investor track?
By role: cost per appointment and per contract by campaign for marketing, time to first contact for the lead manager, appointments, offers and contracts for acquisitions, days to assign for dispositions, on-time closings and cancellations for the transaction coordinator, and profit on closed deals by campaign and market for the owner.
What KPIs should a wholesaling acquisitions team track?
Appointments set and completed, offers made, offer to contract rate and contracts signed, by rep. Also track open leads with no next step and overdue follow-ups, because those are the leads that quietly die.
What KPIs does a dispositions manager track?
Days from contract to an assigned buyer, projected against actual fee, deals with no buyer after a set number of days, and repeat buyers over the last 12 months.
How do I measure speed to lead in Salesforce?
Stamp the time of the first logged call or text on the lead with a Flow, and use a formula for the minutes since the lead arrived. Flag leads that arrive after hours and measure them from the next business morning, so they don't distort the number.
Should I track cost per lead or cost per contract?
Both, but judge channels on cost per appointment and cost per contract, and settle budgets on ROI from deals that actually closed. A cheap lead that never answers costs more than an expensive one that signs.
Can Salesforce track real estate KPIs with accounting data?
Yes. Enter or sync monthly spend per campaign and the final fee or profit on each closed deal from your accounting system, for example QuickBooks Online through a connector, and reconcile monthly so ROI matches the books.
How many KPIs should a real estate team track?
One or two per role, and about five for the owner's weekly meeting. Past that, people stop reading them.
