## Salesforce Lead Routing for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-lead-routing-real-estate.html

Salesforce lead routing for real estate investors: round robin, queues and missed calls
Routing decides who calls a seller back, and how fast. For a home-buying company spending thousands a month on mail, PPC and cold calling, it's the cheapest place to lose a deal: the lead was paid for, it came in, and it sat with the wrong person or nobody. This guide covers how lead routing works in Salesforce, four ways to do round robin, what your phone system should handle versus Salesforce, after-hours and escalation, and how to check that routing is actually working.
In Salesforce, a lead assignment rule sends each new lead to a rep or a queue based on criteria like market or source. Only one rule can be active at a time, and its entries are checked in order. There's no simple round robin switch for leads, so teams use an auto-number formula with assignment rules, a Flow, Omni-Channel or an app. Routing the live call belongs to your phone system. Salesforce's job is to create or match the lead from the call, tag its source, alert someone when a call is missed and escalate when nobody follows up.
How does lead routing work in Salesforce?
The core tool is the lead assignment rule . A few things about it trip people up:
Only one lead assignment rule can be active at a time. That rule holds as many entries as you need, for example one per market or per source.
Entries are checked in order, and the first match wins. Put the specific entries (a PPC campaign in one market) above the general ones (everything in that market).
Each entry assigns to a user or a queue and can send an email notification.
Leads that match no entry go to the default lead owner in Lead Settings. Make that a queue someone watches, not a person who might be on vacation.
Web-to-Lead forms and imports can use the rule , but check that they do. A form or import set up without it puts every lead with one default owner.
Flow can't run assignment rules on its own. The "assign using active assignment rule" checkbox exists only on the page layout. If leads are created by a Flow or an integration, running the rules takes a small piece of Apex called from the Flow, or the routing has to be built in the Flow itself.
That last point catches a lot of investor teams, because so many leads arrive through integrations: the dialer, a texting tool, Zapier, a list upload.
Should leads go to a queue or straight to a rep?
Both work. They fail differently.
 | Shared queue | Straight to a rep
How it works | New leads land in a queue and the first available rep claims them | Each lead gets an owner the moment it's created
Good for | Speed, when several reps are on the phones at once | Clear ownership and accountability
Fails when | Everyone assumes someone else has it | The owner is busy, out sick or on a call for an hour
Fix | A time limit, then automatic assignment or an alert | Escalation when the lead isn't touched in time
The company I work with runs shared inbound queues. What makes a queue work is a clock: a queue without a time limit is just a place where leads wait.
How do you set up round robin for leads?
Salesforce doesn't have a simple built-in round robin switch for leads. These are the four ways teams do it, from simplest to most capable.
1. Auto-number and a formula, with assignment rules
This one is documented by Salesforce in its sample lead management formulas. Add an auto-number field to leads, then a formula field that turns it into a repeating sequence. For three reps:
MOD(VALUE(Lead_Number__c), 3)
Each new lead gets 0, 1 or 2 in turn, and your assignment rule has one entry per value, each pointing to a rep or a queue. It needs no code and it's easy to understand. The downsides: it doesn't know who's out today, and adding a fourth rep means changing the formula and the entries.
2. A Flow that picks the next rep
A record-triggered Flow looks up who's in the rotation (a checkbox on the user record, or a small custom object), picks the rep who was assigned least recently and sets the owner. This can skip reps who are out, weight by market or cap how many open leads one rep holds. The thing to test is two leads arriving at the same moment, because a simple version can give both to the same rep.
3. Omni-Channel
Omni-Channel routes work, including leads, to people who are available and have capacity. Reps set a status, and work goes to whoever is online. It's built for service teams, it takes more setup, and it only works if reps actually set their status. Salesforce has been moving customers from Standard to Enhanced Omni-Channel, so check which one your org has before you plan around it.
4. A routing app
Dedicated routing apps from the AppExchange handle availability, weighting, territories and reporting out of the box. They cost extra and add another vendor. Worth it at high volume or with complex territories, rarely needed for a team of ten reps in two markets.
For most home-buying teams of 10 to 50, option 1 or 2 is enough. Pick option 1 if your team rarely changes, option 2 if reps come and go or you need to skip people who are out.
What should call routing do, and what should Salesforce do?
When a seller calls a marketing number, two systems are involved, and teams often expect one to do the other's job.
Your phone system (RingCentral, smrtPhone and so on) | Salesforce
Rings the right people: ring groups, simultaneous ring, overflow | Creates the lead from the call, or matches it to an existing seller
Handles voicemail and after-hours messages | Tags the lead with the source and market of the number called
Records the call | Logs the call on the seller record
Sends the call somewhere when nobody answers | Alerts a rep or a channel about the missed call and creates a callback task
The missed call is the moment that matters. Almost nobody leaves a voicemail: in Invoca's 2021 data, only 2% of unanswered callers did (more in my lead response statistics ). So a missed call with no alert is usually a lost seller. In the org I run, calls create leads, and every marketing number sends a missed-call alert to Slack. I wrote up how to build that in missed-call alerts in Salesforce .
What happens to leads after hours?
A web form at 9 p.m. on a Saturday is still a paid lead. Decide on purpose what happens to it:
Flag it. Mark leads that arrive outside business hours, so the morning team can see them first and your speed-to-lead numbers don't punish reps for leads that came in at midnight. The org I run uses an overnight flag for exactly this.
Route it to a morning queue , not to whichever rep the rotation lands on.
Acknowledge it with an automatic text or email, if you have the seller's consent to contact them that way.
Follow the market's clock. If you work markets in different time zones, "after hours" means the seller's evening, not the office's.
What if nobody calls the seller?
Routing isn't finished when the lead has an owner. It's finished when someone has talked to the seller. Build the follow-through:
A scheduled path on the lead checks again after a set time. If there's still no call or text logged, it alerts the owner.
If there's still nothing after a second interval, it alerts the manager or moves the lead back to the queue.
A "time until contacted" field records how long the first touch took, so you can report it by source, market and rep.
Pick the intervals with your team. What matters is that a lead can't sit untouched without somebody finding out.
What about sellers who call back months later?
A seller who called in March and calls again in September shouldn't go into the rotation like a new lead. They should go to the rep who already knows them, with their history attached. That takes duplicate matching on phone number before routing, and a rule that sends a matched seller to the original owner and tells that owner they're back. Duplicate handling that keeps the history and notifies the original owner is part of the setup I run. More in duplicate sellers in Salesforce .
How do you know routing is working?
Four reports, checked weekly:
Leads waiting in queues, by age. Anything older than your time limit is a problem today.
Leads owned by inactive users. Someone left, and the rotation or an old rule still includes them.
Leads that went to the default owner. These matched no entry, which usually means a new source or market nobody added to the rule.
Time until contacted, by source and by rep. The number that tells you whether all of the above is paying off.
And the failures I'd look for first in an investor org:
Rule entries in the wrong order, so a general entry catches leads meant for a specific one.
Leads created by an integration or Flow that never run the assignment rule.
A rep who left still in the rotation.
A new tracking number or form that was never added to the rule, so its leads all go to the default owner.
Duplicates that go to a new rep instead of the seller's original owner.
What I'd set up for a 10 to 50 person team
Every lead created with its source and market already filled in, from the tracking number or form.
Duplicate matching on phone before routing, so returning sellers go to their original owner.
During business hours, new leads go to a shared queue per market, with a short time limit to claim them.
Unclaimed leads go to round robin automatically (formula or Flow, depending on how often the team changes).
After hours, leads are flagged and go to a morning queue.
Every missed call creates a callback task and an alert.
Escalation to the manager if a lead isn't contacted in time.
The four reports above, on one dashboard, checked every Monday.
None of this needs an expensive app. It needs someone to set it up carefully and check it every week.
Questions
How do lead assignment rules work in Salesforce?
One lead assignment rule can be active at a time. It contains entries that are checked in order, and the first entry whose criteria match assigns the lead to a user or a queue. Leads that match no entry go to the default lead owner set in Lead Settings.
Does Salesforce have round robin for leads?
Not as a simple built-in switch. Teams use an auto-number field and a MOD formula with assignment rule entries (documented by Salesforce), a Flow that picks the next rep, Omni-Channel routing, or a routing app from the AppExchange.
Can a Flow run lead assignment rules?
Not natively. The 'assign using active assignment rule' checkbox only exists on the page layout. To run the rules from a Flow you need a small invocable Apex method, or you build the routing logic in the Flow itself.
What's the difference between call routing and lead routing?
Call routing is your phone system deciding which phones ring when a seller calls. Lead routing is Salesforce deciding who owns the seller's record and follow-up. You need both, plus a missed-call alert that connects them.
How do I route leads by market in Salesforce?
Make sure every lead has its market filled in automatically from the tracking number, web form or zip code, then add one assignment rule entry or queue per market. Leads without a market should go to a queue someone checks daily.
What happens to leads that don't match any assignment rule entry?
They go to the default lead owner in Lead Settings. Set that to a queue someone watches, and check a report of leads assigned there every week, because they usually point to a new source or form nobody added to the rule.
Is Omni-Channel a good fit for real estate lead routing?
It can be, if reps reliably set their availability status. It routes leads to people who are online and have capacity. For most home-buying teams of 10 to 50, an assignment rule with a formula-based or Flow-based round robin is simpler.
How do I measure speed to lead in Salesforce?
Record the time of the first call or text on each lead in a field such as time until contacted, then report it by source, market and rep. Flag leads that arrive after hours so they're measured from the start of the next business day.

## 50+ Real Salesforce Requests From an Acquisitions Team
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-real-estate-acquisition-case-log.html

50+ Real Salesforce Requests From a Real Estate Acquisition Company
If you've never worked with a Salesforce consultant, it's hard to picture what the engagement actually looks like. Is it one big project? A list of tickets? Strategy calls?
Here's the honest answer: it's a steady stream of very specific, very practical requests. Below is a categorized log of 50+ real requests I delivered for Pezon Properties , a Pennsylvania real estate acquisition company (identifying details like phone numbers and internal links removed). If you run acquisitions on Salesforce — or are thinking about it — this is the most realistic preview you'll find of what a consultant actually does.
1. Campaign Performance & ROI Reporting
The single biggest request: a dashboard that tracks the entire marketing funnel by campaign , filterable by week, month, and quarter. Twenty-five metrics, including:
Volume: total cost, total mail sent, gross and net lead counts, gross and net response rates
Conversion: opportunity count and conversion rate, appointment count and rate, signed agreement count and rate, closed deal count and rate
Unit economics: cost per gross lead, net lead, opportunity, appointment, signed agreement, and closed deal
Profitability: gross and net profit, profit per unit, and return multiple on marketing spend
Supporting requests: quarterly campaign automation (old campaigns deactivate when new ones start, with consistent naming like "2024 Q4 Municipal Liens"), and reports on time-to-respond for text messages and lead age per path stage.
This is the system I built at Pezon Properties , including real-time net profit per deal. See the full case study →
2. Lead Source & Campaign Attribution
ROI reporting is only as good as attribution. Several requests existed purely to make sure every lead carries the right source and campaign:
Call-tracking attribution — each marketing channel (web, PPC, Google Business Profile per city, direct mail) has a dedicated tracking phone number; the lead source and campaign are set automatically based on the number the seller called
Cross-channel matching — when a web or PPC lead comes in from an address that already received a direct mail letter, the direct mail campaign is automatically associated, matched by street address
Unique numbers per direct mail campaign — inbound calls on a campaign's tracking number auto-generate a homeowner lead record tied to that campaign
Campaign mapping to activities — the campaign field flows from lead/opportunity to tasks and events, so activity reports segment by channel too
3. Lead Lifecycle Automation
Acquisition teams live and die by follow-up discipline. These requests automate it:
Auto status updates — "New" flips to "Working" the moment an outbound call, text, or email is logged; "Working" flips to "Follow-up" after 30 days of no activity
Stale-lead escalation — if a lead sits in "New" for more than 24 hours, the sales inbox and lead manager get an automated email
Follow-up task automation — every new lead spawns an assigned follow-up task with an email notification; overdue tasks trigger reminder emails with leadership CC'd
Disposition-driven branching — call outcomes ("answered", "follow up") route the lead to different statuses and create the right next task automatically
Conversion gates — leads can't be converted to qualified without units, beds/baths, square footage, full name, complete address, and occupancy filled in, with an error message that links to the missing fields
Clean conversion — on conversion, every detail (negotiation notes, campaign, lead source) migrates to the opportunity automatically
4. Data Governance & Compliance
Process enforcement — manual opportunity creation removed for non-admins (the only path is lead conversion); lead-status edit access locked down
Duplicate handling — rules for prospect-vs-homeowner collisions that preserve historical homeowner records and campaign attribution
Do-not-contact compliance — a Do Not Mail campaign where every member is flagged across all four channels: do not mail, do not call, do not text, email opt-out
Role-based access — per-user permission matrices (a transaction coordinator who can edit transactions but only read leads; a marketing coordinator with import and campaign rights)
5. Transaction Coordination App Rebuild
The largest single engagement: rebuilding the transaction coordination application so the checklist adapts to the deal instead of asking the same 60 questions every time.
Cash vs. financed logic — cash purchases automatically hide loan request, lender appraisal, and inspection-financing fields
Unit-count logic — single-family and small multi-family deals hide property-management presale steps; 5+ unit properties keep the full diligence set; seller deliverables default based on unit count
A 40+ field property onboarding checklist stage — everything from utilities, insurance, and mortgage details to laundry rooms, mailbox keys, fire escapes, and lead-paint disclosure — inserted as a new stage between due diligence and contingency management
Quality-control gates — a required QC checkbox (comps and rehab budget reviewed) that blocks stage progression until checked
Field mapping — purchase price, rehab cost, and unit count flow from opportunity to transaction; the opportunity owner maps to acquisition rep and manager fields automatically
Financial fields — carrying cost, closing cost, and selling cost fields with auto-calculated equity and return multiple
6. Call & Response Analytics
For a seller-facing team, answer speed is revenue. These requests measure it honestly:
Speed-to-lead report — elapsed time between lead creation and the first genuine outbound activity (excluding incoming texts, which aren't a response)
Missed-call-to-callback time — measuring only valid missed calls (spam excluded), per rep
Live answer rate — missed calls tagged to the right owner by tracking number so the percentage is real
Activity logging fixes — calls and SMS logged consistently across lead, opportunity, and person account records for the same human being
7. Integrations & Imports
DocuSign — agreements of sale sent from the CRM with status tracked back on the deal
Google Sheets + Zapier lead import — bulk lead uploads assigned to the correct campaign with no manual data entry
Direct mail previews — letter previews routed to the marketing coordinator for approval before sending
Call script tooling — a guided lead call form with inbound/outbound toggles, stacked (not overwritten) notes, and appointment assignment to any user
What This List Teaches You
First: almost nothing on it is exotic. It's flows, validation rules, formula fields, report types, and well-designed page layouts — applied relentlessly to one business model. The value isn't in rare technology; it's in knowing what an acquisition operation needs before they ask.
Second: the requests compound. Call-tracking attribution feeds the ROI dashboard; conversion gates feed clean transaction data; clean transaction data feeds net profit per deal. A consultant who only does tickets in isolation builds none of that compounding.
Third: this is what "ongoing CRM management" means in practice. Not a retainer for emergencies — a steady cadence of improvements, each small enough to ship in days, each making the next one more valuable.
Want a request log like this for your company?

## Build a Real Estate Pipeline Dashboard in Salesforce
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-real-estate-pipeline-dashboard.html

How to build a real estate pipeline dashboard in Salesforce: for home-buying and wholesaling teams
In a lot of home-buying companies, the Monday meeting starts with the same questions. What's under contract? What's stuck? What closes this month? Then someone goes to find out. A Salesforce dashboard can answer those questions every time you open it, as long as it's built around the questions rather than around whatever reports already exist. This guide is for owners and ops leads at investor and wholesaling teams: what to put on the dashboard, how to build each part, and how to keep the numbers right.
Build one dashboard per audience, each answering a few questions. For the owner: leads and appointments by source this month, open deals by stage with days in stage, deals under contract by closing date, and booked revenue against the forecast. For acquisitions: today's follow-ups, offers waiting and leads with no next step. For the transaction coordinator: every file under contract by stage, and anything missing a date. Color the aging deals, and remember that a dashboard shows data as of its last refresh, so schedule a refresh before the meeting that uses it.
What should a pipeline dashboard answer?
Start with the questions, not the charts. For an investor team, the owner's questions are usually these:
Where are this month's leads, and how many became appointments?
Which deals are stuck, and for how long?
What's under contract, and when does each one close?
What did we book this month, and how close was the forecast?
Who on the team needs help?
Every component on the dashboard should answer one of them. If a chart doesn't, take it off. A dashboard with 20 charts gets opened less often than one with six.
The components, and how to build each one
Component | Answers | Build it from | Show it as
Lead funnel, this month | Where the leads are | Leads created this month, grouped by status, split by source | Funnel or bar chart
Appointments and contracts by source | Which marketing produces deals | Deals created this month, grouped by lead source, with campaign spend for cost per contract | Bar chart, with a table under it
Open deals by stage, with days in stage | What's stuck | Open deals grouped by stage, with days in the current stage | Stacked bar by aging band, or a colored table
Under contract, by closing date | What closes when | Deals under contract, grouped by expected closing week | Table
Booked revenue against forecast | Are we on track? | Deals by month: expected fee or profit at contract next to the actual figure at closing | Column chart
Offers waiting | What could become a contract | Offers sent with no answer, older than a few days | Table, oldest first
Activity by rep | Who needs help | Calls, conversations, appointments and offers by rep, this week | Table
Leads with no next step | What's quietly dying | Open leads without a future task (a cross filter) | One number, with a target of zero
Each component is a report underneath. The exact report type, filter and grouping for most of these are in my 20 Salesforce report recipes for wholesalers , and the fields they rely on are in the CRM field kit .
How do you show days in stage?
Days in stage is the number that turns a pipeline chart into something you can act on. Two ways to get it:
If your deals are Opportunities , Salesforce has a standard Stage Duration field that tracks how long each one has been in its current stage. Add it to the report and filter or color by it.
If your deals live on a custom object , which is common in investor orgs that track properties and contracts their own way, stamp the date each stage started with a record-triggered Flow, and add a formula for the days since then.
Then color it. A simple rule to start with: green under 7 days, amber from 7 to 14, red over 14. Tune it per stage with your team, because a deal waiting on title moves at a different pace from a seller waiting on a second appointment. At Pezon Properties, a property tracker with days since the last update, where anything over 14 days flags in red, is the component leadership uses instead of asking "what's the status of..." every week.
The transaction pipeline: from contract to closing
Once a deal is under contract, the question changes from "what's stuck?" to "what's about to slip?". The transaction side needs its own view:
Every file under contract by stage, such as inspection, title, clear to close and scheduled.
Files missing a key date or detail: inspection deadline, closing date, title company.
Closings in the next two weeks, soonest first.
Hours from contract to the first call to the seller, by coordinator. It's one of my Monday 5 numbers, because deals where nobody calls the seller for days are where cancellations start.
Cancellations this month, with the reason for each.
In the org I run, transaction coordination works from its own board and scorecard. How that side is set up is in transaction coordination in Salesforce .
Why one dashboard per role works better
An owner's weekly questions and a rep's daily ones are different, and putting them on one screen makes it worse for both.
Dashboard | Who opens it, and when | What's on it
Owner | Owner and partners, weekly | The Monday 5, deals by stage with aging, under contract by closing date, booked against forecast
Acquisitions | Acquisitions manager and reps, daily | Today's follow-ups and appointments, offers waiting, leads with no next step, activity by rep
Transactions | Transaction coordinator, daily | Files by stage, missing dates, closings in the next two weeks, contract to first seller call
Dispositions | Dispositions manager, weekly | Deals ready to market, days to assign, projected against actual fee
Marketing | Whoever runs marketing, weekly | Leads, appointments and contracts by campaign, cost per appointment and per contract
If you want each rep to see their own numbers on one shared dashboard, Salesforce has dynamic dashboards, but they're limited by edition: five on Enterprise, ten on Unlimited and Performance. A dashboard filter on owner often does the job just as well. Who owns which numbers is covered in wholesaling team roles .
Is a Salesforce dashboard live?
Not quite. A dashboard shows data as of its last refresh, and it says when that was. Anyone viewing it can click Refresh. Users with the Schedule Dashboards permission can schedule refreshes daily, weekly or monthly, and Salesforce emails the people you pick when the refresh is done. Schedule the owner's dashboard to refresh early on Monday, before the meeting.
Every dashboard also runs as someone. If it runs as a user who can't see every record it's meant to count, it undercounts, and nobody can tell from looking at it. That's one of the ten causes in why Salesforce numbers don't match .
How do you keep the numbers right?
Every lead arrives on its own. Calls, forms, texts and lists should create records through your phone system, forms and integrations, not when someone remembers to type them in. See getting every lead source into Salesforce .
Stages mean the same thing to everyone. Write down what "appointment", "under contract" and "closed" mean, and which date each report counts by.
Required fields by stage. A deal can't move to under contract without a closing date, or to closed without the final fee.
Money is checked against the books. Spend by campaign and profit on closed deals should match accounting every month. QuickBooks and Salesforce covers the connection.
Do you need Tableau?
Usually not at first. Salesforce dashboards handle the daily and weekly operating view well. Tableau, which has a native Salesforce connector, makes more sense when leadership wants multi-year trends, market overlays, or data from systems outside Salesforce in one place. Get the Salesforce dashboards right first. Tableau on top of numbers nobody trusts only makes them look better.
Questions
How do I build a pipeline dashboard in Salesforce?
Decide the few questions it should answer, build one report per question, add each report to the dashboard as a component, set it to run as a user who can see every record it counts, and schedule a refresh before the meeting that uses it.
What should a real estate investor's pipeline dashboard include?
Leads and appointments by source this month, open deals by stage with days in stage, deals under contract by closing date, booked revenue against the forecast, offers waiting and open leads with no next step.
Do Salesforce dashboards update in real time?
No. A dashboard shows data as of its last refresh. Viewers can click Refresh, and users with the Schedule Dashboards permission can schedule refreshes daily, weekly or monthly.
How do I track days in stage in Salesforce?
On Opportunities, use the standard Stage Duration field, which tracks how long each one has been in its current stage. On a custom deal object, stamp the date each stage started with a Flow and use a formula for the days since then.
Can each rep see only their own numbers on a Salesforce dashboard?
Yes, with dynamic dashboards, which are limited by edition: five on Enterprise and ten on Unlimited and Performance. A dashboard filter on owner is often a simpler way to do the same thing.
What is a transaction pipeline dashboard?
A view of deals under contract: every file by stage, files missing a key date, closings in the next two weeks, hours from contract to the first call to the seller, and cancellations with their reasons.
Do I need Tableau for real estate reporting?
Usually not at first. Salesforce dashboards cover the daily and weekly view. Tableau makes more sense for multi-year trends or for combining Salesforce with data from other systems.

## Salesforce for Real Estate Brokers: Setup Guide
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-setup-real-estate-brokerage.html

How to Set Up Salesforce for a Real Estate Brokerage (Step-by-Step)
Setting up Salesforce for a real estate brokerage is not the same as setting up a generic sales CRM. The objects are different, the workflows are different, and the way agents think about their work is different. This guide walks through the steps from initial setup to a fully operational brokerage CRM.
If you run a home-buying or wholesaling company, this guide isn't the best fit. Start with Salesforce for real estate investors and home-buying companies instead.
Step 1: Choose the Right Salesforce Edition
Most real estate brokerages start with Salesforce Professional or Enterprise . Pricing depends on the edition and the number of users, and businesses can often get a discount through their Salesforce account manager. Professional covers lead management, basic automation, and standard reports. Enterprise adds Flow Builder's full capability, advanced forecasting, and API access for integrations.
The recommendation: Enterprise for any brokerage planning serious automation or Zapier integration. Professional's Flow restrictions will frustrate you within 6 months.
Step 2: Configure Your Core Objects
Leads — Inbound Buyer and Seller Prospects
Add custom fields: Property Type (residential/commercial/rental), Price Range, Timeline to Buy/Sell, Lead Source (website/referral/Zillow/cold outreach), and Assigned Agent. Set up lead conversion to create a Contact and an Opportunity when a lead qualifies.
Opportunities — Active Transactions
Map your transaction stages: Buyer Consultation → Property Search → Offer Submitted → Under Contract → Due Diligence → Closing → Closed Won. Add fields for Listing Address, Purchase Price, Commission Amount, Closing Date, and Transaction Coordinator.
Properties Custom Object (Optional but Recommended)
Create a custom Property object that links to Opportunities. Track MLS number, address, list price, buyer/seller contact, and all transaction documents. This becomes your single source of truth for every active listing or purchase.
The most common setup mistake: brokerages using only the default Salesforce objects without customizing for real estate. Default Salesforce is built for software sales — not real estate. Always customize before rolling out to agents.
Step 3: Set Up Lead Routing
Inbound leads should be automatically assigned based on: geographic area (zip code-based assignment rules), property type specialization, agent availability (custom field on User object), and round-robin for evenly distributed volume. A Salesforce Flow handles all of this automatically the moment a lead record is created.
Step 4: Build Agent-Facing Dashboards
Each agent should see, on their Salesforce home page: their active leads with next action due dates, their pipeline with expected close dates, their task list for today, and their month-to-date performance vs target. This replaces the "what should I be doing right now" question with a clear answer every morning.
Step 5: Configure Automation
New lead notification — instant email/Slack to assigned agent
Follow-up task creation — automatic task when lead status changes
Closing checklist — when opportunity moves to Under Contract, create a task list for the transaction coordinator
Stale pipeline alert — notify manager when an opportunity hasn't been updated in 14 days
Step 6: Connect Your Lead Sources
Every lead source should feed automatically into Salesforce. Use Zapier for: your website contact forms, Zillow and Realtor.com email notifications, Facebook and Google Ad leads, and any referral tracking platforms. Manual lead entry should be the exception, not the rule.
Step 7: Train Your Team
Role-specific training — not one-size-fits-all. Agents need to know: how to update a lead, how to log a contact attempt, how to advance a deal stage. Managers need to know: how to read dashboards, how to reassign leads, how to run pipeline reports. Give each person exactly what they need and nothing more.

I work with real estate investors, wholesalers and home-buying companies, not brokerages or agent teams. If that’s you, book a free 30-minute call, check your Deal Leak Score , or see the fixed-price CRM Revenue Audit for teams already on Salesforce.

## Salesforce vs Follow Up Boss for Real Estate
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-salesforce-vs-follow-up-boss-real-estate.html

Salesforce vs Follow Up Boss for Real Estate: Which CRM Is Right for You?
Two CRMs dominate the real estate conversation: Follow Up Boss — purpose-built for residential real estate teams — and Salesforce — the world's most powerful CRM platform. Both can run a real estate business. They're built for very different ones.
This comparison is written from the perspective of someone who has configured Salesforce for real estate companies. It's not a sales pitch for either platform — it's an honest breakdown of when each one wins.
Category | Follow Up Boss | Salesforce
Setup complexity | Low — ready in hours | High — needs proper configuration
Real estate-specific features | Built-in (MLS sync, lead routing) | Requires configuration or AppExchange
Automation depth | Good for basic workflows | Unlimited with Flow Builder
Reporting & dashboards | Standard reports | Advanced with Tableau integration
Customization | Limited to platform | Fully customizable objects & fields
Scalability | Good for <50 agents | Enterprise-grade, unlimited scale
Cost (per seat) | Lower ($69 to $500/mo flat) | Higher (depends on edition and users; discounts often available through your Salesforce account manager)
Integration ecosystem | Real estate focused | 5,000+ integrations via AppExchange
AI and predictive tools | Basic | Einstein AI, predictive scoring
Support for multiple business lines | Residential only | Any property type or vertical
When Follow Up Boss Wins
Follow Up Boss is the right choice if you run a residential real estate team of under 20-30 agents and your primary workflow is lead follow-up, showing scheduling, and simple pipeline management. It's genuinely easier to set up, the MLS integrations work out of the box, and your agents will adopt it faster because it's built specifically for how residential agents think.
If your business model is straightforward — inbound leads, agent follow-up, transactions — Follow Up Boss does this well at a lower cost and lower friction.
When Salesforce Wins
Salesforce becomes the clear winner the moment your real estate business gets complex. This includes any of the following:
Property acquisition companies — tracking properties through multi-stage acquisition, renovation, and sale pipelines that Follow Up Boss can't model
Real estate investment firms — needing ROI tracking, investor reporting, and multi-portfolio dashboards
Brokerages with 30+ agents — needing sophisticated territory management, performance analytics, and commission tracking
Companies with multiple business lines — combining residential, commercial, and property management in one CRM
Teams that need deep integrations — connecting CRM to accounting systems, custom databases, or proprietary tools
The companies I work with moved to Salesforce specifically because they outgrew their previous CRM — often Follow Up Boss or similar tools — and needed reporting, automation, and integration capabilities that simpler platforms can't provide.
The Honest Answer: It Depends on Where You're Going
If you're running a small residential team today and don't plan to grow significantly, Follow Up Boss is probably the right call. Salesforce's power comes with complexity, and complexity has a cost — in configuration time, in training, and in ongoing administration.
If you're building toward scale — more agents, more properties, more data, more business lines — Salesforce is worth the investment. A well-configured Salesforce setup grows with you indefinitely. You'll never outgrow it.
The question isn't which CRM is better. It's which one fits where your business is going.

## Connect Your Real Estate Stack to Salesforce with Zapier
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/blog-zapier-salesforce-real-estate.html

Connecting Salesforce to Your Real Estate Stack with Zapier
The average real estate company uses 8-12 software tools. Their CRM is one of them. And most of the time, none of these tools talk to each other — which means data gets manually copied between systems, leads get lost in transitions, and nobody has a complete picture. Zapier is the connective tissue that makes Salesforce the center of your entire operation without writing a single line of code.
The 5 Integrations That Deliver the Most Value
1. Website Forms to Salesforce Lead
Every form submission on your website should instantly create a Lead in Salesforce — not batched overnight, not manually entered from an inbox, but instantly, with all form fields mapped and assignment rules triggered. Build this first. It closes the biggest data gap in most real estate organizations and takes about 20 minutes to configure in Zapier.
2. Zillow and Realtor.com to Salesforce Lead
These platforms email lead notifications. Zapier watches the inbox, parses lead details from the email, and creates a Salesforce Lead record automatically. Combined with assignment rules, the lead reaches an agent before anyone has even opened the email notification.
At Central City Solutions, this kind of integration puts every new lead in front of a rep within minutes instead of waiting in an inbox.
3. Facebook Lead Ads to Salesforce
Facebook Lead Ads is one of the most effective lead generation tools for real estate — and one of the least connected to CRMs. Zapier has a native Facebook Lead Ads trigger that fires the moment someone submits a form, creating an instant Salesforce record with full campaign attribution.
4. Closed Deal to Finance System
When an opportunity is marked Closed Won, Zapier automatically updates your financial tracking spreadsheet, notifies the transaction team, and creates a record in your commission calculation system. Zero manual handoff between CRM and finance.
5. Stale Lead Alert to Slack
Combined with a Salesforce Flow flagging leads with no activity in 72 hours, Zapier posts an automatic Slack message to the relevant channel with the lead name, assigned agent, and days since last contact. This makes the invisible visible in real time — without anyone having to run a report.
Zapier is great until it isn’t — at Central City Solutions I eventually moved most of their Zaps to native Flows. Start simple, plan the graduation path. See the full case study →
Zapier vs Native Salesforce Integrations
When a well-maintained native AppExchange integration exists for a tool you use, prefer it over Zapier — native integrations tend to be more reliable with tighter field mapping. Use Zapier for everything that lacks a quality native connector, or where the native connector is missing specific functionality you need.
Building Your Integration Map
Before touching Zapier, document every tool your team uses and every data flow between them. Identify which flows are currently manual. Start with the one that involves the most manual work or the longest delays — that is your highest-value first integration.

## BRRRR Calculator: Cash Left In, Cash Flow & ROI (Free)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/brrrr-calculator.html

BRRRR calculator.
Buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. Enter the purchase, rehab and refinance terms to see how much of your cash stays in the deal, the new loan payment, monthly cash flow and your cash-on-cash return. Built for real estate investors in the United States, Canada, the UK and Europe. Pick your currency; the math is the same everywhere.
The formula
Total project cost = purchase + rehab + closing + holding + refinance costs
New loan = ARV × refinance LTV
Cash left in the deal = total project cost − new loan
Monthly cash flow = rent − operating costs − new loan payment
Cash-on-cash return = (monthly cash flow × 12) ÷ cash left in the deal
Worked example
Buy at $120,000, spend $35,000 on rehab, $3,000 closing and $4,000 holding. The house appraises at $210,000 and the lender refinances at 75%: a $157,500 loan. With $4,000 of refinance costs, the whole project costs $166,000, so $8,500 of your cash stays in. At 7.5% over 30 years the payment is $1,101 a month. Rent of $1,850 minus $550 of costs and the payment leaves $199 a month, a 28.1% cash-on-cash return.
Questions
What is the BRRRR method?
BRRRR stands for buy, rehab, rent, refinance, repeat. You buy a property below its after-repair value, renovate it, rent it out, then refinance at the new appraised value to pull your cash back out and use it on the next deal.
What does "cash left in the deal" mean?
It is the money you still have tied up after the refinance: everything you spent to buy, fix, hold and refinance the property, minus the new loan. A perfect BRRRR leaves zero or less, which means the refinance paid you back in full.
What loan-to-value do lenders use for a BRRRR refinance?
For investment properties, cash-out refinance lenders commonly lend around 70% to 80% of the appraised value. In Canada, conventional rental refinances are often capped at 80%. Check current terms with your lender, since they change with the market.
Is there a waiting period before refinancing?
Many lenders apply a seasoning period, often around six months of ownership, before they lend on the new appraised value instead of the purchase price. Some DSCR and portfolio lenders are more flexible. Confirm with your lender before you buy.
How do I track BRRRR deals across a portfolio?
Keep purchase, rehab, appraisal, refinance and rent figures as fields on each property record in your CRM, with cash left in and cash-on-cash as formulas. Then a portfolio report shows which deals recycled your capital and which did not.
Related free tools
Rental yield & cap rate calculator · DSCR calculator · Wholesale deal analyzer · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.
Add this calculator to your site
Free to embed on your blog or investor site. Copy the code below.

## Cash Buyers List Template for Wholesalers (Free CSV)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/cash-buyers-list-template.html

Cash buyers list template for wholesalers.
A cash buyers list works when every buyer's buy box is saved as fields, not buried in texts and DMs. Then each new deal goes to the 10 buyers who fit its area, price, property type and rehab level, instead of a blast to everyone. Download the free template below and fill it once per buyer.
Download the CSV template Opens in Google Sheets, Excel or any CRM import.
The fields to capture
How to send each deal to the right buyers
1. Filter: area matches, price between min and max, property type matches, rehab level matches
2. Drop buyers who need vacant if the property is occupied
3. Sort: last bought date (newest first), then reply rate
4. Send to the top 10 first; widen only if nobody bites
5. Log every send and every reply on the buyer
Logging the sends and replies is what turns a list into data. After a few months you can see which buyers actually close, which sources produce them, and which deals got no interest because the price or area was wrong.
Check the deal works for the buyer first
A deal that leaves the buyer no margin sits no matter how good your list is. Run it through the free wholesale deal analyzer to see the buyer's all-in cost and profit after your fee before you send it.
Questions
What is a cash buyers list?
A list of investors who buy properties, usually for cash or with short-term financing, that a wholesaler sends deals to. It is only useful if each buyer's buy box is saved as fields, so every deal goes to the buyers who actually fit.
How many buyers do I need?
Fewer than most people think, if they are the right ones. Ten active buyers who match your areas and price range and have bought recently are worth more than a thousand names that never reply.
Where do cash buyers come from?
Common sources are public records of recent cash purchases, title companies and closing attorneys who work with investors, local real estate investor association meetings, landlords in your target areas, and buyers who reply to your deal posts. Record the source on each buyer.
How do I keep the list clean?
Merge duplicates by phone and email, ask for fresh proof of funds when the date gets old, and move buyers who never reply after several matching deals off the main list instead of deleting them.
Can I use this in a CRM?
Yes. Each column becomes a field on a contact or buyer record. The free CRM field kit has the same buyer fields with picklist values and automation rules for Salesforce, REsimpli, Podio, HubSpot or a spreadsheet.

## Cold Caller to Acquisitions Handoff: Fields & Rules
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/cold-caller-handoff-checklist.html

Cold caller to acquisitions handoff: the fields and rules.
Most cold calling teams lose deals at the handoff, not on the call. The caller marks a lead "warm", acquisitions calls back with no context, and the seller has to start over. Fix it with three things: a short fixed list of call outcomes, fields that must be filled before a lead can be passed, and a callback time rule your CRM enforces. The stage rules on either side of the handoff are in wholesaling pipeline stages . The queue, outcome and scorecard side is in cold-calling team setup .
1. A fixed list of call outcomes
Not interested · Wrong number · Call back later · Warm · Hot
Five options, picked from a list, never typed. Free text makes reporting impossible.
2. Required before a lead is passed
Field | Warm | Hot | Why
Timeline to sell | Required | Required | Sets the follow-up cadence
Reason for selling | Required | Required | The first thing acquisitions needs to hear
Property condition | Required | Required | Feeds the repair estimate and MAO
Asking price (if given) | Optional | Required | Shows the gap to your offer early
Decision makers on title | Optional | Required | Avoids appointments with the wrong person
Best callback time | Required | Required | Gets the second call answered
3. A callback time rule
Set a rule and let the CRM enforce it
Hot leads alert the acquisitions manager and get a callback task due within the hour. Warm leads get a task due the same day. Any task past due shows up on a daily "late callbacks" list. Pick times that fit your team, then make the CRM create the tasks so nobody has to remember.
4. A 20-minute weekly check
1. Pull last week's Warm and Hot leads by caller
2. Compare each caller's outcome with what acquisitions found on the callback
3. Count missing required fields per caller
4. Coach the caller with the biggest gap, one thing at a time
Investors on BiggerPockets debate lead managers vs acquisitions managers and VAs for cold calling ; whichever setup you choose, the handoff rules above stay the same.
Questions
What should a cold caller collect before passing a lead?
At minimum: timeline to sell, reason for selling, property condition and best callback time. For hot leads add asking price and who is on title.
How fast should acquisitions call back a hot lead?
Set a rule your team can keep, such as within the hour for hot and the same day for warm, and have the CRM create the task and flag it when it is late.
How do I check if my VAs are qualifying leads correctly?
Once a week, compare each caller's Warm and Hot leads with what acquisitions found on the callback, and count missing required fields per caller.
Can a CRM block incomplete handoffs?
Yes. Most CRMs, including Salesforce, can require fields before a status changes, so a lead cannot be marked Hot until the key questions are answered.

## Cold Calling Team Setup in Salesforce: Queues and Scorecard
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/cold-calling-team-setup-salesforce.html

Cold calling team setup in Salesforce: lists, outcomes and a scorecard that pays for appointments
The usual cold-calling complaint sounds like this: "my caller makes thousands of calls a week and I get no real leads." Sometimes the caller is the problem. More often the setup is: two callers dial the same owner, nobody knows which list is worn out, "interested" means five different things, calls are logged in a dialer that doesn't talk to the CRM, and the only number anyone watches is dials. This guide is the system around the calls: who owns which list, when to call, what each outcome does next, where the handoff happens, and the scorecard I'd use. It is written for owners and ops leads running one to ten callers, in-house or VAs, on Salesforce or any CRM you can shape.
Give every list one owner and a fixed number of attempts. Call inside legal hours (8 a.m. to 9 p.m. in the person's local time) and scrub against the Do Not Call registry at least every 31 days. Replace vague call notes with a short outcome picklist where every value triggers the next step on its own. Hand off to acquisitions only when required fields are filled in, and score callers on appointments set, accepted handoffs and appointments kept, not on dials.
What are the six parts of a cold-calling system?
List: where the names came from and how clean they are ( importing a list ).
Queue: who calls which records, in what order, how many times.
Call: the dialer and the script, logged back to the seller's record ( dialers and Salesforce ).
Outcome: one value that says what happened and decides what happens next.
Handoff: a real appointment or a warm seller passed to acquisitions with the facts attached ( handoff checklist ).
Scorecard: the few numbers that tell you whether the machine works.
The calls themselves are part 3 of 6. If results are poor, there are five other places to look before blaming the caller.
Who should own a list, and how long?
One owner per record. Set the record's owner when the list is loaded, to a caller or a queue with a claim rule. Two people calling one owner is the fastest way to annoy a seller and start an argument about credit.
A fixed attempt plan per list. For example, a set number of attempts across a number of weeks, at different times of day, then retire the record to nurture with a date. Choose it from your own history: look at which attempt number produced your appointments and where the curve flattens. The cadence builder gives a starting plan.
Record the attempt number on every call, so you can see contact rate by attempt, by list and by time of day.
Retire lists on purpose. When a list's contact rate has dropped for several weeks, stop and ask whether the list, the numbers or the hours are the cause, before you buy a bigger list.
Keep one list per campaign. Mixing a pre-foreclosure list with a probate list in one queue hides which one works.
Which calling rules belong in the system?
Put the rules where a tired caller can't skip them. Two federal ones to build around (this is information, not legal advice; check state rules as well):
Calling hours. The FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule treats outbound telemarketing calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. at the called person's local time as a violation unless they've agreed otherwise. Store a time zone on each record (from the property's state and zip) and have the queue show a record only inside its window.
Do Not Call. Sellers and telemarketers must update their call lists against the National Do Not Call Registry at least every 31 days. Keep a scrub date on each record, and a company do-not-call flag for people who ask you to stop. That flag must beat everything else and copy to duplicate records.
Add a hard stop: a record with the flag set, or with a scrub date older than your limit, doesn't appear in a dial queue at all.
What should the call outcome picklist look like?
Notes are for stories. Outcomes are for the system. Keep the list short, fixed and mutually exclusive, and let each value start the next step automatically.
Outcome | What the system does next
No answer | Increase the attempt count; schedule the next attempt per the plan
Left voicemail | Same as above, and flag that a voicemail was left
Wrong number | Remove that number; try the next phone on the record
Not the owner, owner reachable | Task to get the right contact; note who was spoken to
Spoke, not interested | Ask for the reason (picklist); move to nurture with a longer re-contact date
Spoke, not now | Require a re-contact date and a reason; create the task
Spoke, interested | Require the handoff fields; assign to acquisitions with a callback due time
Appointment set | Create the appointment, confirm text if consent exists, notify the acquisitions rep
Do not call | Set the company do-not-call flag everywhere; stop all sequences
"Interested" is the value that needs the most care. If it can be picked with nothing filled in, your acquisitions team will receive "interested" leads that no one can act on. That is the single most common reason a hot-looking list produces nothing.
When and how should a lead be handed to acquisitions?
Hand off when there is a seller with a real reason and a next step, not when someone says "maybe". The required fields at handoff are in the handoff checklist : reason for selling, timeline, condition, price expectation, who else decides and the agreed next step. Two system rules help:
A handoff creates a task for acquisitions due within a set number of minutes, and the caller sees whether it was accepted.
A handoff that sits unaccepted past its limit alerts the manager, and one that acquisitions rejects returns to the caller with a reason. This feedback loop is how callers learn what a good handoff looks like.
The stage rules around the handoff are in pipeline stages .
What should the daily scorecard show?
One line per caller per day, summed per week, from the CRM, with no spreadsheet:
Measure | Why
Dials | Effort and capacity, not performance
Contact rate (conversations / dials) | Tells you about the list, the hours and the numbers as much as about the caller
Interested rate (interested / conversations) | Script and qualification
Handoffs accepted by acquisitions | The quality check: a handoff that is rejected didn't count
Appointments set, and kept | The number that leads to offers
Cost per appointment | Caller cost and list cost together
Pay and praise follow the measures you choose. If you reward dials you'll get dials; if you reward appointments kept, you'll get callers who qualify and confirm. It also gives you an answer when someone asks about a VA who makes thousands of calls a week with nothing to show: look at contact rate and handoffs accepted first.
How should you coach callers?
Sample recordings weekly. Listen to five calls per caller: two good, two weak, one random. Compare against the outcomes they logged. Mismatches (logged "not interested" when the seller asked for a callback) are the most common problem.
Review by outcome, not by caller. Pull ten "spoke, not interested" calls and listen for the pattern in the first thirty seconds.
Change one thing at a time. A new script and a new list in the same week tell you nothing.
Limit what callers can export. A caller needs their queue, not your database; see stopping reps exporting your list .
What if the numbers are bad?
Work down the chain, from the top, before the caller:
Is the list the problem? Low contact rate on a new list usually points to stale numbers or the wrong hours.
Is the data clean? Duplicates mean the same owner got called repeatedly and some stopped answering.
Are outcomes honest? Compare logged outcomes against recordings.
Is the handoff working? A high interested rate and a low acceptance rate means the qualifying standard differs between caller and acquisitions.
Is acquisitions calling back fast enough? A great handoff that waits a day is a lost one; see speed to lead .
Only then, the script and the caller.
If you'd like to check how many reps you need behind the callers, the acquisitions team capacity calculator shows the load.
Questions
What CRM workflow should a new cold caller start with?
A queue of assigned records, a short outcome picklist, a few required fields before a handoff, and a daily view of their own numbers. Add rules only when you see a repeated mistake.
How do I monitor my cold callers' metrics and calls?
Make sure the dialer logs every call to the seller's record with an outcome and attempt number, then report dials, contact rate, interested rate, handoffs accepted and appointments set and kept per caller per week. Sample recordings weekly to check logged outcomes.
What hours can I legally cold call sellers?
The FTC's Telemarketing Sales Rule treats outbound telemarketing calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. at the called person's local time as a violation, unless they've agreed otherwise. State rules can be stricter. This is information, not legal advice.
How often do I need to scrub my call list against the Do Not Call registry?
The FTC says sellers and telemarketers must update their call lists, removing numbers on the National Do Not Call Registry, at least every 31 days. Keep the scrub date on each record and your own do-not-call flag as well.
Why does my VA make thousands of calls and get no leads?
Check in this order: list quality and contact rate, duplicates, whether logged outcomes match the recordings, whether acquisitions accepts the handoffs and calls back quickly, and only then the script. Dial counts alone say very little.
What should a cold caller be paid on?
Whatever you pay on, you'll get more of. Dials reward dialing. Appointments set and kept, and handoffs accepted by acquisitions, reward the work that leads to offers. Choose measures your CRM can report without a spreadsheet.
How many times should I call a cold list?
Set the number from your own data: look at which attempt produced your appointments and where the curve flattens, then retire the record to nurture with a re-contact date. A starting plan is in the cadence builder.
Related guides
Sources
Checked in October 2026. Compliance notes are information, not legal advice; state rules can be stricter.
FTC: Complying with the Telemarketing Sales Rule . Calling hours 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. local time; update call lists against the Do Not Call Registry at least every 31 days
FTC: National Do Not Call Registry FAQs . Telemarketers can't call before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m. local time

## Free Wholesaling CRM Field Kit: Fields, Picklists, Rules
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/crm-field-kit.html

The wholesaling CRM field kit.
The fields, picklists, automation rules and Monday report that keep deals from leaking between the marketing dollar and the closed deal. Copy them into Salesforce, REsimpli, Podio, HubSpot or a spreadsheet. Free to use and change.
1. Lead fields (13)
Where each lead came from, what happens next and how fast you reached the seller. The two that matter most: Lead Source required before a lead leaves New, and Next Task Date required on every open lead.
Field name | Type | Required when | Why it matters
Lead Source | Picklist | Before Status can leave New | Without it, no report can tie a contract or a closed deal back to the channel that paid for it.
Campaign | Lookup to Campaign (or text) | Before Status can leave New, when Lead Source is a paid channel | Lead Source says which channel; Campaign says which mailer, list or ad. Spend is entered on the campaign, so cost per appointment and ROI need this link.
Market | Picklist | Always | Lets you compare channels and reps market by market instead of mixing a strong market with a weak one.
Status | Picklist | Always | One shared list of stages, so a report can count how many leads sit at each step and how long they stay there.
Next Task Date | Date | While the lead is open (Status is not Dead or Under Contract) | An open lead with no next date is a lead nobody is working. This field makes the gap visible and lets you block it.
Touch Count | Number (auto) | Never entered by hand; counted from logged calls, texts and emails to the seller | Shows how much follow-up a lead actually got before it was marked Dead or went under contract.
Video: Leads with no next step → Video: Missed seller calls →
2. Deal fields (23)
Underwriting on the deal itself: MAO as a formula, your repair estimate next to the buyer's, and booked fees kept separate from the fees you actually receive.
Field name | Type | Required when | Why it matters
Lead Source | Picklist (copied from lead, locked) | Copied when the deal is created; not editable after | Keeps attribution intact from first call to closing so contracts and fees count for the right channel.
Campaign | Lookup to Campaign (copied from lead, locked) | Copied when the deal is created; not editable after | Contracts per campaign and ROI by campaign both read this field.
Deal Status | Picklist | Always | Separates deals that are booked from deals that are actually kept.
ARV | Currency | Before Deal Status can move to Offer Sent | After-repair value from comps. Everything in MAO starts here.
Your Repair Estimate | Currency | Before Deal Status can move to Offer Sent | Your team's repair number, the one MAO uses.
Buyer's Repair Estimate | Currency | When a buyer walks the property (optional) | What the end buyer thinks repairs cost. Comparing it with yours shows whether your estimates run low.
Video: Offers off-formula → Deal analyzer (MAO) →
3. Buyer fields (10)
Turn the buyer list into a database, so each deal goes to the buyers who actually buy that kind of house first.
Field name | Type | Required when | Why it matters
Zips | Long text (comma-separated) or multi-select | Before the buyer gets deal blasts | Lets you send each deal only to buyers who buy in that zip.
Max Price | Currency | Before the buyer gets deal blasts | Filters out buyers who can't pay your price, so the list stays short and relevant.
Rehab Level | Multi-select picklist | Before the buyer gets deal blasts | A buyer who only wants light rehabs ignores a full gut, and the reverse.
Closing Speed (days) | Number | Optional | When an inspection period is short, you want the buyers who actually close fast.
Last Bought Date | Date | Updated when the buyer closes one of your deals (or from public records) | Separates active buyers from names on a list.
Using a spreadsheet for buyers? Start from the free cash buyers list template (CSV).
Wholesaling CRM glossary →
4. Automation rules (10)
Plain-English rules that keep the fields filled in and honest, each with a Salesforce hint and an any-CRM hint.
No lead leaves New without a source
Every logged touch counts, and the first one is stamped
A missed seller call becomes a callback task in 5 minutes
No open lead without a next date
Dead needs a reason
Dead Reason sets the revisit date
Offers above MAO need a second pair of eyes
Signing a contract stamps the numbers that matter later
A fall-out zeroes the fee and records why
Every Monday, list the hot leads nobody touched
5. Monday report spec
The five numbers to look at every Monday and the exact fields each one reads from.
Cost per appointment, by campaign
Contracts per campaign
Contract to first seller call
Booked vs. kept profit
Campaign ROI, including the houses you keep
The Monday 5 → The Kept-Deal Map →
Questions
Is it really free? Do I need to give my email?
Yes, it's free and there's no form. Download the files, copy them, change them. Credit is nice but not required.
Does it only work in Salesforce?
No. Every field and rule has a plain-English version for any CRM, including REsimpli, Podio, HubSpot or a spreadsheet. Where Salesforce needs something specific, there's a one-line Salesforce hint.
Where should I start if I can only do one thing?
Make Lead Source required before a lead leaves New, and make Next Task Date required on every open lead. Those two fields fix the most common leaks: not knowing which marketing pays, and leads nobody follows up.
Why these fields and not others?
Each one exists so a specific weekly number can be counted: cost per appointment by campaign, contracts per campaign, time from contract to first seller call, booked vs. kept profit, and campaign ROI including the houses you keep.

## CRM for a We Buy Houses Company: What It Must Do
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/crm-for-we-buy-houses-company.html

CRM for a "we buy houses" company: the seven jobs it has to do
A we-buy-houses company runs on a very particular loop: spend on marketing, get seller inquiries by phone, text and form, get a person on the phone fast, set an appointment, make an offer, get a contract, then sell the contract or fix and sell the house. Most CRMs weren't built around that loop, and most of the trouble owners describe comes from the gaps between the steps rather than from the steps themselves. This guide describes what a CRM has to do for a cash home-buying company in plain terms, what it should connect to, who needs access, and ends with a ten-question check you can run on your own setup this afternoon. The advice holds on any CRM. I build on Salesforce, and I'll point out where that choice matters.
A CRM for a we-buy-houses company must do seven jobs: capture every inquiry with its source, give every seller one record, get the right person acting within minutes, track appointments and offers on the deal, carry the deal from contract through dispo or rehab to closing, keep consent and opt-outs straight, and report cost per contract by marketing source. Judge any tool, from a spreadsheet to Salesforce, against those seven, not against its feature list.
What loop does the CRM have to support?
Whatever you call yourself (we buy houses, cash home buyer, wholesaler, local investor), the sequence is much the same:
Marketing: mailers, PPC, SEO, cold calling, texting lists, referrals.
Inquiry: a seller calls, texts or fills in a form.
First conversation: a rep or cold caller qualifies the situation.
Appointment: a call or a walkthrough.
Offer, then contract.
Exit: assign to a buyer, close yourself and rehab, or hold.
Close and pay: title company, fees, books.
A brokerage CRM is built around a client over many years. Yours is built around a deal on one house over a few weeks, with a seller who may or may not come back. That difference is why a tool that works for agents often feels wrong for you.
What are the seven jobs?
1. Capture every inquiry with its source
Calls, texts, web forms, list uploads and ad leads should all land in one place, tagged by where they came from. If the source is guessed later, your marketing numbers are guesses too. How to tag cleanly: tags, fields or campaigns .
2. One record per seller and property
The same owner appears on several lists and calls from several numbers. Without matching and merging, you pay to contact the same person repeatedly and your lead count lies. See duplicate seller leads .
3. Get someone acting within minutes
The first call is the highest-leverage activity you have. A new lead should create a task for a named person, a missed call should create a callback, and nothing should depend on someone noticing an email. See speed to lead and missed-call alerts .
4. Track appointments, offers and the numbers behind them
Appointment set and kept, offer amount, your maximum allowable offer, the offer date and the follow-up date should be fields on the deal, not text in a note. That's what lets you see the leak between appointment and offer, and between offer and contract. See pipeline stages with entry and exit rules and offer follow-up .
5. Carry the deal from contract to closing
Once a contract is signed, the work shifts to title, buyers or rehab. Your CRM should hold the signed contract, the closing date, the title company, the assignment or sale price and who is doing what. See dispositions and transaction coordination .
6. Keep consent and opt-outs straight
Texting and calling carry legal obligations. One consent field, one opt-out flag, and every tool reading the same ones. See texting sellers and wholesaling laws and what your CRM has to track .
7. Report cost per contract by source
Marketing is your biggest expense, and the question that matters is which source produces signed contracts, not leads. That needs spend, source and deal outcome in the same place. See cost per deal calculator and which campaign gets credit .
What should the CRM connect to?
You're unlikely to have one tool that does everything well. Typical pieces around the CRM:
A phone or dialer that logs calls to the seller's record ( dialers ).
Texting with registered campaigns and opt-out handling.
List and skip-trace tools that feed leads in without duplicates.
E-signature so signed contracts attach to the deal ( DocuSign ).
Bookkeeping so fees and costs match deals ( QuickBooks ).
Ad platforms receiving which leads became contracts ( Google Ads ).
The point of the CRM is that these write back to one record per seller. If each tool keeps its own copy, you've multiplied the problems above. More on the options: integrations .
Who needs access, and to what?
A company of 10 to 50 usually has cold callers, acquisitions reps, a dispo person, a transaction coordinator, a marketing person, VAs and an owner. They don't all need to see the same things. Decide up front who can see sellers' phone numbers, who can export, who can change a closed deal, and who can edit the pipeline settings. Contractors and VAs often need narrower access and a trail of what they did. See who sees what and stopping reps exporting your list .
Which numbers should it give you without a spreadsheet?
Leads, appointments, offers, contracts and closings by source, for any date range.
Time from lead to first call, by rep and by hour of day.
Offer-to-contract rate, by rep.
Cost per appointment and cost per contract, by source.
Deals sitting in a stage longer than they should.
Leads with no next step.
If getting these takes an export, a spreadsheet and an afternoon, the CRM isn't doing job 7. The five I'd put on an owner's screen every Monday are in the Monday 5 .
What is a 10-question check you can run today?
Answer yes or no. Each "no" is a leak.
Does every lead have a source from the moment it is created?
If the same seller calls from a new number, does the CRM find the old record?
Does a new lead create a task for a named person within minutes?
Does a missed call create a callback task automatically?
Does every open lead have a dated next step?
Can you see offers as fields (amount, date, follow-up), not notes?
Is the signed contract attached to the deal?
Does an opt-out on one record stop messages on all of them?
Can you get cost per contract by source in a few clicks?
Can you tell who last touched any seller, and when?
Eight or more yes: your system is doing its job, and the work is polish. Five to seven: you have specific leaks worth fixing in order. Under five: the CRM is storing contacts, not running the business. You can also score yourself with the Deal Leak Score , which turns this kind of check into an estimate of what the leaks cost.
How do you pick one?
Match it to your size and how unusual your process is. Smaller teams with a standard process often do best on an investor CRM that has the loop built in. Teams of around 10 or more, with several lead sources and their own way of working, often outgrow that and want to control the process and the reports, which is where building on Salesforce makes sense. Side by side: 11 CRMs compared , Salesforce vs investor CRMs and the complete guide . If you're on a small budget, start with what free gets you .
Questions
What CRM do we buy houses companies use?
Companies in this space use a mix: investor-focused CRMs with dialer and skip tracing built in, general CRMs such as HubSpot or GoHighLevel, and Salesforce-based setups for larger teams. The right one depends on team size, lead sources and how unusual your process is. Judge each against seven jobs: capture, one record per seller, speed, offers, contract to closing, consent and cost per contract.
What features does a cash home buyer CRM need?
Lead capture with source, duplicate matching, instant task assignment, call and text logging, pipeline stages with required fields, offer and contract tracking, dispo or rehab tracking, consent and opt-out handling, and reports on cost per contract by source.
Do I need a CRM if I only buy a few houses a month?
You need a system for follow-up and source tracking, but a spreadsheet or a free CRM can be enough at low volume. Move up when more than one person works leads, lists get large, or you can't tell which marketing produces contracts.
How is a CRM for investors different from a real estate agent CRM?
Agent CRMs are built around a long relationship with a client and a transaction. An investor CRM is built around many motivated-seller inquiries, fast first contact, offers on one property and an exit (assignment, rehab or hold). That means stages, fields and reports differ.
How do I track marketing ROI as a home-buying company?
Record the source and campaign on every lead at creation, put the marketing cost on the campaign, and follow each lead through to the contract and closing. Then report cost per appointment and cost per contract by source.
Should my cold callers and VAs have full CRM access?
No. Give them the access their job needs: usually their own leads, not exports of the whole database. Limit who can see all phone numbers, export lists or change closed deals, and keep a log of changes.
Related guides
Want the ten answers turned into a fix list?
The CRM Revenue Audit (USD 1,500, fixed price) goes through your setup against these seven jobs and returns a ranked fix list with the cost of each leak. It's for teams already on Salesforce. On another CRM? A free call will tell you whether a move makes sense.
