## CRM Tags for Wholesalers: Tags, Fields or Campaigns?
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/crm-tags-wholesale-real-estate.html

CRM tags for wholesalers: what belongs in a tag, a field or a campaign
Tags are the easiest thing to add to a CRM and the hardest to keep clean. Within a year you have "hot", "Hot", "hot lead", "HOT!!", three versions of "probate" and a list of 400 tags nobody can search. The cause isn't sloppy people. It's that tags get used for jobs that need a field, a campaign or a flag, so each person invents their own. This guide sorts what a wholesaling or home-buying team actually needs to label, tells you which container fits each, and gives naming rules and a Salesforce setup. Use it whether you're on an investor CRM with tags built in or on Salesforce, which is built around structured fields rather than free-form tags.
Use a field (a picklist) for anything you'll report on or filter by every week: lead source, motivation, property type, dead reason. Use a campaign for a marketing wave or a list, because it carries cost and dates. Use a checkbox or status for consent and do-not-contact, which must never be a tag. Keep free tags, if your tool has them, for short-lived working labels, with a fixed list, one owner and a quarterly clean-up.
Why do tag systems turn into a mess?
Anyone can create one. Free-text tags have no spell check and no owner.
One tag tries to do four jobs. "Probate-hot-Franklin-Nov" is a source, a motivation, a market and a date squeezed into one word you can't count.
Nobody retires them. Tags from a campaign two years ago still sit on thousands of records.
Automation keys off them. Once a text sequence starts from a tag, deleting or renaming it breaks something quietly. See automations that fail quietly .
The people who label are not the people who report. Reps tag what helps them today, and the owner later can't answer "which source works?"
What are you really trying to label?
Almost everything teams tag falls into one of six groups. The group tells you the right container.
Where it came from (source, list, mailer wave, ad).
Who the seller is and why they sell (motivation, situation: probate, divorce, tax delinquent, tired landlord).
What the property is (type, condition, county).
Where the lead is (stage, status, nurture).
What you're allowed to do (consent to text, do not call, opted out).
Temporary working notes ("send to dispo team", "call after the 15th").
Which container fits each?
You are labeling | Use | Why
Lead source and channel | A picklist field with a fixed list, set when the record is created | You'll report on it every week; free text can't be counted
A mailer wave, list or ad campaign | A campaign (and campaign members) | Carries cost, dates and result, so cost per contract works
Seller situation (probate, divorce, tax delinquent) | A picklist , or a small set of checkboxes if a lead can be several | Needed for scoring and for the right message
Property type and county | Fields on the property or deal | Filters, buy-box matching and reporting
Stage and status | The stage or status field, with rules | This drives your pipeline; see pipeline stages
Consent, do not call, opt-out | A checkbox plus date and source , never a tag | A compliance fact needs a record of when and how
Short-lived working labels | A tag if you have them, from a fixed list | The one place free tags are fine, because nothing important depends on them
The test: will I want to count it? If yes, it's a field, and probably a picklist. If it only helps someone find a record this week, a tag is fine.
What naming rules keep it clean?
One list, one owner. One person (ops or an admin) approves new values. Reps can ask, but they can't create.
Lowercase or one consistent style. Pick it once and never mix.
One meaning per value. "Probate" means probate, not "probate and maybe divorce".
No dates, names or markets inside a value. Those belong in their own fields or on the campaign.
Keep the lists short. Ten to fifteen sources and eight to twelve situations is enough for most teams. If a list reaches fifty, you're mixing jobs.
Write the definitions down. One line per value, in a place reps can read it. It prevents most arguments.
How do you build this in Salesforce?
Salesforce is built around structured fields rather than the free-form tags many investor CRMs use, which is a feature here: structure is what keeps data usable.
Picklists for sources and situations. Use one shared list of values (a global value set) across Lead, Opportunity and Campaign, so a source can't mean different things on different objects. Make the field restricted, so a rep or an import can't add a new value by accident.
Campaigns for waves and lists. Create a campaign per mailer wave or list and add records as campaign members with a status (sent, responded, appointment, contract). Cost goes on the campaign, which is what makes cost per contract a normal report. The step-by-step is in lead sources in Salesforce .
Checkboxes for situations a lead can have more than one of. Several short checkboxes report more easily than one long multi-select list.
Consent as its own set of fields. A checkbox, the date, and the source of the consent, plus an opt-out checkbox that Flow copies to every duplicate record. See texting and consent .
Record types and page layouts to show reps only the values that apply to their type of lead.
A data dictionary. A small custom object or a shared sheet listing each field, its values and its owner. It sounds boring and it's the thing future admins thank you for.
The CRM field kit has a starting set of lead, deal and buyer fields you can adapt.
Why are tags that trigger automation risky?
If adding a tag starts a text sequence, anyone who adds it starts messages. Two problems follow: a typo means nothing happens, and a bulk edit can start messages to thousands of sellers, including some who opted out. Safer pattern: automation starts from a stage, a status or a consent-checked field, never from a free tag. Where you can't avoid it, make the tag controlled (only ops can apply it) and have the automation check the consent field before it sends.
What does a 30-minute quarterly clean-up look like?
List every tag or picklist value with its record count.
Merge near-duplicates ("hot" and "Hot lead") and retire the unused.
Check anything that triggers automation, and test it on one record.
Archive campaigns that finished, and keep the results.
Update the one-line definitions and tell the team what changed.
It's the same weekly-and-quarterly rhythm that keeps duplicates from piling up. If your tags are already out of hand, the CRM audit checklist shows where to start.
Questions
How should I tag leads in a wholesaling CRM?
Don't use one tag for everything. Put lead source, seller situation and property type in picklist fields you can report on, record marketing waves as campaigns with cost, and keep consent as a checkbox with a date. Use free tags only for short-lived working labels from a fixed list.
What is the difference between a tag and a field in a CRM?
A field holds one defined piece of data you can filter, count and report on, such as lead source. A tag is a free label that is quick to add but easy to misspell and hard to report on. Use fields for anything you'll count and tags for temporary notes.
Does Salesforce have tags?
Salesforce is built around structured fields rather than free-form tags like many investor CRMs. You use picklist fields, checkboxes, campaigns and record types, which keep the data structured and reportable. It takes more setup but is easier to report on.
How many lead sources should a CRM have?
Ten to fifteen is enough for most home-buying teams. If a source list grows past about fifty values, you're probably mixing the source with the campaign, the market or the date, which belong in their own fields.
Should consent and do-not-call be tags?
No. Consent is a compliance fact that needs a record of when and how it was given, so use a checkbox plus a date and a source, and make sure every duplicate record and every tool reads the same field.
How do I clean up a messy tag list?
Export every tag with its count, merge near-duplicates, retire unused ones, test anything that triggers automation, and write a one-line definition for each remaining value. Do it quarterly and give one person ownership of the list.
Related guides
Want your tags and fields sorted once?
Data structure is part of the fixed-price CRM Revenue Audit (USD 1,500): your fields, sources and tags reviewed against how you report, with a clean-up plan. It's for teams already on Salesforce.
Or just ask one question about your setup: email · WhatsApp · LinkedIn

## Reactivating Dead Seller Leads in Salesforce for Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/dead-seller-leads-salesforce.html

The leads you already paid for. Reactivating dead seller leads in Salesforce
Every home-buying company that has marketed for a few years is sitting on hundreds, often thousands, of seller leads marked dead, lost or not interested. You paid for every one of them. Some of those sellers are ready now: the tenant moved out, the repairs got worse, the estate got settled. This page is for owners and acquisitions managers who want to work that list on purpose, without bothering people who asked you to stop.
Don't blast the whole list. Sort dead leads by why they died and how long ago, remove anyone who asked not to be contacted, and fix bad numbers first. Then run each group as its own Salesforce campaign with its own message, so every reply is tracked and credited. Send responders straight to a rep with a task due now, flag them as re-engaged without overwriting the original source, and judge the campaign on contracts, not replies.
Why are dead leads worth working?
They already know you. A seller who talked to your team once is warmer than any list you can buy.
"Not now" is usually about timing. Situations like a vacant house, a tenant who stopped paying or an inheritance don't stand still after your rep stops calling.
Follow-up stops early. In one large study, 81% of sales reps made five or fewer follow-up attempts on a lead ( InsideSales, 2021 ). Plenty of your "dead" leads were simply never worked to the end.
You've already paid. Every one of those leads cost mail, clicks or caller time. Work out what yours cost with the cost per deal calculator ; it puts a number on the list.
How should you sort dead leads before contacting anyone?
By why they died, then by how long ago. Each group gets a different message, and some get none.
Group | Typical dead reasons | What I'd do
Timing | Not ready yet, tenant in place, waiting on family | The best group. Ask what has changed
Price | Wanted more than you offered | Ask whether their situation has changed. Don't open with a higher number
Listed | Listed with an agent | Check whether the listing expired or was withdrawn, then reach out
Never reached | No answer, bad or wrong number | Refresh the contact details before anything else, and mark the wrong numbers so nothing contacts them again
Sold | Sold to another buyer | Stop marketing that address. Keep the person if they own other property
Not a fit | Outside your buy box, no equity | Leave out, unless your buy box has changed
Do not contact | Asked to stop, represented by an attorney | Never, by any channel
Then split each group by age: dead in the last 3 to 12 months, 1 to 2 years, and older. The recent ones remember you. The old ones need more introduction.
If your dead leads don't have a reliable reason on them, that's the first thing to fix, because it decides everything above. A short required list, set the moment a lead or offer dies, is enough. The offer follow-up guide has the list I'd start with.
Who shouldn't you contact?
Not legal advice, but the stakes are real. The TCPA allows $500 per violation, and a court can raise it to $1,500 when the violation is willful. Get your consent and opt-out rules from whoever advises you on it. What I'd build into Salesforce either way:
Honor every opt-out, from any channel. Since April 11, 2025, FCC rules say people can revoke consent by any reasonable means, and you have to honor it within 10 business days. A seller who told a rep "stop calling me" on a call has opted out, even if they never texted STOP.
Keep one place that says "do not contact". Salesforce has standard Do Not Call and Email Opt Out fields on leads and contacts. Make sure your texting tool's opt-outs land there too, and that every list you pull filters on them.
Check the National Do Not Call Registry and your own do-not-call list before a calling or texting campaign, and don't assume consent from an old web form covers a new campaign years later.
Watch the coming change. A broader FCC rule, under which one opt-out covers all of a company's automated calls and texts, has been delayed to January 31, 2027.
Clean the list before you send anything
Merge duplicates. The same seller on three records gets three messages and decides you're spam. See duplicate sellers in Salesforce .
Fix bad numbers. Skip trace the ones marked wrong or disconnected, and mark the old numbers as bad so nothing texts them again.
Check the property. If county records show it sold, take the address out.
Check the source. Every lead should still carry its original source and campaign, so the reactivation can be credited without overwriting where the seller first came from.
How do you run it in Salesforce?
One Salesforce campaign per group and message , for example "Reactivation: timing, Q4 2026". Add the leads as campaign members and give the campaign its own member statuses: Sent, Responded, Appointment, Contract.
Pull the lists with a report filtered on status, dead reason, date it died, a valid phone number and do-not-contact unchecked. Save it, so next quarter's list takes a minute.
Send from a tool that logs back to Salesforce. Replies have to land on the seller's record, or nobody sees them in time. For mail, use a tracking number for each campaign, as with any other mail piece. More in texting in Salesforce .
Send in batches your team can answer. A thousand texts on Monday morning means replies sitting for a day. Send what your reps can call back within the hour, and spread the rest over the week.
Pause other automations on these records , so a seller who replies doesn't also get pulled into two other sequences.
What should the first message say?
Short, from a real person, and honest about why you're writing. Something like:
"Hi Linda, it's Marcus from [your company]. We talked about your house on Maple a while back. Is selling still something you'd consider?"
That's a made-up example. What makes it work: it says who you are, reminds them you've spoken, and asks one question they can answer in a word. What to avoid: pretending you have a buyer lined up, an offer "expiring today", or a message that reads like it went to five thousand people, even though it did. Make opting out easy, and follow whatever your texting tool and your advisor require.
What happens when a seller answers?
Treat the reply like a new lead. A task due now, assigned to a person, with the same speed-to-lead clock you use for fresh leads. See speed to lead for investors .
Send it back to the rep who knows them , if that rep is still on the team and working that market. In the org I run, a returning seller keeps their full history and the original owner gets told the seller came back.
Keep the original source locked. Set a "latest source" to the reactivation campaign and flag the record as re-engaged. That's how reactivation gets credit without rewriting history. See which campaign gets credit .
Handle the no's automatically. "Stop", "wrong number" and "already sold" should update the record, marking the person, the number or the address, so they never come back on a list.
Open a new deal for a new conversation , linked to the same seller and property, rather than reviving a deal from two years ago. The new deal's dates and stages stay honest, and the old one keeps its history.
How do you measure it?
On contracts and closed deals, the same as any other campaign. The report I'd build, by reactivation campaign:
Column | Why
Members sent | The size of the push
Responded | Interest, nothing more
Appointments | Real conversations about selling
Contracts and closed deals | What it actually produced
Fees or profit on closed deals | What it was worth
Cost: texts, mail, skip tracing | So cost per contract compares with new leads
Reply rates look exciting and mean little. A campaign with fewer replies and two contracts beats one with lots of replies and none.
Make it a habit, not a project
A once-a-year blast is the hardest way to do this. The easier way is a date on every dead lead:
When a lead dies, set a "revisit on" date from its reason. A timing reason might come back in 90 days, a listing after it would have expired, a price reason in a few months. Pick the numbers with your team and write them down.
Each week, a list of revisits due goes to a person or into a small campaign. A few dozen a week is easier to answer well than thousands at once.
Clear open tasks when a lead dies , so reps aren't chasing dead leads by accident and the revisit is the only next step. The org I run does this, along with automatic "review this lead" tasks for leads that go stale.
Done this way, the dead list stops being a graveyard and becomes a source with its own row on the campaign report.
Questions
How do you reactivate dead real estate seller leads?
Sort them by why they died and how long ago, remove anyone who asked not to be contacted, fix bad numbers, then run each group as a campaign with a short personal message. Route every reply to a rep immediately and measure the campaign on contracts.
Is it legal to text old seller leads?
It depends on consent, opt-outs and the Do Not Call rules, so check with whoever advises you on the TCPA. At minimum, honor every opt-out from any channel within 10 business days, scrub against the Do Not Call Registry and your own list, and don't assume old consent covers a new campaign.
How often should you contact dead leads?
Set a revisit date on each dead lead based on why it died, for example a few months for timing or price reasons, and work the leads that come due each week in small batches. A steady rhythm beats one big blast a year.
Should a reactivated seller go back to the original rep?
Usually yes, if that rep is still on the team and working that market, because the seller already knows them. Tell the rep the seller came back, and keep the full history on the record.
How do I track a reactivation campaign in Salesforce?
Create a Salesforce campaign for each group and message, add the leads as campaign members with statuses like Sent, Responded, Appointment and Contract, and report on contracts and revenue by campaign alongside cost.
Does reactivating a lead change its lead source?
It shouldn't. Keep the original source and campaign locked, set a separate latest source to the reactivation campaign, and flag the record as re-engaged, so both campaigns get the right credit.
What should I do with sellers who sold to someone else?
Stop marketing that address and update the record so it doesn't come back on a list. If the person owns other property, keep them as a contact for that, separately.

## Do I Need a CRM Yet? Spreadsheet vs CRM for Wholesalers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/do-i-need-a-crm-wholesaling.html

Do I need a CRM yet? Spreadsheet vs CRM for wholesalers.
You need a CRM when a lead can be forgotten without anyone noticing. Deal count matters less than people, follow-up and lead source. If one person works every lead and checks the sheet daily, a spreadsheet can carry you. Once two people touch leads, follow-ups run past a week, or you can't say which list paid for your last deal, the sheet starts costing you deals. Not ready to pay for one yet? Use the free seller lead tracker and read where free CRMs stop working .
Seven signs you've outgrown the spreadsheet
Check the ones that are true
☐ More than one person calls or texts sellers ☐ Follow-ups depend on someone remembering ☐ You can't say which list or campaign produced your last closed deal ☐ A missed call doesn't turn into a callback task by itself ☐ Leads with "not right now" have no next date ☐ Your buyers list is a text thread or a column of phone numbers ☐ Monday numbers take an hour to rebuild by hand
Two or more checked: the spreadsheet is already costing you. Wholesalers describe it the same way on BiggerPockets: "leads die in the follow-up" .
What a spreadsheet still does well
Keep it if
You're solo, every lead is touched daily, and you're still testing which marketing works. A sheet with lead source, status, next follow-up date and notes is a fine start. Make next follow-up date a column you sort by every morning.
The cheapest next step
1. Write your stages from new lead to closed on one page
2. Make lead source, next follow-up date and status required on every lead
3. Move the sheet into a free or low-cost CRM trial and test it for 2 weeks
4. Turn on two automations: missed call = callback task, no next date = alert
5. Only then compare paid tools against the flow you wrote in step 1
Looking at low-cost options? A recent BiggerPockets thread compares them: low to no cost wholesaling CRMs . Whatever you pick, check it against the wholesaling CRM checklist .
Questions
How many leads before I need a CRM?
There is no single number. The trigger is people and follow-up: once two people touch leads, or follow-ups depend on memory, a CRM pays for itself by keeping leads from going quiet.
Can I use Google Sheets as a CRM?
Yes at the start, if one person works every lead daily and the sheet has lead source, status, next follow-up date and notes. It breaks when you add people, texting and automated reminders.
What should I set up first in a new CRM?
Required lead source, a next follow-up date on every open lead, a missed call creating a callback task, and a short list of stages. Fancy dashboards can wait.
Is Salesforce too much for a new wholesaler?
Usually yes. Start with a spreadsheet or an investor CRM. Salesforce makes sense once you have several people, markets or reporting needs your tool cannot handle.

## Double Closing Costs: What You Pay on Both Sides
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/double-closing-costs.html

Double closing costs: both sides, one formula.
In a double close you buy the property from the seller and resell it to your end buyer, usually the same day. You pay buyer-side costs on the first closing and seller-side costs on the second, plus transactional funding if you borrow the purchase money. What you keep is the resale price minus your contract price minus all of that.
The formula
Closing A (you buy) = settlement fee + title insurance and recording you pay + any transfer tax your side pays
Closing B (you sell) = settlement fee + transfer tax, deed prep and any title costs your side pays
Funding = transactional funding fee, if you do not use your own cash
You keep = resale price − contract price − Closing A − Closing B − Funding
Which side pays transfer tax and owner's title insurance depends on the state, county and contract. Ask your title company for a settlement estimate for each closing and put every line in one of the two buckets above.
Double close or assignment?
An assignment has one closing, and your fee is paid at it. A double close keeps your spread off the assignment paperwork, and works when the contract can't be assigned, but costs a second closing and often funding. Put your numbers into the free assignment vs double close calculator to see what you keep each way. If the assignment fee would be large enough to put the buyer off, also check that the deal still works for them in the wholesale deal analyzer .
Ask your title company before you sign
1. Do you close back-to-back transactions?
Some title companies don't. Find one that does before you go under contract.
2. What will each closing cost?
A settlement estimate for closing A and closing B, line by line, at your contract and resale prices.
3. Will the end buyer's lender accept it?
If your buyer is financing, some lenders have rules about how recently the seller took title. Cash buyers avoid this.
4. Can transactional funding be used here?
Confirm the title company works with your funder and when the funds must arrive.
What to track in your CRM
Exit type and both sets of costs
A picklist for assignment or double close on every deal, with closing A, closing B and funding costs as fields. Reports by exit type then show what you actually kept, not just the spread.
Questions
What is a double close?
Two closings back to back, often the same day. In the first you buy the property from the seller; in the second you sell it to your end buyer. You are the buyer in one and the seller in the other, so you pay closing costs on both.
Why double close instead of assigning?
Usually because the spread is large and you do not want the seller or buyer to see it on the assignment paperwork, or because the contract does not allow assignment. The cost is a second set of closing costs and, if you do not use your own cash, transactional funding.
How much does a double close cost?
It depends on the state, county, title company and price, so there is no single number. Ask your title company for a settlement estimate for each closing before you choose, and add any transactional funding fee.
Who pays transfer tax and title insurance?
It depends on local custom and the contract. In some places the seller pays transfer tax, in others the buyer, or it is split. In a double close you are on both sides, so check each line of both estimates.
Can every title company do a double close?
No. Some will not close back-to-back transactions, and some end-buyer lenders have rules about how recently the seller bought the property. Ask before you go under contract. This page is not legal or tax advice.

## Driving for Dollars with Salesforce: Mobile & Maps
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/driving-for-dollars-salesforce.html

Driving for dollars with Salesforce.
You can run driving for dollars from the Salesforce mobile app, which works offline and syncs later, and add Salesforce Maps or a partner app like Geopointe for routes. Here’s what to capture on each property, what the mobile app and map tools do, and what happens after the drive so the house becomes a lead you can measure.
Driving for dollars works in Salesforce with the mobile app: it caches recent records, and Offline Edit lets you create and edit records with no signal , syncing later. source
For routes and map views you need an add-on: Salesforce Maps (routes, territories, nearby search) or a partner app like Geopointe. source · Geopointe
The rule that matters: one Property record per address, checked for duplicates, so a house you drive past twice isn’t two leads.
What should a driving-for-dollars record capture?
Field | Type | Why
Address | Address fields | The match key for duplicates and mapping
Distress signs | Multi-select picklist (overgrown, boarded, tarp, code notice, mail piling up, vacant) | Lets you filter and score; free text can’t be filtered
Occupancy guess | Picklist | Changes the outreach
Photo | File on the record | Proof for the acquisitions call
Driver and date | Lookup and date | Which driver’s routes produce deals
Lead source | Picklist = Driving for dollars | So cost per deal works for this channel too
What does the Salesforce mobile app do in the field?
Offline caching and Offline Edit
By default the app caches up to 30 recent records for each of your 5 most recent objects. With Offline Edit, users create, edit and delete records offline, and changes sync when the device reconnects. source
Quick create actions
Mobile smart actions give one-tap create on leads and other core objects; a custom action can open a short “new property” form with only the fields above. source
Business card scan
Meeting a neighbour, contractor or agent on the street? The app can scan a business card into a contact. source
Do you need Salesforce Maps for driving for dollars?
Option | What it does | Note
Salesforce Maps | Records on a map, route optimization, territory planning, nearby prospecting, external property data via connectors | Add-on; bundled in Agentforce 1 Sales. Maps Advanced plans routes up to 4 months out
Geopointe (Ascent Cloud) | Maps leads and deals, radius search, optimized routes, mobile check-ins with notes, territories | AppExchange partner app
No map add-on | Export addresses to a route app; capture in the mobile app | Fine to start
Sources: Salesforce Maps · Trailhead · Geopointe
What happens after the drive?
1. Deduplicate
Duplicate rules alert or block when a new record matches an existing address. Up to 5 active duplicate rules per object. source
2. Skip trace
Send the address to your skip tracing provider and write phones and DNC flags back. BatchData’s API, for example, returns phones flagged mobile or landline with DNC and TCPA litigator checks; there’s no native Salesforce connector, so this is middleware or a custom callout. source
3. Outreach with consent rules
Calling and texting rules apply to these numbers too. See the texting guide .
4. Score the driver, not just the house
Report deals and contracts by driver and route. That tells you which areas to drive again.
Questions
Can I use Salesforce offline while driving for dollars?
Yes. The mobile app caches recent records, and Offline Edit lets you create, edit and delete records offline; changes sync when you reconnect.
Does Salesforce have route planning?
Salesforce Maps, an add-on, offers route optimization, territory planning and nearby search. Partner apps such as Geopointe also do routing.
How do I avoid duplicate properties from driving for dollars?
Keep one Property record per address and turn on duplicate rules matching on the address, so a second visit updates the record instead of creating a new lead.

## DSCR Calculator for Rental Property Loans (Free)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/dscr-calculator.html

DSCR calculator.
Debt service coverage ratio for a rental property loan: monthly rent divided by the full payment (principal, interest, taxes, insurance and association dues). It also shows the stricter NOI-based ratio and the largest loan that still meets your target DSCR. DSCR loans are mainly a US product; the ratio itself works anywhere.
The formula
PITIA = principal & interest + property taxes + insurance + association dues
DSCR (lender style) = monthly rent ÷ PITIA
NOI = rent − taxes − insurance − dues − other operating costs
DSCR (NOI-based) = NOI ÷ principal & interest
Maximum loan = the loan whose PITIA equals rent ÷ target DSCR
Worked example
Rent is $2,400 a month. A $260,000 loan at 7.25% over 30 years costs $1,774 in principal and interest. Add $300 of taxes and $120 of insurance and PITIA is $2,194. DSCR is 2400 ÷ 2194 = 1.09.
Questions
What is DSCR in real estate?
The debt service coverage ratio compares a property's rent to its loan payment. A DSCR of 1.25 means the rent is 25% more than the payment. DSCR lenders qualify the property on this ratio instead of the borrower's personal income.
What DSCR do lenders require?
Requirements vary by lender and change with the market. Many DSCR lenders look for at least 1.0 to 1.25, and some offer programs below 1.0 with larger down payments or higher rates. Use the target field to test the number your lender gives you.
Why are there two DSCR numbers?
Most DSCR lenders divide rent by PITIA (principal, interest, taxes, insurance and association dues). Commercial lenders and many investors use net operating income divided by debt service, which also subtracts management, repairs and vacancy. The NOI-based number is stricter and closer to real cash flow.
Does interest-only change DSCR?
Yes. An interest-only payment is smaller, so the ratio is higher. Some lenders qualify interest-only loans on the interest-only payment and others on the fully amortizing one. Try both settings.
How do I keep DSCR visible across deals?
Put rent, taxes, insurance, dues and loan terms on the deal record in your CRM, calculate DSCR as a formula, and block a deal from moving to financing when it is under your lender's minimum.
Related free tools
BRRRR calculator · Rental yield & cap rate calculator · Wholesale deal analyzer · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.

Free to embed on your blog or investor site. Copy the code below.

## Free CRM for Wholesalers: Where Free Stops Working
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/free-crm-for-wholesalers.html

Free CRM for wholesalers: what free gets you and where it stops working
If you're searching for a free CRM, you're probably right to start small. One person, a few leads a week and a spreadsheet can run a wholesaling business for a while. The trouble is that free tools are built for a general business, and wholesaling puts strain on exactly the places where free plans are thin: lots of records at once, several people touching the same seller, calls and texts that need to be logged and honored, and a need to know which marketing produced a contract. This guide is a plain look at what a free setup can do, the limits that bite first, and the signs it is time to move. I build Salesforce for home-buying teams, so I'll say up front that for a solo wholesaler, free is often the right answer.
A free CRM or a spreadsheet works while one person handles a few dozen new leads a month. It stops working when a second or third person (a VA, a cold caller, an acquisitions rep) needs the same seller records, when you load lists of thousands of rows, when you need automatic follow-up tasks and call or text logging, or when you need to know which campaign produced which contract. Check six things before you commit: user limit, record limit, automation, call and text logging, reporting by source, and whether you can export everything.
What does "free CRM" actually mean?
Three different things get called free, and the difference matters:
A spreadsheet. Free forever, fully yours, and it does exactly what you build into it. My seller lead tracker shows how far one can go.
A free tier of a paid CRM. A real CRM with caps on users, records, automation or reporting. The vendor expects you to grow into the paid plan.
A free trial. Free for a few weeks, then it bills. Useful for testing, not a place to run a business.
Free tiers change, so check the vendor's page before you build on one. As of the pages I checked in October 2026, HubSpot's free CRM allows up to 2 users, 1,000 contacts and one automated email action, and Zoho CRM's free edition is free for up to 3 users, with advanced reporting and mass email on paid plans. Neither is built for wholesaling, which isn't a criticism: they're built for a general small business, and you'll be adding the investor-specific parts yourself.
What seven jobs does a wholesaling CRM have to do?
Use this as your scorecard for any tool, free or paid:
Capture every inquiry with its source. Web forms, calls, texts, list uploads. If the source isn't recorded at the door, you can't recover it later.
Keep one record per seller and property. No duplicates when the same owner appears on three lists.
Tell someone to act, fast. A new lead should create a task for a named person within minutes.
Remember the next step. Every open lead has a follow-up date. Without it, a lead is just a name.
Log calls and texts, and honor opt-outs. Including the seller who said stop on one number.
Hold the deal. Offer, contract, dispo and closing on one record, with who did what.
Report cost and result by source. Which campaign, list or caller produced contracts, not just leads.
Which limits bite wholesalers first?
Users
A solo operator needs one seat. A cold caller and a VA make three. If a tool allows two or three users on its free plan, you can hit the cap the week you hire. Check what the next tier costs for each extra person before it surprises you.
Records
A single skip-traced list can run into the thousands of rows. A free tier that caps contacts at 1,000 may be fine for a small team of buyers or sellers, but one list upload can fill it. Ask: how many sellers, properties and buyers will I have in a year?
Automation
The first automation most wholesalers need is "new lead means call task for the owner, due now", then "no contact in seven days means a reminder". If a free plan limits automated actions to one, or locks workflows to paid tiers, you're back to remembering.
Calls and texts
This is the one most people underestimate. If your dialer and texting tool don't write back to the CRM, you have two systems of record, and opt-outs live in one while follow-up runs from the other. Texting also has rules (carrier registration, consent, opt-outs) that a spreadsheet can't enforce. See texting sellers: 10DLC and consent .
Reporting
Free plans usually give you basic reports. The report wholesalers need is cost per contract by lead source, which needs your marketing spend, the source on every lead and the deal outcome in one place. That's rarely a free-tier feature, and it's what tells you where the next dollar should go. A cost per deal calculator can give you the numbers by hand while you're small.
Your data
The cheapest tool becomes the most expensive one if you can't get your data out in a usable form. Before you commit, export a test file and check that notes, activity history, dates and the source on every lead come with it.
Spreadsheet, free CRM, investor CRM or Salesforce: which fits when?
These are rules of thumb from the teams I've worked with, not laws. Your volume and number of people matter more than any label.
Setup | Fits when | Where it strains
Spreadsheet | One person, low lead volume, you are still proving a lead source | Second person, duplicate sellers, no reminders, no history, no opt-out control
Free tier of a general CRM | One to three people, a few hundred contacts, simple follow-up | List uploads, wholesaling stages, call and text logging, source reporting
Investor CRM (paid) | You want dialer, skip tracing, texting and wholesaling stages in one login and you don't want to build anything | Unusual processes, deep reporting, control over how it all fits together
Salesforce | A team of about 10 or more, several lead sources, your own process and reporting, and someone responsible for it | You need to build it, and someone has to look after it
Don't read this as "everyone should end up on Salesforce". Plenty of teams do well on an investor CRM for years. The honest comparison, with the trade-offs, is in the 11 CRMs for wholesalers compared and Salesforce vs investor CRMs .
What are the signs you've outgrown free?
A seller has been called twice by two different people this month.
You can't say which lead source produced last quarter's contracts without an hour of digging.
Follow-up depends on someone's calendar or memory, and leads go quiet when that person is busy.
You cap or avoid uploading a list because of the record limit.
A VA or cold caller needs access, and you can't limit what they see or export.
A seller who opted out got another text.
You're paying for three small tools that don't share data, and you spend time copying between them.
Two or three of these and the cost of staying free is already higher than the cost of moving. You can score your own setup in a few minutes with the Deal Leak Score and decide from there. The question "do I need a CRM at all?" has its own page: outgrown the spreadsheet?
How do you leave a free CRM without losing data?
Export everything now , not on the day you cancel: contacts, deals, notes, tasks and any files.
Write a field map. For each old field, name the new one, and note anything that has no home. The CRM switch field map is a starting point.
Keep the old record's ID or a unique key in a field in the new system, so you can trace anything back.
Move the open pipeline first , not the entire archive, and bring history in after.
Run both for a short, planned overlap , with one clear rule about where new leads go.
If you're weighing a move to Salesforce specifically, how I handle a move covers the plan, and the edition picker narrows the options.
Questions
Is there a free CRM for real estate wholesalers?
There are free tiers of general CRMs and there are spreadsheets, but I'm not aware of a free CRM built around wholesaling stages, dialer and texting. A free setup works for one person with low volume. It strains when a second person joins, when you upload large lists, or when you need follow-up automation and source reporting.
What is the best free CRM for real estate investors?
It depends on volume and people. A spreadsheet suits a solo investor proving a lead source. A free tier of a general CRM suits one to three people with simple follow-up. Check six limits first: users, records, automation, call and text logging, reporting by source, and data export.
Can I use HubSpot's free CRM for wholesaling?
You can, and it can work for a small team. As of the vendor page I checked in October 2026, the free CRM allows up to 2 users and 1,000 contacts with limited automation, and you'd build wholesaling stages, fields and reports yourself. Check HubSpot's current limits before you build on it.
Is Google Sheets enough as a wholesaling CRM?
For one person and a modest number of leads, yes. It has no reminders unless you build them, can't stop duplicate sellers, doesn't log calls or texts, and can't enforce opt-outs. The seller lead tracker on this site shows a setup that goes about as far as a sheet can.
What does a free CRM cost you in the end?
Your time and your leads. Time goes into building fields, stages and reports a wholesaling tool would include. Leads go missing when follow-up depends on memory. The cost shows up as slower response and no clear view of which marketing paid off.
Is there a cheap CRM for wholesalers?
Yes, several paid investor CRMs and general CRMs are inexpensive per user. Compare the total, including extra users, dialer minutes, skip tracing and texting, not just the seat price. The 11-option comparison on this site lays out what each includes.
When should a wholesaler move from a free CRM to Salesforce?
Usually around the point you have several people working leads, more than one lead source, and a process of your own that you want reported on, often a team of about 10 or more. Before that, an investor CRM or a free tier is often the better fit.

## Google Ads Offline Conversions from Salesforce for Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/google-ads-offline-conversions-salesforce.html

Send your Salesforce deals back to Google Ads. Offline conversions for investor PPC
If your Google Ads account counts a form fill as a conversion, Google is learning to find people who fill in forms. Some of them are motivated sellers. Many are retail sellers who want full price, agents, renters and spam. The answer to which clicks turned into contracts lives in Salesforce, and Google never sees it. This page is for owners and marketing leads at home-buying and wholesaling companies who spend real money on PPC and want Google to bid for deals, not leads.
Store the Google click ID (GCLID) on every lead that comes from an ad, copy it to the deal when the lead converts, and connect Salesforce to Google Ads through Data manager, which replaced the legacy Salesforce integration Google stopped supporting on May 31, 2025. Send the stages that mean money, such as a qualified appointment, a signed contract and a closed deal with its fee, and bid on the one you have enough of. Add enhanced conversions for leads so matching doesn't rest on the click ID alone, and make sure your calls carry the click too.
Why are form fills the wrong thing to optimize for?
Google's automated bidding learns from whatever you tell it is a conversion. Tell it a form fill is a conversion and it gets very good at finding people who fill in forms. Your cost per lead looks great in Google Ads while your cost per contract in Salesforce keeps climbing, and nobody can say which campaigns, keywords or search terms produce the sellers who actually sign.
Investor PPC has a long funnel with a lot of loss at every step: lead, contact, appointment, offer, contract, closed. Only your CRM knows how far each click got. Offline conversion import is the bridge. Salesforce tells Google which clicks became appointments, contracts and closed deals, and Google bids toward more of those instead of more forms.
It also changes what you can see. With imports running, Google Ads can show cost per appointment and cost per contract by campaign and search term, next to the numbers you already watch in Salesforce. The two will never match to the dollar, but they stop telling different stories.
What changed in 2025 and 2026?
A lot of setup guides online still describe Google's old Salesforce integration and its "milestones". That integration is gone. Here's what changed, from Google's own help pages:
When | What changed | What it means for you
May 31, 2025 | Google ended support for the legacy Salesforce integration. Salesforce connections now live in Data manager. | If someone set this up before 2025, check that every conversion action still gets data under Data manager.
Since the move | Each connection is linked to exactly one Salesforce object, either Lead or Opportunity. | A lead status and a deal stage are two connections and two conversion actions, not one.
From June 15, 2026 | Google began moving offline conversion and enhanced conversions for leads uploads from the Google Ads API to its Data Manager API, and blocking them on the old path. | If a developer or a tool built a custom upload, ask whether it moved.
Google also recommends enhanced conversions for leads over the older click-ID-only import. It adds hashed contact details from your form, so a conversion can still be matched when a click ID is missing. Google says to keep sending the GCLID whenever you have it, and that it's required if you don't collect contact details with the Google tag.
Which Salesforce stages should you send?
Map your funnel to a few conversion actions, then decide which one Google bids on. In Google Ads, primary conversion actions drive bidding and show in the Conversions column. Secondary ones are for observation only, so you can watch contracts and closed deals without letting a thin number steer the budget.
Stage in Salesforce | Send it? | Why
New lead (form or call) | Usually no; your website tag already counts it | Importing it again counts the same lead twice
Qualified lead: a real owner, a property in your buy box, some reason to sell | Yes | Google's own advice is to pick a qualified or converted lead as the goal
Appointment set or held | Yes, often the primary | Close enough to money, and frequent enough for bidding to learn from
Offer made | Optional | Useful to watch, but it depends on your reps as much as on the lead
Contract signed | Yes | The strongest signal most teams have enough of; primary once volume allows
Closed, with the fee or profit | Yes, as secondary | The truth, but it arrives late and in small numbers
Volume is the catch. A team signing a handful of contracts a month gives Google very little to learn from, while appointments happen several times as often. For most investor teams I'd make the qualified appointment the primary conversion, send contracts and closed deals as secondary, and switch the primary to contracts once there are enough of them to steer by.
Timing matters too. Google only accepts click-based conversions within 90 days of the click. A seller who clicks in March and signs in August won't import. That's fine; it's one more reason the earlier stages carry the bidding.
How do you set it up?
Turn on auto-tagging in Google Ads. It adds a GCLID to the landing page address on every ad click. Without it there's nothing to send back.
Capture the GCLID on your site. Google publishes a short script that reads the GCLID from the address, stores it for 90 days and fills a hidden field on your forms. Put it on every page of the site, because sellers click around before they fill anything in.
Add a GCLID field to Lead and Opportunity in Salesforce. Google's setup page asks for a 255-character text field on both, read-only for users, with the lead field mapped to the opportunity field so the value survives lead conversion.
Turn on field history tracking for Lead Status and Opportunity Stage. Google reads the time of the status or stage change from that history and uses it as the conversion time.
Test every form. Submit a test lead with ?gclid=test on the end of the page address, check that the value lands on the lead, convert it, and check it on the opportunity. Then do the same for every other form and landing page.
Connect Salesforce in Google Ads. Create a conversion action that imports from a CRM, choose Salesforce, sign in, pick the object (Lead or Opportunity), set the condition (for example, Stage changes to Contract Signed) and map the GCLID. For enhanced conversions for leads, also map email and phone; Google prefers email and needs at least one of the two.
Use a dedicated integration user with only the access the connection needs. Not the owner's login, and not a rep who might leave. When that user is deactivated, the imports stop.
Set a daily schedule and give it a day. Google says a new conversion action needs 4 to 6 hours before uploads, conversions can take up to 24 hours to show, and the first run only looks back 14 days.
One limit catches investor orgs more than any other: Google's Salesforce connector reads Leads and Opportunities. If your deals live on a custom object, such as a Property or Deal record, the connector can't see them. You can track the stages you need on an opportunity linked to that record, or send conversions through a file or another tool. Decide this before you build, not after.
What about phone calls?
A lot of motivated sellers call instead of filling in a form, so a setup that only handles forms misses some of your best leads. There are three kinds of calls to think about:
Calls straight from the ad , through a call asset or call-only ad with a Google forwarding number. Google already knows about the call. To tell it what happened next, its phone call import matches on the caller's number and the call start time, so your phone system needs to log both on the Salesforce record.
Calls from your website after an ad click. These only tie back to the click if your call tracking swaps numbers per visitor (dynamic number insertion with a number pool). Check whether your call tracking writes the click ID or the campaign onto the lead it creates in Salesforce, or sends the conversion to Google itself. Pick one path. Doing both counts the same seller twice.
Calls from a mailer number , even when the seller found you by searching your name. That isn't an ad click, and forcing it into Google Ads makes the numbers worse, not better.
Whichever way calls come in, the lead your phone system creates in Salesforce has to carry its source and, where there is one, the click ID. If it doesn't, the import quietly skips every seller who called. More on getting calls onto the right record in dialers in Salesforce .
Should you send a value with each conversion?
Yes, if you can do it consistently. A value lets Google bid toward money instead of a count, which matters when one campaign brings in assignment-fee deals and another brings in properties you keep.
Closed deals: the fee or profit, from the same field your ROI reports use. Gross on some deals and net on others makes the value useless.
Contracts and appointments: a fixed estimate, such as your average fee times the share of contracts that close. Revisit it every quarter.
Leads: Google's upgrade notes say expected revenue carries over for opportunities but isn't supported for leads, so set the value on the conversion action instead.
If you don't map a value, Google uses the conversion action's default. That's a reasonable start while you get the basics working.
What usually goes wrong
The GCLID is only on one form. The landing page has it; the contact page, the chat widget and the second landing page don't.
It doesn't survive conversion. The lead has a GCLID, the opportunity doesn't, so every contract arrives with nothing to match.
Stages get skipped. A rep moves a deal from New straight to Contract, so the appointment conversion never fires. A date field such as "appointment held on", set by a Flow whenever a deal passes that point, is a safer trigger than the stage itself.
A status gets renamed. Someone tidies the picklist, the condition no longer matches, and imports drop to zero without an error anyone sees.
The connection belongs to someone who left. Google says a failed event isn't retried automatically, so days can go missing for good. The admin handover plan covers the logins that should never belong to one person.
Two primary conversions count the same thing. A tag-based form conversion and an imported "new lead" both drive bidding, and Google thinks every lead is two.
Bidding on closed deals too early. Small numbers make the bidding jumpy. Watch them as secondary first.
How do you know it's working?
Once a week, compare counts. Appointments imported to Google Ads against a Salesforce report of appointments from leads with a GCLID, for the same week. They won't match exactly, because of the 90-day window and Google's own attribution, but they should be close.
Watch for blanks. A Salesforce report of PPC form leads with an empty GCLID should be close to empty. If it isn't, a form or a landing page isn't capturing it.
Check the schedule. Look at the last run in Data manager every week. Failed runs don't fix themselves.
Judge spend in Salesforce. Google Ads will show conversions, but the budget decision belongs on cost per contract and profit by campaign from your CRM, using the original source. See which campaign gets credit and the cost per deal calculator .
In the org I run, PPC sits in the same campaign ROI reports as TV, mail and every other source: appointments, contracts and booked revenue by campaign and market, checked against the books. Offline conversion import doesn't replace that. It gives Google the same answer your reports already give you.
Questions
Can Google Ads import conversions from Salesforce?
Yes. Google Ads connects to Salesforce through Data manager and imports conversions when a lead status or opportunity stage changes, matched by the Google click ID (GCLID) and, with enhanced conversions for leads, by hashed email or phone.
Is the Google Ads Salesforce integration still available?
The legacy integration isn't. Google ended support for it on May 31, 2025, and Salesforce connections now run through Data manager, with each connection linked to one object, either Lead or Opportunity.
Where do I store the GCLID in Salesforce?
In a 255-character text field on both Lead and Opportunity, read-only for users, with the lead field mapped to the opportunity field so the value carries over when the lead converts. Your website fills it through a hidden form field.
Do I still need the GCLID with enhanced conversions for leads?
Google says to include GCLIDs whenever you can, and that they're required if you don't use the Google tag to collect contact details from your forms. Enhanced conversions add hashed email or phone so more conversions can be matched.
Which conversion should a real estate investor bid on?
For most teams, a qualified appointment, because it's close to money and happens often enough for bidding to learn. Send contracts and closed deals too, as secondary conversions, and make contracts the primary goal once you have enough of them.
Can Google Ads import conversions from a Salesforce custom object?
Google's Salesforce connector works with Leads and Opportunities. If your deals live on a custom object, track the stages you want on a linked opportunity, or send conversions through a file upload or another tool.
How long after a click can I import a conversion?
Google accepts click-based conversions within 90 days of the click. Its Salesforce connection also only looks back 14 days on the first run, so older conversions from before the setup won't come in.
How do I track Google Ads phone calls in Salesforce?
Calls from call assets with a Google forwarding number can be imported with the caller's number and call start time. Calls from your website need call tracking that swaps numbers per visitor, so the call can be tied to the click. Either way, the Salesforce lead has to carry the source.

## How to Choose a Salesforce Consultant for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/hire-salesforce-consultant-real-estate.html

Choosing a Salesforce consultant for an investor team, and what it should cost
This is for owners and ops leads about to hire someone to build, fix or move their Salesforce. I'm one of the people you might hire, so read it with that in mind. I've tried to write what I'd tell a friend who runs a home-buying company: how to tell the good ones from the expensive ones, what the market charges in 2026, and what you should never sign away.
Pick someone who has worked inside a home-buying or wholesaling pipeline, start with a small fixed-price piece of work before any big build, and make sure you keep the org, admin access and the documentation. Compare quotes by what's included, not the hourly rate. In 2026, freelancers commonly charge $50 to $150 an hour and US partner firms $100 to $250, and small-business implementations often land between $10,000 and $30,000.
What kind of help do you actually need?
Most bad consulting projects start with the wrong kind of help. Work out which of these you're buying before you talk to anyone:
Your situation | What you're buying | Usual shape
You're on Salesforce, it mostly works, but leads slip and the numbers feel wrong | A review and targeted fixes | A fixed-price audit, then a short list of fixes
You're on Podio, REsimpli, GoHighLevel or spreadsheets and outgrowing it | A move to Salesforce | A scoped project with phases and a switch-over plan
Someone built your org, left, and nobody knows how it works | A handover and clean-up | Documentation first, then fixes, often followed by a retainer
You have a steady stream of changes and no admin | Ongoing admin and development | A monthly retainer
One specific job: dialer sync, accounting, a dashboard | A specialist for one project | Fixed scope, fixed price
If you can't tell which row you're in, that's normal, and it's what a free first call is for. Any consultant worth hiring should be able to tell you in 30 minutes which row fits, including when the answer is "you don't need me yet".
Freelancer, partner firm or offshore team?
All three can work. They fail in different ways, so pick the failure you can live with.
 | Independent consultant | Salesforce partner firm | Offshore development team
Who does the work | The person you talked to | Often a team, sometimes junior staff after a senior sale | A team working from your written specs
Knows real estate investing | Varies a lot; ask for specifics | Rarely, unless they focus on it | Rarely
Strength | Direct, fast decisions, one person who knows your org | Bench depth, process, can cover big projects | Low hourly rate for well-defined work
Main risk | One person; ask what happens when they're sick or busy | Cost, and the people who sold the project aren't the ones building it | You end up writing the specs and testing everything yourself
Best for | Teams of 10 to 50 who want someone who understands the business | Large, multi-department builds | Teams that already have a strong admin to direct the work
If you're on an investor CRM built on Salesforce, the vendor's own services team knows their package best. Ask them whether they'll build things outside the package, how changes are priced, and who supports custom work after it's live.
What does a Salesforce consultant cost in 2026?
Rates vary a lot by region and experience. Codleo, a Salesforce consultancy, published these ranges in October 2026. Use them as a rough guide:
What | Typical 2026 range
Freelance consultant | $50 to $150 an hour
Certified US partner firm | $100 to $250 an hour
Offshore team | $40 to $80 an hour
Small-business implementation | $10,000 to $30,000
Org health check or audit | $5,000 to $20,000
Managed support (retainer) | $2,500 to $15,000+ a month
Two things the rate card hides. First, hours spent learning your business are hours you pay for, so a cheaper consultant who has never seen a wholesaling pipeline can cost more in the end. Second, the cheapest quote is often the one with the vaguest scope, and vague scope is where projects drag.
Salesforce licenses are a separate cost, paid to Salesforce. I don't quote list prices here because they change and they're negotiable. Teams can often get a discount through their Salesforce account executive, depending on the business and the number of users, so ask before you sign.
For what it's worth, here's what I charge. The CRM Revenue Audit is a fixed USD 1,500 for teams already on Salesforce, and the full fee comes off a build if you go ahead within 30 days. Builds and moves are quoted as projects once the scope is written down. Ongoing support is a monthly retainer with no long-term contract.
Eleven questions to ask any Salesforce consultant
Have you worked inside a home-buying or wholesaling company's Salesforce? What did you build? Listen for specifics: missed-call handling, lead source by marketing number, offers and contract dates, buyer lists. "We've done lots of real estate" usually means brokerages, which is a different business.
Who will actually do the work? Get names. If it's a firm, ask to meet the person building it.
What would you look at first in our org? Good answers start with how leads come in and where the money goes, not with a list of features.
How do you test changes before they reach my team? You want to hear "sandbox" and "we test with real scenarios before release".
What's the smallest paid piece of work we can start with? A consultant who only takes big projects is a risk for a team your size.
How do you handle changes to the scope? Changes are normal. Surprise invoices aren't. Get the process in writing.
Who owns what you build? The answer should be "you do", including documentation.
What happens if something you built breaks after go-live? Ask how long they support their own work and what it costs.
How will you train my team? Acquisitions reps, transaction coordinators and the owner use Salesforce differently. One generic training session isn't training.
When would you tell us we don't need you? If they can't name a case, they'll sell you something either way.
What hours do you overlap with us? Seller leads come in during your business day. So do the problems.
Red flags
Quotes a full rebuild before looking at your org.
Can't explain what they'll do without jargon.
No written scope, or a scope that lists features instead of outcomes for your team.
Wants to be the only person with admin access.
Pushes a long contract before you've seen any work.
Answers every problem with an app you have to buy.
Talks about what Salesforce can do but never asks how a lead moves through your business.
Why you should start small
The best test of a consultant is a small, fixed-price piece of work with a clear deliverable. You find out how they think, how they communicate, whether they finish things and whether your team likes working with them, for a fraction of the cost of finding out halfway through a build.
A good first project ends with something you can use even if you never hire them again:
A written list of what's broken or leaking, with what each one is likely costing you.
A plan in order of impact, so you know what to fix first.
A couple of quick fixes done, so you can judge the quality of their work.
That's how I built my own audit, but the advice holds whoever you hire.
What you should always own
Whoever you hire, keep these in your company's hands from day one:
The Salesforce contract, in your company's name
System Administrator access for at least two people on your side
Integrations running under a dedicated integration user, not the consultant's login
Documentation of every automation and change, delivered as you go, not at the end
Everything built in your org in a form your next admin can open and edit
Passwords for your dialer, texting and other tools, held by you
If a consultant leaves and you can't run your org without them, you didn't hire a consultant, you hired a dependency. My admin handover plan shows what it takes to untangle that after the fact.
How to judge me
Hold me to the same list. I'm in Cairo and I work US business hours. I've spent two years running the Salesforce for a two-market home-buying company in Ohio: missed-call alerts on every marketing number, shared lead queues, follow-up that stops when a seller replies, campaign ROI checked against the books and a board for every file under contract. I do the work myself. The first paid step is a fixed-price audit for teams already on Salesforce, with a full refund if it doesn't find at least five fixable issues worth more than the fee. If you're on another CRM, the first step is a scoping call for a move to Salesforce instead.
And if a free call shows you don't need me yet, I'll say so.
Questions
How much does a Salesforce consultant cost in 2026?
Freelance Salesforce consultants commonly charge $50 to $150 an hour, US partner firms $100 to $250, and offshore teams $40 to $80, based on ranges Codleo published in October 2026. Small-business implementations often cost $10,000 to $30,000, and managed support runs from about $2,500 a month.
Should I hire a Salesforce partner firm or an independent consultant?
For a 10 to 50 person investor team, an independent consultant who knows real estate investing is often the better fit: one person who learns your business and does the work. Partner firms make more sense for large, multi-department builds that need a team.
How much does a Salesforce implementation cost for a small real estate investment company?
Small-business Salesforce implementations commonly land between $10,000 and $30,000, plus Salesforce licenses. The range depends on how many integrations you need (dialer, texting, accounting), how much data you're moving and how much automation you want on day one.
How long does a Salesforce implementation take?
Small, well-scoped builds take weeks. A move from Podio or another CRM usually runs in phases over one to three months, with both systems running side by side for a short time so no leads are lost. A written scope is what keeps it on schedule.
What should be in a Salesforce consulting scope of work?
The outcomes for your team (for example, every missed call gets a callback task), what's included and excluded, who does the work, how changes to scope are priced, testing and training, support after go-live, and who owns the work and documentation.
Do we need a consultant if we're on an investor CRM built on Salesforce?
Sometimes. The vendor supports their package. Custom automations, reports, integrations and clean-up beyond the package usually fall to you, and that's where a consultant or admin comes in. Ask the vendor in writing what they support.
Can a consultant work alongside our existing admin?
Yes, and it's often the best setup. The admin keeps day-to-day changes moving and the consultant handles a build, a migration or a second opinion. Agree on who approves changes so you don't get two people editing the same automation.

The investor CRM audit checklist: 60 checks you can run yourself
This is for owners and ops leads at home-buying and wholesaling companies who want to know how well their CRM actually runs the business. It works for any CRM: Salesforce, Podio, REsimpli, GoHighLevel or an investor CRM. The checks follow a deal from the marketing that paid for it to the closing that paid you back, plus the health of the system underneath.
Answer each check yes or no for how things work today. Start with the sections closest to the money: whether every seller gets answered and followed up, and whether every deal traces back to the campaign that paid for it. Then fix your three most expensive no's first and check again in a month.
How to use it
Go through it with whoever runs your CRM, and answer each line yes or no about how things work today, not how they're supposed to work. If you're not sure, it's a no. Tick the yeses; your score updates as you go.
Don't worry much about the total. Look at which sections have the most no's, and start with the ones closest to the money: Answer, then Follow-up, then Spend.
Your score: 0 of 60 Nothing is saved or sent anywhere. Refreshing the page clears it.

1. Every new lead gets a source and campaign automatically, without a rep picking it

## The Kept-Deal Map: 5 Places Wholesaling Deals Leak
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/kept-deal-map.html

The Kept-Deal Map: find where your deals leak.
Most investors don't have a lead problem, they have a leak problem. Money disappears between the marketing dollar and the kept deal, at five points a CRM can measure if it's set up to. This map names the five leak points, what each looks like, what a system that closes it does, and the free tool to measure it from your own numbers.
Tap Yes or No on each leak point below. Nothing is sent anywhere.
Want the detailed version? Take the 10-point Deal Leak Score and compare answers with your team.
1. Spend
Which campaigns produce kept deals, not just leads?
How the leak looks
Leads are counted by source, but contracts and closings are not tied back to the campaign that paid for them. Cost per lead looks fine while cost per deal is unknown.
What a system that closes it does
Lead source is a required field that carries from lead to contract to closing. A report shows spend, leads, appointments, contracts and closed deals by campaign and market.
Measure it
Cost per deal calculator
2. Answer
How many seller calls go unanswered, and what does that cost?
How the leak looks
Calls to marketing numbers roll to voicemail after hours or when reps are busy, and nobody sees the list. A seller calling several investors usually talks to whoever answers first.
What a system that closes it does
Every missed call to a marketing number creates a callback task on the lead with a due time minutes out, assigned to the next available rep, plus a report of missed calls and time to callback.
Measure it
Missed seller call cost calculator
3. Follow-up
How fast does the team act once a seller is engaged, and does anyone fall through?
How the leak looks
Follow-up lives in reps' heads, phones and sticky notes. Leads with no next task quietly die, and nobody can say how long a new lead waited for a first touch.
What a system that closes it does
No open lead without a next task. Time to first touch and time from contract to first seller call are measured, and stalled leads surface automatically in a shared queue.
Measure it
Deal Leak Score
4. Offer
Is every offer made from the same disciplined numbers?
How the leak looks
Each rep underwrites differently, in a spreadsheet nobody else sees. Offers go out above the real maximum, and the spread disappears after the contract is signed.
What a system that closes it does
Underwriting sits on the deal record: ARV, repairs, rule percentage and fee as fields, MAO as a formula, and a required review step before an offer goes out.
Measure it
Deal analyzer (MAO)
5. Keep
Does your ROI count only the deals that actually closed?
How the leak looks
Revenue is reported when a contract is signed. Cancelled contracts and reduced fees never come back out of the numbers, so campaigns look more profitable than they are.
What a system that closes it does
Booked revenue and closed revenue are separate fields. ROI by campaign is calculated on kept deals only, and fall-outs are tracked with a reason.
Measure it
The Monday 5
Watch the series
Six short videos, one leak each, with a "steal this" fix you can set up in any CRM. Example numbers are labeled as examples.
1. The 5 leaks
2. Missed seller calls
3. Leads with no next step
4. Offers off-formula
5. Fall-outs in your ROI
6. The Monday 5
All Deal Leak videos, with the free tool for each
Questions
What is Deal Leak?
Deal Leak is the profit a home-buying or wholesaling business loses between paying for a seller lead and keeping a closed deal: the unanswered call, the lead with no next step, the offer made off-formula, and the contract that falls out but still sits in the ROI numbers. It is usually unmeasured, which is why it keeps happening.
What is a kept deal?
A deal that actually closed and paid, at the fee or profit that was actually received. ROI on kept deals leaves out contracts that cancelled or were renegotiated, so it shows what each campaign really returned.
Is speed to lead really that important?
The best-known study (InsideSales.com with MIT's Dr. James Oldroyd, 2007, about 15,000 web leads across six companies, not real estate) found that calling within 5 minutes instead of 30 gave roughly 100x higher odds of making contact and 21x higher odds of qualifying the lead. A Harvard Business Review study (2011) found firms that responded within an hour were about 7x more likely to qualify the lead. No comparable study exists yet for real estate investors.
Do I need Salesforce to close these leaks?
No. Any CRM can close most of them if lead source carries through to closing, every lead has a next task, underwriting lives on the deal, and ROI is calculated on kept deals. Salesforce makes sense when you run several markets, teams or channels and have outgrown simpler investor CRMs.
What does the CRM Revenue Audit do with this map?
The audit (USD 1,500, fixed price) goes through your CRM and phone data leak point by leak point, sizes each leak from your own numbers, and gives you a prioritized fix list. You can implement it yourself or with me.
