## Lead, Opportunity or Property? Sellers in Salesforce
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/lead-vs-opportunity-salesforce-real-estate.html

Lead, Opportunity or Property: how to model a seller and a deal in Salesforce
Salesforce was built around a sales story that doesn't quite fit a home-buying company: a company becomes a prospect, a prospect becomes an account, and a deal belongs to that account. Your story is different. A person calls about a house, one person can own several houses, one house can have several owners (heirs, ex-spouses), and a seller who said no in March can come back in September with a new number. How you model that on day one decides what your reports can say two years later. This guide is for ops leads and owners on Salesforce, or about to be: what each standard object should mean, when to convert, what conversion carries across, and when a custom Property object earns its place.
Use the Lead for the inquiry (an unqualified person asking about a property), the Contact for the seller as a person, the Opportunity for a deal on one property, and a custom Property object when a person can have several houses or a house can have several owners. Convert a lead when there is a real deal to track, usually at the appointment, not at first touch and not at the offer. Treat a returning seller as a new opportunity on the existing contact, not a new lead, and remember duplicate rules don't run on conversion unless you turn that on.
Why does the data model matter so much?
Because every report you'll ever want is a question about the model. "How many deals did this mailer produce?" needs the source to survive from inquiry to closing. "What is our offer-to-contract rate?" needs offers to be records, not notes. "How many houses has this seller sold us?" needs the seller to be a person who outlives a single deal. If the model is wrong, you can still get answers, but only by exporting to a spreadsheet and fixing it by hand every month. That's the usual reason a Salesforce dashboard disagrees with the bank account, and it's the cause behind several items in ten reasons your numbers are off .
What should each Salesforce object mean for a home-buying team?
Object | Should mean | Example
Lead | An inquiry that hasn't become a real deal yet | A mailer response with an address, a phone and a source
Contact (and Account) | The seller as a person, kept for good | The owner who sold you one house and may sell another
Opportunity | One deal on one property, with stages, offer, contract and result | "123 Main St, offer made, MAO set, closing date"
Property (custom object) | The house itself, independent of any one seller or deal | Parcel number, address, condition, every deal and owner linked to it
Campaign | A marketing effort with a cost, a market and a list or wave | "Probate mailer, Franklin County, November"
Keep the Opportunity as the thing your pipeline report counts. When it is, "deals in stage" and "cost per contract" are simple reports instead of projects.
When should you convert a lead?
Convert when there is a real deal worth tracking, which for most teams is the moment an appointment is set. The reasoning:
Too early (at first contact) and your opportunity list fills with people who never answer again. Pipeline reports inflate and the forecast gets noisy.
Too late (at the offer or contract) and reps work seller conversations on the Lead with no stage rules, and the time between "appointment" and "offer" can't be measured.
Never (everything stays on the Lead) is a real option for some small teams, and it works until you want reports on deals rather than on leads.
The early steps (New lead, Contacted, Nurture) live on the Lead, and the deal steps live on the Opportunity. The stage rules for each are in wholesaling pipeline stages .
What does conversion carry over, and what does it leave behind?
When you convert a lead, Salesforce creates an account and a contact, and optionally an opportunity, and moves the lead's related items across. According to Salesforce's help documentation, open activities, activity history and files carry over to the resulting records, and the new notes go to the account, contact or person account but not to the opportunity. A few things to plan for:
Field mapping isn't automatic for custom fields. If you add "motivation", "property address" or "lead source detail" on the Lead, map each one to the matching Contact or Opportunity field, or the data stays on a converted lead nobody opens again.
Duplicate rules don't run on conversion unless the "Use Apex Lead Convert" setting is on, so convert only after you've checked for an existing contact. See duplicate seller leads .
Notes on the Opportunity are not carried. If the seller's story lives in notes on the Lead, copy the key facts into fields before you convert, or the deal record starts out blank.
A converted lead can't be turned back. Test your conversion on a handful of records in a sandbox before using it on live data.
Person accounts change the rules. With person accounts enabled, Lightning converts leads with no value in Company to person accounts and leads with a Company to business accounts. Treat enabling person accounts as a one-way door and read Salesforce's documentation first.
Which of three patterns fits your team?
Pattern A: Lead, then Contact and Opportunity at the appointment
The standard approach. Good for most teams where one seller means one or two deals. Cheap to build and everything native works.
Pattern B: A, plus a custom Property object
Add a Property record (address, parcel, condition, county) that Opportunities and Contacts link to. Choose it when a seller has several houses, when heirs or co-owners each talk to you about the same house, or when you want repeat deals on the same property to show as one history. This is the pattern I'd lean toward past about 10 people, because property history is where a lot of your real knowledge lives.
Pattern C: Opportunity first
Skip the Lead for inquiries and create an Opportunity on first contact. This can suit a very small team that only wants one list, but it mixes "unreachable" with "real deal" in your pipeline numbers, so you'll need a clear early stage that reports exclude.
What happens when a seller comes back?
This is where the model proves itself. A returning seller should:
match their existing Contact on phone, email or property,
get a new Opportunity under that Contact (or on the same Property) instead of a brand-new Lead,
carry the original lead source and the new one, so attribution isn't overwritten, and
notify the original owner.
This is the routing logic in lead and call routing and the attribution question in which campaign gets credit .
What should you check before you convert?
No existing contact or open opportunity for this phone, email or address.
The must-have fields from the Contacted stage are filled in.
Lead source and campaign are set, and will map across.
Consent and opt-out flags are correct and will carry to the contact.
Key facts from notes are copied into fields.
An owner is assigned for the opportunity, and a next step is dated.
Put these in a screen flow or a validation rule instead of a document, so reps can't skip them under pressure. And if you'd like someone to review your setup against these questions, that's what the CRM Revenue Audit does.
Questions
How do I track leads in Salesforce as a real estate investor?
Record every inquiry as a Lead with a source and campaign, assign an owner, log calls and tasks against it, and report on leads by source and status. Convert to a contact and opportunity when there is a real deal, so the pipeline report counts deals instead of inquiries.
Should I convert every lead in Salesforce?
No. Convert when there is a real deal to track, usually when an appointment is set. Converting every lead floods your opportunity reports with people who never answered, and it makes the forecast unreliable.
What happens to my notes and activity when I convert a lead?
According to Salesforce Help, open activities, activity history and files carry over to the resulting records. New notes go to the account, contact or person account but not the opportunity, so copy key facts into fields before converting.
Can you undo a lead conversion in Salesforce?
A converted lead can't be turned back into a lead. Test conversion on a few records in a sandbox, and set the required checks before the Convert button is used on live data.
How do I find converted leads in Salesforce?
Run a report on leads with converted lead information, which shows the lead alongside the account, contact and opportunity it became. Filter by converted date to see the conversions for a month.
How should I handle a seller with two properties in Salesforce?
One Contact for the person, one Opportunity per property or deal. If this happens often, add a custom Property object so each house has its own history and can be linked to its owners and deals.
Do duplicate rules run when a lead is converted?
Not unless the "Use Apex Lead Convert" setting is on. Check for an existing contact or open opportunity before converting, ideally with a flow or screen that does it for the rep.
Should I enable person accounts for sellers?
Think carefully. Person accounts let sellers exist as individuals without a company, but enabling them changes how conversion and some features behave and is treated as a one-way change. Ask your admin to review Salesforce's person accounts documentation first.

Sources
Checked in October 2026. Salesforce and vendor features change with each release, so check the linked page before you rely on a detail.
Salesforce Help: Considerations for Converting Leads . What carries over on conversion; person accounts and the Company field; notes
Salesforce Help: Things to know about duplicate rules . Duplicate rules and lead conversion

## Missed-Call Alerts in Salesforce for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/missed-call-alerts-salesforce.html

Missed-call alerts in Salesforce: turn every missed seller call into a callback
A seller calls one of your marketing numbers, nobody picks up, and the seller hangs up. Almost nobody leaves a voicemail: in Invoca's 2021 data, only 2% of unanswered callers did. So unless something tells a rep right away, that paid lead is gone, and the next investor on the seller's list gets the deal. This guide is for ops leads and acquisitions managers on Salesforce: what has to be in place first, how the automation works, who should get the alert, and how to know it's working.
First, your phone system has to write every call to Salesforce, missed ones included, with the direction, the result and the number that was called. Then a record-triggered Flow on that call creates a callback task for the lead's owner, or a queue if there's no owner, sends an alert to the rep and a Slack channel, and escalates to a manager if the callback isn't logged in time. Measure missed calls without a callback every day.
What has to be in place first?
A missed-call alert is only as good as the data under it. Before you build anything, check three things:
Missed calls reach Salesforce. Most phone systems investor teams use connect to Salesforce, but some only log calls that were answered. Make a test call, let it ring out, and see whether a call record shows up on the lead, with a direction (inbound) and a result (missed or no answer).
The call lands on the right seller. The integration should match the caller's number to an existing lead or contact. If the caller is new, something has to create a lead, or the missed call has nowhere to live.
The number they called is captured. That's what tells you the source and market. Each marketing number should map to one campaign. See lead sources in Salesforce .
If any of those fail, fix the integration first. More on that side in dialers in Salesforce and the RingCentral integration guide .
In the org I run, calls create leads and every marketing number sends a missed-call alert to Slack. Everything below assumes the same starting point.
How the automation works
One record-triggered Flow does most of the work. In plain words:
Step | What happens
1. Trigger | A call activity is created where the direction is inbound and the result is missed or no answer.
2. Find the seller | Use the lead or contact the call is linked to. If there isn't one, create a lead with the source and market of the number that was called.
3. Check for an open callback | If the seller already has an open callback task, update it instead of creating another one. Sellers often call two or three times in a row.
4. Create the callback task | Assigned to the lead's owner, due within your time limit, with the number they called in the subject.
5. Alert | A notification to the owner's phone, and a message to the acquisitions channel in Slack for that market.
6. Stamp the lead | Record the time of the last missed call, so it can be measured and reported.
7. Escalate | A scheduled path checks again after your time limit. If the callback task is still open, it alerts the manager and can move the lead to a shared queue.
Slack alerts from a Flow need Salesforce and Slack connected through Salesforce's Slack app, with the right permission set on the users involved. Without that, a Zap or your phone system's own Slack integration can post the message, but then you have one more thing to monitor.
When a notification turns out to be noisy, ops should be able to switch it off without editing the Flow. I build that with a configuration object , a settings record that turns individual alerts on or off.
Who should get the alert?
The seller's owner , if the seller already has one and that person is working today.
A shared queue and channel , if the seller is new or the owner is out. One channel per market, so people only see calls they can act on.
The manager , only on escalation. If managers get every alert, they stop reading them.
Alert fatigue is real. If the Slack channel gets so busy that people mute it, the alert stops working. Keep the message short (seller name, number called, link to the record) and send it to as few people as can act on it.
What about calls after hours?
A callback task due at 11:40 p.m. is due before anyone sees it, and it makes your speed-to-lead numbers look worse than they are. For calls outside business hours:
Set the callback task due at the start of the next business morning.
Flag the lead as an overnight lead, so the morning team calls those first. The org I run uses an overnight flag for exactly this.
Route it to the morning queue rather than a rep who may not be on shift.
If you work markets in different time zones, use the seller's local time.
Should you send an automatic text back?
A short text after a missed call ("Sorry we missed you, we'll call you right back") can keep a seller from dialing the next investor on their list. A few cautions:
Check your consent and opt-out handling with whoever advises you on TCPA. Not legal advice, but the stakes are real: statutory damages are $500 per violation, up to $1,500 if willful.
Business texting in the US runs through 10DLC registration, which your texting tool handles. Make sure your number is registered before you automate anything.
Stop the text if the seller has opted out on any record.
The text doesn't replace the call. Keep the callback task and the clock.
What usually goes wrong
The integration only logs answered calls , so missed calls never reach Salesforce.
Calls from new numbers create nothing , so the sellers you most want to catch are the ones that slip.
Three calls, three tasks. Without step 3 above, reps get a pile of tasks for one seller and start ignoring them.
Alerts go to someone who left. See the admin handover plan for everything that keeps pointing at a former user.
The Slack channel is muted. Ask the team. Honestly.
Nobody tests it. It worked the day it was built, and then a picklist value changed. A test call once a week catches that. More in monitoring Salesforce automations .
How do you know it's working?
One daily report and one weekly test:
Missed calls yesterday , by number and market, with how many got a callback within your time limit, and how many got none at all. The "none at all" column should be zero.
Time from missed call to callback , by rep, measured from the next business morning for overnight calls.
A test call every week to one of your numbers, left to ring out, to see the task and the alert appear.
To put a dollar figure on what missed calls cost you each month, use the missed call cost calculator . For the research on response times, see my lead response statistics .
Questions
How do I get missed-call alerts in Salesforce?
Make sure your phone system logs missed calls to Salesforce with the direction, result and number called. Then build a record-triggered Flow on those call records that creates a callback task, alerts the owner and a Slack channel, and escalates if the task isn't done in time.
Can Salesforce send missed-call alerts to Slack?
Yes. Flow has Slack actions once Salesforce and Slack are connected through Salesforce's Slack app and users have the right permission set. Teams without that connection often post alerts through a Zap or their phone system's own Slack integration.
Can Salesforce text a missed caller back automatically?
Yes, if your texting tool is connected to Salesforce, a Flow can send a short text after a missed call. Check consent and opt-out handling with whoever advises you on TCPA, make sure your number is 10DLC registered, and keep the callback task too.
What happens if the caller isn't in Salesforce yet?
Something has to create a lead from the call, with the source and market of the number they dialed. If nothing does, the missed call has no record to attach to, and the alert never fires for the sellers you most want to catch.
How do I stop duplicate callback tasks when a seller calls several times?
Before creating a task, have the Flow check whether the seller already has an open callback task. If so, update that task (and its due time) instead of creating a new one.
Why aren't missed calls showing up in Salesforce?
Usually because the phone integration only logs answered calls, the call is logged under a user without access to the record, or the caller's number doesn't match any record. Make a test call, let it ring out and check what gets created.
How fast should a missed seller call be returned?
As fast as you can. In Harvard Business Review's 2011 study, firms that contacted a lead within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify it as firms that waited longer. Set a time limit with your team and escalate when it's missed.

## Missed Seller Call Cost Calculator (Speed to Lead)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/missed-call-cost-calculator.html

What do missed seller calls cost you?
Use your own numbers from your phone system and CRM. The calculator turns unanswered calls into lost deals and lost profit, per month and per year. Nothing you type leaves your browser.
An estimate from your inputs, not a promise. Example numbers are made up for illustration.
How the math works
How is the cost of missed seller calls calculated here?
Missed calls = inbound calls × missed %. Lost leads = missed calls × the share of those callers who never get reached. Lost deals = lost leads × lead-to-contract % × contract-to-close %. Lost profit = lost deals × average profit per deal. Every number comes from your inputs.
What is speed to lead?
The time between a seller reaching out (call, form, text) and a real person on your team responding. A seller who is calling several investors usually talks to whoever answers first.
How do I find my missed-call rate?
From your phone system's call log (RingCentral, CallRail, Aircall and similar): inbound calls to marketing numbers that went to voicemail or were abandoned, divided by all inbound calls in the same period.
What does a missed-call alert look like in a CRM?
When a call to a marketing number is missed, the CRM creates a task on the lead with a due time a few minutes out, assigns it to the next available rep, and alerts them. A report then shows missed calls and how long each took to get a callback.

## The Monday 5: KPIs for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/monday-5-real-estate-kpis.html

The Monday 5: five numbers to see before the week starts.
For teams that buy houses and pay for their own seller marketing. You know what these numbers mean for your business, so this page sticks to the Salesforce side: what each one needs so it's on one dashboard Monday morning, without a spreadsheet.
Cost per appointment, by campaign
What it is
Campaign spend ÷ appointments set from that campaign's leads.
In Salesforce
Actual Cost on each campaign, an Appointment Set Date on the lead, and one report grouped by campaign.
Contracts per campaign
What it is
Signed contracts, counted by the campaign the seller first came from.
In Salesforce
The campaign copied from lead to deal and locked once the contract is signed, so a repeat seller keeps the first source.
Contract to first seller call
What it is
Hours from “under contract” to the first logged call with the seller.
In Salesforce
A Contract Signed Date, a small flow that stamps the first completed call after it, and a list of signed deals with no call yet.
Booked vs. kept profit
What it is
The profit expected when a deal went under contract, next to the profit kept at closing.
In Salesforce
Expected profit locked at signing, kept profit entered at closing, and a fall-out reason on every deal that didn't close.
Campaign ROI, including the houses you keep
What it is
(Kept profit + equity in houses you kept − campaign spend) ÷ campaign spend.
In Salesforce
A “kept” flag and an equity value on the deal (after-repair value minus all-in cost), counted in each campaign's ROI.
Questions
What are the most important KPIs for a real estate wholesaling business?
The Monday 5: cost per appointment by campaign, contracts per campaign, time from contract to first seller call, booked vs. kept profit, and campaign ROI that includes the houses you keep.
Why cost per appointment instead of cost per lead?
Lead counts include wrong numbers, tire-kickers and duplicates. An appointment means a real seller conversation, so cost per appointment is much closer to what a channel actually costs you.
Can I track these without Salesforce?
Yes, in any CRM that keeps lead source on the record from first contact to closing and logs calls with timestamps. The hard part is usually attribution: making sure the source survives from lead to contract to closed deal.
Work out your numbers

## Motivated Seller Lead Scoring in Salesforce (Investor Guide)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/motivated-seller-lead-scoring-salesforce.html

Which sellers should your team call first? Motivated seller lead scoring in Salesforce
When a team gets more leads than it can work, someone decides who gets called first. Usually it's whoever came in last, or whoever the rep likes the sound of. A lead score makes that call the same way every time. This page is for owners and acquisitions managers who want a score their reps trust, built from what actually leads to contracts in their market rather than from a template.
Start with a simple points score on the lead, built from what your reps already ask: why they're selling, how soon, the condition of the property, whether it's vacant, and how the asking price compares with your numbers. Show it as A, B and C bands, not a raw number, and check it against your own closed deals every quarter. Einstein Lead Scoring needs at least 1,000 leads created and 120 converted in 200 days, costs extra on Enterprise Edition, and learns whatever "converted" means in your org, so most investor teams should start with rules.
Why score seller leads at all?
Order matters when you can't call everyone at once. Response time is one of the most studied levers in lead conversion: in Harvard Business Review's 2011 study, firms that reached a lead within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify it ( sources here ). The best leads should get that first hour.
It makes reps consistent. A new rep learns what your team thinks a good lead looks like on day one, instead of after fifty bad calls.
It decides who works what. Your strongest closer gets the A leads, and a VA or a cadence handles the C's.
What should a motivated seller score include?
The things your reps already ask on the first call, recorded as picklists rather than buried in notes:
Reason for selling: behind on payments, inherited or in probate , vacant, tired landlord, major repairs, relocating, or just curious.
Timeline: within 30 days, one to three months, three to six months, no timeline.
Condition: major repairs, some updates, move-in ready.
Occupancy: vacant, tenant, owner lives there.
Price: the seller's asking price against your maximum offer. See the deal analyzer .
Decision makers: whether everyone on title is on board.
Engagement: whether they called you, answered, or replied to a text.
Score the property and the situation, never the person. Leave out race, color, national origin, religion, sex, familial status and disability, the characteristics the Fair Housing Act protects, and anything that stands in for them, such as a seller's name. State and local laws can protect more, so check yours. It's the wrong signal and a real legal risk. Not legal advice.
A starting model you can adjust
The points below are a made-up starting point, not a formula from any company. Your own closed deals decide the real weights.
Signal | Answers and points | Max
Timeline | Within 30 days: 25 · 1 to 3 months: 15 · 3 to 6 months: 5 · no timeline: 0 | 25
Price | Asking at or under your MAO: 25 · up to about 10% over: 10 · well over, or won't say: 0 | 25
Reason | Behind on payments, inherited, vacant, tired landlord or major repairs: 20 · relocating or downsizing: 10 · just curious: 0 | 20
Condition | Major repairs: 15 · some updates: 8 · move-in ready: 0 | 15
Occupancy | Vacant: 10 · tenant: 5 · owner lives there: 0 | 10
Decision makers | Everyone on title agrees: 5 · not yet known: 0 | 5
That adds up to 100. A reasonable first cut: 70 and up is an A, 45 to 69 a B, 20 to 44 a C, under 20 a D. Move the lines once you've seen a quarter of results.
Show the band, not the number. "A" tells a rep what to do. "62" starts an argument about why it isn't 64.
How do you build it in Salesforce?
Add a picklist for each signal on the lead, and make them required when a rep marks the lead qualified, not when it's created.
Add the points up. A formula field with a CASE() for each picklist is enough for most teams. A second formula turns the total into a band.
Show why. A short text formula like "30 days · Vacant · Under MAO" next to the band. Reps trust a score they can read.
Use it everywhere reps look. Sort queues and list views by band, and put it on the lead page and the mobile layout.
Route on it. A leads go to your best closer with a task due now; B's the same day; C's into a follow-up cadence. More in lead routing for real estate teams .
One technical catch: a formula is calculated when someone reads it, so a change in a formula score doesn't start an automation by itself. If routing should react when a score changes, have a Flow write the score into a regular number field and trigger from that.
Keep a second, frozen copy: the score at first contact. Today's score changes as reps learn more. The first one is what you need to judge whether the model works.
How do you know the score works?
Once a quarter, run one report: leads created three to six months ago, old enough for deals to have closed, grouped by their score at first contact, with the share that reached contract and the share that closed.
The bands should separate clearly. A leads should reach contract at several times the rate of C leads. If the rates are close, the weights are wrong.
Read the misses. Look at closed deals that scored C or D, and at A leads that died. What did the score not see? Often it's a signal nobody records, like a tenant who stopped paying.
Change one thing at a time , and note the date you changed it, so you can tell what helped.
Check by source and market too. A score that works for PPC leads in one city can be wrong for cold-call leads in another, because the people and the reasons differ.
What about Einstein Lead Scoring?
Salesforce's own scoring learns from your past leads. The details, from Salesforce's help pages:
It needs at least 1,000 leads created in the last 200 days, and at least 120 of them converted. The same thresholds apply to each segment you set up.
Without enough data of your own, it uses a global model built from anonymous data across many Salesforce customers.
It reanalyzes your leads about every 10 days.
It comes with Sales Cloud Einstein, included in Performance and Unlimited Editions and an extra cost on Enterprise Edition.
The catch for investor teams is the word "converted". Einstein predicts lead conversion, and in many investor orgs a lead converts when an appointment is set, or never, because the team works everything on the lead or on a custom deal record. So it learns to predict appointments, not contracts. And it doesn't know your MAO math unless that's on the lead.
My view: start with rules everyone can read. If you have the volume and the license, run Einstein alongside them and compare both against closed deals each quarter. For where AI fits more broadly, see AI in Salesforce for real estate investors .
What usually goes wrong
Scoring what nobody asks. If reps don't ask about the timeline, the field is blank and every lead becomes a C.
Too many inputs. Fifteen picklists don't get filled in. Six or seven do.
Inflated answers. If whoever qualifies the lead is paid or praised on A leads, the answers drift upward. Score facts the rep records, and spot-check a few calls.
Never checking it. A score nobody tests against contracts is an opinion with a number on it.
Treating C's as dead. A low score means a different cadence, not no follow-up. Plenty of deals come from leads that weren't ready yet; see reactivating dead seller leads .
Questions
What is motivated seller lead scoring?
A way to rank seller leads by how likely they are to sell to you soon, using answers your reps record, such as reason for selling, timeline, condition, occupancy and asking price against your maximum offer. The score decides who gets called first and by whom.
How do you score leads in Salesforce without Einstein?
Add a picklist for each signal on the lead, add up points in a formula field, and turn the total into A, B, C and D bands. If automations should react to score changes, have a Flow store the score in a number field.
What makes a seller motivated?
Usually a reason and a timeline: behind on payments, an inherited or vacant house, a tired landlord, major repairs or a move, combined with wanting to sell soon at a price that works for you. Score the situation and the property, never the person.
How many leads do you need for Einstein Lead Scoring?
Salesforce says at least 1,000 leads created in the last 200 days, with at least 120 of them converted. Without that, Einstein uses a global model built from anonymous data across Salesforce customers.
Is Einstein Lead Scoring included in Salesforce?
It comes with Sales Cloud Einstein, which Salesforce includes in Performance and Unlimited Editions and sells as an extra on Enterprise Edition. Check your contract, because Salesforce renames its bundles often.
How often should you update a lead scoring model?
Review it every quarter against leads created three to six months earlier, using each lead's score at first contact. Change one weight at a time and note the date.
Should a low lead score mean we stop following up?
No. A low score means a slower cadence or a different person, not no follow-up. Many deals come from sellers who weren't ready the first time.

## Opening a New Market? A CRM Checklist for Home Buyers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/new-market-crm-checklist.html

Opening a new market? Set up your CRM before the first mailer drops.
When a home-buying company opens a second market, the marketing usually goes live before the CRM is ready for it. Leads from both markets land in the same lists, reps get leads from a city they've never seen, and three months in, nobody can say whether the new market is making money. I run the Salesforce for a two-market home-buying company in Ohio, so this is the checklist I'd work through before the first mailer, ad or cold call goes out.
Make market a field on every lead, deal, campaign and buyer, filled in automatically from the phone number, web form or zip code, never typed by a rep. Then add market to routing, spend tracking, underwriting assumptions, contract templates, buyer lists and every dashboard. Before launch, call every new number and submit every new form, and check that each test lead lands with the right market, source and owner.
What goes wrong when you add a market without changing the CRM?
Nothing breaks on day one, which is why it's easy to skip. The problems show up a few weeks later:
You can't tell if the new market is profitable. Spend, leads and contracts from both markets blend together, so the new market's numbers hide inside the old one's.
Leads go to the wrong people. Round robin doesn't know a lead is in a city your rep has never driven through.
Offers use the wrong assumptions. Repair costs, ARV comps and the offer formula from your first market don't fit the second.
Dispo blasts the wrong buyers. Buyers in one city get deals from another and start ignoring your emails.
Contracts go out on the wrong template. A new state can mean different contract language, disclosures and closing steps.
All of these are cheap to prevent before launch and expensive to untangle after, because by then you have months of leads with no market on them.
The new market checklist
1. Market on every record
A Market field on leads, deals, campaigns, buyers and transactions, with the same values everywhere
Filled automatically: from the tracking number the seller called, a hidden field on the web form, or the property's zip code or county
Reps can't leave it blank or change it without a reason
A report of records with no market, checked weekly until it stays at zero
In the org I run, leads, deals and campaigns all carry their market. That one field is what makes everything below possible.
2. Numbers, forms and lead sources
Every new call-tracking number mapped to its market and channel before it goes on a mailer or ad
Web forms for the new market send the market with the lead
PPC and social campaigns named with the market, so spend matches leads
New lead sources added to your picklists, not typed as free text
3. Spend by market
Monthly spend recorded per campaign and per market
The same split in your accounting (a class or location per market in QuickBooks, for example), so the CRM can be checked against the books
Cost per lead and cost per contract reported by market from day one
Campaign ROI by market and source, checked against the books, is part of what I built for the company I work with. Without the same split in accounting, you end up arguing with your own dashboard.
4. Routing and response
A queue or assignment rule entry per market, so new-market leads go to the people working that market
After-hours rules that follow the new market's clock if it's in another time zone
Missed-call alerts on every new marketing number
A "time until contacted" measure you can split by market
More on the routing side in Salesforce lead routing for real estate investors .
5. People and roles
Who owns a new-market lead from first call to appointment, written down
Field reps or appointment setters in the market set up as users, with access to what they need and nothing more
Appointments on a map, so you can see where people are driving
A manager who can see every lead in the market
6. Underwriting
ARV and maximum offer on the deal record, not in a spreadsheet
Repair cost assumptions and the offer percentage set per market, so the formula fits local numbers
Comps sources noted for the new market
An underwriting queue, so new-market deals get reviewed by someone who knows the area
The deal analyzer shows the offer math if you want to sanity-check the formula.
7. Contracts, title and closing
Contract templates for the new state in DocuSign or whatever you use, chosen automatically by the property's state
State disclosure requirements for wholesaling checked and tracked (see wholesaling laws and CRM tracking )
Title companies or closing attorneys for the new market on file, depending on how closings work in that state
Closing tasks adjusted for local steps
8. Dispositions
Buyers tagged by market, with the zip codes they buy in
Deal blasts filtered by market and zip
Buyer tiers based on what each buyer has actually bought, so your best buyers in the new market see deals first
Buyer tiers updated from repeat purchases and preferred zips are part of the dispo setup I run, and they matter more in a new market, where you don't know the buyers yet.
9. Reports and dashboards
A market filter on every dashboard the owner and managers use
Your weekly numbers split by market (the Monday 5 works well for this)
A market view: spend, leads, contacts, appointments, offers, contracts, closed deals and net profit per deal
10. Duplicates across markets
Duplicate matching on phone and email across all markets, not within each one
A rule for sellers who own property in both markets: one person, separate deals
When a duplicate comes in, the original owner is told instead of the lead being quietly reassigned
The launch test
The week before launch, do this with whoever runs your CRM:
Call every new marketing number and let one call ring out.
Submit every new web form.
Check each test lead: right market, right source, right owner or queue, a task created, the missed-call alert fired.
Move one test deal from offer to closing and check the right contract template and tasks appear.
Open the dashboard filtered to the new market and make sure the test records show up.
Delete the test records.
It takes about an hour, and it's the cheapest hour of the whole launch.
What should you measure in the first 90 days?
The same funnel you track in your first market, split by market: spend, leads, contact rate, appointments, offers, contracts, cost per contract and, once deals close, net profit per deal.
One thing that helps: compare the new market with how your first market did in its first three months, not with how it does today. A mature market has a buyer list, a reputation and reps who know the streets. A new market has none of that, and judging it against your best numbers can kill a market that was on track.
Decide up front what would make you keep going, change the channel mix or pull out, and write it down before the first mailer goes out. Otherwise the decision gets made on feel.
What changes for a virtual market?
If you're working the new market remotely, with local field reps or appointment setters, a few extra things matter:
Appointments assigned to a local person , with the address, time and seller notes on their phone before they get in the car.
Photos and documents on the deal , in a folder per deal that the whole team can see, not in a field rep's camera roll.
A clear handoff from the remote caller to the local rep and back, with a task at each step so nothing waits on a text message.
Local title or closing contacts on file, because nobody on your team can drive over to fix a problem.
Questions
How do I track marketing ROI by market?
Put a Market field on every lead, deal and campaign, filled automatically from the tracking number, web form or zip code. Record monthly spend per campaign and market, split the same way in your accounting, and report cost per contract and net profit per deal by market.
Should each market have its own Salesforce org?
Almost never for a 10 to 50 person company. One org with a market field on every record lets you share buyers, reports and automations while still splitting everything by market. Separate orgs make sense only for separate businesses.
How do I route leads by market in Salesforce?
Use a queue or an assignment rule entry per market, based on the Market field. Make sure the market is set before assignment runs, which is why it should come from the phone number, form or zip code rather than a rep.
How do I compare a new market with my existing one?
Compare it with your first market's first three months, not with your first market today. Track the same funnel by market: leads, contact rate, appointments, offers, contracts and cost per contract.
What changes in the CRM for a virtual wholesaling market?
Appointments assigned to local field reps, photos and documents stored on the deal, a tracked handoff between remote callers and local reps, and local title or closing contacts on file.
When should a new market get its own dashboard?
From day one, but as a filter on your existing dashboards rather than a separate set. Everyone looks at the same numbers, split by market, so the new market can't hide inside the old one.
Related guides
Opening a market soon?
Book a free call and I'll go through this checklist against your setup. If you're already on Salesforce, the fixed-price CRM Revenue Audit (USD 1,500) covers campaign ROI, routing and reporting in writing, with a fix plan. On another CRM? A move to Salesforce can be planned around the launch.
Or just ask one question about your setup: email · WhatsApp · LinkedIn

## Offer Follow-Up in Salesforce for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/offer-follow-up-salesforce.html

The offer went out. Then what? Offer follow-up in Salesforce
Most wholesaling and home-buying teams track leads well and offers badly. The offer gets made on the phone or at the kitchen table, the seller says they need to think about it, and a week later nobody is sure who was supposed to call back. This page is for owners and acquisitions managers who want every open offer on one list, with a named owner and a next step, until it's signed or truly dead.
Give every offer four required fields in Salesforce: the amount, the date, how it was made (in person or virtual) and a next follow-up date. Let Salesforce create the follow-up task, warn before the offer expires and flag any open offer with no seller contact for a set number of days. Put all open offers on one list the acquisitions manager reviews every morning. When an offer dies, require a reason, because those reasons tell you whether you have a pricing problem or a follow-up problem.
Why do offers go cold?
"Let me think about it" isn't a no. It's an open loop, and open loops close on whoever calls back. Often that's another investor.
The offer never makes it into the CRM. It was said out loud at the house or over the phone. If the amount and the date aren't on the record, the offer doesn't exist as far as anyone else is concerned.
Nobody clearly owns it. The lead manager set the appointment, the acquisitions rep made the offer, and each assumes the other is following up.
New leads are more fun. A rep with ten fresh leads today will call those before the seller who said "maybe" last Tuesday.
The deadline lives in someone's head. The offer was good "through Friday", and Friday comes and goes.
The habit isn't special to real estate. In one large study of sales leads, half were never called a second time ( Velocify, 2012 ). An offer is a much warmer lead than a web form, and it gets the same treatment when nobody owns the next step.
Where should offers live in Salesforce?
Two workable setups:
Setup | How it works | Good for | Watch out for
Offer fields and an "Offer Made" stage on the deal | One record per property; the offer amount, date and status sit on the deal | Most teams, especially to start | Only the latest offer is visible unless you track history on the amount
A separate Offer record linked to the deal | Every offer and counteroffer is its own row with amount, date and status | Teams that negotiate several rounds, or want offer-to-contract by spread and rep | More clicks for reps; keep the form to a handful of fields
I'd start with the first and turn on field history tracking for the offer amount. Salesforce tracks up to 20 fields per object this way and shows 18 months of history on the record. Opportunity stage changes are tracked out of the box, including how long each deal sat in each stage, so you get "days from offer to contract" without building anything. Move to a separate Offer record when your team routinely goes back and forth three or four times per deal.
The fields every offer needs
Field | Required? | Why it's there
Offer amount | Yes | The number, with history, so a later counter doesn't erase the first offer
Offer date | Yes | Starts every clock: follow-up, aging, days to contract
Made in person or virtually | Yes | The two close at different rates, and you'll want to know by how much
Next follow-up date | Yes | No open offer without a next step. This one field does most of the work
Offer good through | If you use deadlines | Drives a reminder before it passes
MAO when offered | Recommended | Shows offers made over your maximum, by rep. See the deal analyzer
Seller's asking price | Recommended | The gap between ask and offer is the negotiation
Status | Yes | Open, Countered, Accepted, Declined, Expired
Dead reason | When declined or expired | The only way to learn from the ones you lose
Make the required fields required at the moment the deal moves to "Offer Made", not when the lead is created. A rep can't know the offer amount on day one, and a form full of required fields nobody can fill gets filled with junk.
What should Salesforce do on its own?
Create the first follow-up task the moment an offer is logged, assigned to the person who made it and due on the follow-up date.
Warn before the deadline. A record-triggered Flow with a scheduled path can create a "call before the offer expires" task a day or two before the "offer good through" date. If the date changes, the scheduled action moves with it.
Flag offers with no contact. If an open offer has had no logged call, text or completed task with the seller for a set number of days, create an "offer made, no activity" task and tell the manager. Base this on a "last seller contact" date stamped by your calls and texts. The standard Last Activity field can mislead: it follows the primary contact on an activity, so a call logged against a second owner may not move it.
Stop automated texts when the seller replies , so a seller in the middle of a conversation doesn't get a canned "just checking in".
Clean up when it's decided. Accepted moves the deal to contract and closes the follow-up tasks. Declined or expired asks for a reason, closes open tasks and sets a date to try again.
In the org I run there's an offer-deadline task, an "offer made, no activity" task, and on-site and virtual offers are tracked separately, so the owners can see which offers close and how. None of it is complicated. It just means the follow-up happens because the system says so, not because someone remembers.
What does a good follow-up rhythm look like after an offer?
There's no magic sequence, and your market and team will shape it. Here's a starting point I'd adjust with the team:
When | Touch | What it adds
Same day | Text or email with the offer in writing | The number in front of everyone who has a say, including the people you didn't meet
Next day | Call | Questions they thought of overnight; who else needs to say yes
Day 3 to 4 | Call | Anything that changed: a repair quote, another offer, a move date
Before the deadline | Call | A real decision point, if your offer has one
Weekly, then monthly | Call or text | Until they sign, sell to someone else or tell you to stop
Two rules matter more than the exact days. Every touch should add something, a question, an answer or a changed number, rather than "just checking in". And when a seller asks you to stop, stop, and record it so no automation or other rep contacts them again. To build a cadence your team can follow, try the seller follow-up cadence builder .
How do you handle counteroffers?
Log every counter as a new amount. With history on the field, the first offer stays visible. With Offer records, each counter is its own row.
Keep the seller's number next to yours. First offer, latest offer and the seller's counter on one screen show the gap at a glance.
Route anything over MAO to the manager. A Flow can hold the status until the manager approves, and record who approved it. That's the paper trail for the deals that lose money.
What happens when an offer dies?
Require a reason from a short list: price too low, listed with an agent, sold to another buyer, decided not to sell, couldn't reach them, and other (with a note). Keep it short enough that reps pick honestly.
Then look at the reasons every month. Mostly "price too low" with offers well under MAO points to how you price. Mostly "couldn't reach them" or "sold to another buyer" points to follow-up. Those are different fixes, and the reason field is the only way to tell them apart.
A dead offer isn't a dead seller. Set a date to try again, because situations change: the repair estimate comes in, the tenant leaves, the listing expires. That's where reactivating dead seller leads picks up. And review dead offers as a manager once a week, so "dead" doesn't become the way a busy rep clears their list.
The reports that matter
Open offers by owner and age , with last seller contact. This is the morning list. If you build one thing from this page, build this.
Open offers with no contact in your set number of days. It should be empty. When it isn't, it's a to-do list.
Offer-to-contract rate by rep, and by in-person versus virtual.
Days from offer to contract , from the stage history.
Dead reasons by month , by lead source and by rep.
Offers over MAO , by rep, and how those deals turned out.
The first two belong on the acquisitions manager's home page. The rest feed the weekly meeting and the Monday 5 .
Questions
How do you follow up after making an offer to a motivated seller?
Put the offer in writing the same day, call the next day and again a few days later, and keep a dated next step on the record until the seller signs, sells elsewhere or asks you to stop. Each touch should add something new rather than check in.
How long should you keep following up on a real estate offer?
Until the seller signs, sells to someone else or asks you to stop. After the first couple of weeks, move to a weekly and then monthly rhythm, and set a date to try again on offers that die, because sellers' situations change.
Should offers be a separate object in Salesforce?
Not at first. Offer fields and an Offer Made stage on the deal, with history tracked on the amount, work for most teams. A separate Offer record makes sense when you negotiate several rounds per deal or want to analyze offers by spread and rep.
How do I find offers nobody followed up on?
Build a report of open offers where the last seller contact is older than your limit, grouped by owner. Stamp that date from logged calls and texts rather than relying on the standard Last Activity field.
Can Salesforce remind reps before an offer expires?
Yes. A record-triggered Flow with a scheduled path can create a task a set number of days before the offer's deadline date, and it adjusts automatically if the date changes.
How do I track counteroffers in Salesforce?
Log each counter as a new offer amount with field history turned on, or as its own Offer record. Keep the first offer, latest offer and seller's counter visible together, and route anything over MAO to a manager for approval.
What dead reasons should wholesalers track?
A short list reps will use honestly: price too low, listed with an agent, sold to another buyer, decided not to sell, couldn't reach them, and other with a note. Review them monthly by source and rep.

## Moving Off Podio: A Migration Checklist for Wholesalers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/podio-alternative-wholesalers.html

Moving off Podio: a migration checklist for wholesalers.
Leaving Podio is mostly a data decision, not a software one. Decide what history you keep, carry lead source through to every closed deal, plan for what Podio's Excel export leaves out, and test with 50 records before you move the rest. The checklist below covers it in ten steps.
Signs you've outgrown your current setup
Check the ones that are true
☐ Monday numbers get rebuilt in a spreadsheet by hand ☐ Closed deals don't show which campaign produced them ☐ Missed seller calls don't become callback tasks on their own ☐ The person who built the workspace has left, and nobody wants to touch it ☐ A second market or a bigger team is coming
Two or more checked usually means it's time to rebuild or move. Score the whole funnel in two minutes with the free Deal Leak Score .
Three options
1. Rebuild in Podio
Cheapest when the team knows Podio and the problems are messy fields and missing automations. Rebuild against the wholesaling CRM checklist .
2. Move to an investor CRM
Built for wholesaling and quick to start. Check lead source carried to the closed deal and fall-out reasons before you sign.
3. Move to Salesforce
More setup, but it fits teams with their own process, several markets or custom reporting. I build on Salesforce, so weigh that.
The 10-step migration checklist
1. List every app, field and automation in the workspace
2. Decide what moves: open leads, active deals, buyers, closed deals with source
3. Map each field to the new system; fix picklists and drop unused fields
4. Keep lead source, created date and closed date on every record
5. Export each app (Excel export, filtered batches above 20,000 items)
6. Plan separately for comments, files and tasks (not in the export)
7. Merge duplicate sellers by phone and email
8. Import 50 records, check them with the team, fix the mapping
9. Move the rest, reconnect phone, text and web forms, then cut over
10. Keep Podio read-only for 30 days; compare Monday numbers in both
Export details from Podio's help page on exporting to Excel : an export from the first All items view includes all fields plus created on, created by and tags; images, files, tasks, comments and activity are not included; each export is capped at 20,000 items.
Questions
What does a Podio Excel export include?
Per the Podio help page, an export from the first All items view includes all app fields plus metadata such as created on, created by and tags. Images, files, tasks, comments and activity are not included, and each export is capped at 20,000 items, so larger apps are exported in filtered batches.
How do I keep comments and call notes when I leave Podio?
They are not in the Excel export, so plan for them separately: decide which notes matter (often only open deals and active sellers), and move those through the Podio API or by hand. Archive the rest as a read-only export.
How long does a migration take?
It depends on the number of apps, records and integrations. The slow parts are usually deciding what to keep and cleaning duplicates, not the import itself. Run a 50-record test before the full move.
Should I rebuild in Podio instead?
Sometimes yes. If the team knows Podio and the problems are messy fields and missing automations, a clean rebuild against the checklist can be the cheapest fix.
Can you migrate Podio to Salesforce?
Yes, that is part of my work. I build Salesforce for real estate investors and wholesalers, so weigh my view with that in mind.

## Podio's 25,000 Automation Limit: What Wholesalers Can Do
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/podio-automation-limit.html

Podio's new automation limit: what it means for a wholesaling team
A lot of wholesaling companies run on Podio, and most of the work in those setups is done by Podio Workflow Automation, the tool many teams still call Globiflow. Since September 1, 2026, that automation comes with a monthly allowance. If your Podio was built by a template vendor or a consultant a few years ago, you may not know how close you are to it. This page explains what changed, what counts, what happens when you hit the cap and how to decide what to do.
Podio now includes 25,000 Workflow Automation actions a month . Extra capacity comes in prepaid, non-refundable add-ons, only on the Premium plan. There are no automatic overage charges: once you're over, automations above your capacity may be limited or fail until capacity frees up or you buy more. The flows that burn through the allowance are usually the ones that loop over many items or sync databases, not the ones that run once per new lead. Check your usage on the Workflow Automation Account Details page before you decide anything.
What changed with Podio pricing in 2026?
Podio, now owned by Progress Software, moved to what it calls hybrid pricing: you still pay for seats, and some usage now has limits with paid add-ons on top. The dates, from Podio's own FAQ:
Date | What happened
July 1, 2026 | Customers notified, grace period started
August 1, 2026 | Usage add-ons went on sale
September 1, 2026 | Grace period ended and the new limits applied to existing customers
Two kinds of usage are covered:
Workflow Automation : the included base limit is now 25,000 actions a month . Add-ons are available only on the Premium plan.
API : the limits didn't change. It's 250 calls an hour for resource-intensive calls and 1,000 an hour for everything else, measured on a rolling hour. API add-ons are available on Plus and Premium. This is the one that matters if Zapier, Make or other tools talk to your Podio.
The add-on rules are worth reading twice, because they're stricter than most software:
Add-ons are prepaid, and Podio says to treat them as non-refundable.
They bill on the same monthly or annual cycle as your plan. Buying mid-cycle is prorated.
If you cancel, it takes effect at the end of the billing cycle.
Only the contract owner, the person on your account who handles billing, can buy them.
What counts as an action?
This is where teams get surprised. According to Podio:
A single action generally counts once each time it runs.
Actions that process several items may count once per item.
Loops may count based on the items and the number of times they repeat.
Database syncs count toward usage.
Some preparation or lookup steps may not count.
So a flow that runs once when a new lead comes in is cheap. A flow that runs every night and touches every open lead is not, because it can count once for every lead it touches, every night. Most wholesaling setups have a few of those: "days since last contact" updates, nightly status clean-ups, buyer list syncs, follow-up sweeps.
What does that look like for a real team?
Made-up example. The numbers below are invented to show the math, not taken from any company.
A 15-person wholesaling team gets 1,200 new seller leads a month. Here's what three common automations could cost, if each item counts once:
Automation | How it runs | Actions a month
New lead setup | On each new lead: set status, assign a rep, create two tasks, send one text, post a notification. About 6 actions, 1,200 times. | About 7,200
Days-since-contact update | Every night, loops through 2,500 open leads and updates a field on each | About 75,000
Buyer list sync | Every night, syncs 1,000 buyer records with another app | About 30,000
Total |  | About 112,000, against 25,000 included
The automations that do the real work, setting up each new lead, fit easily. The nightly loop and the sync are what break the allowance, and those are usually the easiest to redesign.
What happens when you hit the cap?
Podio's wording is that activity above your included or purchased capacity "may be limited or fail until capacity becomes available again", or until you buy an add-on. There's no automatic overage charge, so you won't get a surprise bill. You may get something worse for a wholesaler: automations that quietly don't run.
Think about what that means late in the month. A seller fills in your web form, the lead gets created, and the flow that assigns it to a rep, creates the callback task and sends the first text doesn't fire. Nobody notices until the seller has signed with someone faster.
Podio says alerts for contract owners and admins are planned. Until they arrive, someone on your team should look at usage every week, on the Workflow Automation Account Details page. API usage shows on the API Keys Settings page.
What are your options?
In the order I'd try them:
1. Measure
Look at last month's usage before you decide anything. If you're at 8,000 actions, you have time and this page is just a heads-up. If you're at 40,000, you need a plan this month. If someone else built your Podio, like a template vendor or a consultant, ask them for last month's number and which flows use the most.
2. Find the multipliers and redesign them
List every flow and mark the ones that run on a schedule, loop over items or sync data. For each one, ask whether it could run only when something changes instead of on everything every night. Archive dead leads so loops touch fewer items. Sync weekly instead of nightly where nobody needs fresh data. This is often enough on its own.
3. Buy add-ons
Fine for a short spike, or as a bridge while you redesign or move. Remember the rules: Premium only, prepaid, non-refundable, bought by the contract owner. If you find yourself buying them every month, that's a signal, not a fix.
4. Move some jobs out of Podio Workflow Automation
Some teams move heavy jobs to Make or Zapier. That doesn't make the work free: those tools connect through Podio's API, which has its own hourly limits, and they bill separately. Do it for specific jobs, not as a blanket fix.
5. Move off Podio
If your team has grown, your automations are what keep leads alive, and you can't get the reporting you need, this may be the push to move. For smaller teams, an all-in-one investor CRM can be a good landing spot. For teams of 10 or more who want their own system and real numbers, Salesforce is the option I build. My Podio migration checklist compares the three paths honestly, and Salesforce vs Podio puts the two side by side.
How do you decide?
Your situation | What I'd do
Under the cap, or under it after trimming the loops | Stay. Redesign the scheduled flows, check usage weekly and move on.
Over the cap for a month or two because of a spike or a one-off import | Buy an add-on for the spike, then trim.
Over every month, and you're already planning to move within a year | Add-ons as a bridge, and start the move now rather than later.
Over every month, 10 or more people, and you can't see cost per contract by source | Plan the move. You're paying more for a setup that's already limiting you.
Small team, few automations, happy with Podio | Stay. This change probably doesn't affect you much.
If you move to Salesforce, are there limits there too?
Yes, and anyone who says otherwise is selling. Salesforce limits how much a single automation can do in one go, and it has daily allowances for scheduled jobs and API calls that grow with the number of licenses you have. What it doesn't have is a monthly action allowance for ordinary record-triggered automations that you top up in prepaid packs. The flows that create the callback task, send the alert and stop the follow-up when a seller replies run each time a record changes, without counting against a monthly meter.
The honest trade-off: Salesforce costs more to set up and needs someone to run it. It pays off when your team is big enough that missed leads and blind marketing spend cost more than the system. If that's you, see how a move to Salesforce works , or read the full Podio to Salesforce switch guide with the field map and a 30-60-90 day plan.
If you'd rather stay on Podio, that's a fine answer too. Do the redesign in option 2 and check your usage every week.
Questions
What is Podio's automation limit?
Since September 1, 2026, Podio Workflow Automation includes a base of 25,000 actions a month. Extra capacity is sold as add-ons, which are available only on the Premium plan.
When did the Podio usage limits start?
Podio notified customers and started a grace period on July 1, 2026, put add-ons on sale on August 1, 2026, and applied the new limits to existing customers on September 1, 2026.
What happens when we go over Podio's automation limit?
There are no automatic overage charges. Podio says activity above your included or purchased capacity may be limited or fail until capacity becomes available again or you buy an add-on. For a wholesaler, that can mean new leads that don't get assigned, tasked or texted.
Can we buy more Workflow Automation actions on Podio Plus?
No. Workflow Automation add-ons are available only on Podio Premium. API add-ons are available on Plus and Premium.
Are Podio add-ons refundable?
Podio says add-ons are prepaid and should be treated as non-refundable. They bill on the same cycle as your plan, mid-cycle purchases are prorated, and a cancellation takes effect at the end of the billing cycle.
Do Zapier and Make count against Podio's 25,000 actions?
Zapier and Make connect through Podio's API, which has its own limits that didn't change: 250 resource-intensive calls an hour and 1,000 other calls an hour, on a rolling hour. API add-ons are available on Plus and Premium.
How do I check my Podio automation usage?
Workflow Automation usage is on the Workflow Automation Account Details page, and API usage is on the API Keys Settings page. Podio says alerts for contract owners, admins and automation account owners are planned.
What uses up Podio automation actions fastest?
Flows that loop over many items, flows that process many items at once, and database syncs, because they can count once per item. A nightly flow that touches every open lead can use more actions in a month than all your new-lead automations combined.
Should we leave Podio because of the new limits?
Not automatically. If you're under the cap, or can get under it by redesigning scheduled flows, stay. If you're over every month, have 10 or more people and can't get the reporting you need, it's a good time to plan a move.

## Privacy | Amr Magdy
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/privacy.html

Privacy
What this site collects, and why
The short version: I only get what you send me and basic visit counts, I never sell any of it, and you can ask me to delete your details any time.
Updated October 27, 2026
Who runs this site
I'm Amr Magdy, an independent Salesforce CRM Consultant working from Cairo, Egypt, as Amr Magdy CRM Consulting. I decide what happens to the details collected here. Questions about them go to info@AmrMagdy.com .
What I collect and why
Forms. When you ask for an audit or a move to Salesforce, send a question or join the newsletter, I get what you type: your name and email, and where the form asks for them, your company, phone, CRM and message. Web3Forms delivers it to my inbox. I use it to reply, to send what you asked for and, if you joined the newsletter, to send the newsletter.
Calls. When you book a call, Calendly takes your booking details on its own site and shares them with me so we can meet.
Email, WhatsApp and LinkedIn. If you message me there, I get what you send. Those services have their own privacy rules.
Visit counts. Google Analytics shows me which pages get read, which buttons and forms get used, your rough location (city or country), your device and browser, and the site that sent you. It doesn't tell me who you are. Form sends and booking clicks are counted there as leads, without names or emails.
Cookies
The only cookies on this site are Google Analytics cookies, _ga and _ga_66PK4JKWSF . They hold a random ID so a return visit isn't counted as a new visitor, and they last up to two years.
If you visit from the UK, the EU, the EEA or Switzerland, they stay off unless you choose Accept, and you can change your mind any time with Cookie choices at the bottom of each page. Before you choose, and if you choose No thanks, Google Analytics still gets a basic count of the visit, with no cookie and no ID.
The site also saves two small settings in your browser: your cookie choice and light or dark mode. They stay on your device. To block Google Analytics on every site, use your browser's tracking protection or Google's opt-out add-on .
Who else handles it
A few services do part of the work, each under its own privacy policy:
GitHub Pages hosts this site and keeps server logs, including IP addresses, for security.
Web3Forms delivers form messages, and Zoho Mail holds my inbox.
Calendly runs call bookings.
Google runs Google Analytics. The fonts are served from this site, not by Google.
These services are based in the US and elsewhere, and I work from Egypt, so your details may be handled outside your country.
I don't sell or rent your details, I don't share them with advertisers, and this site has no ads.
How long I keep it
Messages and bookings: while we're talking or working together. Ask me and I'll delete them, unless the law says I have to keep them, like invoices for tax.
The newsletter list: until you leave it.
Google Analytics: visit-level data is deleted automatically after 14 months at most. Totals in reports stay.
Your choices
Email info@AmrMagdy.com to see the details I hold about you, fix them, delete them or ask me to stop using them. To leave the newsletter, reply to any issue or email me. I reply within one working day and act within 30 days.
If you're in the UK, the EU or the EEA: I reply to messages and bookings because you asked me to, and I use analytics cookies and send the newsletter only with your consent, which you can take back any time. You can complain to your data protection authority (in the UK, the ICO), though I'd like the chance to put it right first.
Changes
If I change this page, the date at the top changes too.
