## Probate Leads in Salesforce: A CRM Setup for Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/probate-leads-salesforce.html

Probate deals run on the court's clock. Tracking probate leads in Salesforce
Probate is one of the steadiest lead sources in investing, and one of the easiest to work badly. The person you need to reach is grieving, the decision may belong to someone other than the person you're talking to, and the court sets the pace. A CRM built for "call fast and close in two weeks" loses these deals. This page is for owners and acquisitions managers who work probate leads, or want to, and need Salesforce to keep track of a deal that can take most of a year.
Build a probate lead around the whole estate rather than the house alone: the person who died, the personal representative who can sell, the attorney, the heirs, and the case with its county, case number, filing date and the date letters were issued. Track the dates that decide when a sale can happen, follow up on a slow, respectful cadence that can run for months, and keep probate deals in their own pipeline so your usual "no activity in seven days" alarms don't fire on them. Rules vary by state, and none of this is legal advice.
Why are probate leads different?
The owner isn't the one deciding. The person who owned the house has died. The personal representative, called the executor when a will names one and the administrator when the court appoints one, acts for the estate once the court issues letters testamentary or letters of administration.
The court sets the pace. Depending on the state, probate typically takes six to twelve months, faster for simple estates and a year or more for complex ones.
A sale may need the court's OK. In many states the executor needs court approval before selling real estate. Some require the court to confirm the sale, which can mean a hearing where other buyers can bid more. Some wills give the executor authority to sell without approval.
Families are involved. Heirs in other states, siblings who disagree, someone living in the house. Patience and a record of every conversation matter more here than anywhere else.
The filings are public. Probate records usually include the will, the petition, the inventory and the representative's name, sometimes with contact details. That's where most probate lead lists come from.
Who's who in a probate deal?
Person | Role | In Salesforce
The person who died | Owned the property | A field on the case or deal, never a contact anyone calls
Personal representative | Can sell once the court issues letters | The main contact on the deal
Probate attorney | Advises the representative and often knows the timing | A contact linked to the deal with the role "Attorney"
Heirs | May need to agree; one may want to keep the house | Contacts linked with the role "Heir"
The court | Sets the timeline and may approve or confirm the sale | Case number, county and hearing dates
Opportunity contact roles handle the people side: one deal, several contacts, each with a role. Then anyone opening the deal sees who to call and who not to.
How do you set it up in Salesforce?
Lead source "Probate" , with each list tracked as its own campaign, such as one county and month, so you know which lists pay.
A deal for each property once the lead is qualified, with the representative as the main contact and the attorney and heirs linked by role.
A probate case record if you work more than a handful: case number, county, filing date, letters date, decedent, representative and attorney, linked to every property in the estate. One estate can hold several properties, and a case record means you enter those details once.
Its own pipeline. A separate record type or sales process for probate, with stages that match the case: researching, letter sent, talking with the representative, waiting on letters, offer made, waiting on court approval, under contract.
Duplicate checks on case number and property address. The same estate often shows up on a probate list, a vacant list and a tax list. See duplicate sellers in Salesforce .
Which fields and dates matter?
Field | Why it's there
Case number and county | To look up the case and catch duplicates
Date of death | Context, and the start of your "wait before contacting" rule
Filing date | Starts the court's clock
Letters issued date | When the representative can act for the estate
Executor or administrator | Whether there was a will
Court approval needed to sell | Yes, no or unknown. Ask the attorney rather than guess
Creditor claim deadline | Often shapes when the estate is ready to sell or distribute
Who lives in the property | Vacant, an heir or a tenant changes the conversation
Heirs in agreement | Yes, no or unknown
Next follow-up date | Required, like every other open deal
What timeline are you working with?
A typical sequence for an estate with a will, from LegalZoom's guides. Every state differs, so treat the durations as rough.
Step | Typical timing | What it means for you
Petition filed with the court | Often within 30 to 60 days of the death | The case appears in public records
Hearing, appointment and letters issued | About 2 to 8 weeks after filing | The representative can now act for the estate
Notice to creditors and claim period | Usually 3 to 6 months | Debts get sorted, often the longest step
Inventory and appraisal | About 30 to 90 days | The estate learns what the house is worth
Sale, with court approval or confirmation where required | A confirmation hearing is often 2 to 4 weeks after an offer is accepted | Your offer may face higher bids at the hearing
LegalZoom puts the whole run, from filing to closing a probate sale, at typically six to twelve months, with simple estates closing in three or four and complex ones taking eighteen months or more.
That timeline breaks most investor CRMs. A deal that sits in one stage for four months isn't stale; it's waiting on a court. Keep probate out of your normal aging alarms and give it alarms of its own, built on the case dates above.
What follow-up fits probate?
Start slow and in writing. I'd lead with a letter to the representative rather than a call, and give the family time first. Whatever your rule is, put it in Salesforce so every rep follows it, such as no first contact until a set number of weeks after the date of death.
Let the case dates drive the tasks. A check-in a week after letters are issued, another before the creditor deadline, another after the inventory. Scheduled paths in a Flow can create those tasks from the dates, and they move if the dates change.
Space calls weeks apart , not days. A representative handling an estate gets a lot of calls from investors. Being the patient, organized one helps.
Bring in the attorney when the representative is comfortable with it. Attorneys often know when the estate will be ready to sell.
Write everything down. A probate deal can pass between reps over the months it takes. The next person needs to know who said what, and who doesn't want calls.
Opt-outs still apply. The consent and do-not-call rules in reactivating dead seller leads apply here too.
How do you get probate data into Salesforce?
Probate filings are public, and anyone can usually see the case file through the local court, online in some counties and in person in others. Most teams buy lists from a data vendor or pull them from county records. Either way:
Import with the case details : case number, county, filing date, decedent, representative's name and mailing address, and the property address.
Match duplicates on the way in , by case number and property address, before anyone sends a letter.
Tag each list as a campaign , one per county and month, so cost per contract by list is a report, not a guess.
Find phone numbers for the representative , not the decedent, if your process includes calls.
Which reports matter?
Probate pipeline by stage and case milestone : letters issued or not, creditor period over or not.
Case dates coming up in the next 30 days , so every milestone gets a call.
Cost per contract by probate list , by county and month.
Letter to conversation to contract , to see where probate deals drop out.
Probate deals by age , judged against your own history rather than your two-week wholesale deals.
Questions
How do you track probate leads in a CRM?
Link each property to the estate: the decedent, the personal representative, the attorney, the heirs and the case details, including county, case number, filing date and letters date. Keep probate deals in their own pipeline with follow-up tied to the case dates.
Who can sell a house in probate?
The personal representative, called the executor when named in a will or the administrator when appointed by the court, once the court issues letters testamentary or letters of administration. Many states also require court approval or confirmation of the sale.
How long does a probate sale take?
LegalZoom puts typical probate real estate sales at six to twelve months from the probate filing to closing, with simple estates sometimes closing in three or four months and complex ones taking eighteen months or more.
Are probate records public?
Generally yes. Once a case is filed, the will, petition and inventory are usually part of the public record, available through the local probate court, and some counties put them online.
Should probate leads have their own pipeline in Salesforce?
Yes. Probate deals wait on the court for months, so they trip normal aging alarms and need different stages, dates and follow-up. A separate record type or sales process keeps them visible without false alarms.
When should you first contact a probate lead?
There's no rule that fits every family. I'd start with a letter to the personal representative rather than a call and give the family time. Whatever you decide, set it as a rule in Salesforce so every rep follows it.
How do you handle several heirs on one property?
Link each heir to the deal with a contact role, track whether they agree, and keep the personal representative as the main contact, since they act for the estate.
Related guides
Sources
Checked in October 2026. Probate rules vary by state and change, so check with a probate attorney before you rely on any timing or requirement. Nothing here is legal advice.

## Wholesaling CRM Questions, Answered Plainly | Amr Magdy
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/questions-from-wholesalers.html

Wholesaling CRM questions, answered plainly.
Fifteen questions wholesalers and investors asked in Facebook groups, BiggerPockets and Quora in October 2026, paraphrased with names removed. Each answer is short, practical advice with one concrete step to set up in your CRM, whichever CRM you use, and a link to the free tool or video that goes deeper. Any dollar figure here is an example, not a result. For short answers on 40 more pain points, by topic, see the wholesaling systems FAQ .
The questions
Do motivated sellers drop off in the last two or three months of the year?
I'm starting out with a full-time cold caller. What workflow should I set up first?
How do you monitor cold callers’ metrics and calls when they use your dialer account?
Which CRM should I use to build pipelines for my VAs: REsimpli, FreedomSoft, XLeads or something else?
I sent seven contracts last month and none got signed. What am I doing wrong?
My VA makes over 4,500 calls a week and gets no solid leads. What should I check?
What's the most consistent source of motivated seller leads?
How do I calculate my offer price, or maximum allowable offer (MAO)?
How fast should I call back a missed seller call?
How do I know which marketing actually makes money?
I pull pre-foreclosure, probate and driving-for-dollars lists. How do I stop calling the same owner three times?
If my marketing budget went to zero tomorrow, where would my next deal come from?
What is the best CRM for real estate investors?
How much should a real estate investor spend on a CRM?
After a BRRRR refinance, how do you pay back the new loan?
Do motivated sellers drop off in the last two or three months of the year?
Not in a way you should plan around without checking your own numbers. Seller motivation comes from situations like probate, vacancy, divorce, back taxes and repairs the owner can't afford, and those don't stop for the holidays. What often changes is contact: people are busier, travel more and pick up fewer unknown calls. Some investors also pause marketing at year end, which can mean less competition for the sellers who are ready. The honest answer for your market is in your own history, not in a group thread.
Do this in your CRM: Build one report of leads, appointments and signed contracts by month and by lead source, going back at least twelve months. Compare November and December with the rest of the year for each channel, then decide whether to cut, hold or shift spend.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → The Monday 5 →
I'm starting out with a full-time cold caller. What workflow should I set up first?
Set up the handoff before the dialing. A cold caller's job is to find interested sellers and pass them on cleanly, so the first thing to build is what happens after a yes: which details get captured (address, motivation, timeline, asking price, condition), who gets the lead, and how fast they call back. Then define a short list of call outcomes the caller picks on every call, such as no answer, wrong number, not interested, call back later and interested. Without those, you can't coach the caller and you can't tell a bad list from a bad pitch.
Do this in your CRM: Create a qualified lead stage with those details as required fields, and an automation that assigns each new qualified lead to you with a callback task due the same hour. Make call outcome a required field on every logged call.
Video: Leads with no next step → Wholesaling CRM glossary →
How do you monitor cold callers’ metrics and calls when they use your dialer account?
Give every caller their own login, even on one dialer account. With a shared login, nobody can see who did what. With separate users, each call, recording and outcome is tied to one person, and you can compare callers working the same list. Track a few numbers per caller per day: dials, conversations with a real person, interested leads passed on, and the mix of call outcomes. Then listen to a handful of recordings each week, some picked at random and some marked interested. The numbers tell you where to look; the recordings tell you why.
Do this in your CRM: Sync dialer calls to the lead record with the caller as the owner, and build a daily dashboard grouped by user that shows dials, conversations, leads passed on and outcomes.
The Monday 5 → Deal Leak Score →
Which CRM should I use to build pipelines for my VAs: REsimpli, FreedomSoft, XLeads or something else?
The brand matters less than whether it does four things for your setup. One: separate logins and permissions, so each VA sees only the leads and stages they work. Two: pipeline stages you name yourself, with required fields before a lead moves forward. Three: your dialer and texting tools log calls and outcomes onto the lead automatically, not by copy and paste. Four: lead source stays on the record from first contact to closed deal, so you can report cost per deal by channel. Test any investor CRM against those four points during a trial, with a VA doing real work in it. Salesforce makes sense once you run several markets, teams or channels.
Do this in your CRM: Before you buy, write your stages on paper (new, contacted, qualified, appointment, offer, contract, closed, dead), rebuild them in the trial, and run five real leads through end to end.
Salesforce for real estate investors → The Kept-Deal Map →
I sent seven contracts last month and none got signed. What am I doing wrong?
Look at the system before the script. Three things usually explain a run of unsigned contracts. First, the offer: if each one is worked out differently, some will be too low for that seller's situation and others too high to work for you. Use one formula and write down the inputs. Second, follow-up: a sent contract with no scheduled next touch goes cold, and a seller talking to several investors often signs with whoever followed up. Third, reasons: if you don't record why each contract wasn't signed (price, timing, family, another buyer, no response), you'll keep guessing. After a month of recorded reasons, the pattern is usually clear.
Do this in your CRM: Add a contract sent stage that requires a follow-up task within 24 hours, and a required “reason not signed” picklist when a deal moves to dead.
Deal analyzer (MAO) → Video: Offers off-formula →
My VA makes over 4,500 calls a week and gets no solid leads. What should I check?
Check four things, in this order. List quality: how old is the list, how was it skip traced, and how many numbers come back wrong or disconnected? If wrong numbers dominate, more dials won't help. Numbers tracked: dials alone say little; you need conversations, interested sellers and appointments to see where the drop happens. Call timing: compare contact rates by hour and day of week, because the hours that work vary by list and market. Call outcomes: if an outcome isn't logged on every call, you can't tell a bad list from a bad pitch. Then listen to a few recorded conversations.
Do this in your CRM: Make call outcome required, tag each lead with its list name and pull date, and run a weekly report of conversations and interested sellers by list and by hour of day.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → Wholesaling CRM glossary →
What's the most consistent source of motivated seller leads?
The one that produces closed deals at the lowest cost in your market, and the only way to know which one that is, is to measure it. Ask a group and you'll hear cold calling, texting, direct mail, PPC and driving for dollars, and each answer is true for somebody. Comparing sources by cost per lead misleads, because cheap leads often convert worse. Compare cost per signed contract and cost per closed deal by source, over at least a quarter. For example, a channel with expensive leads can still be your cheapest per deal if more of its leads close.
Do this in your CRM: Make lead source a required field that stays on the record from first contact to closing, and report spend, leads, contracts and closed deals by source every month.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → Video: The 5 leaks →
How do I calculate my offer price, or maximum allowable offer (MAO)?
Start with the common formula: MAO = after-repair value (ARV) × your rule percentage − repairs − your wholesale fee. Many buyers use 70%, but markets often use anything from 65% to 80% depending on price point and competition, so treat it as a dial, not a law. Example only: with an ARV of $200,000 at 70%, repairs of $30,000 and a $10,000 fee, MAO is $140,000 − $30,000 − $10,000 = $100,000. ARV should come from recent sold comps of similar renovated homes nearby, and repairs from a walkthrough plus a contingency. The formula is only as good as those two inputs.
Do this in your CRM: Put ARV, repairs, rule percentage and fee as fields on the deal, calculate MAO with a formula field, and require a review before any offer above MAO goes out.
Deal analyzer (MAO) → Video: Offers off-formula →
How fast should I call back a missed seller call?
As fast as you can: within minutes if possible, and the same hour at the latest. A seller calling from your marketing may be calling other investors too, and usually talks to whoever answers first. The research on speed to lead isn't from real estate, but it points the same way. A Harvard Business Review study (2011) found firms that responded to a lead within an hour were about 7x more likely to qualify it. No comparable study exists yet for real estate investors, so measure your own time to callback and what it costs you.
Do this in your CRM: Have every missed call to a marketing number create a callback task on the lead, due in a few minutes and assigned to the next available rep, plus a daily report of missed calls and time to callback.
Missed seller call cost calculator → Video: Missed seller calls →
How do I know which marketing actually makes money?
Count only the deals you keep. Many reports count revenue when a contract is signed, but cancelled contracts and renegotiated fees never come back out, so some campaigns look profitable when they aren't. Kept-deal ROI compares what a campaign cost with the fees you actually received on deals that actually closed. To get there, lead source has to stay attached from first call to closing, and booked revenue and closed revenue have to be separate numbers. Review it every week with a short list of numbers rather than a crowded dashboard.
Do this in your CRM: Add separate booked fee and closed fee fields on the deal, a required fall-out reason, and a report of spend against closed fees by campaign. Check it every Monday.
The Kept-Deal Map → The Monday 5 →
I pull pre-foreclosure, probate and driving-for-dollars lists. How do I stop calling the same owner three times?
Match on the property, not the person. The same owner often shows up on several lists with slightly different names or mailing addresses, so matching on owner name misses duplicates. Standardize the property address before you import (street suffixes, unit numbers, ZIP) and keep one record per property, with every list it came from attached as a source. Add the filing or pull date as a field so the newest records get called first. That stops three people calling one seller with three different stories, and when one of those leads becomes a deal you can see which list produced it.
Do this in your CRM: Use the standardized property address as the duplicate rule on import, store each list as a related source record, and add a filing date field your call queue sorts by.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → CRM field kit →
If my marketing budget went to zero tomorrow, where would my next deal come from?
Start with the leads you already paid for. Most investor CRMs hold sellers who said not now and never got a second or third call. Pull every lead from the last 12 to 24 months that never reached a contract, sort by last contact date, and call the oldest first. Some of those situations have changed since: the tenant left, the repairs got worse, the probate settled. Nobody else is calling them because the list is yours. It isn't free, since it costs rep time, but it's usually the cheapest deal flow you have.
Do this in your CRM: Build a list view of leads with no contract and no activity in 90+ days, sorted by last contact date, and give it to one rep as a weekly call block.
Deal Leak Score → Missed seller call cost calculator →
What is the best CRM for real estate investors?
There isn't one best CRM for everyone. Pick the one your team will actually keep updated, and check that it answers three questions: which marketing campaign produced each closed deal (not just each lead), whether every open lead has a next task with a date, and what each closed deal cost by source without exporting to a spreadsheet. Most investor-specific CRMs, such as REsimpli, InvestorFuse and Podio-based setups, can do all three if they're set up that way. Salesforce makes sense once you run several markets, teams or channels and need reporting and automation the simpler tools can't do; it costs more to set up and needs someone to own it.
Do this in your CRM: Before choosing, run five real leads from first call to closed deal in a trial and check you can answer those three questions at the end.
Deal Leak Score → CRM field kit →
How much should a real estate investor spend on a CRM?
Judge it by cost per closed deal, not by the monthly software price. The subscription is usually the smaller cost; the bigger costs are setup time and the deals that slip through when the CRM isn't used. Spend what it takes to get three things working: every lead keeps its marketing source through to closing, every open lead has a next task, and you can see cost per closed deal by source each month. If a cheaper tool does that and your team uses it every day, it's the right one. Move up to something like Salesforce when several markets or teams need reports or automation the simpler tool can't give you.
Do this in your CRM: Measure one month first: leads in, leads followed up within a day, and leads that became contracts. That tells you what problem the CRM has to solve.
Cost per deal by lead source calculator → Acquisitions team capacity calculator →
After a BRRRR refinance, how do you pay back the new loan?
The refinance doesn't make the debt go away, it replaces it, and the rent pays it back. You buy and rehab with cash or a short-term loan. Once the property is rented and appraised at its new value, a long-term lender gives you a new mortgage, often 70% to 80% of the appraised value for an investment property. That loan pays off the short-term loan and returns some or all of your cash. From then on, the rent covers the monthly payment, taxes, insurance and repairs, and what is left is your cash flow. So the test of a good BRRRR is not only whether you got your cash back, but whether the rent still covers the new payment with room to spare.
Do this in your CRM: Keep purchase, rehab, appraisal, new loan and rent as fields on each property, with cash left in the deal and monthly cash flow as formulas, so every refinance is checked the same way.
BRRRR calculator → DSCR calculator →

## Real Estate CRM for Investors: The Complete Guide (2026)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/real-estate-crm-guide.html

Real estate CRM for investors: the complete guide.
A real estate CRM for investors is the system that tracks every seller, property, offer and buyer and makes sure no lead is forgotten. This guide covers how to choose one, the records and stages it needs, what to automate and connect, the numbers to review weekly, compliance, and a 30-day setup plan, with links to every free tool on this site.
A real estate CRM is the system that holds every seller, property, offer and buyer, and makes sure no lead is forgotten . For investors it replaces sticky notes, spreadsheets and memory.
The parts that matter: a data model built around properties, pipeline stages with rules, automation for follow-up, integrations with your phone and lead sources, and five numbers you review every week.
This guide links every free tool, checklist and deep dive on this site, so you can build or fix your CRM in order.
Contents: What it is Do you need one Types Data model Stages Automation Follow-up Integrations Reports Compliance 30-day setup Mistakes Toolkit
What is a real estate CRM?
A CRM (customer relationship management system) is a database plus rules. For a real estate investor, the database holds sellers, properties, offers, contracts and buyers; the rules decide who calls a lead, when, and what must be captured before a lead moves forward. A real estate agent CRM is built around buyers and listings; an investor CRM is built around motivated sellers, offers and dispositions. That difference is why generic advice often doesn’t fit wholesalers.
When does an investor need a CRM?
When a lead can be forgotten and nobody notices. In practice: more than one person talks to sellers, follow-ups depend on memory, or you can’t say which list paid for your last deal. The 7-sign checklist walks through it, including what a spreadsheet still does well.
What kinds of real estate CRMs are there?
Type | Good at | Watch for
Investor-specific CRMs | Ready on day one: seller fields, stages, often calling and texting built in | Limits on custom data and reports as you grow
General CRMs (HubSpot, Pipedrive and similar) | Clean pipelines, email, easy start | Built for B2B sales; property and offer tracking is on you
Salesforce | Your own data model, deep automation, any report, large integration ecosystem | Needs setup; edition decides what’s possible
Podio and no-code tools | Flexible and cheap to start | Becomes hard to maintain; see moving off Podio
Side-by-side with sources: Salesforce vs investor CRMs · Salesforce vs Follow Up Boss · wholesaling CRM .
What records and fields should a real estate CRM have?
Record | One per | Must-have fields
Lead / Seller | Person who might sell | Lead source (picklist), phone, motivation, timeline, consent and opt-out, next follow-up date, owner
Property | Address | Address, type, beds/baths, condition, ARV, repair estimate, occupancy, list/owner status
Deal (Opportunity) | Property you’re working to contract | Stage, offer amount, MAO, contract price, closing date, exit type, dead reason
Offer | Each offer made | Amount, date, rep, status (so offers made vs signed is reportable)
Buyer | Cash buyer or fund | Buy box (zips, price range, property types), proof of funds, last deal
Campaign | List, mailer, PPC or channel | Spend, dates, channel, so cost per lead and per deal compute
Activities | Call, text, email, task | Outcome (picklist), attempt number, recording link
The full field list with picklist values is in the free CRM field kit . Definitions of every term: wholesaling CRM glossary .
What pipeline stages should a wholesaler use?
Stage | Enters when | Can’t leave without
New | Lead created | First contact attempt logged
Contacted | Talked to the seller | Timeline, reason, condition, next follow-up date
Appointment | Walkthrough or call booked | Date, address confirmed, decision makers known
Offer made | Offer sent | Offer amount, MAO, offer date
Under contract | Seller signed | Contract price, signed contract on file, closing date, title company
Marketing to buyers | Dispo started | Assignment ask, buyers sent
Assigned / Closed | Buyer signed or closed | Buyer, assignment price, fee, exit type
Dead | Any stage | Dead reason (picklist) and a re-contact date if it’s “not now”
Rules like “can’t leave without” are validation rules in Salesforce; most investor CRMs support required fields per stage too. See data quality features . The entry rule, exit rule, owner and time limit for each stage are in wholesaling pipeline stages .
What should a real estate CRM automate?
New lead → assigned owner and a call task due within minutes. Contacting within an hour made firms nearly 7× as likely to qualify a lead .
Missed inbound call → callback task plus a text, if you have consent. Only 2% of unanswered callers leave a voicemail .
No activity in 7 days → follow-up task for the owner.
“Not now” → re-contact date and a long-term cadence, not a dead lead.
Under contract → title task, dispo alert and buyer list match.
Offer above MAO → manager approval.
Duplicate lead → alert and merge, keeping the first source.
Monday → the five KPI numbers emailed to the owner.
Examples in Salesforce: 15 automation recipes for wholesalers .
How much follow-up does a seller lead need?
More than most teams give it. 93% of converted leads were reached by the sixth call attempt in Velocify’s 2012 data, yet half of leads in the same research were never called a second time. Build the cadence into the CRM so it doesn’t depend on memory: follow-up cadence builder · speed to lead guide · all 62 statistics .
What should a real estate CRM connect to?
Tool | Why connect it | Guide
Phone / dialer | Every call and outcome on the lead | Dialers
Texting | Texts in the same timeline; opt-outs respected | Texting and 10DLC
Lead sources | Source on every lead, through to the deal | Lead sources
E-signature | Contracts on the deal | DocuSign
Accounting | Fees invoiced and collected, reportable | QuickBooks
Everything else | Email, files, Slack, maps, scheduling | All integrations
Which numbers should an investor review every week?
Five is enough to run the business: new leads by source, speed to first contact, offers made, contracts signed, and cost per kept deal. Fall-outs come out of the count. More on weekly numbers: the Monday 5 · KPIs in Salesforce · pipeline dashboard · kept deal map .
Calculators: cost per deal · deal analyzer (MAO) · team capacity · missed call cost .
AI on top of the CRM: Salesforce AI and Agentforce for investors .
What compliance rules affect an investor’s CRM?
Texting: app-to-person texts over 10DLC numbers in the US require brand and campaign registration, per Twilio. CTIA’s guidance calls for express written consent for marketing texts and advises against rented, sold or shared lists. Store consent and opt-out on the lead. Texting guide
Calling: keep DNC flags from your list or skip-tracing provider on the record, and make every dialer respect them.
Platform changes: Salesforce’s Open CTI, used by many dialers, reaches end of life on February 28, 2028. Dialer guide
This is not legal advice; state wholesaling and telemarketing rules vary.
How do you set up a real estate CRM in 30 days?
Week 1: Decide the model
Write your stages on one page, with the fields required to leave each one. Pick lead source values. Decide who owns which leads.
Week 2: Build and import
Create fields, stages and rules. Clean and import one list first; the Data Import Wizard handles up to 50,000 records at a time in Salesforce. Check duplicates before the rest.
Week 3: Connect and automate
Phone and texting first, then web forms and lead sources. Turn on the new-lead task, missed-call task and no-activity sweep.
Week 4: Train and measure
Train on the five things each role does daily. Start the Monday review with the five numbers. Fix the field people skip most. See getting your team to use it .
Moving from another system: switching to Salesforce · Podio migration checklist · replacing Zapier chains .
What are the most common real estate CRM mistakes?
Mistake | Fix
Lead source typed as free text | One picklist, set automatically
Leads with no next step | Every open lead has a task with a due date
“Dead” used for “not now” | A not-now status with a re-contact date
Source lost when the lead becomes a deal | Map the source to the deal and keep it to close
Each rep with their own offer math | One MAO formula on the deal
Fall-outs counted as wins | Cancelled contracts out of campaign ROI
Calls logged in the dialer only | Outcome fields on the Salesforce record
Building everything before anyone uses it | Launch the core in 30 days, then add

Questions
What is the best CRM for real estate investors?
It depends on team size and how custom your process is. Investor-specific CRMs are fastest to start; Salesforce fits teams that need their own data model, deep automation and custom reports. Compare on data model, follow-up automation, phone integration and reporting, not feature counts.
What should a real estate investor CRM track?
Sellers with lead source and next follow-up date, properties, every offer, contracts, buyers with buy boxes, campaigns with spend, and every call and text with an outcome.
How is an investor CRM different from a realtor CRM?
A realtor CRM centers on buyers, listings and the sphere of influence. An investor CRM centers on motivated sellers, offers, contracts, dispositions to cash buyers and cost per deal by lead source.
How long does it take to set up a real estate CRM?
A usable core (stages, required fields, lead sources, phone logging and the key automations) can be live in about 30 days. Reports and extra integrations come after the team is using it.
Can a CRM help with speed to lead?
Yes. Automatic assignment and a task due within minutes for every new lead, plus a callback task for missed calls, make response time a process instead of a habit.

## Real Estate Lead Attribution: Which Campaign Gets Credit?
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/real-estate-lead-attribution.html

Which campaign gets credit for the deal? Lead attribution for real estate investors
A seller gets six of your mailers, sees your ad on Google, calls the number on your website and tells your rep, "I got your letter." The deal closes. Which campaign earned it? If you can't answer that the same way every time, your cost per deal by channel is a guess, and so is your marketing budget. This page is for owners and marketing leads at home-buying and wholesaling companies who want a rule they can apply consistently, and the fields and reports that make it work.
Pick one rule and apply it to every deal: credit the campaign that produced the seller's first response, meaning their first inbound call, form, text reply or real cold-call conversation. Record it automatically from the tracking number, form or list, copy it to the deal and lock it. Keep two more fields for context, the latest source that brought them back and what the seller said, and judge channels on deals that actually closed, not contracts.
Why is attribution hard for investors?
Sellers are touched many times before they respond. Several mailers, a few cold calls, a text, maybe a postcard from someone else entirely.
Sellers don't remember. Someone who gets letters from ten investors often can't tell you whose letter they're holding.
Channels overlap. Mail drives people to Google, Google sends them to your site, and your site has its own number.
Deals take months. A lead from January can close in August, after three other campaigns have touched it.
Records get edited. A rep changes the lead source on a deal "to fix it", and the original answer is gone.
None of this has a perfect answer. It has a consistent one, and consistency is what lets you compare channels month to month.
What are the options?
Approach | Credits | Good at | Weak at
First response | The campaign behind the seller's first inbound call, form, text reply or real conversation | Showing which spend starts relationships | Gives no credit to whatever brought a cold seller back later
Latest source | The campaign behind the most recent response before the deal | Showing what makes sellers act now | Undervalues the mail that warmed them up
Seller says | Whatever the seller tells the rep | Color, and catching referrals and signs | Unreliable on its own; "your letter" is a common default answer
Split credit | Several campaigns share each deal | Teams with heavy multi-channel spend and someone to maintain it | Complex, and hard to explain in a Monday meeting
Salesforce can do split credit through its campaign influence features. For most teams of 10 to 50, I'd skip it. A simple rule everyone understands beats a sophisticated one nobody trusts.
The rule I'd use
Credit goes to the campaign that produced the seller's first response. Then lock it.
A seller who calls a direct mail tracking number: that mail campaign.
A seller who fills in a form from a PPC ad: that PPC campaign.
A seller a cold caller actually talked to and qualified: that cold-calling list.
A seller on a list who was mailed and called but never answered, then called in from a bandit sign: the bandit sign. Being on a list isn't a response.
Two things make this work. The source is captured by the system at the moment of response, not typed in by a rep. And once the deal exists, the original source and campaign are copied to it and locked, so nobody can "fix" them later. That's the same rule behind the deal fields in my CRM field kit .
How do you capture the source automatically?
Channel | How the source gets captured
Direct mail | A unique tracking number per campaign (or per list and market), mapped to the campaign in your CRM
PPC and social ads | Tagged landing page links, with the campaign passed into a hidden field on the form, plus a tracking number on the page
Cold calling | The list name on every imported record, and a lead created only when a caller has a real conversation
Texting campaigns | Replies tied to the list and campaign that sent the text
Bandit signs, TV, radio | A dedicated number for each
Referrals and repeat sellers | A required field when a rep creates a lead by hand: who referred them
Organic search and your website | A website tracking number and form source, separate from paid traffic
The tracking number is the backbone. When every campaign has its own number and every number maps to a campaign, most attribution arguments go away. More on the setup in getting every lead source into Salesforce .
The fields to keep
Field | Set by | Used for
Original source and campaign | The system, at first response; copied to the deal and locked | Cost per deal and ROI by channel and campaign
Latest source | The system, every time the seller responds again | Seeing what brings sellers back
Seller says | The rep, from the first conversation | Color, and spotting sources your tracking misses
Market | The system, from the number, form or zip code | Splitting all of the above by market
Re-engaged | The system, when a dead or quiet seller responds again | Counting comebacks separately
If "seller says" disagrees with the original source a lot for one channel, look at that channel's tracking. A mail campaign that sellers keep mentioning but that never shows up as a source usually has a number that isn't mapped.
What about sellers who come back months later?
Keep the original source locked, set the latest source to whatever brought them back, and flag the record as re-engaged. Then decide how long "quiet" has to be before a comeback counts as re-engaged; six months is a reasonable place to start, but pick a number with your team and write it down.
This lets you answer two different questions without arguing: which campaigns start relationships, and which ones bring old sellers back. Follow-up and re-engagement campaigns often look like they produce nothing under a strict first-response rule. The re-engaged flag is how they get seen. If you run reactivation campaigns on purpose, the dead seller leads guide covers the campaign side.
Returning sellers also need to land with the right person. See duplicate sellers in Salesforce for how matching and routing handle that.
The reports that matter
Cost per appointment and cost per contract by campaign , using the original source. This is the budget report.
ROI on kept deals. Profit from deals that actually closed, plus the equity in any house you kept as a rental (after-repair value minus all-in cost), minus spend, divided by spend, by campaign. Contracts that fell apart don't count. This is the last of my Monday 5 numbers, and it's the one I'd look at before changing a budget.
Deals by latest source , next to deals by original source, to see what brings sellers back.
Re-engaged deals by campaign , so follow-up spend gets credit.
Deals with no source , which should be an empty report. If it isn't, fix it before you trust anything above.
Spend has to be on the same campaigns, month by month, and checked against your books. If it isn't, the ROI numbers are wrong however good the attribution is. Why Salesforce numbers don't match covers that side.
Campaign ROI by market and source, checked against the books, is part of what I built for a two-market home-buying company in Ohio. Whatever rule you pick, it has to be applied the same way to every deal, or those numbers aren't worth reading.
Questions
What is lead attribution in real estate investing?
It's the rule for which marketing campaign gets credit for a seller lead and the deal it becomes. Without a consistent rule, cost per deal by channel and campaign ROI can't be compared month to month.
Should wholesalers use first-touch or last-touch attribution?
For most investor teams I'd use a first-response rule: credit the campaign behind the seller's first inbound call, form, text reply or real conversation, and lock it on the deal. Track the latest source separately, so campaigns that bring sellers back still show up.
Should I trust 'how did you hear about us'?
As color, not as the record. Sellers who get mail from many investors often can't say whose letter they're holding. Capture the source from tracking numbers and forms, and keep what the seller says in its own field.
How do I track direct mail ROI?
Give each mail campaign its own tracking number, map the number to the campaign in your CRM, record spend per campaign each month, and report cost per contract and profit on closed deals by campaign.
How do I attribute a seller who comes back a year later?
Keep the original source locked, set a latest source field to whatever brought them back, and flag the record as re-engaged. Report re-engaged deals separately so follow-up campaigns get credit.
What's the difference between lead source and campaign?
Lead source is the channel, like direct mail, PPC or cold calling. A campaign is a specific effort with its own spend, like a July absentee-owner mailer in one market. You need both: source for the big picture, campaign for ROI.
Should marketing ROI count contracts or closed deals?
Closed deals. Contracts that fall apart cost you marketing money and produce nothing. ROI that counts only kept deals shows which channels produce deals that actually close.
Related guides
Want to know which marketing actually pays?
Campaign ROI is the first thing the fixed-price CRM Revenue Audit (USD 1,500) checks: whether every deal carries its source, whether spend matches the books and what your kept-deal ROI really is. It's for teams already on Salesforce. On another CRM? A move to Salesforce can build this in from day one.

## Lead Response Time Statistics (2026): 50+ Sourced Stats
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/real-estate-lead-response-statistics.html

Speed to lead & follow-up statistics for real estate investors (2026).
Speed to lead is the time between a seller reaching out and a real person responding. Below are 62 statistics on lead response, follow-up, missed calls, CRM data and the 2026 investor market, each linked to the page it came from, plus 8 widely quoted “stats” I couldn’t verify.
Jump to: Speed to lead Follow-up Missed calls CRM data 2026 market Channels Myths What it means
Lead response time (speed to lead)
Answering fast is the single most studied lever in lead conversion. The research is old, mostly outside real estate, and still consistent: minutes matter, and most companies are slow.
Statistic | Source | Sample
In an audit of 2,241 US companies, only 37% responded to a web lead within an hour. | Harvard Business Review, “The Short Life of Online Sales Leads” (Oldroyd, McElheran, Elkington) (2011) | 2,241 US companies sent a web-generated test lead
Companies that responded to a web lead within 30 days took an average of 42 hours. | Harvard Business Review, “The Short Life of Online Sales Leads” (Oldroyd, McElheran, Elkington) (2011) | 2,241 US companies sent a web-generated test lead
23% of the audited companies never responded to the web lead at all. | Harvard Business Review, “The Short Life of Online Sales Leads” (Oldroyd, McElheran, Elkington) (2011) | 2,241 US companies sent a web-generated test lead
Firms that contacted a lead within an hour were nearly 7 times as likely to qualify it as firms that waited even one hour longer. | Harvard Business Review, “The Short Life of Online Sales Leads” (Oldroyd, McElheran, Elkington) (2011) | 1.25 million leads across 29 B2C and 13 B2B companies
Those same firms were more than 60 times as likely to qualify a lead as firms that waited 24 hours or more. | Harvard Business Review, “The Short Life of Online Sales Leads” (Oldroyd, McElheran, Elkington) (2011) | 1.25 million leads across 29 B2C and 13 B2B companies
Calling a lead within 5 minutes instead of 30 minutes made the odds of contacting it 100 times higher. | InsideSales.com / Dr. James Oldroyd (MIT Sloan), “Lead Response Management Study” (2007) | 6 companies, 15,000+ leads, 100,000+ call attempts over 3 years
Calling within 5 minutes instead of 30 minutes made the odds of qualifying the lead 21 times higher. | InsideSales.com / Dr. James Oldroyd (MIT Sloan), “Lead Response Management Study” (2007) | 6 companies, 15,000+ leads, 100,000+ call attempts over 3 years
Waiting one hour cut the odds of contact by more than 10 times and the odds of qualification by more than 6 times. | InsideSales.com / Dr. James Oldroyd (MIT Sloan), “Lead Response Management Study” (2007) | 6 companies, 15,000+ leads, 100,000+ call attempts over 3 years
In a 2013 secret-shopper audit, 47% of companies never responded to a web-form lead. | InsideSales.com, “Annual 2014 Lead Response Report” (2014) | 9,538 companies that received a successful form submission (from 14,061 sampled)
Companies that called back took 61 hours on average to place the first call. The median was 3 hours 8 minutes. | InsideSales.com, “Annual 2014 Lead Response Report” (2014) | 2,142 companies that responded by phone
Leads converted at 8 times the rate when worked within 5 minutes than at 6 minutes or later. | InsideSales (XANT), “Lead Response Management 2021” infographic (2021) | 400+ companies, 5.7M leads, 55M+ sales activities over 3 years
Fewer than 1% of lead contact attempts happened within the first 5 minutes, and 57.1% came more than a week after the lead arrived. | InsideSales (XANT), “Lead Response Management 2021” infographic (2021) | ~30M contact attempts by 10,000+ North American users, 2018-2020
Calling a new lead within one minute raised conversion by 391% over calling later. The lift fell to 160% in the second minute. | Velocify (Leads360) lead-conversion study (2012) | ~3.5M leads, 400+ companies, H1 2012
In a secret-shopper test of 74 top US real estate brokerages, 41% never answered a website inquiry. | Roof AI, “Testing response times of the top 74 brokerages” (Test date not given) | 74 brokerages, web-form inquiry
Only 9% of those 74 brokerages (7 firms) replied within 5 minutes, and all 7 had a website chatbot. | Roof AI, “Testing response times of the top 74 brokerages” (Test date not given) | 74 brokerages, web-form inquiry
B2B buyers chose the vendor they first contacted about 80% of the time. In the main survey, 77% of buyers' first vendor conversation was with the eventual winner. | 6sense, “The B2B Buyer Experience Report for 2025” (2025) | ~4,000 B2B buyers (main n=3,744), plus a supplemental n=766
Follow-up and persistence
Most leads get one or two attempts. The data says more attempts, at better times, reach more people.
Statistic | Source | Sample
50% of leads were never called a second time. | Velocify (Leads360) study (2012) | ~3.5M leads, 400+ companies
93% of leads that converted had been reached by the sixth call attempt. | Velocify (Leads360) study (2012) | ~3.5M leads, 400+ companies
Leads that needed 7 or more calls before first contact were 45% less likely to convert than leads reached in 6 or fewer. | Velocify (Leads360) study (2012) | ~3.5M leads, 400+ companies
81% of sellers made 5 or fewer follow-up attempts on a lead. | InsideSales (XANT), “Lead Response Management 2021” (2021) | ~30M attempts, 10,000+ users, 2018-2020
Making 7 or more follow-up attempts produced 15% more connections. | InsideSales (XANT), “Lead Response Management 2021” (2021) | ~30M attempts, 10,000+ users, 2018-2020
The median number of contact attempts on an inbound web lead was 1, and the average was 2.2. | InsideSales.com, “Annual 2014 Lead Response Report” (2014) | 9,538 audited companies
Thursday was the best day to reach a lead, 49.7% better than the worst day (Tuesday). Contact rates were highest from 4-6 pm. | InsideSales / Oldroyd, “Lead Response Management Study” (2007) | 15,000+ leads, 100,000+ dials
Contact rates from 9-10 a.m. were 28.4% higher than the full-day average. | InsideSales (XANT), “Lead Response Management 2021” (2021) | ~30M attempts
Among daily cold callers, the most common connect rate was 11-20% (38% of respondents). Only 5% reported more than 30%. | HubSpot, “2025 State of Cold Calling Report” (2025) | 379 sales professionals, self-reported
Among daily cold callers, 35% said 2-5% of their calls turned into appointments, the most common answer. | HubSpot, “2025 State of Cold Calling Report” (2025) | 379 sales professionals, self-reported
Missed calls and phone answering
Sellers call. If nobody answers, almost nobody leaves a message.
Statistic | Source | Sample
On average, 26% of calls from potential customers went unanswered across industries. | Invoca press release (aggregate customer call data) (2021) | Invoca's aggregate 2021 platform data
Only 2% of callers whose calls went unanswered left a voicemail. | Invoca press release (aggregate customer call data) (2021) | Invoca's aggregate 2021 platform data
Missed-call rates reached 60% in some industries, such as professional services. | Invoca press release (aggregate customer call data) (2021) | Invoca's aggregate 2021 platform data
Missed-call rates varied by industry: 32% in healthcare, 28% in legal, 14% in home services and 9% in real estate. | CallRail small business marketing benchmark report (Business Wire release) (2025) | 1.1M de-identified conversations across 7 industries, including real estate and real estate investment
About 80% of Americans said they generally don't answer cellphone calls from unknown numbers. Only 19% said they do. | Pew Research Center, “Most Americans don't answer cellphone calls from unknown numbers” (2020) | 10,211 US adults, July 13-19, 2020
CRM data quality and selling time
A CRM only helps if the data in it is trusted and reps have time to sell.
Statistic | Source | Sample
76% of CRM users said less than half of their organization's CRM data is accurate and complete. | Validity, “The State of CRM Data Management in 2025” (2025) | 602 CRM users and admins in the US, UK and Australia
37% of respondents said their organization lost revenue as a direct result of poor CRM data quality. | Validity, “The State of CRM Data Management in 2025” (2025) | 602 CRM users and admins in the US, UK and Australia
Companies lost an average of 16 deals per quarter to poor-quality data. | Validity release (2025) | 602 CRM users and admins in the US, UK and Australia
Workers spent an average of 13 hours a week hunting for basic information in the CRM. | Validity release (2025) | 602 CRM users and admins in the US, UK and Australia
37% of CRM users admitted they regularly fabricate data to tell leaders what they want to hear. | Validity release (2025) | 602 CRM users and admins in the US, UK and Australia
The average seller spent only 40% of their time selling. | Salesforce, State of Sales report (7th edition) announcement (2026) | 4,050 sales professionals in 22 countries, Aug-Sep 2025

In the prior edition, reps said they spent 70% of their time on non-selling tasks. | Salesforce, State of Sales (6th edition) stats story (2024) | 5,500 sales professionals in 27 countries, Mar-Apr 2024

56% of US small businesses with fewer than 100 employees did not use a CRM. 39% of those relied on spreadsheets, email and personal productivity tools instead. | Bigin by Zoho CRM + SMB Group, “2023 State of Customer Operations for U.S. Small Businesses” ( (2023) | 1,500 US small businesses
Real estate investing and wholesaling market
The market context for 2026: thinner flip margins, fewer investor purchases, more foreclosures and more wholesaling laws.
Statistic | Source | Sample
297,045 US single-family homes and condos were flipped in 2025, 7.4% of all home sales and the fewest since 2020. | ATTOM, “2025 Year-End U.S. Home Flipping Report” (2026) | National recorded sales
The typical gross flip profit in 2025 was $65,981, down from $77,000 in 2024. | ATTOM, “2025 Year-End U.S. Home Flipping Report” (2026) | National recorded sales
Gross flipping ROI fell to 25.5% in 2025 from 32.1% in 2024, the lowest since 2008. | ATTOM, “2025 Year-End U.S. Home Flipping Report” (2026) | National recorded sales
77,991 homes were flipped in Q2 2026, 6.2% of all home sales, down from 8.0% in Q1 2026 and 7.3% a year earlier. | ATTOM, “Q2 2026 U.S. Home Flipping Report” (2026) | National recorded sales
The typical Q2 2026 flip earned a $60,526 gross profit, a 21.5% gross margin, and took 161 days from purchase to resale. | ATTOM, “Q2 2026 U.S. Home Flipping Report” (2026) | National recorded sales
Investors made 26.7% of US home purchases in Q2 2026 (284,068 homes), the lowest share in five quarters and 22% fewer purchases than in Q2 2025. | BatchData, “Investor Pulse: Q2 2026” (prepared by CJ Patrick Co.) (2026) | 86M+ single-family homes and townhomes, county recordings; preliminary
Investors with 1-10 properties owned about 96% of investor-owned homes. | BatchData, “Investor Pulse: Q2 2026” (prepared by CJ Patrick Co.) (2026) | ~15.9M investor-owned homes
Investors bought 19% of homes sold in Q1 2026 (45,397 purchases across 39 metros), down 6% year over year and the lowest level since 2020. | Redfin, “Investor Home Purchases Fall to Lowest Level Since 2020” (2026) | 39 major metros. "Investor" = any institution or business buyer
Only 5% of US home sellers sold FSBO, an all-time low. 91% used an agent. | NAR, “2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers” (2025) | 6,103 primary-residence buyer responses for transactions Jul 2024 - Jun 2025
Sellers had owned their homes for a median of 11 years before selling, an all-time high. | NAR, “2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers” (2025) | 6,103 primary-residence buyer responses for transactions Jul 2024 - Jun 2025
First-time buyers made up 21% of buyers, the lowest share since NAR began tracking in 1981. Their median age was 40. | NAR, “2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers” (2025) | 6,103 primary-residence buyer responses for transactions Jul 2024 - Jun 2025
41.1% of mortgaged US homes were equity-rich (LTV of 50% or less) in Q2 2026, down from 47.4% a year earlier. | ATTOM, “Q2 2026 U.S. Home Equity & Underwater Report” (2026) | Mortgaged residential properties
227,548 US properties had a foreclosure filing in the first half of 2026, up 21% year over year. That is 1 in every 632 housing units. | ATTOM, “Mid-Year 2026 U.S. Foreclosure Market Report” (2026) | National

Five states enacted six new laws regulating real estate wholesaling in 2025: Connecticut, Maryland (2 laws), North Dakota, Oklahoma and Tennessee. | Leonine Public Affairs, “New State Laws for Real Estate Wholesaling in 2025” (2025) | State legislative tracking
17.43% of surveyed real estate investors named wholesaling as their strategy, compared with 44.08% for buy-and-hold and 38.49% for fix-and-flip. | RCN Capital / CJ Patrick, “Investor Sentiment Survey, Fall 2025” (2025) | Sample size not stated (appears to be about 300)

No aggregate sample given
8 statistics everyone quotes that I couldn't verify
These appear on hundreds of blogs and sales decks. I traced each one and could not find a primary source, or found it was misquoted. Don't repeat them as fact.
“78% of customers buy from the company that responds first.”
Usually credited to a “Lead Connect survey” with no title, year, sample or link. No primary source found. Closest real data: in 6sense’s 2025 B2B survey, buyers chose the vendor they first contacted about 80% of the time.
“35–50% of sales go to the vendor that responds first.”
Credited to InsideSales.com, but it is not in their 2007, 2014 or 2021 studies.
“80% of sales need 5 follow-ups; 2% close on first contact.”
Credited to a “National Sales Executive Association” that VentureBeat found does not exist. Use the Velocify and InsideSales follow-up data above instead.
“44% of salespeople give up after one follow-up.”
No primary source found. Real data: half of leads were never called a second time (Velocify 2012).
“85% of callers who reach voicemail won’t call back.”
Repeated widely with no original survey. Real data: 26% of calls unanswered and only 2% of those callers left a voicemail (Invoca 2021).
“The MIT study: respond in 5 minutes and you’re 100x more likely to close.”
The 100x is the odds of contacting the lead, not closing. And it is InsideSales.com data analyzed by an MIT professor, not an MIT publication.
“The average lead response time is 47 hours.”
A misquote of HBR’s 42 hours.
“Investors buy 1 in 3 homes.”
Out of date. BatchData puts investors at 26.7% of purchases in Q2 2026; Redfin puts it at 19% in Q1 2026 using a different method. Quote one with its source.
What this means for a wholesaling team
1. Measure your own speed to lead
Every study above says minutes matter, and most companies don't know their number. Stamp the time a lead arrives and the time someone actually talks to the seller, and report the gap weekly. The speed to lead guide shows how.
2. Make the sixth attempt automatic
93% of converted leads were reached by the sixth call attempt, yet most leads get one or two. Let the CRM schedule the attempts so persistence doesn't depend on memory. Copy a follow-up cadence .
3. Treat a missed call as a lead, not a voicemail
Only 2% of unanswered callers leave a voicemail. Turn every missed call into a callback task and a text within minutes. See what yours cost with the missed call calculator .
4. Fix the data before buying more leads
76% of CRM users say less than half their data is accurate. Required lead source, next follow-up date and dead reason fix most of it. Use the CRM field kit .
5. Margins are thinner, so every lead counts
Flip ROI fell to 25.5% in 2025, the lowest since 2008, and investor purchases are down. Teams that keep more of the leads they already pay for will outlast teams that just buy more.
How these were checked
Every statistic was read on the linked page in October 2026. Where the original was paywalled or blocked (the HBR article and the Velocify study), I used a contemporaneous report of it and say so. Vendor research (InsideSales, Velocify, Invoca, CallRail, Validity, HubSpot, Carrot, BatchData) is labeled by publisher so you can weigh it. Most lead-response research is not specific to real estate. Spotted an error or a newer source? Email a correction .

## Rental Yield & Cap Rate Calculator (USD, CAD, GBP, EUR)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/rental-yield-calculator.html

Rental yield & cap rate calculator.
Gross yield, net yield, cap rate and cash-on-cash return for any rental or buy-to-let property. Include purchase costs such as closing costs, stamp duty or transfer tax as one figure. Built for real estate investors in the United States, Canada, the UK and Europe. Pick your currency; the math is the same everywhere.
The formula
Gross yield = annual rent ÷ purchase price
Net operating income (NOI) = annual rent × (1 − vacancy) − running costs
Net yield = NOI ÷ (price + purchase costs + renovation)
Cap rate = NOI ÷ purchase price
Cash-on-cash = (NOI − annual mortgage payments) ÷ cash invested
Worked example
A $250,000 property with $10,000 of purchase costs rents for $1,750 a month. Gross yield is 8.40%. Allow 5% for vacancy and $4,500 a year of running costs and the net operating income is $15,450, a 5.94% net yield and a 6.18% cap rate. With a $187,500 repayment mortgage at 5.5% over 25 years ($13,817 a year), cash flow is $1,633 a year on $72,500 invested.
Questions
What is the difference between gross and net rental yield?
Gross yield is the annual rent divided by the purchase price, before any costs. Net yield subtracts running costs and vacancy, and divides by everything you paid including purchase costs and renovation. Net yield is the one to compare properties with.
Is cap rate the same as net yield?
Close, but not the same. Cap rate is net operating income divided by the purchase price only. Net yield in this calculator divides by price plus purchase costs and renovation, so it is usually a little lower. US investors tend to quote cap rate; UK and European investors tend to quote yield.
What is a good rental yield?
There is no single number. Yields depend on the country, city, property type and interest rates. Compare a property against similar rentals in the same area, and check that the cash flow is positive after the mortgage.
Should I include stamp duty or transfer tax?
Yes, in purchase costs. Stamp duty in the UK, land transfer tax in Canada, transfer tax in the US and registration or transfer taxes across Europe all add to what you paid, so they lower your net yield. Rates and surcharges for additional properties vary; check the current rules where you buy.
How do I track yield across a portfolio?
Store rent, running costs, purchase costs and loan terms as fields on each property record in your CRM, with yield and cash flow as formulas. A portfolio report then ranks properties by net yield every month.
Related free tools
BRRRR calculator · DSCR calculator · Cost per deal by lead source · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.

## Your Salesforce Admin Left: A 2-Week Handover Plan
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-admin-left.html

Your Salesforce admin just left. Here are the first two weeks.
This is for the owner or ops lead at a home-buying or wholesaling company whose Salesforce person just quit, gave notice or stopped answering. Salesforce keeps running for a while on its own, which is the dangerous part: the things that break first are the quiet ones, and you usually find out from a seller who never got a callback. Here's what I'd do, in order.
Don't delete or deactivate their user on day one. Freeze it so they can't log in, make sure someone still with you has System Administrator access, and then find everything that runs under their name: flows and their error emails, integrations logged in as them, scheduled reports, records and queues they own. Move those first, then deactivate. Budget about two weeks to do it properly.
What should you do in the first hour?
Four things, and none of them involve changing how Salesforce works yet.
Make sure you still have an admin. Go to Setup, then Users, and look at who has the System Administrator profile. If the person who left was the only one, that's the first problem to fix. Give a second trusted person admin access today. If nobody still with you has it, contact Salesforce Support or your Salesforce account executive now. They'll need to confirm you're authorized for the org before they can help, and that takes time.
Freeze their user. On the user's record there's a Freeze button. It stops them logging in without touching anything they own. More on why not to deactivate below.
Change the shared passwords they knew. Dialer, texting tool, Zapier, the Gmail or Outlook account used for lead notifications, your website forms. In investor companies these are often shared logins, and the admin had all of them.
Check Login History. Setup has a Login History page. If you see their user logging in after they left, or logins from an integration you don't recognize, you know where to look next.
If you're on an investor CRM built on Salesforce, call the vendor too. Ask them, in writing, what they look after and what was your admin's job. Teams often find out at this point that some of the automations were built by their own person on top of the vendor's setup, and the vendor doesn't support those.
Should you freeze or deactivate a Salesforce user who left?
Freeze first. Deactivate later, once you've moved what depends on them.
Freezing only blocks login. Everything they own stays as it is, and every automation that references them keeps working. The catch is that a frozen user still uses a license, so you keep paying for the seat until you deactivate.
Deactivating is where things go wrong if you rush it. Salesforce's own list of things to consider before deactivating a user includes several that hit investor orgs:
You can't deactivate someone who's the only recipient of a workflow email alert, or who's selected in a custom hierarchy field, until you change those.
A dashboard whose running user is deactivated can show unexpected results. If your admin built the owner's dashboard and it runs as them, that's your Monday numbers.
Older Process Builder automations can't update records owned by an inactive user, so any lead or deal still owned by them can quietly stop updating.
Files they uploaded stay owned by them.
If they own more than 10,000 records of one object, Salesforce recommends transferring those before you deactivate.
One more thing people don't expect: deactivating frees the license for someone else, but your bill doesn't go down unless you also lower the number of licenses with Salesforce. If you don't plan to backfill the seat, ask your account executive about it at renewal. That's also a good moment to ask about a discount, which teams can often get depending on the business and the number of users.
What runs under their name?
This is the real work of the first week. Most of what an admin builds keeps running without them, but a lot of it reports to them, logs in as them or is owned by them. Go through each row. If nobody left on your team is comfortable in Setup, hand this table to whoever covers Salesforce next. It's the list I'd work through if I took over your org.
Where to look | Why it matters | What to do
Flow error emails | By default, when a flow fails, Salesforce emails the person who last edited that flow. If that was your admin, failures now go to a dead inbox and nobody hears about them. | In Setup, open Process Automation Settings and send flow error emails to the Apex Exception Email recipients instead. Then add two people who are staying (Setup, Email, Apex Exception Email).
Default Workflow User | Scheduled flows and some time-based steps run as this user. If it's set to your admin, those jobs are tied to a person who's gone. | Change it in Process Automation Settings to an admin who's staying, or to a dedicated automation user.
Integrations | Dialer call sync, texting, DocuSign, QuickBooks, Zapier, Make, your website forms. If any of them connected to Salesforce with your admin's login, they stop the day you deactivate. | List every connected tool and which Salesforce user it signs in as. Move each one to a dedicated integration user. Enterprise and higher editions have included free Salesforce Integration user licenses since 2023, built for exactly this.
Connected apps | Apps your admin authorized can keep a token after they leave. | Check Connected Apps OAuth Usage in Setup and revoke anything you don't recognize.
Scheduled reports and dashboards | Weekly emails to the owner, daily numbers to Slack, a TV dashboard in the office. If they're scheduled by or run as your admin, they break or show the wrong data. | Reassign the running user and the schedule owner. Open each dashboard and check the numbers still look right.
Records, queues and assignment rules | Leads, deals and tasks owned by them. Assignment rules or the default lead owner pointing at them. New leads can land with a user nobody watches. | Use Mass Transfer Records in Setup for leads and accounts, and fix the assignment rule entries and the default lead owner in Lead Settings.
Email alerts and templates | Alerts sent to them alone, or "from" their address. | Point alerts at a role, a queue or a shared inbox instead of one person.
Scheduled jobs and exports | Scheduled Apex and data exports keep running under the user who scheduled them. | Check Scheduled Jobs and Data Export in Setup, and reschedule under someone who's staying.
Company information | If they're the primary contact on the org, Salesforce's security and billing notices go to them. | Update the primary contact in Company Information.
While you're in there, open the Automation app (it's in the app launcher in recent releases). Its Monitor tab lists failed and paused flow runs with the reason, which is the fastest way to see whether anything has already started failing since your admin left.
What breaks first in a home-buying company?
I run the Salesforce for a two-market home-buying company in Ohio. If I left tomorrow, these are the things I'd want the next person to check first, because they run every day, they fail without any noise, and the team notices last:
Missed-call alerts. A seller calls a marketing number, nobody picks up, and the alert that should go to a rep or a Slack channel doesn't fire. You find out when the seller signs with someone else.
Dialer call sync. Calls stop landing on the seller record. Reps keep working, the record goes quiet, and the "no activity in 7 days" list fills with leads that were actually called.
New marketing numbers. The admin was the one who added each new call-tracking number and mapped it to a lead source. Nobody does it now, so new campaigns show up as "unknown" and your cost per contract by source drifts without anyone noticing.
Follow-up that stops on reply. If the text cadence breaks, it either stops for everyone or keeps texting sellers who already answered. The second one is the expensive one.
Contract and closing alerts. Unsigned DocuSign reminders, title and closing tasks, deadline tasks on deals under contract.
New hires. Nobody knows how to set up a new rep: user, permission set, dialer, texting, assignment. The new rep ends up working out of a spreadsheet for two weeks.
For each one, do a live test this week: call a marketing number and let it ring out, text a test lead and reply, create a test lead from your web form. Watching it work is faster than reading how it was built.
What should you ask your admin before they go?
If they gave notice and you're on good terms, pay them for a few hours of handover and record the calls. These are the questions I'd ask, and I'd want my own replacement to ask me the same:
What breaks most often, and what do you do when it does?
What do you check by hand every week that isn't automated?
Which logins, API connections or accounts are in your name?
Which automations are you nervous about, and why?
What's held together with a workaround you meant to fix?
Is anything scheduled to run monthly or quarterly that we haven't seen yet?
Who else has admin access, and why?
Which reports does the owner actually read, and which ones are wrong?
What were you halfway through building?
If you had a week to rebuild one thing, what would it be?
If they've already gone and won't help, don't panic. Everything below can be worked out from the org itself. It just takes longer.
How do you write down what they built?
You don't need a 40-page document. You need enough that the next person can find their way around without guessing. I'd write three things.
1. A one-page map of how a lead moves
From the first call or form to a closed deal: lead sources, how leads are created, how they're assigned, what follow-up runs, what happens at offer, contract, closing and dispo. For each step, note which automation runs and which report shows it. If you use the Kept-Deal Map , its five stages (spend, answer, follow-up, offer, keep) are a good skeleton.
2. A list of every automation
Setup lists every flow. Put each one in a sheet with one line each: what it does, which object it runs on, whether it's active, and who asked for it, if anyone knows. Add every Zap and Make scenario that touches Salesforce, because those don't show up in Setup at all.
3. A record of recent changes, before it disappears
Download the Setup Audit Trail this week. It's the only record of what your admin changed in Setup, and Salesforce only keeps 180 days of it. After that, the history of how your org got this way is gone. It downloads as a CSV from the View Setup Audit Trail page.
Who covers Salesforce now?
Three honest options, and the right one depends on how much changes in your business month to month:
Hire a replacement. Right if you have a full week of Salesforce work every week. Hiring takes time, so plan for a gap. My guide to hiring a Salesforce admin for a real estate team has the job post, ten interview questions and salary data.
A monthly retainer. Right if you have a steady trickle of changes but not a full-time job's worth. It also works as a bridge while you hire. The trade-offs are in hire, freelancer or retainer .
Your ops lead covers it. Fine for small changes, as long as they have a backup and someone checks the automations every month.
Whatever you choose, make it a rule from now on that two people have admin access, and that nothing important runs as one person's login.
The two-week checklist
Copy this into a task list and tick it off.
Day one
A second person who's staying has System Administrator access
Their user is frozen, not deactivated
Shared passwords they knew are changed (dialer, texting, Zapier, notification inbox, web forms)
Login History checked for activity after they left
Vendor called, if you're on an investor CRM built on Salesforce
Week one
Flow error emails go to Apex Exception Email recipients, with two people listed
Default Workflow User changed
Every integration moved to a dedicated integration user
Connected Apps OAuth Usage checked and unknown apps revoked
Scheduled reports and dashboards reassigned, and the numbers checked
Records, queues, assignment rule entries and the default lead owner moved
Email alerts that go only to them pointed somewhere else
Scheduled jobs and data exports rescheduled
Company Information primary contact updated
Live tests: missed call, text reply, web form lead, a test deal moved to closing
Automation app Monitor tab checked for failed flow runs
Week two
Setup Audit Trail downloaded and saved
One-page lead-to-close map written
Automation list written, including Zaps and Make scenarios
Handover questions answered, if they're willing
Decision made on who covers Salesforce now
User deactivated, and the license count reviewed with Salesforce
Questions
Should I freeze or deactivate a Salesforce user who left?
Freeze first. Freezing blocks login without changing anything they own. Deactivate after you've moved their records, integrations, scheduled reports and anything else that depends on their user, because deactivating too early can break dashboards and automations.
Does freezing a Salesforce user free up the license?
No. A frozen user still counts against your licenses. You have to deactivate the user to free the license, and even then your bill only drops if you lower the license count with Salesforce.
Why won't Salesforce let me deactivate a user?
Common reasons are that the user is the only recipient of a workflow email alert, or is selected in a custom hierarchy field. Salesforce's advice is to freeze the user, change or reassign what depends on them, then deactivate.
What happens to flows when the admin who built them leaves?
Most flows keep running. Record-triggered flows run when records change, whoever built them. The risk is that failure emails go to the person who last edited the flow by default, so nobody hears about errors once that inbox is gone. Change the setting in Process Automation Settings.
What happens to the leads and deals the admin owned?
They stay owned by that user until you move them. Use Mass Transfer Records in Setup for leads and accounts, and check your assignment rules and default lead owner so new leads don't keep landing with them.
Can someone take over a Salesforce org they didn't build?
Yes, and it's common. Start with the checklist on this page, then document the org before changing anything. If you're short on time, a retainer admin can do the handover work and keep things running while you decide on a long-term hire.
How long does a Salesforce admin handover take?
For a 10 to 50 person investor team, plan on about two weeks to do it properly: day one for access, week one for everything that runs under their name, week two for documentation. It goes faster if the person leaving helps.
