## Salesforce Admin for Real Estate Investors: Hire or Retainer?
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-admin-real-estate-investors.html

A Salesforce admin for your investor team: hire, freelancer or retainer?
Most home-buying and wholesaling teams of 10 to 50 people reach the same point. Salesforce runs the business, the person who set it up has moved on, and every change now waits on a support ticket or a favor. This page is for the owner or ops lead deciding what to do about it: what an admin actually does in an investor org, the three ways to cover it, and how to tell which one fits. If you decide to hire, it has a job post you can copy, interview questions you can ask without knowing Salesforce yourself, a short paid test for finalists, what admins are paid in 2026 and what their first month should look like.
Signs the admin gap is costing you
You don't need a full-time admin because you're on Salesforce. You need some admin time when changes start piling up. These are the signs I see most:
Changes wait weeks. A new lead source, a new market, a new field for the acquisitions team. Nobody owns it, so it sits.
Automations fail and nobody knows. A missed-call alert stops firing after someone edits a flow, and you find out when a seller says nobody called back.
The dashboard and the bank account disagree. Cost per contract looks fine in Salesforce, but the money doesn't feel that way.
Your ops lead is the admin by accident. They know the most about the CRM, so every request lands on them on top of their real job.
Zapier is doing a lot of the heavy lifting. Every Zap is a thing that can break quietly, and the bill keeps growing.
You're about to grow. New reps, a new market, a new dialer. Every one of those is a set of CRM changes.
If two or three of those sound familiar, the gap is already costing you deals. The question is how to cover it.
What an admin actually does in an investor org
In a home-buying company the work is mostly the same few things, every month:
Area | Typical requests
Lead intake | New marketing numbers and lead sources, web forms, duplicate rules, routing to the right rep or queue
Speed to lead | Missed-call alerts, callback tasks, text follow-up that stops when a seller replies
Acquisitions | Offer fields, appointment outcomes, stale-offer reviews, reassigning leads when a rep leaves
Contract to close | Transaction stages, title and closing tasks, DocuSign status, deadlines
Dispositions | Buyer list fields, buyer tiers, deal blasts, assignment tracking
Reporting | Campaign ROI, cost per contract, the owner's Monday numbers, fixing reports that drifted
Users and access | New reps and VAs, permission sets, turning off people who left
Integrations | Dialer and call logs, texting, DocuSign, QuickBooks, Zaps that need moving to Flows
For a longer list of real requests from one acquisitions team, see 50+ real Salesforce requests from an acquisitions team .
Three ways to cover it
 | Full-time hire | Hourly freelancer | Monthly retainer (fractional admin)
Best when | You have a backlog that fills 40 hours a week, every week | You have one clear project with a start and an end | You have a steady stream of changes but not a full-time job's worth
Knows real estate | Depends who you find; most Salesforce admins have never seen a wholesaling pipeline | Usually not; you explain your process every time | Pick one who does, so you don't pay for the learning curve
Who watches the automations | They do, if it's in the job description | Nobody, between jobs | Should be part of the retainer (see below)
Risk | One person holds everything; when they leave, you start over | Changes with no documentation, made by different people | Retainer that gets used for nothing; fix it with a monthly report
Commitment | Salary, benefits, hiring time | Per job | Month to month
Honest version: if you're under 10 people and nothing changes month to month, you probably don't need any of these. Fix the setup once and leave it. If you're past 40 or 50 people with several markets, a full-time admin starts to make sense, and a retainer can bridge until you find the right one.
What to put on a retainer
A retainer only works if both sides know what "covered" means. This is what I'd put in writing, whoever you hire:
A request queue. One place where requests go, with a status. Not WhatsApp messages to one person.
A monthly check of the automations. Flows, Zaps and integrations that should have fired, checked against what actually happened.
A monthly report. What was asked, what was done, what's next, and anything that looks wrong in the data.
Documentation as you go. Every change gets one line: what, why, who asked. The next admin will thank you.
Response times you can plan around. Something broken that stops leads gets looked at the same day. A new report can wait for the next slot.
Training for new hires. A short walkthrough for every new rep, so they don't end up working out of a spreadsheet.
No long contract. If it isn't worth it, you should be able to stop.
That's how I run Ongoing Support & Development . It's a monthly retainer with no long-term contract.
If you hire someone full time
Good. Hire for your process as much as for Salesforce skill: write the job post around how a lead moves through your business, ask scenario questions about missed calls, duplicates and cost per contract instead of certification trivia, and give your top two candidates a short paid test. A few things that save pain:
Ask them to walk you through how they'd track a lead from a mailer number to a closed assignment. If they can't picture it, they'll learn on your org.
Give them read-only access to a sandbox during the interview and ask what they'd fix first. You'll learn more in 20 minutes than from the CV.
Get the org documented before the handover, not after. If the person who built it is still around, pay them for a week of write-up.
Check that one person isn't the only system administrator. Two people with full access, always.
Hiring well takes time, and Salesforce doesn't wait. A retainer admin can keep things running, handle the handover and get the org documented, so your new hire starts with a clean desk. If your admin has already left, start with the two-week handover plan .
A job post you can copy
Most Salesforce admin job posts are a list of Salesforce features. Write yours around your business instead, and the right people will recognize themselves in it. Replace the parts in brackets.
Salesforce Administrator, real estate investment company ([full time], [remote or city])
About us. We buy houses directly from homeowners in [markets]. We're [number] people across acquisitions, dispositions, transaction coordination and marketing, and Salesforce runs everything from the first seller call to closing.
What you'll own
Lead intake: new marketing numbers, web forms and lead sources, duplicate rules, and routing to the right rep or queue.
Speed to lead: missed-call alerts, callback tasks, and text follow-up that stops when a seller replies.
Deals: offer, contract and closing stages, required dates, and tasks for our transaction team.
Reporting: the owner's weekly numbers, cost per contract by campaign, and fixing reports that drift.
Users: setting up new reps and VAs, permissions, and turning off people who leave on their last day.
Integrations: [dialer], [texting tool], DocuSign, QuickBooks, and moving what still runs in Zapier into Salesforce where it makes sense.
A written log of every change: what, why and who asked.
You have
Two or more years running a Salesforce org day to day, not only project work.
Flow Builder experience, including record-triggered and scheduled flows, and fixing failed runs.
Reports and dashboards, including custom report types.
The habit of testing in a sandbox before you touch production.
Clear writing. You can explain a trade-off to a non-technical owner in two sentences.
Nice to have : experience with real estate investors, wholesalers or another high-volume inbound sales team; [your dialer] or call-tracking integrations; the Salesforce Administrator or Platform App Builder certification.
Pay : $[range] base, plus [benefits]. Hours : [your hours and time zone].
To apply : send your resume and answer this in a few sentences: "A seller calls one of our marketing numbers and nobody answers. What should happen in Salesforce?"
That last question does a lot of the screening for you. People who've run a sales org answer it in terms of records, tasks and reports. People who haven't talk about the phone system.
Put a pay range in the post. Several US states and cities now require one, and it stops you interviewing people you can't afford.
Ten interview questions any owner can ask
You don't need to know Salesforce to run a good interview. Ask about your own business and listen for whether the answer is about records, rules and reports, or about vague promises. I run the Salesforce for a home-buying company in Ohio, so these are the things I'd want my own replacement to know.
Ask the candidate | A strong answer sounds like | Red flag
1. A seller calls one of our marketing numbers and nobody answers. Walk me through what should happen in Salesforce. | A lead is created or matched to an existing one, the source is captured from the number, someone gets a task or alert within minutes, and missed calls show on a report. | Talks only about the phone system, never the record.
2. How would you stop the same seller from being created twice? | Matching and duplicate rules on phone and address, a merge routine, and checks on what web forms and dialers create. | "We clean it up once a month."
3. I want cost per contract by campaign. What do you need to build that? | A campaign or source on every lead, spend entered per campaign per month, contract status on the deal, then a report or dashboard that joins them. | Jumps to a dashboard without asking where spend lives.
4. When would you use a Flow, and when would you call a developer? | Flows for most automation (tasks, alerts, field updates, simple integrations). Code only for heavy logic or volume. Tests in a sandbox first. | Wants code for everything, or has never used a sandbox.
5. We run a lot of Zapier between tools. What would you do with it? | Lists every Zap, moves the ones touching Salesforce data into native Flows where it makes sense, and keeps a record of what still runs outside. | "Zapier is fine," with no inventory.
6. How do you make sure calls and texts from our dialer show up on the seller record? | Checks the integration settings, field mapping and activity owner, then spot-checks real records every week. | Assumes the integration "just works."
7. An acquisitions rep says Salesforce has too many clicks. What do you do? | Sits with the rep, removes fields they don't need, and builds a simpler page or task queue for their role. | Tells the rep to get used to it.
8. What would you check in your first week? | Users and permissions, broken automations and error emails, duplicate counts, and which reports the owner actually reads. | Starts building new things on day one.
9. How do you track a deal from contract to close so nothing slips? | Stages with required dates (inspection, title, closing), automatic tasks per stage, and a report of deals missing a date. | Relies on reps remembering.
10. What do you do with a request from me that would break something else? | Explains the trade-off in plain words, offers an option, documents the change and tests it before release. | Says yes to everything, or no to everything.
Ask four or five of these in a first interview. Save the rest for the finalists, along with the test below.
A paid test for your top two candidates
Ask each finalist to sign up for a free Salesforce Developer Edition org and spend two to three paid hours on this:
Add a field to leads called "Last call result" with the values Answered, No answer and Wrong number.
When it's set to No answer, create a callback task for the lead owner due in 15 minutes, and send the owner a notification.
Build a report of open leads with no activity in the last 48 hours.
Write half a page: what they built, what they'd test before going live, and what could go wrong.
Then have them walk you through it on a call. The write-up tells you more than the build. Anyone can follow a tutorial to make a flow. The candidates worth hiring bring up the edge cases on their own: what happens after hours, what if the lead has no owner, what if the rep is out sick, how to avoid creating three callback tasks for the same lead.
Pay for the test. It's a few hundred dollars, it's fair to the candidate, and it gets you real work instead of a performance.
Last step: have each finalist spend 20 minutes with your ops lead and one acquisitions rep. Those are the people they'll work with every day, and the rep will tell you quickly whether the candidate listens.
What do Salesforce certifications tell you?
The Administrator certification tells you someone studied how Salesforce works and passed an exam. That's worth something. It doesn't tell you whether they've kept a busy org running, handled a broken integration at 8 a.m. or said no to an owner. I hold the Administrator and Platform App Builder certifications myself, and I'd still rather hire someone who can walk me through a real org they've run than someone with more badges.
Treat certifications as a tie-breaker, and the scenario questions and the test as the real interview.
What does a Salesforce admin cost in 2026?
Salesforce Ben pulled together three US salary sources in August 2026. All figures are base salary in US dollars.
Source (2026, US) | Figure | Notes
Mason Frank | $110,000 median | Middle half earns $75,000 to $140,500. Contract admins: $75 to $135 an hour.
Stott and May | $120,000 median | Range of $90,000 to $150,000.
Salesforce Ben survey | $78,000 junior, $92,000 intermediate, $109,000 senior | Medians from a survey of 2,316 people across Salesforce roles.
Add benefits, payroll taxes, equipment and the weeks it takes to hire, and you have the real cost. For many 10 to 50 person investor teams, that number is the reason they use a part-time admin or a retainer instead, at least until the workload proves itself.
Where the person is based matters less than two things: how many of your working hours they overlap with, and whether they've seen a home-buying pipeline before. I work from Cairo during US business hours, so I'm not neutral on the first point. The second is the one I'd weigh more.
Red flags in candidates
Wants to rebuild everything in the first month.
Has never used a sandbox, or thinks testing in production is fine "for small changes".
Can't explain a past change without jargon.
No habit of writing down what they changed.
Answers every scenario with "we'd buy an app for that".
Talks about Salesforce features but never asks how your business works.
What should their first 30 days look like?
Agree on this before they start, so they don't spend a month building things nobody asked for.
Week | Focus | You should see
Week 1 | Access and a look under the hood: users, admin access, failed automations, error emails, integrations, duplicate counts | A short list of what's broken or risky, in plain words
Week 2 | Write it down: a one-page map of how a lead moves, and a list of every automation and Zap | The map and the list, shared with the ops lead
Week 3 | Fix the top three problems from week one | Each fix tested and logged
Week 4 | One improvement the team asked for, plus the first monthly report | What was asked, what was done, what's next
The Deal Leak Score is a good week-one starting point, and the handover plan lists everything that can be running under the previous admin's name.
Questions
Do I need a full-time Salesforce admin for a team of 10 to 50?
Usually not. Most investor teams that size have a steady stream of changes but not 40 hours a week of them. A part-time or retainer admin who knows real estate covers it, as long as automations are checked monthly and changes are documented.
What is a fractional Salesforce admin?
Someone who acts as your admin for part of the month on a retainer: handles requests, watches automations and integrations, keeps reports right and trains new users, without the cost of a full-time hire.
Can my ops manager just be the admin?
They can for small changes, and many do. The risk is that CRM work eats their real job and nobody checks the automations. Give them a backup, even a part-time one.
We're on Podio or REsimpli. Does this apply?
The retainer covers Salesforce orgs. If you're on another CRM and outgrowing it, the first step is a move to Salesforce , which we can scope on a free call.
How much does a Salesforce admin cost in 2026?
US median base salaries for Salesforce admins run about $110,000 (Mason Frank) to $120,000 (Stott and May) in 2026, according to Salesforce Ben's August 2026 roundup. Salesforce Ben's own survey puts juniors at $78,000 and seniors at $109,000. Contract admins charge about $75 to $135 an hour.
Should our Salesforce admin know real estate?
It helps a lot. An admin who has seen a home-buying or wholesaling pipeline already knows what a missed call, a stale offer or a closing deadline costs, so you don't pay for the learning curve. Salesforce skills can be tested; process knowledge is harder to teach.
Is the Salesforce Administrator certification required?
No. It shows someone studied the platform and passed an exam. It doesn't show they've run a busy org. Use scenario questions and a short paid test to judge candidates, and treat certifications as a tie-breaker.
How do I test a Salesforce admin candidate if I don't know Salesforce?
Ask scenario questions about your business, like what should happen when a seller's call goes unanswered, and listen for answers about records, tasks and reports. Then give finalists a short paid task in a free Developer Edition org and have them walk you through it.
Can a VA be our Salesforce admin?
A VA can handle data clean-up, list views and simple report changes with the right permissions. Designing automations, integrations and security needs admin-level skills. If a VA does the day-to-day, have someone with those skills review changes.
What should a new Salesforce admin do in the first week?
Check users and admin access, failed automations and where error emails go, integrations and which user they log in as, duplicate counts, and which reports the owner actually reads. Then write a short list of what's broken or risky before building anything new.

## Salesforce AI & Agentforce for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-ai-agentforce-real-estate.html

Salesforce AI and Agentforce for real estate investors.
Salesforce’s 2026 AI for sales is Agentforce, plus Einstein features like Conversation Insights and Lead Scoring. For real estate investors, the useful parts today are call analysis and activity capture on data you already have; agents that write to sellers need consent rules first. Here’s what each feature does, where it’s available and how to get your CRM ready. Which follow-up jobs to hand to AI first, and the consent rules, are in AI for wholesalers .
Salesforce’s 2026 sales AI is Agentforce : agents for prospecting, lead engagement, pipeline management and coaching. They consume usage-based credits, and Salesforce says to confirm licensing with your account team. source
For investors, the most practical AI is not an agent writing to sellers. It’s call analysis (Einstein Conversation Insights) and activity capture , which work on data you already have. source · EAC
AI on top of messy data repeats the mess. Fix lead source, call outcomes and stages first.
What AI does Salesforce Sales Cloud offer in 2026?
Feature | What it does | Availability (per Salesforce Help)
Agentforce Prospecting | Builds a prioritized list of contacts and accounts for reps | Usage-based credits; confirm with account team
Agentforce Engagement (formerly Lead Nurturing) | Web chat to leads and email nurturing via Outlook or Gmail | Enterprise, Performance or Unlimited with Sales and Einstein for Sales
Agentforce Sales Management | Pipeline and account management assistance | Usage-based credits
Agentforce Sales Coach | Real-time feedback and role-play | Usage-based credits
Einstein Conversation Insights | Analyzes recorded calls for keywords, mentions and next steps; connectors include RingCentral, Dialpad and Aircall | Starter, Pro, Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, Agentforce 1 Sales
Einstein Lead Scoring | Scores leads from your past conversions, refreshed every 10 days | Needs Sales Cloud Einstein
Einstein Activity Capture | Syncs email and calendar activity to Salesforce | Standard in Starter through Enterprise
Sources: Sales Cloud agents · Agentforce Engagement · Conversation Insights · Lead Scoring · Activity Capture . In June 2025, Agentforce 1 editions replaced Einstein 1 editions. source
Which AI uses actually help a wholesaling team?
Call review at scale
Conversation Insights can flag calls where sellers mention keywords you choose, like foreclosure, probate, divorce or a deadline. A manager reviews the flagged calls instead of random ones.
Lead scoring, once you have history
Einstein Lead Scoring learns from your past converted leads. A team with few closed deals gets a weak model; Salesforce uses a global model when you lack data. source
Summaries for the handoff
Summaries of long seller conversations help acquisitions pick up where the caller left off. The structured fields (timeline, reason, condition) still matter more; see the handoff checklist .
Careful with agents that write to sellers
An agent emailing or texting sellers is still marketing outreach. Consent, opt-outs and tone apply, and CTIA’s guidance calls for express written consent for marketing texts. source See the texting guide .
Is your CRM ready for AI?
Check | Why
Lead source is a picklist, set automatically | Scoring and attribution learn from it
Calls are recorded and logged to the lead | Conversation analysis needs the recordings on the record
Stages have entry rules | Otherwise the model learns from inconsistent stages
Dead reasons are required | So the model can tell bad leads from bad follow-up
Enough closed deals | Scoring from your own history needs history
Score your setup in two minutes with the Deal Leak Score .
Questions
What is Agentforce in Salesforce?
Agentforce is Salesforce’s family of AI agents. In Sales Cloud they include Prospecting, Engagement (lead nurturing), Sales Management and Sales Coach, billed with usage-based credits.
Can Salesforce AI analyze my acquisition calls?
Einstein Conversation Insights analyzes recorded calls for keywords and next steps, with voice connectors including RingCentral, Dialpad and Aircall.
Should an AI agent text or email my sellers?
Only with consent and opt-outs in place. Marketing messages to sellers are still marketing, and CTIA’s guidance calls for express written consent for marketing texts.
Do I need clean data before using Salesforce AI?
Yes. Scoring and analysis learn from your fields; free-text lead sources, unlogged calls and inconsistent stages produce unreliable results.

## How to Know When Salesforce Automations Fail (and Zaps)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-automation-monitoring.html

Your automations fail quietly. Here's how to find out before a seller does.
In an investor company, automations do the work nobody remembers to do: the callback task after a missed call, the text that stops when a seller replies, the reminder about a contract nobody signed. When one of them breaks, nothing looks wrong. The CRM still opens, the dashboards still load, and leads quietly stop getting followed up. This guide is for owners and ops leads who want to know about a failure the day it happens, not a month later.
Send flow error emails to two people through the Apex Exception Email list, instead of the default of whoever last edited the flow. Check the Automation app's Monitor tab every week for failed and paused flow runs. Turn on Zapier's error notifications, and remember Zapier switches a Zap off by itself when 95% of its runs in the last seven days errored. Then add heartbeat reports: daily counts of things that should always happen, like calls logged and tasks created, so you notice when one drops to zero.
Why do automations break?
Almost never on their own. Something around them changes:
Someone renames a picklist value, and the flow that checks for the old value never fires again.
A new validation rule stops the flow from saving the record it's updating.
The user an integration logs in as is deactivated, or their password expires.
A texting or dialer vendor changes how their integration works.
A Zapier plan hits its limit. At the company I work with, that's what pushed us to move Zaps into Flows.
Volume jumps after a big mailer, and an automation that worked at 50 leads a day struggles at 500.
Notice that most of these follow a change someone made on purpose. That's why a change log is part of monitoring, not paperwork.
The three kinds of failure
Kind | Example | How you find out
Loud | A flow throws an error when it runs | An error email, if it goes to someone who reads it
Logged | A flow run fails or pauses; a Zap run errors | Only if someone looks at the logs
Silent | The flow never fires because its conditions stopped matching | Only by noticing that something which should happen every day didn't
If error emails are all you have, you only cover the first kind, and only when they reach someone.
Who gets the error emails?
By default, when a flow fails, Salesforce emails the person who last modified that flow. In practice that's whoever built it, often a consultant who's gone or an admin who left. The errors go to an inbox nobody reads.
Fix it in two places in Setup:
Process Automation Settings : set "Send Process or Flow Error Email to" to the Apex Exception Email recipients instead of the last person who modified the flow.
Apex Exception Email (under Email in Setup): add the people who should get them. You can add Salesforce users and outside email addresses, so a shared ops inbox works.
Put two people on the list, so a vacation doesn't mean a week of unread failures. Do the same in Zapier and in each integration's own settings: error notifications should go to a person who's still with you and who knows what to do with them.
Where do you look for failures?
Salesforce: the Automation app
Recent Salesforce releases include an Automation app, in the app launcher. Its Monitor tab lists failed and paused flow runs with the reason for each, and from there you can debug a failed run or resume a paused one. Check it weekly. A run that failed on Tuesday is a seller who didn't get a task on Tuesday.
Zapier: Zap history
Errored runs show up in Zap history. Zapier also turns a Zap off automatically if 95% of its runs in the last seven days errored. That protects your account, but it means a Zap that's been failing for a week can simply stop, and the leads it was supposed to create stop with it. Whether you get an email depends on your notification settings, so check them.
Your integrations
Dialer, texting, DocuSign and accounting integrations usually have their own sync logs or error pages. Know where each one is, and look at them when a heartbeat number drops.
How do you catch the silent failures?
With heartbeat reports: daily counts of things that should always happen in a working day. If one drops to zero, or far below normal, something broke even if no error was raised.
Heartbeat | What a drop usually means
New leads yesterday, by source | A form, number or integration stopped creating leads
Calls logged yesterday | The dialer sync stopped
Tasks created by automation yesterday | A follow-up flow stopped firing
Missed-call alerts sent yesterday | The alert broke, or nobody missed a call (rare)
Texts sent, and cadences stopped by a reply | The texting integration or the stop rule broke
Deals that changed stage this week | Stage updates from DocuSign or the team stopped
Put them on one dashboard, or better, post them to a Slack channel every morning so people see them without opening Salesforce. Daily numbers in Slack are part of the setup I run, and a zero in the morning post is hard to miss.
The 15-minute weekly check
Automation app, Monitor tab: any failed or paused runs this week?
Flow error emails: anything new in the shared inbox?
Zap history: any errored runs, and are all the Zaps that should be on still on?
Heartbeat dashboard: anything at zero or far below normal?
Integration sync logs: dialer, texting, DocuSign, accounting
Leads with no owner or owned by inactive users: zero?
Change log: what changed this week, and did anything break after it?
The monthly tests
Once a month, walk the paths that make money and watch each automation fire:
Call a marketing number and let it ring out. Did the lead, the alert and the callback task appear?
Submit each web form. Right source, market and owner?
Reply to an automated text from a test number. Did the cadence stop?
Move a test deal to under contract. Did the transaction tasks appear?
Send a test DocuSign envelope and leave it unsigned. Did the reminder fire?
Set up a test user the way you would a new rep. Does assignment pick them up?
Delete the test records afterwards. It should take under an hour, and it's the only way to be sure the silent failures aren't happening.
If a notification misfires and you need to stop it fast, it helps when ops can switch it off without editing the automation. I build that with a configuration object , a settings record that turns individual notifications and rules on or off.
Keep a change log
Every change to an automation, field, picklist or integration gets one line: date, what changed, why and who asked. When a heartbeat drops, the first question is "what changed?", and the log answers it in seconds.
Salesforce keeps its own record of setup changes in the Setup Audit Trail, but only for 180 days. Download it regularly if you want the history.
Monthly monitoring with a short written report is part of what I do on Ongoing Support & Development : what failed, what was fixed, what was tested and what changed.
Questions
Who gets Salesforce flow error emails?
By default, the person who last modified the flow. You can change it in Process Automation Settings so errors go to the Apex Exception Email recipients instead, and then list who should get them under Apex Exception Email in Setup.
Can flow error emails go to an address outside Salesforce?
Yes. The Apex Exception Email list accepts Salesforce users and external email addresses, so you can send flow errors to a shared ops inbox.
How do I see failed flows in Salesforce?
Open the Automation app from the app launcher and go to the Monitor tab. It lists failed and paused flow runs with the reason, and lets you debug a failed run or resume a paused one.
Why did Zapier turn off my Zap?
Zapier turns a Zap off automatically if 95% of its runs in the last seven days errored. Check Zap history for the errors, fix the cause, then turn it back on and check that the runs it missed are handled.
What is a heartbeat report?
A daily count of something that should always happen, like calls logged, leads created or tasks created by automation. When the count drops to zero or far below normal, something broke, even if no error was raised.
How often should we check our Salesforce automations?
A 15-minute check every week (failed runs, error emails, Zap history, heartbeat numbers) and a test of the money-making paths every month: a missed call, each web form, a text reply, a deal moving to contract.
Related guides
Sources
Checked in October 2026. Salesforce and vendor features change with each release, so check the linked page before you rely on a detail.

Milestone: Spring '25 release notes . The Automation app and its Monitor tab
Zapier: error handling . Zap history, notifications, and the automatic turn-off at a 95% error ratio over seven days
Gearset: Salesforce audit trail . 180 days of setup history

## 15 Salesforce Automations for Wholesalers (Recipes)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-automation-recipes-wholesalers.html

15 automation recipes for a wholesaling CRM.
The automations that pay off first in a wholesaling CRM are a call task for every new lead, a callback for every missed call, required fields before a lead is passed, and long follow-up for “not now” leads. Here are 15 recipes written as trigger → action, which Salesforce tool to use for each, and the order to build them.
These are the automations I’d build first for a wholesaling team, written as trigger → action so you can hand them to whoever builds your CRM.
Count them before you pick an edition: Salesforce Professional allows 5 flows; Enterprise allows 2,000 active. source · source
Several are better as validation rules, approval processes or dashboard subscriptions than as flows.
15 automations for a wholesaling CRM
Automation | Trigger | Action | Fixes | Salesforce tool
New lead → owner and call task | Lead created | Assign by market or round robin ; create call task due in 5 minutes; alert owner | Speed to lead | Record-triggered
Missed inbound call → callback | Call logged with outcome = missed, direction = inbound | Task due in 10 minutes for lead owner; if consented, send text | Missed calls | Record-triggered on Task
No activity in 7 days | Daily at 7am: open leads with last activity > 7 days | Follow-up task for owner; after 3 sweeps, flag for manager | Follow-up | Schedule-triggered
“Not now” → re-contact date | Status changes to Not now | Require re-contact date; create task on that date; enroll in long cadence | Long follow-up | Record-triggered
Warm/hot handoff check | Status changes to Warm or Hot | Block save without timeline, reason, condition, callback time (validation rule); task for acquisitions due same day / within 1 hour | Handoff | Validation rule + record-triggered
Offer above MAO → approval | Offer amount > MAO on the deal | Route to acquisitions manager for approval before status can be Sent | Offer discipline | Flow Approval Process
Offer expires | Daily: offers sent > 5 days with no response | Task to follow up; mark expired after 14 days | Offers | Schedule-triggered
Signed contract → under contract | Signed document written back by e-signature tool | Stage = Under contract; task for TC; post to #dispo | Contract to dispo | Record-triggered
Under contract → buyer match | Stage = Under contract | Create Deal Sent records for top 10 matching buyers; task for dispo | Dispo speed | Record-triggered
Closing date in 3 days | Daily: deals closing in 3 days | Checklist task for TC (title, funds, buyer confirmation) | Closing | Schedule-triggered
Deal dies → reason and source kept | Stage = Dead | Require dead reason; if “not now”, create re-contact date | Clean ROI | Validation rule + record-triggered
Fall-out → out of ROI | Contract cancelled | Uncheck “counts in ROI”; notify owner; reopen lead with reason | Honest reporting | Record-triggered
Duplicate seller → merge task | Duplicate rule alert on new lead | Task to merge; keep first lead source | Data quality | Duplicate rule + task
Proof of funds stale | Daily: buyers with POF date > 90 days | Task to request a new POF | Dispo | Schedule-triggered
Monday numbers | Monday 7am | Dashboard emailed to owner and managers | Weekly review | Dashboard subscription
Flow, validation rule or approval: which tool for which job?
Job | Tool | Why
Stop bad data being saved | Validation rule | Enforced everywhere, including imports and integrations
React to a change | Record-triggered flow | Runs when a record is created, updated or deleted
Sweep records on a timetable | Schedule-triggered flow | Runs at set times on batches of records
Guide a rep through a script | Screen flow | Shows only the questions that apply
Manager sign-off | Flow Approval Process | Multistep approvals with work items; Enterprise and up
Sources: Flow types · Flow Approval Processes .
Which automations should you build first?
Week 1
New lead task, missed call callback, warm/hot validation. These protect the leads you already pay for. See speed to lead and the handoff checklist .
Week 2
No activity sweep, not-now re-contact, dead reason. These protect the long follow-up where most conversions happen .
Week 3
Contract to dispo, buyer match, closing checklist. These shorten days to assignment.
Week 4
Offer approvals, fall-outs out of ROI, Monday dashboard. These make the numbers honest.
What goes wrong with CRM automation?
Building automations before the fields are clean: a flow that reads a free-text lead source does nothing useful.
Too many alerts: if every change pings someone, people mute them. Alert on exceptions only.
No owner: every automation should have a person who gets told when it fails.
Overlapping tools: a Zapier chain and a flow both creating tasks doubles the work. See replacing Zapier chains .
Questions
What should a wholesaler automate first in a CRM?
The new-lead call task, a callback task for missed calls, and required fields before a lead is marked warm or hot. They protect leads you already paid for.
How many flows can Salesforce Professional run?
Salesforce’s Professional Edition allocation page lists 5 flows. Enterprise and Unlimited allow 4,000 total and 2,000 active.
Should required fields be a flow or a validation rule?
A validation rule. It blocks the save everywhere, including imports and integrations, and can be conditional on stage or status.

Salesforce Help: Flow types
Salesforce Help: Professional Edition allocations
Salesforce Help: Enterprise Edition allocations
Salesforce Help: Flow Approval Processes

## Salesforce CRM for Canadian Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-consultant-canada-real-estate.html

Salesforce for Canadian real estate investors: the same deal system, set up for Canadian rules
I build Salesforce for home-buying companies and wholesalers. If you run an investing business in Canada, two questions matter before anything else: does the same system work there, and what has to change? This page answers both, for owners of home-buying, wholesaling and BRRRR businesses. I work remotely, and Eastern and Central business hours fall inside my working day.
The core system is the same: every seller lead answered fast, offers on the deal record, a pipeline to closing, and ROI counted on deals that actually closed and properties you keep. What changes in Canada is mostly consent. Calls fall under the CRTC's telemarketing rules and the National Do Not Call List, and texts and emails under CASL, so the CRM should record consent, do-not-call status and unsubscribes for every person. Set CAD as the currency, put the province on every lead and deal, and get each province's assignment and wholesaling rules from a local lawyer.
What stays the same as a US home-buying team?
The deal flow doesn't change at the border. A Canadian team still needs:
Every seller lead captured with its source. Calls and forms create leads on their own, and every missed call becomes a callback task. See missed-call alerts in Salesforce .
Offers made from the same numbers. After-repair value, repairs and maximum offer on the deal record, not in separate spreadsheets. The deal analyzer shows the math.
A pipeline from first call to closing , with a board for every deal under contract. See transaction coordination in Salesforce .
Buyers stored with the areas and property types they buy , so a new deal goes to the right people first. See dispositions in Salesforce .
ROI by campaign on deals that actually closed , with one consistent rule for which campaign gets credit. See lead attribution for investors .
The full picture of how a home-buying company runs on Salesforce is in my Salesforce for real estate investors guide. The rest of this page is what's different in Canada.
Cold calling: the CRTC rules and the National Do Not Call List
If your team calls homeowners, plan for the CRTC's Unsolicited Telecommunications Rules to apply, and confirm with a lawyer how they apply to your calls. According to the CRTC:
Telemarketers must register with the National Do Not Call List (DNCL), even for exempt calls. Anyone making calls that aren't exempt must also subscribe to the list while calling, and must not call numbers on it.
Calls are allowed from 9:00 a.m. to 9:30 p.m. on weekdays, and from 10:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. on weekends.
Telemarketers must keep their own do-not-call list, add a request within 14 days, and keep the number on it for 3 years and 14 days.
Callers must clearly identify themselves.
What that means in the CRM:
Every imported list is screened before it's loaded, and each phone number carries the date it was checked and the result.
An internal do-not-call flag follows the person across every record, including duplicates. See duplicate sellers in Salesforce .
Your dialer's calling windows follow the seller's province and time zone.
A report of calls to flagged numbers, which should always be empty.
Texts and emails: what CASL means for your CRM
Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation (CASL) covers commercial electronic messages: messages where one of the purposes is to get the recipient to do business with you. That includes email, texts and direct messages on social platforms. According to the CRTC's CASL guidance, each one needs consent, identification of the sender and a way to unsubscribe.
Express consent doesn't expire, though people can withdraw it at any time. Implied consent lasts for set periods, such as six months after an inquiry or two years after a purchase.
Unsubscribe requests must be processed without delay, and within 10 business days.
The sender has to prove consent, so keep the record for as long as you contact the person.
The maximum penalty per violation is $1 million for an individual and $10 million for a business.
In the CRM, that means a consent record on every person, with the type (express or implied), the date and where it came from; unsubscribes that stop every cadence at once; and texting through a tool that logs to Salesforce, never from a rep's own phone. My texting in Salesforce guide is written for US rules, so read its compliance notes with CASL in mind. None of this is legal advice.
Privacy
Personal information about sellers and buyers falls under Canada's private-sector privacy law, PIPEDA, or under a provincial law in Alberta, British Columbia and Quebec. For the CRM, the practical side is the same everywhere: collect what you need, limit who can export it, and be able to find and delete a person's information when you're asked to. Only owners and ops should be able to export lists. See VA access in Salesforce for how to limit what callers see.
Currency, provinces and time zones
Currency. Set the org's corporate currency to CAD. If you buy on both sides of the border, Salesforce's multiple currencies feature lets each deal carry its own currency. Once it's turned on it can't be turned off, so decide before you build.
Province on everything. Every lead, deal and campaign carries its province, with the city or market under it, so every report splits by province. My new market checklist covers the rest of a launch.
Time zones. Canada spans six of them. Route leads by province, and set callback due times and calling windows in the seller's local time.
Assignment and wholesaling rules. They differ by province, and some have changed recently. Track the province on every deal, record any disclosure or deadline your lawyer says applies, and report on deals missing it. The approach is the same one I describe for US states in tracking wholesaling rules in your CRM .
BRRRR investors: count the properties you keep
If you run BRRRR and keep properties as rentals, an ROI report that only counts assignment fees makes the campaigns that found your rentals look worse than they are. The ROI in my Monday 5 adds the equity in the houses you keep for exactly this reason. Flag kept deals, give each one an equity value (after-repair value minus all-in cost), and include them in campaign ROI. The BRRRR calculator and the rental yield and cap rate calculator both work in CAD.

On Podio, REsimpli, GoHighLevel or spreadsheets? The audit isn't for you. The next step is a free call about a move to Salesforce , and the free CRM field kit works in any CRM in the meantime.

Ask a lawyer how they apply to your calls, and set up the CRM for them either way. ## Salesforce CRM for UK Property Investors & Deal Sourcers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-consultant-uk-estate-agents.html

Salesforce for UK property investors and deal sourcers: the same deal system, set up for UK rules
I build Salesforce for property businesses that buy direct from owners. If you run an investing or deal sourcing business in the UK, two questions matter before anything else: does the system fit how you work, and what has to change? This page answers both, for buy-to-let, HMO and BRR investors, deal sourcers and packagers. I work remotely, and UK afternoons sit inside my working day.
The core is the same as for a US home-buying company: every vendor lead answered fast, offers and their numbers on the deal record, investors matched to the right deals, and ROI counted on deals that actually complete. What changes in the UK is the stages and the consent rules. Build the pipeline around offer accepted, solicitors instructed, searches, mortgage offer, exchange and completion. Screen cold-call lists against the TPS, get consent before marketing texts and emails, and record all of it in the CRM. Set GBP as the currency, and track sourcing fees from invoice to payment.
What stays the same?
Whether you buy for your own portfolio or source for investors, the system underneath is the one a US home-buying company runs:
Every vendor lead captured with its source , from letters, leaflets, portals, PPC and referrals, and every missed call turned into a callback task. See missed-call alerts in Salesforce .
Offers and the numbers behind them on the deal record , so you can see why a deal was won or lost, instead of digging through WhatsApp.
One rule for which campaign gets credit when a vendor has had three letters and a leaflet. See lead attribution for investors .
ROI counted on deals that complete , not offers accepted.
The full picture is in my Salesforce for real estate investors guide. It's written in US terms, so read "seller" as vendor and "closing" as completion.
A pipeline from offer to completion
UK deals move through stages a US template doesn't have. A pipeline that fits:
Stage | What the CRM should hold | Alert when
New lead | Vendor, property, source, motivation, timescale | No contact within your time limit
Viewing booked | Date, who's going | A viewing with no notes the next day
Offer made | Amount, how it was worked out, date | No answer after a few days
Offer accepted | Agreed price and date | Solicitors not instructed within your limit
Solicitors instructed | Both firms and contacts | No update for a set number of days
Searches and survey | Dates ordered and returned, survey result | Searches overdue
Mortgage offer, if any | Lender and offer date | Offer date approaching its expiry
Exchange | Exchange date and deposit | Target exchange date passed
Completion | Completion date, final price, fee or profit | Completion date passed with no update
Every deal that falls through gets a reason from a fixed list, so you can see whether deals die at searches, survey, finance or with the vendor. If you buy in Scotland, the process is different, with missives instead of exchange, so give it its own pipeline. How the contract-to-completion side runs day to day is in transaction coordination in Salesforce .
Deal sourcing: investors, packs and fees
If you source deals for investors, the CRM has a second side, much like dispositions in a US wholesaling business:
Investors stored with what they buy: strategy (buy-to-let, HMO, BRR, serviced accommodation), areas, budget, and cash or mortgage.
Every deal pack logged against the investor and the deal, so you can see who's had it and who replied.
Matching. A new deal goes first to investors whose areas, strategy and budget fit, ranked by what they've already bought from you. See dispositions in Salesforce .
Sourcing fees tracked from agreement to invoice to payment, with the date each step happened.
Check whether your business needs to register with HMRC for anti-money laundering supervision and join a property redress scheme. In December 2025, The Negotiator reported industry research finding that almost all property-sourcing agents were breaching anti-money laundering rules. Whatever applies to you, the CRM is where the ID checks and the records should live, so you can show them when asked.
Cold calling: the TPS
Treat calls offering to buy someone's property as marketing calls unless an adviser tells you otherwise. Under the ICO's guidance on the Privacy and Electronic Communications Regulations (PECR):
Don't make live marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) unless the person has agreed to your calls, and screen your call lists against it.
Keep your own do-not-call list of people who object or opt out, and screen against that too.
Always say who's calling, and let your number display.
Automated, recorded marketing calls need consent that specifically covers them.
What that means in the CRM:
Every list is screened before it's loaded, and each number carries the date it was checked and the result.
An objection flag follows the person across every record, including duplicates. See duplicate sellers in Salesforce .
A report of calls to flagged numbers, which should always be empty.
Texts and emails: PECR
The ICO says you must not send marketing texts or emails to individuals without specific consent. The soft opt-in covers existing customers who bought, or negotiated to buy, something similar from you, so it won't usually cover a vendor you've never dealt with. Every message has to say who it's from and give a simple way to opt out, and people who opt out go on a suppression list.
In the CRM, that means consent recorded with the date and where it came from, opt-outs that stop every automation at once, and texts sent through a tool that logs to Salesforce, never from someone's own phone. None of this is legal advice.
UK GDPR
UK GDPR covers the personal data you hold on vendors and investors. The CRM side is practical: record where each person's details came from, limit exports to owners and ops, decide how long you keep dead leads, and be able to find, export or delete one person's data when they ask. Get the details from a data protection adviser. For limiting what callers and VAs can see, see VA access in Salesforce .
GBP, areas and portals
Currency. Set the org's corporate currency to GBP. If you also buy abroad, Salesforce's multiple currencies feature lets each deal carry its own currency. It can't be turned off once enabled, so decide before you build.
Areas. Store the postcode district on every lead, deal and investor. It's the simplest key for matching deals to investors and splitting reports by area.
Sources. Give each letter campaign, leaflet drop, portal and PPC campaign its own tracking number or landing page, so every lead arrives with its source.
Tax and legal figures. I don't give tax or legal advice. If you want stamp duty or other figures in your reports, store the numbers your accountant gives you on the deal.
How working together works

On another CRM, or spreadsheets? The audit isn't for you. The next step is a free call about a move to Salesforce , and the free CRM field kit works in any CRM in the meantime.
Need someone to run it? Ongoing Support & Development is a monthly retainer with no long-term contract.

## Salesforce Dashboard Numbers Wrong? 10 Causes and a Fix
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-dashboard-wrong-numbers.html

Your Salesforce dashboard and your bank account disagree. Here's why.
Every owner I talk to has a version of this: the dashboard says cost per contract is fine, but the money doesn't feel that way. Or the report says 14 contracts last month, the acquisitions manager says 17 and the title company closed 11. This page is for owners and ops leads at home-buying and wholesaling companies who want numbers they can make decisions on. It covers the ten causes I see most in investor orgs, how to check each one, and a 20-minute check you can run this week.
Most mismatches come from a handful of causes: lead source and market not carried over when a lead becomes a deal, reports counting by different date fields, report types that leave records out, dashboards running as a user who can't see everything or showing data from the last refresh, and spend in Salesforce that doesn't match what accounting paid. Fix the definitions first (what counts as a contract, and by which date), then reconcile one month against your books, record by record.
Ten reasons your Salesforce numbers don't match
Starting with the ones I'd check first.
1. Source and market get lost when a lead becomes a deal
When a lead is converted, Salesforce copies standard fields like Lead Source to the new records automatically. Custom fields don't carry over unless someone maps them. If your market, campaign, channel or tracking number live in custom fields, the deal can arrive with them blank, and your "unknown" bucket grows every month.
Check: run a report of deals created last month grouped by source and market. If "blank" or "unknown" is more than a sliver, this is your problem. Fix: map the custom lead fields to the matching deal fields in the lead field mapping settings, then fix the past records with a one-time update.
2. Two reports count by different dates
"Contracts this month" can mean deals created this month, deals that reached the contract stage this month, or contracts signed this month. Three reports, three answers, all technically right.
Check: open each report and look at which date field the time filter uses. Fix: agree on one date per number (contracts by contract signed date, closings by closing date) and use it everywhere. See the definitions below .
3. The report type leaves records out
A custom report type can be set so that each record must have at least one related record, or so that related records are optional. If a "Leads with Activities" style report requires activities, every lead nobody has touched yet disappears from it, which is exactly the lead you most want to see.
Check: look at the report type's settings for the "at least one related record" option. Fix: use a type where related records are optional. To find records missing something, use a cross filter such as "Accounts without Opportunities". A report can have up to three cross filters.
4. The dashboard runs as someone else
Salesforce's own rule: folders control who can open a dashboard, but the running user determines what data it shows. If the dashboard runs as a rep, it may only count that rep's records. If it runs as an admin, everyone sees everyone's numbers, which may not be what you want either.
Check: the "view dashboard as" setting on the dashboard. Fix: pick a running user who can see all the records the dashboard is meant to count. Dynamic dashboards, which show each viewer their own data, are limited by edition: 5 in Enterprise and 10 in Unlimited and Performance.
5. The dashboard hasn't refreshed
A report shows live data when you open it. A dashboard shows data as of its last refresh, and the time is printed at the top. On a Monday morning, last Friday's dashboard and today's report won't agree.
Fix: refresh before you read it, or schedule a refresh before your weekly meeting.
6. Filters and scope
One report shows "my leads", another shows "all leads". One excludes dead leads, the other doesn't. Someone added a filter months ago to answer a one-off question and never took it out.
Fix: open the filter panel on both reports and compare them line by line. Rename reports so the scope is in the name.
7. Duplicates
The same seller as two leads, or the same deal entered twice, inflates lead counts and makes cost per lead look better than it is. It's common: in a 2025 Validity survey, 76% of CRM users said less than half their CRM data was accurate (more in my lead response statistics ).
Fix: matching and duplicate rules on phone, email and property address, and a regular merge routine. I go deeper in duplicate sellers in Salesforce .
8. The chart only shows the top values
Dashboard components can be set to show a maximum number of values. The report lists all 23 lead sources, the chart shows the top 10, and the small ones vanish from the picture.
Fix: check the component's display settings, or group small sources into an "other" bucket on purpose.
9. New sources never made it into the groupings
Bucket fields and picklists group your sources into channels like direct mail, PPC and cold calling. When marketing adds a new source and nobody updates the bucket, it lands in "other" or goes missing from the channel totals.
Fix: make "update the buckets and picklists" part of adding any new lead source or tracking number.
10. Spend doesn't match what accounting paid
This one is behind most "the dashboard says we're profitable" conversations. Spend in Salesforce was typed in by hand, a mailer was prepaid for three drops but recorded in one month, a refund from a lead vendor never made it back, or PPC spend was entered as budgeted rather than actual.
Fix: record spend per campaign per month from the accounting records, not from memory, and check the total against your books every month. Campaign ROI checked against the books is part of what I built for the company I work with, and it's the step that makes the owner believe the dashboard.
The 20-minute check
Pick last month and do this with whoever runs your Salesforce, with QuickBooks or your closing list open next to it.
Contracts. Count contracts signed last month in Salesforce, by contract signed date. Count them in your own list. Write both numbers down.
Closings. Do the same for closings, by closing date, against what title actually closed and what hit the bank.
List the differences. For every deal that's on one list but not the other, find out why: wrong date, wrong stage, duplicate, deleted, never entered.
Source on every contract. Check that each of last month's contracts has a lead source and a market. Count the blanks.
Spend. Compare total marketing spend in Salesforce for last month with the marketing lines in your books. If they differ by more than a rounding error, cost per contract is wrong too.
Dashboard settings. On the owner's dashboard, check the running user, the last refresh time and each chart's maximum values.
Whatever you find in step 3 is your fix list. Don't expect all ten causes. Fix whichever ones the check turns up.
Write the definitions down
Half of the arguments about numbers are really arguments about words. Write one line for each number and put it at the top of the dashboard:
Number | Counted when | By which date
Lead | A seller record is created from a marketing source (not a duplicate) | Created date
Contact made | A two-way conversation happened, logged as a call or text with an outcome | Activity date
Appointment | A meeting or walkthrough is set with the seller | Appointment date
Offer | A number was given to the seller and recorded on the deal | Offer date
Contract | The seller signed the purchase agreement | Contract signed date
Closed | Funds received from the closing or assignment | Closing date
Cost per contract | Marketing spend in the period divided by contracts in the period | Spend month and contract signed date
Net profit per deal | Revenue minus the deal's direct costs, including its share of marketing | Closing date
Your definitions may differ. That's fine, as long as everyone uses the same ones. The Monday 5 builds on definitions like these to give an owner five numbers to check every week.
How to stop it happening again
One owner for the numbers. Someone whose job includes the monthly reconciliation.
A monthly reconciliation of contracts, closings and spend against the books, using the check above.
A "missing source" report that should always be empty, checked weekly.
A rule for new lead sources: picklist, bucket, field mapping and tracking number all updated before the campaign goes live.
Fewer reports. Twelve reports that answer the same question twelve slightly different ways is how teams stop trusting all of them. Keep the ones the owner reads and archive the rest.
Questions
Why doesn't my Salesforce dashboard match the report?
The usual reasons are that the dashboard hasn't been refreshed since the data changed, it runs as a user who can't see all the records, a chart is set to show only the top values, or the dashboard component uses a different report or filter than the one you're comparing it with.
What is the running user on a Salesforce dashboard?
It's the user whose access decides what data the dashboard shows. Folders control who can open the dashboard, but the running user determines which records are counted. Pick a running user who can see everything the dashboard is meant to count.
Why is my Salesforce report missing records?
Check the report type first: some custom report types only include records that have at least one related record. Then check the filters, the scope (my records or all records) and whether the running user can see the records.
Why does lead source show as blank on deals in Salesforce?
Standard fields like Lead Source carry over when a lead is converted, but custom fields such as market, campaign or tracking number only carry over if someone maps them to fields on the deal. Map them, then fix past records with a one-time update.
How many dynamic dashboards can I have in Salesforce?
According to Salesforce's dynamic dashboards cheat sheet, Enterprise Edition allows 5, Unlimited and Performance allow 10, and Developer Edition allows 3.
How do I make Salesforce match QuickBooks?
Record marketing spend per campaign per month from the accounting records, split by market the same way in both systems, count contracts and closings by agreed dates, and reconcile one month at a time, listing every deal that appears in one place but not the other.
How often should we reconcile Salesforce numbers?
Monthly for contracts, closings and marketing spend, and weekly for a quick look at records with no lead source or market. Once the monthly check comes back clean a few times in a row, the owner starts trusting the dashboard.

## Salesforce Dialers for Real Estate: Open CTI Ends 2028
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-dialer-real-estate.html

Dialers in Salesforce for real estate teams.
RingCentral, Aircall, Dialpad and Twilio all log calls into Salesforce, but Salesforce’s Open CTI, which many of them use, reaches end of life on February 28, 2028. Here’s how each dialer connects, which edition it needs, what a wholesaling team should log, and how to plan for 2028. The system around the calls (queues, outcomes and a caller scorecard) is in cold-calling team setup .
Salesforce says Open CTI reaches end of life on February 28, 2028, and existing implementations stop working after that. Salesforce Voice is the recommended replacement. source
Many dialer integrations use Open CTI; Twilio Flex’s docs say its Salesforce integration will stop working after that date. source
Edition matters: RingCentral supports Professional and above; Aircall and Dialpad require Enterprise or Unlimited. RingCentral · Aircall · Dialpad
The last two numbers are from my speed to lead statistics page , with sources.
How do the main dialers connect to Salesforce?
Dialer | What it does in Salesforce | Salesforce edition | Other requirements
RingCentral for Salesforce | Click to dial and click to text, automatic call and message logging, screen pops, voicemail, in-app calling | Professional and above | RingCentral Advanced or Ultra; admin install
Aircall | Calls in and out from Salesforce; logs details, tags and recordings; works across leads, contacts and accounts | Enterprise or Unlimited | Aircall Professional plan; same email in both systems
Dialpad | CTI, power dialer, call logging; SMS logged as completed tasks on the contact (not opportunities) | Enterprise or Unlimited, API enabled | Dialpad Connect, Support or Sell license
Twilio Flex | Agent UI inside Salesforce; click to dial, screen pop, activity logging | Not stated | Flex account; subject to the Open CTI retirement
Salesforce Voice | Native telephony with Amazon Connect; Salesforce’s recommended Open CTI replacement | Licensed separately | —
Sources: RingCentral · RingCentral FAQ · Aircall · Dialpad · Dialpad SMS logging · Twilio Flex · Salesforce Voice
What does the Open CTI retirement mean for an investor?
If your dialer runs inside Salesforce today, ask the vendor whether it uses Open CTI. Nothing breaks before February 28, 2028, but anything you build now should have a path past it. Dialpad, for example, says Dialpad for Salesforce is not being retired and lists Salesforce Voice or Dialpad Everywhere as options. source
Ask your dialer vendor, in writing, what their post-2028 Salesforce integration is.
Keep call outcomes in your own Salesforce fields, not only in the vendor’s objects, so reports survive a switch.
If you’re choosing a dialer now, weigh the vendor’s 2028 plan as much as today’s features.
What should a dialer integration log for a wholesaling team?
Field | Why
Call outcome (picklist) | Contact rate and conversion by list; see the handoff checklist
Call direction and duration | Separates inbound sellers from outbound dials
Recording link | Coaching and dispute checks
Missed inbound call → task | Only 2% of unanswered callers leave a voicemail; the task is the callback. See the missed call calculator
Attempt number | Follow-up cadence reporting; the median web lead got one contact attempt (InsideSales, 2014)
Recorded calls can also feed Einstein Conversation Insights, which lists RingCentral, Dialpad and Aircall among its voice connectors. source
Questions
Is Salesforce Open CTI being retired?
Yes. Salesforce Help says Open CTI reaches end of life on February 28, 2028, existing implementations stop working after that, and Salesforce Voice is the recommended replacement.
Which dialer works with Salesforce Professional Edition?
RingCentral lists Professional and above. Aircall and Dialpad require Enterprise or Unlimited.
Can Salesforce log texts from my dialer?
Some dialers do. Dialpad logs SMS as completed tasks on the contact’s activity history, but not on opportunities and not from shared lines. RingCentral logs calls and messages.
What is the best dialer for wholesalers using Salesforce?
It depends on your edition and volume. Check the Salesforce edition each vendor requires, how calls are logged, and the vendor’s plan after Open CTI ends in 2028.

## Wholesale Dispositions in Salesforce: Buyers & Deals
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-dispositions-real-estate.html

Wholesale dispositions in Salesforce.
A dispo system in Salesforce has three parts: buyer records with a structured buy box, a record of every deal sent to every buyer, and a fast way to send new contracts to the best-matched buyers first. Here’s the data model, matching rules, sending options, automations and the numbers that show whether your buyer list is real.
Dispo in a CRM means three things: buyers with a buy box , a record of which buyers saw which deal , and a fast way to send a new deal to the right buyers first .
In Salesforce that’s a Buyer record, a junction object between Property and Buyer, and List Email or an email tool. List Email sends to up to 200 leads or contacts at once. source
The payoff: when a contract is signed, the 10 buyers most likely to close get it in minutes, and you can see who actually buys.
What records does a dispo system need?
Record | Key fields | Why
Buyer (Contact or custom object) | Zips or counties, min/max price, property types, rehab level, financing (cash or hard money), proof of funds date, last purchase date | Matching a deal to the buy box
Property / Deal | Address, ARV, repairs, contract price, assignment ask, access instructions, photos folder | What you’re selling
Deal Sent (junction: Property ↔ Buyer) | Date sent, opened or viewed, interested, offer amount, outcome | Who saw what, who offered, who closes
The junction record is the part most teams skip. In Salesforce it’s two master-detail relationships, and it can roll up to both sides: offers per deal and deals sent per buyer. source · roll-up limits
How do you match a deal to the right buyers?
Start with the buy box
A list view or report filtered by the deal’s zip, price band and property type gives the candidate buyers. Keep the buy box as picklists and numbers, not a notes field, or the filter can’t work.
Rank by behaviour, not list size
Sort candidates by deals closed in the last 12 months, then by offers made. A roll-up on the buyer record makes this one column.
Send to the top 10 first
Give your best buyers a head start, then widen. The Deal Sent records show who had the chance, which settles “I never got that one.”
How do you send deals to buyers from Salesforce?
Option | Good for | Limit or note
List Email | Up to 200 buyers at a time from a list view | Counts toward the mass email limit, typically 5,000 recipients a day
Mailchimp (Beaufort 12 integration) | Designed deal emails to segmented buyer audiences | Third-party integration; email activity shows on Salesforce records
Account Engagement | Larger lists, scoring and automation | Syncs with Professional and higher every 2–4 minutes
Text | Buyers who agreed to texts | See the texting and 10DLC guide
Sources: List Email · Mailchimp · Account Engagement
Should buyers get a portal?
A buyer portal lets buyers log in and see available deals, request access and submit offers. In Salesforce that’s Experience Cloud, which needs Enterprise or higher and licenses bought separately. For most wholesalers, a good email and a deal page per property is enough until volume justifies it. source
What should dispo automate?
Under contract → post to the #dispo Slack channel with address, ARV and assignment ask. Flow has a Send Message to Slack action. source
Under contract → create the deal folder (Box for Salesforce puts a folder on each record). source
Buyer offer received → task for the dispo rep and update the Deal Sent record.
No buyer interest in 72 hours → task to re-price or widen the list.
Proof of funds older than 90 days → task to request a new one.
Which dispo numbers matter?
Number | Tells you
Days from contract to assignment | Whether your buyer list is deep enough
Buyers who closed in the last 12 months | Your real buyer list (often a small fraction of the total)
Offers per deal sent | Pricing and deal quality
Assignment fee vs ask | How much you give up to close
Fall-outs by buyer | Who to stop sending deals to first
A Kanban view of the dispo pipeline, summarized by expected fee, gives the team a daily board. source Free template: cash buyers list .
Questions
How do wholesalers track cash buyers in a CRM?
Store each buyer with a structured buy box (areas, price range, property types, rehab level, financing, proof of funds date) and log every deal sent to them, so you can filter matching buyers and see who actually buys.
Can Salesforce send a new deal to my buyers list?
Yes. List Email sends a template to up to 200 contacts or leads at a time from a list view. For larger lists or designed emails, use an email tool connected to Salesforce.
Do I need a buyer portal?
Usually not at first. Salesforce portals use Experience Cloud, which needs Enterprise or higher and separate licenses. Email plus a deal page works for most wholesalers.
What is a buy box?
A buyer’s criteria for deals: locations, price range, property types, condition and how they fund purchases.

## DocuSign + Salesforce for Real Estate Investors
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-docusign-real-estate.html

DocuSign + Salesforce for real estate investors.
DocuSign connects to Salesforce through Docusign’s own AppExchange package : you send purchase and assignment contracts from the deal record, templates fill themselves from Salesforce fields, and signed documents come back to the record. Here’s what it does, what it needs and how I set it up for wholesalers.
Docusign builds Docusign eSignature for Salesforce , an AppExchange package that sends agreements from Salesforce records and writes signed documents and signer data back. source
Templates pull record fields through merge fields, so seller name, property address and price fill themselves. source
Salesforce lists it as working with Professional, Enterprise, Unlimited, Developer, Starter and Performance. It needs a separate Docusign subscription. source
What does DocuSign do inside Salesforce?
Capability | What Docusign’s listing says | What I use it for in wholesaling
Send from a record | Send agreements to Salesforce contacts or any email, with messages, reminders and authentication | Purchase agreement to the seller from the deal, not from someone’s inbox
Templates with merge fields | “Create agreements from Docusign templates that use Salesforce data through merge fields” | Seller name, address, price and closing date typed once in Salesforce, never retyped in a PDF
Write-back | “Signed documents and signer-provided data are written back to Salesforce” | The signed contract lives on the deal; title, dispo and the owner all see the same file
Mobile | Mobile-responsive signing and Salesforce mobile support | Sellers sign on a phone at the kitchen table
Setup | “Clicks-not-code”; the package’s tabs and objects don’t count against org limits | No custom code needed for the basic flow
Sources: AppExchange listing · Salesforce integration page . Docusign also sells Gen for Salesforce (documents generated from Salesforce data) and CLM for Salesforce (contract templates and workflows). source
What does a contract flow look like for a wholesaler?
1. Offer accepted
The acquisitions rep clicks Send with Docusign on the deal. The purchase agreement template fills from the deal: seller, address, price, earnest money, closing date.
2. Seller signs
The signed PDF and signer data come back to the deal. I key a Flow on that write-back to move the stage to Under Contract and create the title-company task.
3. Dispo assigns
The assignment contract template goes to the end buyer from the same deal, with the assignment price and fee filled in.
4. Everything in one place
Both signed contracts sit on the deal. When a closing gets delayed or a buyer backs out, nobody has to search email for “the latest version”.
Before you build this, make sure the fields exist: contract price, assignment price, assignment fee , closing date, title company. Those are what the templates merge.
What should you check before installing?
A Docusign plan with the Salesforce integration. The AppExchange listing shows a published price of “starts at $30 per user per month” and a 30-day free trial (as of October 2026). source
Your contract templates reviewed by your attorney for each state you buy in. The integration fills fields; it doesn’t make a contract valid.
Which record you send from. I send from the deal (Opportunity or a custom Deal object), not the lead, so every contract stays with the property.
Docusign’s status-object details. I couldn’t read Docusign’s admin guide pages (they only load with JavaScript), so confirm the exact objects in the admin guide before building reports on them.
Questions
Can I send a purchase agreement from Salesforce with DocuSign?
Yes. With Docusign eSignature for Salesforce installed, you send agreements from a record using a Docusign template whose merge fields pull data from Salesforce, and the signed document is written back to Salesforce.
Does DocuSign for Salesforce work on Professional Edition?
Salesforce lists Docusign as working with Professional, Enterprise, Unlimited, Developer, Starter and Performance editions.
Can a signed DocuSign contract update the deal stage?
The package writes signed documents and signer data back to Salesforce. A record-triggered Flow can react to that write-back and move the stage. Confirm which object changes in Docusign’s admin guide before you build it.
Do I need a separate DocuSign subscription?
Yes. The integration requires a Docusign plan; the AppExchange listing shows pricing and a 30-day free trial.
