## Salesforce vs Podio for Wholesalers (2026)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-vs-podio.html

Salesforce vs Podio for wholesalers. Where each one wins in 2026
Podio has been the default first CRM for wholesalers for years: cheap, flexible and full of workspaces other investors built. Salesforce is what many of those teams look at once they have several reps, a second market or an owner who wants real numbers. This page compares the two honestly, with Podio's own published limits linked, and says when staying on Podio is the right call. I build on Salesforce, so weigh my view with that in mind.
Stay on Podio if you're a small team, your workspace works and you're under its automation allowance. Look at Salesforce when you have several reps or markets, need reports like cost per contract by source that you can't get from Podio, need per-field and per-record permissions, or keep running into Podio's limits, such as 25,000 Workflow Automation actions a month (since September 2026), 100 fields per app and 20,000 rows per Excel export. Salesforce costs more to set up and run, so a move only pays when one of those is costing you deals.
Salesforce and Podio side by side
 | Podio | Salesforce
Owned by | Progress Software | Salesforce
How it's built | Workspaces and apps you or a template vendor design, with items, relationships and calculation fields | Objects, fields and automations configured around your process: standard leads and opportunities plus your own records for properties, offers and buyers
Fields | Up to 100 fields per app | Up to 500 custom fields per object on Enterprise Edition, 800 on Unlimited; 25 on Starter
Automation | Podio Workflow Automation, the tool many teams still call Globiflow. 25,000 actions a month included since September 1, 2026; add-ons on Premium only | Flow. Limits apply per transaction, plus daily allowances for scheduled jobs that grow with your licenses; no monthly action count
Reporting | Views with filters and groupings, and up to 50 reports per app | Reports across related records, dashboards, scheduled reports and stage history
Permissions | Workspace roles (light, regular and admin) and sharing single items with guests | Profiles, permission sets, field-level security and sharing rules
Data in and out | Excel import and export, 20,000 rows per file | Import wizard and Data Loader; full API on Enterprise and up, an add-on on Professional
Integrations | Podio API: 250 resource-intensive calls an hour and 1,000 others | Salesforce API and AppExchange apps for dialers, texting and e-signature
Price | Published per seat, plus usage add-ons | List prices are published, but what you pay is set in a quote from Salesforce
I don't list Salesforce prices, because what businesses actually pay depends on the quote. Podio's prices are on its own site.
Where Podio wins
Cost to start. A small team can run Podio for a fraction of what Salesforce costs once you count licenses and setup.
Anyone can build in it. An owner or an ops person can add an app or a field in an afternoon, and a lot of wholesaling workspaces are available to copy.
Your team already knows it. Many wholesaling VAs and reps have worked in Podio before.
It's enough for a small, simple operation. One market, a few people and a workspace that works is a good reason to stay.
Where Salesforce wins
Structure that holds up as you grow. Leads, deals, properties, offers, buyers and assignments each have their own record and rules, so a second market or a rental side doesn't mean starting over.
Reports owners actually use. Cost per contract by source, days from offer to contract, offers over MAO by rep, all from the same data the team works in. See the Monday 5 for the ones I'd start with.
Permissions. VAs see only their queue, each market sees its own deals, and financial fields stay hidden from the people who don't need them. See Salesforce access for VAs and cold callers .
Automation without a monthly meter. Flow has limits per transaction and daily allowances for scheduled jobs that grow with your licenses, but no monthly count of actions to top up. The record-triggered automations that create tasks and stop cadences run each time a record changes, without counting against a monthly meter.
History. Opportunity stage changes are tracked out of the box, and field history tracking covers up to 20 fields per object, so you can see who changed what and when.
Which Podio limits matter for wholesalers?
From Podio's own documentation:
Limit | Podio's number | Where wholesalers hit it
Workflow Automation actions | 25,000 a month included since September 1, 2026 | Nightly loops over every open lead and buyer list syncs. More in Podio's new automation limit
Fields per app | 100 | Lead apps that grew a field for every question anyone ever asked
Items per app | 500,000 | Teams that import cold-calling and texting lists into the same app as leads
Excel import and export | 20,000 rows per file | Any export of the full lead list, which has to go in filtered batches
Reports per app | 50 | Owners who want a report for every source, rep and market
Items in a relationship field | 250 | A buyer linked to every deal they've bought
API calls | 250 resource-intensive and 1,000 other calls an hour | Zapier, Make and dialer syncs during busy hours
Podio also says that many fields and calculation fields slow an app down, which matches what a lot of teams feel after a few years of adding to the same workspace.
The cost question, honestly
Salesforce is not the cheap option. You pay for licenses, setup and someone to look after it, plus the dialer, texting and data tools you connect. Podio's per-seat price is low and public.
The move pays when something you can't do in Podio is costing you deals: leads that slip because an automation hit its cap, marketing money spent without knowing cost per contract by source, or a second market you can't keep separate. If none of that is true, stay. To see which Salesforce edition you'd be quoted for, use the edition picker .
How do you decide?
Your situation | What I'd do
A few people, one market, Podio works and you're under the cap | Stay on Podio
Over the automation cap because of nightly loops or syncs | Redesign those flows first. A move isn't the only fix
Ten or more people, several markets, and nobody can tell you cost per contract by source | Plan a move
You need VAs, markets or entities kept apart and can't do it in workspaces | Plan a move
The person who built your Podio left and nobody understands it | Either rebuild in Podio or move. A mess moves with you if you copy it, so rebuild either way
What does moving from Podio involve?
Mostly data decisions: what history you keep, how lead source carries through to every closed deal, and what Podio's Excel export leaves out (files, comments, tasks and activity aren't in it). Run a 50-record test before you move the rest, and keep Podio read-only for a while after. The details are in two guides:
Moving off Podio: a migration checklist , with three options compared, including staying.
Podio, REsimpli or GoHighLevel to Salesforce , with the field map and a 30-60-90 day plan.
Questions
Is Salesforce better than Podio for wholesalers?
For a small team with a simple process, Podio is usually enough and much cheaper. Salesforce is better when you have several reps or markets, need reports like cost per contract by source, need field- and record-level permissions, or keep hitting Podio's limits.
What are Podio's limits?
Podio's documentation lists 100 fields per app, 500,000 items per app, 20,000 rows per Excel import or export, 50 reports per app and API limits of 250 resource-intensive and 1,000 other calls an hour. Since September 1, 2026, Workflow Automation includes 25,000 actions a month.
Who owns Podio?
Podio is owned by Progress Software, which publishes its documentation and the 2026 hybrid pricing changes.
Can Salesforce do what Globiflow does?
Yes. Salesforce Flow handles the same kinds of jobs as Podio Workflow Automation, the tool formerly called Globiflow: creating tasks, updating records, sending texts through a connected app and running on a schedule, without a monthly action allowance.
Is Podio cheaper than Salesforce?
Yes, almost always, especially for small teams. Salesforce adds licenses, setup and ongoing admin. It's worth it only when something Podio can't do is costing you deals.
How long does it take to move from Podio to Salesforce?
It depends on the number of apps, records and integrations. The slow part is usually deciding what to keep and cleaning duplicates. The switch guide on this site lays out a 30-60-90 day plan.
Can I run Podio and Salesforce together?
For a short time during a move, yes, so no lead is lost. Long term, two CRMs means two versions of the truth, so pick one as the system of record.

## Salesforce vs REsimpli for Wholesalers (2026)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/salesforce-vs-resimpli.html

Salesforce vs REsimpli for wholesalers.
REsimpli is an investor CRM with the dialer, texting and data already inside. Salesforce is a CRM you build around your own process. Here’s where each one wins, with every claim linked to the vendor’s own page.
REsimpli gives a wholesaling team calling, texting, lists, skip tracing and buyer sites in one login, priced by team size.
Salesforce gives you a CRM you shape around your own process: your records, your automations, your reports. Dialing, texting and data come from integrations.
Pick REsimpli if you want it working this week and your process fits its pipeline. Pick Salesforce if you have several reps, markets or entities, or need custom reports or permission rules beyond what REsimpli offers. Test it in the trial.
Disclosure: I build Salesforce CRMs for investors, so I have a bias. To keep it in check, every feature and price below comes from the vendor’s own site, linked in the row. I don’t list Salesforce prices: most businesses get a discount from a Salesforce account executive based on the business and number of users.

Time to first call. Dialer, texting, lists and skip tracing are already wired together.

Questions
Is REsimpli better than Salesforce for wholesalers?
For a small team that wants calling, texting, lists and skip tracing in one login, REsimpli is usually the faster choice. Salesforce is better when you need your own records, deeper reports or permissions across several reps, markets or entities.
Does Salesforce have a dialer and texting for real estate?
Not built for wholesaling out of the box. Sales Dialer is a paid add-on that Salesforce is retiring in favor of Salesforce Voice, and teams typically add AppExchange dialer and texting apps.
How much does REsimpli cost?
REsimpli’s blog, updated October 1, 2026, lists Solo at $299 a month monthly or $249 on annual billing, Team at $899 and Business at $2,199 a month. Check the pricing page before you buy.
Can I use REsimpli and Salesforce together?
REsimpli lists an open API, so a sync is possible, but running two CRMs usually means two versions of the truth. Most teams pick one as the system of record.

## Sample CRM Revenue Audit report | Amr Magdy
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/sample-audit-report.html

Sample Salesforce audit report for a home-buying company
This is a shortened sample for a made-up company, “Example Home Buyers”, so you can see the format before you buy. It isn’t a real client and there are no real numbers in it. A real report covers your org, uses your data and runs much longer.
$1,500 fixed , for teams already on Salesforce.
The company in this sample: a home-buying team in two markets with 6 Salesforce users, acquisitions reps, a lead manager, a dispo lead and a transaction coordinator. Leads come from mail, PPC, cold calling and texting.
1. Summary for the owner
The org is in decent shape for day-to-day work. The money leaks sit in three places: missed calls on marketing numbers that nobody gets alerted on, offers that go quiet because nobody owns the next step, and campaign ROI that counts contracts instead of deals that closed. Fixing those three comes first.
2. Findings
Every finding says where it is, why it matters, how much it matters and how big the fix is.
# | Finding | Where | Why it matters | Impact | Fix size
1 | The missed-call alert flow has been failing silently since a field was renamed | Flow “Missed Call Alert”, phone integration | Sellers who call after hours get no callback | High | Small
2 | Offers sent with no follow-up task and no owner for the next step | Opportunity, stage “Offer Made” | Offers go cold while the seller shops other buyers | High | Small
3 | Lead Source is a free-text field with many spellings of the same source | Lead and Opportunity | Campaign reports split one source into several rows | Medium | Medium
4 | Campaign ROI counts signed contracts, including ones that fell out | Campaign reports and dashboard | Spend goes to sources that look good but don’t close | High | Medium
5 | No duplicate rule on seller phone number | Duplicate and matching rules | Two reps call the same seller with two different offers | Medium | Small
6 | Dead and lost deals have no required reason | Opportunity close | No way to see why deals are lost, by rep or by market | Low | Small
7 | Three old automations still run on the same field and fight each other | Process Builder and Flow | Status changes back after a rep updates it | Medium | Medium
8 | The owner dashboard runs on reports nobody has checked in months | Home dashboard | Monday decisions get made on wrong numbers | Medium | Medium
3. The 30 / 60 / 90 roadmap
First 30 days: fix the missed-call alert, add the follow-up task on every offer, and add the duplicate rule on phone. These stop the biggest leaks for the least work.
Days 31 to 60: clean up Lead Source into one picklist and map the old values, add required lost reasons, and retire the old automations into one flow.
Days 61 to 90: rebuild campaign ROI on closed deals only, then build the Monday 5 dashboard below.
4. The Monday 5 dashboard spec (excerpt)
Each number is defined field by field, so your team or anyone you hire can build it.
Number | Report type | Filter | Grouped by
Cost per appointment by campaign | Campaigns with Opportunities | Appointment date this month | Campaign
Contracts per campaign | Opportunities with Campaign | Stage reached “Under Contract” | Campaign, market
Time from contract to first seller call | Opportunities with Activities | Contract date last 30 days | Acquisitions rep
The full spec also covers booked vs. kept profit and campaign ROI, including the houses you keep.
5. Three quick fixes, done during the audit
Repaired the missed-call alert so the lead manager gets a text and a task within minutes.
Added an automatic follow-up task, owned by the rep, the moment a deal moves to “Offer Made”.
Turned on a duplicate rule that warns a rep when a seller’s phone number is already in the system.
The three fixes are agreed with you before I touch anything.
6. The walkthrough
A recorded call where I go through every finding with you and your team, answer questions and agree the order of the fixes.
If the report doesn’t give you at least five specific, fixable issues worth more than the fee, you get the fee back.

## Seller Appointment No-Shows and Reminders in Salesforce
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/seller-appointment-no-shows-salesforce.html

Fewer wasted drives. Seller appointment reminders and no-shows in Salesforce
An acquisitions rep who drives across town to a house where nobody answers loses half a morning, and the seller who didn't show is often talking to someone else. Most teams can't say how often it happens, because the appointment just quietly disappears from the calendar. This page is for owners and acquisitions managers who want fewer no-shows and an honest number for the ones that still happen.
Treat every set appointment as something the system keeps track of. Confirm it in writing the moment it's booked, remind the seller the day before and a couple of hours before, and have the rep text on the way. Record an outcome on every appointment: held, no-show, rescheduled or canceled. A no-show then creates a reschedule task on its own, and a weekly report shows the show rate by rep, source and day, which is where the real fixes come from.
What does a no-show actually cost?
The rep's time. The drive, the prep and the comps pulled for a house you never saw.
The slot. That time could have gone to a seller who would have been home.
Often the deal. A seller who skips the appointment may have signed with another buyer, or got cold feet that one more call would have settled.
The truth in your numbers. If no-shows aren't recorded, "appointments set" and "appointments held" look the same in reports. Lead managers look better than they are, and nobody can see where the leak is.
Where should appointments live in Salesforce?
In two places, kept in step:
A calendar event linked to the lead or deal, synced to the rep's Google or Outlook calendar, so the appointment exists where the rep actually looks.
A few fields on the lead or deal: appointment date and time, in person or virtual, who set it, and the outcome. Fields make the reports simple and give your reminders a date to count from.
If sellers book themselves online, Calendly's Salesforce integration can create the lead and the event and track cancellations and reschedules. Calendly says it needs Salesforce Enterprise Edition or higher.
A map helps more than you'd think. The org I run has an appointment map inside Salesforce, so a rep can see the day's appointments and the leads near them, and plan the route.
How should you confirm and remind?
When | What | Sent by
Right after booking | Confirmation with the day, time, address and the rep's name | Salesforce, automatically
The day before | Reminder that asks for a quick reply to confirm | Salesforce, automatically
A couple of hours before | Short reminder | Salesforce, automatically
On the way | "Leaving now, see you at 2" | The rep, personally
The automatic ones run from a record-triggered Flow with scheduled paths counted from the appointment date and time, sent through your texting tool. When the appointment moves, the scheduled reminders move with it, so a rescheduled seller doesn't get a reminder for the old time.
Route every reply to the rep. "Can't make it" should create a reschedule task right away, not sit in an inbox.
Stop on opt-out. Reminders a seller expects are different from marketing, but the opt-out rules still apply. Check your setup with whoever advises you on the TCPA. Not legal advice.
Keep the rep's own text. The automatic messages make sure nobody forgets. The personal one is what makes a seller feel bad about not being there.
Record an outcome on every appointment
One required field, filled in after the appointment time passes:
Held
No-show
Rescheduled
Canceled by the seller
Canceled by us
Then two rules. The morning after any appointment with no outcome, the rep gets a task to record it, and the manager sees the list. And a held appointment needs a next step before it can be saved: an offer, a follow-up date or a dead reason. That's how appointments stop vanishing between the calendar and the deal. The next step after "held" is usually an offer, and the offer follow-up guide picks up from there.
What should happen after a no-show?
From the driveway: the rep calls and texts before leaving. "I'm outside" often finds a seller who is ten minutes away.
Same day: marking the no-show creates a reschedule task due today and starts a short follow-up of two or three touches offering a new time. It stops when the seller replies.
After a second no-show: move the seller to a longer follow-up cadence rather than blocking more calendar time.
When you learn why, record it: forgot, changed their mind, family disagreed, sold to someone else. A month of reasons tells you whether the fix is reminders, qualifying or speed.
What about virtual appointments?
Many teams make offers by phone or video instead of at the house. They need the same tracking: the reminder carries the link or the number to call, and the outcome is recorded the same way. Keep in-person and virtual separate in your reports, because they show up and close at different rates. The org I run tracks on-site and virtual offers separately for exactly that reason.
The reports that matter
Show rate , held divided by held plus no-shows, by who set the appointment, by lead source, by day and time, and by how many days ahead it was booked. If appointments booked far ahead no-show more often, book sooner.
Appointments with no outcome. It should be empty.
Held appointments with no next step. Also empty. If it isn't, offers are leaking.
Set versus held, by lead manager. If you pay on appointments, pay on held ones.
Cost per held appointment by source , next to cost per contract. For PPC, that's also the number worth sending back to Google Ads .
To see whether your team has room for more appointments at all, try the acquisitions capacity calculator .
Questions
How do you reduce no-shows for seller appointments?
Confirm in writing as soon as the appointment is booked, send reminders the day before and a couple of hours before, have the rep text on the way, and book as soon as the seller can meet. Then track the show rate by rep and source to find what else needs fixing.
Can Salesforce send appointment reminder texts?
Yes, through a texting app connected to Salesforce. A record-triggered Flow with scheduled paths can send reminders a set time before the appointment, and the reminders move automatically if the appointment is rescheduled.
How do I track no-shows in Salesforce?
Add a required outcome field for each appointment, with values like held, no-show, rescheduled and canceled, and create a task the morning after any appointment that has no outcome yet. Report on held divided by held plus no-shows.
What is a good show rate for seller appointments?
There's no reliable public benchmark for investor teams. Measure your own by rep, source and day, and work on the biggest gaps; the trend matters more than any outside number.
Does Calendly work with Salesforce?
Yes. Calendly's Salesforce integration can create leads and events and track cancellations and reschedules. Calendly says it requires Salesforce Enterprise Edition or higher.
What should a rep do when a seller doesn't show?
Call and text from the driveway before leaving, then let Salesforce create a same-day reschedule task and a short follow-up offering a new time. After a second no-show, move the seller to a longer follow-up cadence.
Related guides
Sources
Checked in October 2026. Salesforce and vendor features change with each release, so check the linked page before you rely on a detail.
Salesforce Developers: Schedule your path in Salesforce Flow . Reminders a day and an hour before an appointment, and how scheduled actions follow a changed appointment time
Calendly Help: How to integrate Calendly with Salesforce . Leads and events by default, canceled and rescheduled events, and the Enterprise Edition requirement

## Seller Lead Follow-Up Cadence Builder for Investors (Free)
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/seller-follow-up-cadence.html

Seller follow-up cadence builder.
Silence is not a no. Pick how hot the lead is, the date you first spoke, and the channels you use. You get a dated touch plan you can follow by hand or import into your CRM as tasks. It is a starting template: adjust it to your market and your own results. The words for each touch are in 12 follow-up message templates .
Your touch plan
# | Date | Day | Channel | Purpose
Rules that make any cadence work
Every open lead has a next touch date
A lead with no next task is a lead nobody will call. Make the next touch date required before a rep can save a call outcome.
Stop on a no, not on silence
Silence is not a no. Move a quiet lead to a slower cadence instead of closing it. Close it only when the seller says no, sells, or the property no longer fits, and record the reason.
Log channel and outcome on every touch
After a few hundred touches you can see which channel and which touch number actually gets replies, and replace guesses with your own numbers.
Re-rate the temperature after each conversation
A cold lead whose situation changes (a job move, a vacancy, a repair bill) becomes hot. Changing the temperature should restart the cadence from that date.
Questions
How many times should I follow up with a seller lead?
Until they say no or sell, not until you get tired. The cadence changes with the lead: a seller with a near deadline gets touches every few days, a seller who said "not now" gets a touch every month or quarter. What matters is that every open lead has a next touch date.
Should I call or text first?
Test it on your own list rather than guessing. Split a list in half, call first on one half and text first on the other, and compare reply rates after a few weeks. Log the channel on every touch so you can see the answer.
What is a hot, warm and cold seller lead?
In this builder, hot means a seller with a reason and a timeline under about a month, warm means interested but one to six months out, and cold means not now. Use your own definitions, but write them down so every rep labels leads the same way.
Is texting sellers legal?
Rules on texts and calls to consumers vary by country and US state, and several states are stricter than federal law. Check the rules that apply to you, and consent requirements, before you scale texting. This builder plans touches; it does not send anything.
How do I load the plan into my CRM?
Download the CSV and import it as tasks, or create the same steps as an automated cadence in your CRM. Most CRMs, including Salesforce, can create the next task automatically when the last one is completed.

## Seller Follow-Up Messages: Text, Voicemail, Email Templates
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/seller-follow-up-message-templates.html

Seller follow-up messages: 12 templates, and the rules that decide when they send
Most wholesalers don't have a follow-up problem, they have a message problem and a trigger problem. The messages sound like a form letter, and they go out when someone remembers rather than when the seller's situation calls for them. This page gives you twelve short templates for the moments that matter (a missed call, a confirmed appointment, a quiet offer, a seller who said "not now"), written to sound like a person typed them. Under each is the rule that should send it, so the CRM does the remembering and a human does the talking. Timing for the whole sequence is in the cadence builder; this page is the words and the triggers.
Keep each message short, from a named person, with one question or one next step. Send a text only to sellers who've agreed to be texted, identify yourself, and honor STOP. Let the CRM trigger each message from an event (missed call, appointment set, offer sent, re-contact date reached), stop the sequence the moment the seller replies, and log every message on the record. Use the templates below as a starting point and change the words to sound like you.
What rules should every message follow?
Short and human. Text messages of one to three sentences. Written the way you'd text a neighbor, not a lead.
One ask. A question they can answer in a word, or a single next step. Never two.
No pressure and no promises. Don't state prices, timelines or terms you haven't agreed. Don't invent urgency.
Name yourself and your company in the first message to someone, and include an easy way to stop (a "reply STOP" line) in texts, as your texting provider requires.
Consent first for texts. A skip-traced number is not agreement to be texted. See texting sellers: 10DLC and consent . If you're unsure, call or send mail instead and ask for text permission on the call.
Honor opt-outs everywhere. One STOP covers every duplicate record and every channel you control. Opt-outs must be processed within 10 business days at the latest under the FCC's rules since April 2025; do it immediately.
Quiet hours. Send in the seller's daytime, in their time zone.
This is information, not legal advice; confirm the rules for your states and your texting provider. Merge fields appear as {first_name}, {address}, {rep_name} and {company}.
Missed call and new lead
1. Missed call text-back (sends within minutes, only with consent)
Hi {first_name}, it's {rep_name} with {company}. Sorry I missed your call. Are you still looking to sell {address}? Reply STOP to opt out.
Trigger: missed inbound call from a known seller who has agreed to texts. Owner: the lead owner, who also gets a callback task. Stops when: the seller replies or a person calls them.
2. First reply after a web form or ad lead
Hi {first_name}, {rep_name} here from {company}. Got your note about {address}. Good time for a quick call today, or is later better?
Trigger: new lead with consent recorded on the form. Stops when: they reply or a call connects.
3. After the first conversation
Thanks for talking with me, {first_name}. I'll {next_step} by {date}. If anything changes before then, text me here.
Trigger: outcome set to "spoke, interested" with a next step and a date. The text uses the fields the caller filled in, which is another reason to require them.
Appointment
4. Appointment confirmation
Confirming {day} at {time} at {address}. Anyone else who helps decide, like a spouse or heir, is welcome. See you then, {rep_name}.
Trigger: appointment created. A second reminder the morning of, from the same rule. Asking about other decision-makers here is a system trick: it fills the "who else decides" field before the visit.
5. No-show or missed appointment
Hi {first_name}, we missed each other today. No problem. Want to pick a new time, or should I check back in a few weeks?
Trigger: appointment time passed with no outcome. Gives the seller an easy way out and keeps the lead alive. More in seller no-shows .
Offer
6. Offer sent, day one
Hi {first_name}, I just emailed the offer for {address}. Any questions on it, text or call me. I'm around today.
Trigger: offer date set. Also creates the follow-up task with a date; the pipeline needs that date to leave the stage ( pipeline stages ).
7. Offer gone quiet
Hi {first_name}, checking back on the offer for {address}. Is there anything I can answer, or is the timing off right now?
Trigger: a set number of days after the offer with no activity. Gives two honest ways to answer, and the second ("timing") feeds your not-now reason field. More in offer follow-up .
8. Seller says yes
Great, {first_name}. I'll send the agreement now. Once it's signed, I'll introduce you to {tc_name}, who will handle the title side.
Trigger: stage moved to Under contract. Starts dispo and the transaction checklist on the same day.
Not now and reactivation
9. Not-now check-in on the re-contact date
Hi {first_name}, it's {rep_name}. You mentioned {date_reason} would be the time to talk about {address}. Is now better?
Trigger: re-contact date reached. The reason field written weeks ago is what makes this feel like memory rather than automation.
10. Reactivation wave for a quiet lead
Hi {first_name}, {rep_name} with {company}. We spoke a while back about {address}. Is it still something you're thinking about?
Trigger: a person-approved segment, in small waves, consent confirmed. Never run on the whole database at once; see reactivating dead seller leads .
Voicemail
11. Voicemail script (about 15 seconds)
Hi {first_name}, this is {rep_name} with {company}, calling about {address}. No pressure. If it's still something you're considering, call or text me back at {number}. Thanks.
Trigger: call outcome "left voicemail". Say the number slowly, once at the end. Don't leave a voicemail on every attempt; one on the first and another much later is plenty.
Email
12. Email after the offer
Subject: Your offer for {address}
Hi {first_name}, thanks for your time. The offer is attached. In short: {offer_summary}. If something in it doesn't work, tell me which part and I'll see what I can do. I'll check back on {date}. {rep_name}, {number}
Trigger: offer sent. Email is the place for detail, and it leaves a record the seller can show a family member.
How should the CRM send them?
Trigger from events, not from calendars. Each template above starts from something that happened: a missed call, an appointment, an offer date, a re-contact date.
Check consent and opt-out before every send, in the same step that sends.
Stop on reply. Any inbound text, call or email ends the automated sequence and creates a task for the owner.
One channel per touch. Don't text, email and call within the same hour. It reads as pressure and as spam.
Log it all on the seller's record: what, when and how they responded, so the next person doesn't repeat it.
Keep templates in one place with an owner. Edit them as a team, review replies monthly and retire the ones that get "stop" responses.
The same pieces also tell you what to ask of an AI tool that drafts messages: the triggers, the consent check and the stop rule stay yours. See AI for wholesalers . When to send what, across weeks, is in the follow-up cadence builder .
Questions
What should I text a motivated seller after a missed call?
Keep it short and human: say who you are, that you missed their call, and ask one question, such as whether they're still looking to sell the property. Only text people who have agreed to be texted, and include a way to opt out.
How do I follow up with a seller who went quiet after an offer?
Send a short message a few days after the offer asking whether you can answer anything or whether the timing is off, and record their answer in a reason field. Make the follow-up date required when the offer is sent so it never depends on memory.
Do I need consent to text seller leads?
Generally yes. A skip-traced phone number isn't permission to text. Get consent on the form or during a call, record it on the record, include opt-out language and check the rules for your states. This is information, not legal advice.
What should a follow-up voicemail for a seller say?
Say your name and company, the property you're calling about, that there's no pressure, and your number, slowly, once. Keep it around 15 seconds, and don't leave one on every attempt.
How often should I send follow-up messages to sellers?
Space them by event and by seller type rather than a fixed rhythm, use one channel per touch, and stop the automation when the seller replies. The cadence builder gives a touch plan by seller type.
Can AI write my seller follow-up messages?
It can draft them for a person to review, which is a low-risk use. The triggers, the consent check, opt-out handling and the rule that stops a sequence on reply should stay in your CRM, whatever writes the words.
Related guides
Sources
Checked in October 2026. Templates are examples to adapt, and compliance notes are information, not legal advice.
National Law Review: TCPA global revocation rule extended to January 2027 . Opt-outs processed within 10 business days since April 11, 2025
Want these sent by the CRM, not by memory?
The CRM Revenue Audit (USD 1,500, fixed price) reviews your follow-up triggers, consent fields and message logging, and returns a fix plan. It's for teams already on Salesforce.

## Seller Lead Tracker Spreadsheet (Free CSV) for Wholesalers
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/seller-lead-tracker-spreadsheet.html

Seller lead tracker spreadsheet: a free CSV, a daily routine, and when to leave it
If you are tracking seller leads on paper, in your phone or across three half-finished sheets, a good spreadsheet is a real upgrade, and it costs nothing. This page gives you a seller lead tracker with 28 columns set up the way a wholesaling or home-buying business actually works: source on every lead, a next follow-up date, consent, offers and dead reasons. It also gives you the dropdown lists, the two formulas that matter, a 15-minute daily routine and the weekly counts. Then, because I build CRMs for a living, an honest list of five signs the sheet has stopped being enough.
Download the CSV, import it into Google Sheets or Excel, add dropdown lists for Lead source, Status, Situation and Dead reason, and add two formulas: days since last contact and an overdue flag. Every working day, spend 15 minutes on the overdue list, oldest first. Every Friday, count leads, appointments, offers and contracts by source. When a second person needs the sheet, lists grow past a few thousand rows, or you can't tell who changed what, move to a CRM.
Where is the free seller lead tracker?
Download the seller lead tracker (CSV) . It opens in Google Sheets (File, Import) and Excel. It has the 28 headers and three clearly marked example rows to delete. No sign-up. The fields line up with the CRM field kit , so when you move to a CRM the columns map across instead of being redesigned.
What are the 28 columns, and why each one?
Column | Why it's there
Lead ID, Date added | A unique key and the clock for speed and aging
Lead source, Campaign or list | The two columns that let you work out cost per contract later. Fill them in the day the lead arrives
Seller name, Phone, Second phone, Email | Sellers call from several numbers; keeping two lets you spot repeats
Property address, City, State, Zip | The property is the real key. Search this column before you add a new row
Situation, Motivation (1-5), Timeline, Asking price, Condition | The five facts that decide whether and how to make an offer
Owner | One name per lead, so nobody assumes someone else has it
Status | One list for where the lead stands (see the lists below)
Last contact date, Next follow-up date, Next step | The most important three. A lead without a next follow-up date is already lost
OK to text, Do not contact | Consent and opt-outs belong in their own columns, not in notes. See texting and consent
Offer amount, Offer date | Lets you count offers and measure time from appointment to offer
Dead reason | A short dropdown, so you learn why deals die
Notes | Free text, last. Anything you want to count belongs in a column, not here
Which dropdown lists should you add?
In Google Sheets use Data, Data validation, Dropdown, and set the rule to reject other values. Keep each list short. A list you can read in one glance gets used.
Lead source: Direct mail, Cold call, Text, PPC, SEO, Driving for dollars, Referral, Other.
Status: New, Contacted, Appointment set, Offer made, Under contract, Marketing to buyers, Closed, Nurture, Dead. These follow the eight stages and the nurture status .
Situation: Probate, Divorce, Tax delinquent, Pre-foreclosure, Tired landlord, Relocation, Inherited, Other.
Dead reason: Bought elsewhere, Listed with an agent, Price too far apart, Not selling, Asked to stop, Unreachable.
Y/N columns: Y or N only.
Use the same words every time. A spelling change creates a new category, which is the same problem described in tags, fields or campaigns .
Which formulas and colors matter?
Add two helper columns to the right of Notes.
Days since last contact (column AC, row 2, copy down):
=IF(T2="","",TODAY()-T2)
Overdue flag (column AD):
=IF(AND(U2<>"",U2<TODAY(),S2<>"Dead",S2<>"Closed"),"Overdue","")
Then add conditional formatting: color the whole row when AD says "Overdue", and a second color when Next follow-up date is empty and Status isn't Dead or Closed. Sort by the follow-up date, oldest first, with a saved filter view called "Today" that shows only overdue and due-today rows. That one view is the whole point of the sheet.
What does the 15-minute daily routine look like?
Open the "Today" view. Work it from the oldest follow-up date down.
After every contact, update Last contact date, Status, Next step and Next follow-up date before you move on. This takes a few seconds and it's the habit that makes the sheet work.
Add new leads the moment they arrive, source first.
Before adding a row, search the phone and address columns for an existing one.
At the end, check for rows with no follow-up date. Give each one a date or mark it Dead with a reason.
For how often to follow up, the follow-up cadence builder gives you a touch plan by seller type.
What should you count every Friday?
Five minutes, same numbers, every week. With a Date added column, a count of last week's leads for a source is:
=COUNTIFS(C:C,"Direct mail",B:B,">="&TODAY()-7)
Build a small table of sources down the side and these across the top: leads, appointments set, offers made, contracts, and money spent. The spend you type in yourself. Then divide: spend by contracts is your cost per contract for each source, and the cost per deal calculator will do the arithmetic for you. If one source has produced many leads and no contracts for a month, you've found the first thing to change.
When should you leave the spreadsheet?
A spreadsheet is a good tool for one person. These are the signs it has stopped being enough:
A second person needs it. Two people editing means overwritten rows, no history of who changed what, and no way to limit what a VA can see or download.
Lists get big. Once you import thousands of rows from list providers, duplicates multiply and the sheet slows down.
You need automatic follow-up. A sheet can show overdue leads but it can't create a task, text a seller or alert you to a missed call.
Calls and texts matter. Logging them by hand falls apart at volume, and opt-outs can't be enforced.
You can't answer "which marketing works?" in five minutes. That's the signal to bring spend, source and deal results together in a real system.
If two or more are true, read what free CRMs give you and where they stop and do I need a CRM? . When you do move, a clean move checklist and how I handle a move to Salesforce are there.
Questions
What should a seller lead tracking spreadsheet include?
Lead source and campaign, the seller's contact details, the property address, situation and motivation, an owner, a status, last contact date, next follow-up date, consent columns, offer amount and date, and a dead reason. The next follow-up date and the source are the two that matter most.
Is there a free real estate lead follow-up sheet?
Yes, the seller lead tracker on this page is a free CSV for Google Sheets or Excel with 28 columns, dropdown list suggestions, an overdue flag formula and a weekly counts method. No sign-up is needed.
How do I organize real estate leads in a spreadsheet?
Use one row per property, a dropdown for status and source, a required next follow-up date, and a saved view that shows only overdue and due-today leads. Update the contact dates after every touch and search for the address before adding a row.
How do I know when a lead is overdue in Google Sheets?
Use a helper column with a formula such as =IF(AND(U2<>"",U2<TODAY(),S2<>"Dead",S2<>"Closed"),"Overdue","") and color the row when it says Overdue. Sort by the follow-up date and keep a filter view of overdue rows.
How do I track which lead source works in a spreadsheet?
Record the source on every lead the day it arrives, then count leads, appointments, offers and contracts by source each week with COUNTIFS formulas. Divide your spend on each source by its contracts to get cost per contract.
When is a spreadsheet no longer enough for wholesaling?
When a second person needs it, when lists reach thousands of rows, when you need automatic follow-up tasks or call and text logging, or when you can't tell which marketing produced contracts in a few minutes.
Related guides
Outgrowing the sheet?
A free 30-minute call will tell you whether to move to an investor CRM or build on Salesforce, and I'll tell you if the answer is to stay on the sheet a while longer. If you're already on Salesforce, the fixed-price CRM Revenue Audit (USD 1,500) shows where deals leak.

## Import a Skip-Traced List into Salesforce Without Duplicates
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/skip-traced-list-import-salesforce.html

Import a skip-traced list into Salesforce: clean, split, tag, test, then load
A list from PropStream, BatchLeads or a skip-tracing service is the cheapest way to fill a cold-calling queue, and the fastest way to wreck a Salesforce org. The file arrives with three phone numbers per owner, the same owner on four rows, addresses spelled five ways, and half the people already in your system from last month's list. Loaded straight in, it creates thousands of duplicates, triggers thousands of tasks at once and buries the history of sellers you already know. This guide is the routine I'd run before every list goes in: what to clean, how to split new sellers from existing ones, how to map and tag the file, and how to test and check the load. It works for any list source.
Don't load the file as it comes. Clean phone numbers to digits, standardize the property address, scrub against the Do Not Call registry, and build a match key for each row. Export your existing leads, compare keys, and split the file into new sellers and sellers you already have. Tag every row with a campaign, load 50 rows as a test, check them, then load the rest with the Data Import Wizard (up to 50,000 records at a time) or Data Loader. Hold automations during the load so thousands of tasks don't fire at once.
What should one row in the file mean?
Decide this before anything else. List providers usually give you one row per property, with the owner's name and several phone numbers and emails across columns. Salesforce wants one seller record with one main phone, and the other numbers stored somewhere you can still use them. A workable rule for most teams:
One row = one property and its owner. The property address is the key, because it is the one thing that is stable. Owners change numbers, and spellings of names vary.
Best phone in Phone, the others in their own fields (Phone 2, Phone 3, or a related record if your setup uses one), so a caller can try the next number without a second lead.
Owners with several properties get several rows. Whether they become one seller with several deals depends on your data model; see Lead, Opportunity or Property .
How do you clean the file before it goes in?
Phones to digits. One column per phone, ten digits, no brackets or dashes. This is the same cleaned-phone key your duplicate rule should match on; see duplicate seller leads .
Standardize the address. One street column, one city, state and zip. "123 N Main St" and "123 North Main Street" should be one value. A free address-cleaning step in your list tool or spreadsheet is worth the ten minutes.
Remove rows with no usable number or address. A row you can't call or mail only adds noise.
Scrub against the Do Not Call registry. The FTC says sellers and telemarketers must update their call lists, deleting numbers on the National Do Not Call Registry, at least every 31 days. Do it before you load and keep a flag for your own internal do-not-call list too. Load the result as a field, so it travels with the record.
Set consent to "no" by default. A skip-traced number is not permission to text. Leave the text-consent field empty or "No" until the seller gives it, and see texting sellers .
De-duplicate inside the file. Salesforce doesn't compare rows saved together, so the same owner twice in one file becomes two records. Sort by property key and remove repeats first.
How do you split new sellers from sellers you already have?
Build a match key in the file: cleaned property street plus zip, and separately each cleaned phone.
Export your existing leads, contacts and open deals with the same keys (add the cleaned phone and a property key field in Salesforce if you don't have them).
Compare the two. A lookup in a spreadsheet works; so does a database or Power Query. Mark each row new (no match on property or phone), existing (matches a known seller) or conflict (matches on phone but not property, or the other way round).
Handle each group on purpose. New: load as new leads. Existing: don't create a lead. Add them to the new campaign, and update fields such as a better phone number, keeping the record and its history. Conflict: review by hand. Same phone and a different property is often a seller with a second house.
This is the step most teams skip, and it is what keeps a returning seller from becoming a stranger in your system. Without it, a duplicate rule that blocks the load will fail the import instead of warning anyone, which is the cause of imports that stop with a duplicates-detected error.
How should the columns map to Salesforce fields?
In the list | In Salesforce | Note
Owner name | First and last name on the Lead | If the list gives one string, split it first. Companies and trusts go in a separate field.
Cleaned phone 1, 2, 3 | Phone, Phone 2, Phone 3 | Digits only; add a column for phone type if the list has it
Email | Email | Often wrong on skip-traced lists; mark the source
Property street, city, state, zip | Property address fields | Not the owner's mailing address, which goes in its own fields
Owner mailing address | Mailing address fields | Absentee owners are your best signal
List filters (equity, years owned, absentee, tax delinquent) | One field each, or a single picklist for situation | Keep what you'll score or filter on; drop the rest
DNC result and date | Do-not-call checkbox and scrub date | So you know how stale the scrub is
(you add) Lead source | Lead Source picklist | For example "Cold call list"
(you add) Campaign | Campaign member | See below
Use the lead source, campaign, market and status fields from the CRM field kit as your base, add the phone and address fields above, and take picklist values from the tagging rules , so a list never invents a new category.
How do you tag which list produced the deal?
Create one campaign per list pull, named so it sorts: provider, filter, date and market. Add every loaded row as a campaign member with a status such as "Loaded". Put the cost of the list on the campaign. Then your reports can answer the question that matters later, which is not "how many leads did this list give me" but "how many contracts, and what did each cost". The campaign setup is covered in lead sources in Salesforce , and the arithmetic in the cost per deal calculator .
What should you hold back during the load?
An import is an event your automations will react to. Imagine a flow that creates a call task for every new lead, an assignment rule that spreads leads across reps, and a text sequence that starts on a new record. Load 8,000 rows and you create 8,000 tasks, assign them in one lump and possibly send messages you didn't mean to. Before you load:
Decide who owns the list (one caller group or queue), and set the owner in the file, so assignment doesn't scatter it.
Add a "list import" flag your flows can check, so call-now tasks and speed-to-lead alerts skip it; those are for inbound sellers.
Make sure nothing sends a message to a record just because it was created.
Switch on duplicate reporting, so any match is logged rather than lost.
How do you test, load and check?
Test with 50 rows. Pick a mix: new, existing and a few ugly ones. Load them and open ten records. Check phones, addresses, source, campaign, owner and consent.
Load the rest. The Data Import Wizard handles up to 50,000 records at a time. For more, or when you need to update existing records by ID, use Data Loader.
Check the counts. Rows in the file equal records created plus records updated plus rows you set aside. If the numbers don't add up, find the gap before anyone starts dialing.
Run a duplicate report. Group the new leads by cleaned phone and by property key. Anything with two or more records goes to the clean-up list.
Spot-check 20. Pick twenty at random, find each in the CRM and compare with the file.
Keep the file. Store the original and the cleaned version with the campaign. If a seller disputes where you got their number, you'll want it.
Then let the callers in, with their queue set up as in the cold-calling team setup .
Questions
Can I connect PropStream to Salesforce?
I found no native PropStream integration with Salesforce. PropStream exports lists as spreadsheets, which you clean and then import with the Data Import Wizard (up to 50,000 records at a time) or Data Loader. The same approach works for BatchLeads and other skip-tracing exports.
How do I import a list into Salesforce without creating duplicates?
Clean phone numbers and addresses, build match keys, export your existing leads and compare, then split the file into new sellers, existing sellers and conflicts. Load only the new ones as leads, and update or add existing ones to the campaign. Also remove repeats inside the file, because Salesforce doesn't compare rows saved together.
How many records can I import with the Data Import Wizard?
Up to 50,000 records at a time, according to Salesforce Help. For larger files, or to update existing records by ID, use Data Loader.
Should every row of a skip-traced list become a lead?
No. Remove rows with no usable number, scrub against the Do Not Call registry, and don't create a new lead for someone you already have. Add known sellers to the campaign instead, so their history stays on one record.
How do I track which list produced a deal?
Create one campaign per list with the cost on it, add every loaded record as a campaign member, and keep the lead source on the record. Then report contracts and cost per contract by campaign.
How often do I have to scrub a list against the Do Not Call registry?
The FTC says sellers and telemarketers must update their call lists, removing numbers on the National Do Not Call Registry, at least every 31 days. Store the scrub date on the record so you can see how old it is. This is information, not legal advice.
Why did my Salesforce import fail with a duplicates error?
An active duplicate rule matched records in your file. Imports can't show an alert to a person, so the rule can stop those records from being saved. Split new from existing sellers before the load, so the file doesn't contain records that match.
Related guides
Sources
Checked in October 2026. Compliance notes are information, not legal advice.
Salesforce Help: Data Import Wizard, how many records . Up to 50,000 records at a time
FTC: Complying with the Telemarketing Sales Rule . Update call lists against the National Do Not Call Registry at least every 31 days
Salesforce Help: Things to know about duplicate rules . Records saved together aren't compared; imports can't show alerts

The CRM Revenue Audit (USD 1,500, fixed price) checks how lists, duplicates and campaigns behave in your org today and returns a fix plan. It's for teams already on Salesforce. On another CRM and moving? List loading is the first routine we set up.

## Wholesaling SOPs That Live Inside Your CRM, Not a Doc
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/sops-inside-your-crm-wholesaling.html

Wholesaling SOPs that live inside your CRM: shown at the moment of the task, checked without a meeting
Every wholesaling company eventually writes SOPs: a shared document with how a cold caller handles a lead, how acquisitions runs an appointment, how dispo sends a deal. A month later, nobody opens it. New hires read it once, the team drifts, and the owner is back to correcting the same mistakes by message. The fix isn't a better document, it's moving each rule to the place the work happens, so the CRM shows it when it matters, requires it when it must be right and reports on whether it was followed. This guide shows the five-line format I use for an SOP, the SOPs a 10 to 50 person team needs by role, and where in Salesforce each part belongs.
Write each SOP in five lines: the trigger, the owner, up to seven steps, a done-when check and a clock. Then put each piece where work happens: the steps as guidance on the Path or as tasks a flow creates, the must-haves as required fields and validation messages, the clock as an alert, and the done-when check as a report that shows how often it was met. Keep a short document only as an index and for the why.
Why do SOP documents stop being used?
They live somewhere else. The rule is in a document and the work is in the CRM, so reading the rule is an extra step nobody takes under pressure.
They're too long. A ten-page SOP is read once. A seven-step one is used.
Nothing checks them. If skipping a step costs nothing and shows nowhere, it gets skipped.
They go stale. The process changes, the document doesn't, and the team learns to ignore it.
They describe an ideal, not the job. They say what should happen, not what the system shows, requires and records.
What is the five-line SOP?
Trigger: the event that starts it. "A seller sets an appointment."
Owner: one role or person. "The acquisitions rep on the lead."
Steps: seven at most, each starting with a verb. If it needs more than seven, it's two SOPs.
Done when: the observable result. "The appointment has a date, a confirmed address and every decision maker named."
Clock: how long it may take, and what happens if it doesn't. "Confirmed by the morning of; alert to the manager if not."
A "done-when" that you can't check in the CRM is a warning sign. Either the CRM is missing a field or the SOP is too vague.
Which SOPs does each role need?
Role | SOPs (one each)
Cold caller or VA | Working a list; logging a call outcome; handing off an interested seller; handling do-not-call and wrong numbers
Lead manager | First response to an inbound lead or missed call; reassigning an unclaimed lead; weekly duplicate clean-up
Acquisitions | Running an appointment; making and sending an offer; following up an offer; closing out a dead deal with a reason and a date
Dispositions | Marketing a contract to buyers; recording buyer responses; assigning and collecting the fee
Transaction coordinator | Opening title; tracking closing dates; confirming funding; filing documents on the deal
Marketing | Launching a campaign with its cost and source tags; loading a list ( importing a list )
Ops or admin | Adding a user and their access; checking automations for errors; changing a field or stage safely
That's about twenty SOPs for a full team, and a new company doesn't need all of them on day one; see "start with three" below. Who owns what in more detail is on team roles and the CRM .
Where does each part live in Salesforce?
SOP part | Where it lives
Trigger | A record-triggered flow or a stage change, so the SOP starts itself
Owner | The record owner or a queue with a claim rule
Steps | Guidance on the Path step (up to 1,000 characters), or tasks created by a flow, one per step, with the instruction in the task description
Must-haves | Required fields and validation rules with specific messages ("Add the closing date before moving to Under contract")
Done when | The fields filled in, plus a checkbox or status that a manager can report on
Clock | A date field and a scheduled flow that creates a task or alerts a manager when it's late
Guided data entry | A screen flow for multi-step jobs such as logging an offer, so the user fills in the right things in the right order
The why and the exceptions | A short document linked from the record or the Path, kept to a page
The pipeline stage rules in pipeline stages are SOPs in this form: entry, exit, owner and clock for each stage. The call outcomes in the cold-calling setup are another.
How do you check that SOPs are followed?
For each SOP, pick one measure the CRM can report and put it on a manager's screen:
Appointment SOP: percentage of appointments with all decision makers named.
Offer SOP: percentage of offers with a follow-up date set within a day.
Handoff SOP: percentage of handoffs accepted by acquisitions without being sent back.
Dispo SOP: time from contract to buyers contacted.
Do-not-call SOP: number of records with a do-not-call flag that still have an open task.
A weekly look, five minutes, with one question per measure: who needs help? Not who to blame. If most of the team misses a step, the SOP or the system is wrong, not the people. The Monday numbers in the Monday 5 give the owner's view on top.
How should you train and update?
Day one, on a practice record. A new hire works a test lead from new to closed, with the Path and tasks guiding them. They learn the SOPs by doing them, and you see where they stumble.
One owner per SOP, who reviews it every quarter and whenever a mistake repeats.
Change the system and the guidance together. If you rename a stage or add a field, update the Path guidance in the same change.
Write down the reason. One line, "we require the closing date here because title can't open without it", saves a lot of arguments.
Keep access narrow. People follow the SOP for their role more easily when they see only what that role needs; see who sees what .
What are the three to write first?
First response to a new lead or missed call. It's where most money leaks ( speed to lead ).
The cold-caller-to-acquisitions handoff. It's where most deals get lost between two people ( handoff checklist ).
Offer sent to offer answered. It's where the pipeline sits longest ( offer follow-up ).
Write those three in the five-line form, build each into the CRM, run them for a month and look at the measures. Then add the next three. If you want the setup done once and properly, that's included in an audit and in ongoing support.
Questions
What SOPs does a wholesaling company need?
Roughly twenty for a full team, grouped by role: caller and VA, lead manager, acquisitions, dispositions, transaction coordinator, marketing and ops. A new company can start with three: first response to a new lead, the caller-to-acquisitions handoff, and offer follow-up.
How do I make my team actually follow SOPs?
Put each step where the work happens: guidance on the Path, tasks a flow creates, required fields with clear messages, and a manager report on whether it was followed. A document nobody opens can't change behavior; a field that won't save without the right data does.
How long should an SOP be?
Seven steps at most. If it needs more, it's two SOPs. Add a trigger, an owner, a done-when check and a clock, and keep the explanation of why on one page.
Where should SOPs live, in a doc or in the CRM?
In the CRM wherever possible, because that's where the work is done. Keep a short document as an index and for the reasons behind the rules, and link it from the record or the Path.
How do I train a new VA on my CRM?
Give them a practice record to work from new to closed, with the Path guidance and tasks leading them, limited access to what their role needs and a manager who checks their first week of work against the SOP measures.
How do I know whether an SOP is being followed?
Pick one measure per SOP that the CRM can report, such as the percentage of offers with a follow-up date set within a day, and review it weekly. If most people miss a step, fix the SOP or the system rather than blaming the team.

Sources
Checked in October 2026. Salesforce and vendor features change with each release, so check the linked page before you rely on a detail.
Trailhead: Visualize Success with Path and Kanban . Up to five key fields and up to 1,000 characters of guidance per path step

## Speed to Lead for Real Estate Investors: The First-Hour Rule
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/speed-to-lead-real-estate-investors.html

Speed to lead for real estate investors: the first-hour rule.
Speed to lead is the time between a seller reaching out and a real person on your team talking to them. For investors and wholesalers it decides who gets the deal: motivated sellers usually contact several buyers, and they often go with the first one who answers and sounds able to help. Aim to reach every inbound lead within the hour, and measure it.
What the research says
The best-known study is The Short Life of Online Sales Leads (Harvard Business Review, March 2011) by James Oldroyd, Kristina McElheran and David Elkington. Looking at 1.25 million leads across 42 US companies, firms that contacted a lead within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify it as firms that waited longer, and more than 60 times as likely as firms that waited 24 hours or more. In a separate audit of 2,241 US companies, only 37% responded within an hour and 23% never responded.
That study covered web leads in general, not seller calls. A missed seller call is the same problem in a sharper form: the seller already reached out, and the clock is running against every other investor they called.
How to measure your speed to lead
Lead created time = when the call, form or text came in
First conversation time = when a person on your team actually spoke with the seller
Speed to lead (minutes) = first conversation time − lead created time
Report: median by lead source, by hour of day, and by rep, every Monday
Use the median, because one lead that waited three days will distort an average. Split by hour of day: most teams find their gap is evenings and weekends, which is when many sellers call.
Five rules that fix it in any CRM
1. Every missed call becomes a task
When a call to a marketing number is not answered, the CRM creates the lead if it does not exist and a callback task due in minutes. No missed call should exist only in the phone system.
2. Route to whoever is free
New leads and missed-call tasks go to the next available rep, not to the person who owns the number or the market. A lead waiting for one busy rep is a slow lead.
3. Escalate after 15 minutes
If nobody has touched a new lead or a callback task in 15 minutes, it moves to a second person or a manager. Pick the number that fits your team, then enforce it.
4. Acknowledge after hours, call first thing
Outside business hours, send the seller a short text that a person will call at a set time, then make that call the first task of the morning. Track the acknowledgment and the conversation as separate times.
5. Put the number on the Monday report
Median speed to lead and missed calls not returned, by source. What gets reviewed every week gets faster.
What it costs you
Put your own numbers into the free missed seller call cost calculator : inbound calls, the share you miss, the share you never reach, your conversion rates and average profit. It turns missed calls into lost deals and lost profit per month and per year.
Questions
What is speed to lead?
The time between a seller reaching out (a call, a web form, a text reply) and a real person on your team having a conversation with them. Measure it to the first conversation, not to the first automated text.
What is a good speed to lead for a wholesaler or home-buying company?
Under an hour is the bar the research supports, and in practice the goal is minutes for inbound calls and web forms during business hours. More important than a target is knowing your real number by lead source and by hour of day.
Does an automatic text count as a response?
It helps, because the seller knows they reached someone. But it is not a conversation. Track automated acknowledgment and first human conversation as two separate times.
How do I measure speed to lead if my CRM does not track it?
Add two date-time fields to the lead: when the lead came in and when the first real conversation happened. A formula field gives the minutes between them. Report the median, not the average, by source and by hour.
Why do missed calls matter so much?
A missed inbound call is a seller who already chose to call you. If nobody calls back fast, they talk to the next investor on their list, and the lead never shows up in your CRM at all, so your reports cannot see the loss.
Related
Missed-call alerts in Salesforce · Motivated seller lead scoring · Seller appointment no-shows · Lead sources into Salesforce · Speed to lead & follow-up statistics · Cold caller handoff checklist · Missed seller call cost · Acquisitions team capacity · Deal Leak Score · The Monday 5 · Follow-up cadence builder · All guides · All free tools

## Stop Reps Exporting Your Seller List from Salesforce
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/stop-reps-exporting-leads-salesforce.html

Your seller list is the business. Stopping reps from exporting it in Salesforce
Every owner who has watched a rep leave for a competitor, or start their own wholesaling company, has wondered what walked out the door with them. Your seller list, with years of conversations, numbers and reasons to sell, is one of the most valuable things the business owns. This page is for owners and ops managers who want to know what a rep can actually take out of Salesforce, what to switch off, and what to do when someone gives notice.
Turn off Export Reports for everyone who doesn't need it, keep API Enabled, Weekly Data Export, View All Data and Modify All Data for admins, and set sharing so reps see their own leads and their market's queue rather than every seller you've ever had. Add login hours or IP ranges if your team works set hours or from an office. Know the limits: nothing stops a screenshot, and seeing who exported what needs the paid Event Monitoring add-on. When a rep gives notice, reassign their records and freeze their user the same day.
How can data leave Salesforce?
Route | What controls it | Notes
Exporting a report, or its printable view | The Export Reports permission | The most common route, and the easiest to close
Data Loader, spreadsheet add-ins and other tools that use the API | The API Enabled permission | Check what else depends on it before switching it off
The weekly data export in Setup | The Weekly Data Export permission | A copy of everything. Admins only
Records beyond their own | Sharing settings, and View All Data | The more a rep can see, the more they can copy
Report subscriptions and scheduled emails | Report and subscription permissions | Results land in an inbox, possibly a personal one
Contact sync to email and phone | Your email and calendar sync settings | Check whether contacts sync into reps' own accounts
Your dialer and texting tools | Those tools' own settings | Many keep their own copy of your contacts
Screenshots and copying from the screen | Nothing | Limiting what each rep can see is the only defense
No setting makes leaking impossible. The goal is to close the easy routes, make the hard ones slow and visible, and keep what each person can see to what they need.
Which permissions should you remove?
From Salesforce's own permission descriptions:
Export Reports "allows the user to use Export Details and Printable View to export reports." Take it off reps, callers and VAs. Keep it for the owner, the manager who runs reports and the admin.
API Enabled "allows the user [to] execute API calls," which is what Data Loader and similar tools need. Remove it from people who don't need it, but test first: some phone, texting and email tools connect as each user and stop working without it.
Weekly Data Export lets a user run the weekly Data Export Service. Admins only.
View All Data and Modify All Data let a user see or change everything in the org, regardless of sharing. Admins only, and as few of them as possible.
The clean way to set this up is a rep profile with none of these, plus an "Export" permission set you assign to the two or three people who need it. Then the answer to "who can export?" is a list you can read in Setup. More on profiles and permission sets for each role in Salesforce access for VAs and cold callers .
Setup Audit Trail shows changes made in Setup, including many profile and permission changes, so you can spot someone quietly given export rights. Salesforce keeps it for 180 days and shows the 20 most recent entries on screen; download it to see the rest.
Limit what each rep can see
This is the biggest lever, and the one most investor orgs skip. A rep who can see 40,000 sellers can photograph 40,000 sellers. A rep who sees their own 300 and their market's open queue can't.
Set leads to private by default , then open up what each role needs with queues and sharing rules: their own records, their market's shared queue, and the deals they work on.
Keep the archive for managers. Closed deals, dead leads and other markets don't need to be visible to every rep.
Hide what callers don't need with field-level security: assignment fees, profit, buyer lists.
There's a trade-off. Investor teams like shared queues because they're fast, and locking everything down slows the team. The middle path above keeps speed where it matters, on new and open leads, and protects the years of history behind them.
Login hours and IP ranges
Both are set per profile. Login IP ranges limit logins to addresses you list, such as your office or VPN, which works well for VA teams in one office. Login hours limit logins to set times, such as a calling shift. Neither suits reps who work from their phones at odd hours, so use them where they fit.
Give every person their own login. Shared logins for a dialer, a texting tool or Salesforce itself mean you can't tell who did what, and you can't shut one person out without locking out everyone.
Can you see who exported what?
Partly, and the useful part costs extra.
Free: login history shows who logged in, when and from where. Salesforce's free Event Monitoring tier covers a few event types, such as logins, logouts and total API usage, with one day of storage.
Paid: report exports are a separate event type that needs the Event Monitoring add-on, also part of Salesforce Shield. It covers more than 70 event types, with up to 30 days of storage.
Blocking: with that add-on, a Transaction Security policy can block a report export above a set number of rows and email someone when a user tries.
For most teams of 10 to 50, the add-on isn't worth it. Removing the permission is the cheap control. It starts to make sense when you have many users, a history of leaks, or a lot of money riding on one list.
What should you do when a rep gives notice?
Decide on access first. Whether they work their notice period, and with what access, is the owner's call. Make it before anything else happens.
Reassign their open leads, deals and tasks the same day , and take them out of round robin , queues and alerts. The steps are in the new rep and offboarding checklist .
Freeze their user. Freezing blocks login right away; it doesn't free the license. Deactivate once nothing depends on the user, such as a report, an automation or an integration running under their name. The admin handover plan covers what to check.
Close the side doors. Their dialer and texting logins, shared drives, the data tools where your lists live, and any password they knew.
Look at recent activity: logins, and report exports if you have Event Monitoring.
Keep the phone numbers. If sellers have been calling a rep's personal cell, they'll keep calling it after the rep leaves. Company numbers in your dialer stay with the company.
What about agreements and the law?
Permissions slow people down. Agreements give you recourse. Whether a confidentiality or non-solicitation agreement holds up depends on your state, so that's a conversation for an employment attorney. Not legal advice.
One thing worth knowing: under the federal trade secrets law, information only counts as a trade secret if the owner took reasonable measures to keep it secret. Removing export rights, limiting who sees what and giving everyone their own login are part of showing that you did.
Questions
Can you stop users exporting data from Salesforce?
You can close the main routes: remove Export Reports, API Enabled, Weekly Data Export, View All Data and Modify All Data from users who don't need them, and limit which records each user can see. Nothing stops screenshots, so limiting what each rep can see matters most.
What does the Export Reports permission do in Salesforce?
Salesforce describes it as allowing the user to use Export Details and Printable View to export reports. Without it, a user can still run reports they have access to but can't export them.
Can Salesforce show who exported a report?
Yes, with the paid Event Monitoring add-on (also part of Salesforce Shield), which logs report exports. The free tier only covers a few event types, such as logins, logouts and total API usage, kept for one day.
Can I block large report exports in Salesforce?
With Event Monitoring or Shield, a Transaction Security policy can block a report export above a set number of rows and send an email alert when someone tries.
Should I freeze or deactivate a rep who quits?
Freeze them right away, which blocks login, then reassign their records. Deactivate once nothing depends on the user, such as reports, automations or integrations running under their name.
Will removing API access break my integrations?
It can. Some phone, texting and email tools connect to Salesforce as each user and need API Enabled. Test with one user before removing it from everyone, and run integrations under a dedicated integration user where you can.
Is my seller list a trade secret?
It may be, but that's a question for an attorney. Under federal law, information only qualifies if the owner took reasonable measures to keep it secret, so access controls and permissions help make the case.
Related guides
Sources
Checked in October 2026. Salesforce features and add-ons change, so check the linked page before you rely on a detail. Nothing here is legal advice.
