## Podio, REsimpli or GoHighLevel to Salesforce: Switch Guide
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/switch-to-salesforce-real-estate-investors.html

Moving from Podio, REsimpli or GoHighLevel to Salesforce.
A switch to Salesforce is mostly a data and habits project. The software part is the easy bit. This guide gives you an honest side-by-side with prices checked on each vendor's site, a field map from each tool to Salesforce, what usually breaks, and a 30-60-90 day plan that keeps new leads flowing while both systems run.
Free download: the CRM switch field map (CSV, about 50 rows). Typical fields in each tool, where they go in Salesforce, and what usually breaks.
Side by side
Prices for the other tools are the vendors' own list prices, checked on October 20, 2026. Salesforce pricing depends on edition and number of users, and businesses can often get a discount through their Salesforce account manager. They change, so click through before you decide. "Built in" lists what the vendor says is included; it is not a review.
Tool | List price | Users | Built in (per vendor) | Getting your data out
Podio | Free; Plus $11.20 and Premium $19.20 per user/mo billed annually ( pricing ) | Free up to 5 employees; once you upgrade, every employee is billed ( billing ) | Custom apps you design; Workflow Automation included with Premium | Excel per app, 20,000 items per export, no comments, files or tasks ( help )
REsimpli | Solo $249/mo billed annually ( pricing ); Team $699/mo annual for 5 users and Business $1,799/mo for 15, per REsimpli's own blog ( source ) | 1, 5 or 15 by plan | Dialer, list stacking, skip tracing, direct mail and KPI dashboards on every plan; AI agents optional, priced per plan | Leads export from the list view ( help ); test what notes and calls come with it
CarrotCRM (formerly InvestorFuse) | Free; Essential $69, Scale $179, Team $349 per month ( pricing ) | 1, 3, 5, 10 | Investor lead follow-up; no setup fees per Carrot | Not documented on the pricing page; ask support
GoHighLevel | Starter $97, Unlimited $297, Agency Pro $497 per month ( pricing ), plus usage fees for calls, texts, email and AI | Unlimited | Funnels, texting, email, workflows; not built for investors specifically | Contacts CSV, admins only, latest note only, no text or email history, per sub-account ( help )
Follow Up Boss | Grow $58/user/mo annual; Pro $416/mo annual for 10 users; Platform $833/mo for 30 ( pricing ) | Per user, 10 or 30 | Lead routing, calling and texting on Pro and up; built for agent teams | CSV with last 50 calls, texts and notes per contact; no emails or recordings ( help )
Spreadsheet | Free | Anyone with the link | Whatever you build | It's already a file
Salesforce Pro Suite | Depends on edition and number of users; API access is an add-on. Most businesses can get a discount through their Salesforce account manager ( editions ) | Per user | Leads, deals, campaigns, forecasting, 50 custom objects, 5 flows total ( limits ) | Data Export every 29 days on Professional-level orgs; Data Loader with API
Salesforce Core | Depends on edition and number of users; ask your Salesforce account manager for a quote and a discount ( editions ) | Per user | Enterprise-level automation, approvals, joined reports, Premier Success | Weekly Data Export on Enterprise-level orgs (per Salesforce); Data Loader up to 5 million records ( help )
Stay where you are if...
Podio: your team knows it, someone can still change it, and the problems are messy fields rather than missing reports. A clean rebuild costs less than a switch.
REsimpli: you are under about five people and use the dialer, list stacking and mail every day. Replacing those means three new vendors.
CarrotCRM: you run Carrot websites and mainly need lead follow-up at a low price.
GoHighLevel: marketing and texting are the job and deals are simple. Flat pricing with unlimited users is hard to beat for that.
Follow Up Boss: you are an agent team more than an investor team.
Any tool: nobody on your side will own a new system. Switching tools won't fix ownership.
Not sure? Score your funnel with the Deal Leak Score . If the leaks are in follow-up and ownership, fix those first in the tool you have.
The field map: where your data goes in Salesforce
Every investor CRM stores the same five things under different names. Here is where each lands. The CSV has the field-level version.
What it is | Podio | REsimpli / CarrotCRM | GoHighLevel / Follow Up Boss | Salesforce
Seller inquiry | Leads app item | Lead | Contact / Person | Lead (converts to Account + Contact)
Property | Properties app or fields on the lead | Fields on the lead | Custom fields on the contact | Custom Property object, so a repeat seller gets a second deal, not a duplicate
Deal | Deals or Opportunities app | Lead status / deal stage | Opportunity in a pipeline / deal stage | Opportunity with your stages and a Path
Cash buyer | Buyers app | Buyers module or tag | Contact with a tag | Contact with buy-box fields
Closing | Transactions app or deal fields | Deal fields | Often outside the CRM | Custom Transaction object with actual profit
Marketing source | Category field | Lead source / list | Source, tags | Lead source picklist + Campaign Member
Calls and notes | Comments (not in Excel export) | Activity history | Conversations / notes | Tasks, Notes, call logs from your phone system
Automations | Workflow Automation (Globiflow) | Drip campaigns | Workflows / Action Plans | Flows, rebuilt by hand
Names vary by setup. Podio workspaces in particular are custom, so map from your own apps, not from this table.
What usually breaks
Duplicate sellers
Stacked lists and repeat inquiries mean the same owner appears three or four times with different phone formats. Normalize phones and addresses before import, then turn on matching and duplicate rules . Duplicate rules, even ones set to allow with an alert, can make import rows fail with a DUPLICATES_DETECTED error ( Salesforce Help ), so read the error file after every load.
Call logs and notes
Every source cuts history short: GoHighLevel exports the latest note only, Follow Up Boss the last 50 calls, texts and notes, and Podio's Excel export carries no comments. Load what you have as completed Tasks and Notes with Data Loader, and only for open deals and active sellers. Archive the rest.
Tags
Tags come out as one cell of comma-separated text. Decide tag by tag: picklist value, campaign, or delete. Importing every tag as one huge multi-select field gives you a field nobody can report on.
Attachments
The Data Import Wizard can't load files. Data Loader can, with limits on request size ( Salesforce Help ). For years of photos, a link to a shared drive folder per property is often enough.
Automations
No tool exports its automations. List every Podio flow, REsimpli drip, GoHighLevel workflow or Follow Up Boss action plan, keep the ones that still matter, and rebuild them as Flows.
Original dates
Imported records get today's created date unless the admin enables the "Set Audit Fields upon Record Creation" permission (Setup > User Interface, then a permission set) or stores the original date in a custom field. Without it, your first month of reports says every lead came in on cutover day.
Import limits: the Data Import Wizard handles up to 50,000 records at a time; Data Loader handles up to 5 million and needs API access ( Salesforce Help ).
The 30-60-90 day switch plan
Days | Do | Done when
1–30: map and build | Inventory every field, app and automation. Fill in the CSV. Decide what history moves. Build objects, fields, stages, the shared lead queue, missed-call alert and duplicate rules in a sandbox or a copy. Connect the phone system. | Reps have worked 20 real leads in the test org and signed off on the stages.
31–60: move and run both | Load buyers, then sellers and properties, then open deals, then activity history. Pick a cutover day: every web form, phone number and list import points to Salesforce from that morning. The old tool goes read-only. | Two weeks with zero new leads created in the old tool.
61–90: earn the switch | Follow-up cadences, transactions board, buyer matching, campaign ROI and the Monday dashboard. Train on the five reports people use. Cancel the old subscription after the last lookup. | The Monday meeting runs from one dashboard and nobody exports to a spreadsheet.
Risks and how to handle them
Leads slip during cutover. One cutover day, every source moved together, and a daily count of leads created in each system.
Reps keep working the old tool. Make it read-only on cutover day. A friendly week of both is how leads end up in neither.
Reports look wrong in month one. Expected if original dates or sources didn't move. Fix the mapping in the 50-record test, not after the full load.
Edition surprise. Pro Suite allows 5 flows in total. Count the automations you plan before you sign.
Texting compliance. If you change texting providers, your A2P 10DLC brand and campaign registration may need to be moved or redone with the new provider, and your opt-out lists must come with you. Check with your provider and counsel; this page isn't legal advice.
Running both systems without losing leads
Write down every lead source: each web form, each phone number, each list vendor, each texting campaign.
Give each one a cutover owner and a time on cutover day.
Keep the old tool open read-only so reps can look up history, not create records.
Every morning for two weeks, run two counts: new leads in Salesforce yesterday, new records in the old tool yesterday. The second number should be zero.
If it isn't, find the source and move it that day.
Compare the Monday numbers from both systems for the first month. Where they differ, one of them is missing data.
Questions
Should I switch from Podio to Salesforce?
Switch if your team has outgrown what Podio can report or automate without a consultant, and you have someone to own the new system. Stay, or rebuild Podio, if the team knows it and the problems are messy fields and missing automations. The checklist on the moving off Podio page covers that choice.
Is REsimpli or Salesforce better for a wholesaler?
REsimpli is the better fit for a small team that wants dialer, list stacking, skip tracing and direct mail in one box with no admin. Salesforce fits a larger team with its own process, several markets, or reporting REsimpli can't produce. Many teams that switch keep their dialer and data vendors and connect them to Salesforce.
Can I keep GoHighLevel and add Salesforce?
Yes. Some teams keep GoHighLevel for marketing and texting and make Salesforce the record of every deal. The risk is duplicates: decide which system creates the person and sync on one key, usually phone number, with a duplicate rule on the Salesforce side.
Will I lose my call history and notes?
Some of it, often. GoHighLevel's contact export carries only the latest note, Follow Up Boss caps calls, texts and notes at the last 50 per contact, and Podio's Excel export leaves out comments and files. Move history for open deals and active sellers, and keep the old account read-only for a few months for lookups.
How long does a switch take?
The plan on this page runs 90 days, with new leads flowing into Salesforce by about day 45. Clean data and few integrations make it faster; five tools and three years of tags make it slower.
How do I avoid losing leads during the switch?
Pick one cutover day for new leads, move every web form and phone number on that day, and run a daily check for two weeks: leads created in each system yesterday. If the old system got any, a source was missed.
What is the field mapping template?
A free CSV with about 50 rows: typical fields in Podio, REsimpli, GoHighLevel, Follow Up Boss, CarrotCRM and spreadsheets, the Salesforce object and field each one maps to, and what usually breaks. Open it in Excel or Google Sheets and add a column for your own field names.

## Wholesale Assignment Fee: Set It So the Deal Still Sells
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesale-assignment-fee.html

Wholesale assignment fee: set it from the buyer's margin.
An assignment fee is what a wholesaler is paid for assigning the purchase contract to a cash buyer. The fee that works is not a round number you pick in advance: it is whatever is left after the buyer's repairs, costs and required profit come out of the after-repair value, minus your contract price. Price it from the buyer's side and deals sell instead of sitting.
The max-fee formula
Buyer's costs = ARV × closing, holding and selling %
Buyer's profit = the profit active buyers in that market need on this kind of deal
Max fee = ARV − repairs − buyer's costs − buyer's profit − your contract price
If max fee is below the fee you need, renegotiate the contract price or pass
Worked example
Made-up numbers to show the math. A house has a $250,000 after-repair value and needs $40,000 of repairs. The buyer's closing, holding and selling costs run about 10% of ARV, so $25,000. Buyers in that area want around 15% of ARV in profit on a medium rehab, so $37,500. Your contract price is $130,000. Max fee = $250,000 − $40,000 − $25,000 − $37,500 − $130,000 = $17,500 . Ask $25,000 and the buyer's profit drops to $30,000; some will pass, and the ones who stay may try to renegotiate before closing.
Run your own numbers in the free wholesale deal analyzer : it shows your MAO, the room under it, the buyer's all-in cost and the buyer's profit and return after your fee.
Assign or double close?
An assignment is usually cheaper: one closing, and the fee is paid at that closing. A double close means you buy the property and resell it, often the same day, so you pay a second set of closing costs and may need transactional funding, but the buyer does not see your spread on the assignment paperwork. Compare the two with your numbers in the assignment vs double close calculator .
What to track in your CRM
Planned fee vs closed fee
Save the fee you expected when you went under contract and the fee that actually closed. The gap shows how often buyers push back and on which kinds of deals.
Fee by lead source and campaign
Average fee per closed deal by source tells you more than lead counts do. A source with fewer leads and bigger fees can beat a cheaper one.
Assignment or double close
A picklist on the deal, plus the extra closing costs on double closes, so the report shows what you actually kept.
Questions
What is an assignment fee?
The amount a wholesaler is paid for assigning their purchase contract with the seller to an end buyer. The buyer pays the seller the contract price and pays the wholesaler the fee, usually at closing.
How much is a typical assignment fee?
There is no standard amount. It depends on the spread between your contract price and what buyers in that market will pay. The useful question is not what is typical but how much fee this deal can carry while the buyer still makes the profit they need.
Does the buyer see my fee?
With an assignment, usually yes: the fee appears in the assignment agreement and on the settlement statement. If a large fee would put the buyer or seller off, a double close is the common alternative, at the cost of a second set of closing costs.
Is assigning a contract legal everywhere?
Rules on wholesaling, assignment and disclosure vary by state and change over time, and some purchase contracts forbid assignment. For example, Oklahoma's SB 1075, in effect since November 1, 2025, requires written disclosures to the seller and a two-business-day right to cancel. This page is not legal advice; check the contract and ask a local real estate attorney before you assign.
What should my CRM track about fees?
The fee on every closed deal, the fee you planned when you went under contract, the lead source and the campaign. That shows which sources produce the deals with the biggest fees and how often fees get cut before closing.

Several states now regulate how you contract and assign, with disclosures, cancellation windows and closing deadlines. See new wholesaling laws: what your CRM has to track , state by state.

## Wholesale Deal Analyzer: MAO, Your Fee & Buyer Profit
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesale-deal-analyzer.html

Wholesale deal analyzer.
One sheet for one deal: your maximum allowable offer, how much room your contract price leaves, what your cash buyer pays, and whether there is still enough profit in it for them to close. A deal that only works for you does not close. Built for real estate investors in the United States, Canada, the UK and Europe. Pick your currency; the math is the same everywhere.
The formula
MAO = ARV × rule % − repairs − your fee
Room under MAO = MAO − your contract price
Price to buyer = contract price + your fee
Buyer all-in = price to buyer + repairs + (ARV × buyer costs %)
Buyer profit = ARV − buyer all-in
Buyer return on cost = buyer profit ÷ buyer all-in
Worked example
A house with a $250,000 ARV needs $40,000 of repairs. At a 70% rule and a $12,000 fee, MAO is $123,000. You contract at $115,000, which leaves $8,000 of room. Your buyer pays $127,000, spends $40,000 on repairs and $25,000 on closing, holding and selling, for an all-in of $192,000. Sold at ARV, the buyer keeps $58,000, a 30.2% return on cost.
Questions
What is MAO in real estate wholesaling?
MAO (maximum allowable offer) is the highest price you can put a property under contract for and still leave room for your end buyer's profit and your own fee. The common starting formula is ARV × 70% − repair costs − your wholesale fee.
What is a good assignment fee?
There is no fixed number. The fee works when the buyer still has enough profit to take the deal. A useful check is the buyer's return on cost after your fee: if it drops below what active buyers in your market accept, the fee is too big for that deal.
What is the 70% rule?
A rule of thumb that a buyer should pay no more than 70% of the after-repair value minus repairs. It leaves room for closing, holding and selling costs and the buyer's profit. It is a starting point, not a law: adjust the percentage to what buyers in your market actually pay.
Should the wholesale fee come out of MAO?
Yes. Your end buyer's number is ARV × rule % − repairs. Your fee sits on top of your contract price, so your own maximum offer is the buyer's number minus your fee.
Why check the buyer's profit, not just my MAO?
Your MAO tells you what to offer the seller. The buyer's profit tells you whether the deal will sell. Deals that clear your MAO but leave the buyer a thin margin are the ones that sit, get renegotiated or fall out.
Where should the ARV and repair numbers come from?
ARV from recent sold comparables near the property with similar size, age and condition after repairs; active listings and automated estimates are a cross-check, not the number. Repairs from a walkthrough with a contractor or a repair estimate sheet, plus a contingency. The analyzer is only as good as these two inputs.
Can my CRM run this on every deal?
Yes. Put ARV, repairs, rule %, fee and contract price on the deal record as fields and the results as formula fields, so every rep makes offers from the same math and every lost deal shows why.
Related free tools
Assignment vs double close · Deal Leak Score · Cash buyers list template · Assignment fee guide · All free tools
Last updated October 2026. For planning only, not financial, tax or legal advice. Check figures with your lender, accountant or lawyer.

Free to embed on your blog or investor site. Copy the code below.

## Wholesaling Cost Per Deal Calculator by Lead Source
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesaling-cost-per-deal-calculator.html

Wholesaling cost per deal, by lead source.
Put in last month's (or last quarter's) numbers for each marketing channel. The calculator shows cost per lead, cost per contract, cost per closed deal and ROI side by side, so you can see which channel is actually paying for itself. Nothing you type leaves your browser.
Channel | Spend ($) | Leads | Contracts | Closed deals | Gross profit ($)
Results
Channel | Cost / lead | Lead → contract | Cost / contract | Cost / deal | ROI
Enter spend and closed deals for at least one channel.
Gross profit = assignment fees or net profit from the closed deals that came from that channel. Example numbers are made up for illustration only.
How the numbers work
How do you calculate cost per deal in wholesaling?
Divide the total marketing spend for a channel by the number of deals that closed from that channel in the same period. Example: $6,000 on direct mail that produced 2 closed deals is a $3,000 cost per deal.
What is the difference between cost per contract and cost per deal?
Cost per contract divides spend by signed purchase contracts. Cost per deal divides spend by closed (funded) deals. The gap between them shows how many contracts fall out before closing.
How do you calculate marketing ROI per lead source?
ROI = (gross profit from closed deals − marketing spend) ÷ marketing spend. A channel with $20,000 of assignment fees on $5,000 of spend has a 300% ROI.
Where should these numbers come from?
From your CRM. Every lead needs a lead source, every contract and closed deal needs to be linked to the original lead, and spend needs to be logged per channel per month. If any link is missing, the numbers are guesses.
Why most wholesalers can't fill this in
The usual gap is attribution: leads come in from mail, PPC, cold calls and texts, but the closed deal is never tied back to the original lead source in the CRM. That's the first thing I check in a CRM Revenue Audit , and it's the first check in the free Deal Leak Score .

## Wholesaling CRM Glossary: ARV, MAO, Cost per Deal
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesaling-crm-glossary.html

Wholesaling & investor CRM glossary.
Plain-English definitions of the terms acquisitions and dispo teams use every day, and where it helps, what each one looks like inside a CRM.
Acquisitions (acq)
The part of an investor business that finds motivated sellers, qualifies them and gets properties under contract. In a CRM: Usually the lead and opportunity stages owned by acquisition reps.
After-repair value (ARV)
What a property should sell for once repairs are done, based on recent sold comps of similar renovated homes nearby. In a CRM: A currency field on the deal record that feeds the MAO formula.
Assignment contract
A contract that lets a wholesaler transfer their right to buy a property to an end buyer for a fee, instead of buying it themselves.
Assignment fee
The wholesaler's profit on an assigned deal: the difference between the end buyer's price and the wholesaler's contract price. In a CRM: Captured on the transaction so campaign ROI uses real profit.
Attribution (lead source attribution)
Tying every contract and closed deal back to the marketing channel and campaign that produced the original lead. In a CRM: Lead source carried from lead to opportunity to transaction and locked against accidental edits.
Booked revenue
Expected profit recorded when a deal goes under contract, before it closes. In a CRM: Compared weekly against what deals actually closed for (forecast vs. actual).
Comps (comparable sales)
Recently sold properties similar in size, age, condition and location, used to estimate ARV.
Contract-to-close rate
Closed deals ÷ signed contracts. The gap shows how many deals fall out after signing.
Cost per appointment
Campaign spend ÷ seller appointments set from that campaign. Closer to real channel cost than cost per lead. In a CRM: One of the Monday 5 .
Cost per contract
Campaign spend ÷ purchase contracts signed from that campaign's leads.
Cost per deal
Campaign spend ÷ closed deals from that campaign. The number that decides whether a channel pays for itself. In a CRM: See the cost per deal calculator .
Cost per lead (CPL)
Campaign spend ÷ leads generated. Easy to measure but misleading on its own, because lead quality varies by channel.
Deal leak
Profit lost between paying for a seller lead and keeping a closed deal: unanswered calls, leads with no next step, offers made off-formula, and fall-outs still counted in ROI. The Kept-Deal Map breaks it into five leak points. In a CRM: Measured with lead source carried to closing, missed-call and next-task reports, and ROI on kept deals.
Disposition (dispo)
Selling or assigning a contracted property to an end buyer. The dispo team markets deals to a cash buyers list.
Double close
Two back-to-back closings: the wholesaler buys the property and immediately resells it, instead of assigning the contract.
Drip / follow-up sequence
Scheduled calls, texts or emails to sellers who aren't ready yet. Most deals come from follow-up, not first contact. In a CRM: Tasks or cadences triggered by lead status and next follow-up date.
Kept deal
A property the investor keeps (for example as a rental) instead of selling. Leaving these out of ROI undercounts the channel that found them. In a CRM: A flag plus a profit value so it counts in campaign ROI.
Lead queue / round robin
A shared list of new leads assigned to reps in rotation or by rules (market, source, availability) so no lead sits unowned.
MAO (maximum allowable offer)
The highest contract price that still leaves room for the end buyer's margin and the wholesaler's fee. Common formula: ARV × 70% − repairs − fee. In a CRM: See the deal analyzer .
Missed-call alert
An automatic task and notification when a call to a marketing number goes unanswered, so someone calls back within minutes.
Motivated seller
An owner with a reason to sell quickly or as-is: inheritance, divorce, relocation, financial distress, a tired landlord, or a property in poor condition. In a CRM: See motivated seller lead scoring .
Pay per lead (PPL)
Buying seller leads from a vendor at a fixed price per lead, instead of paying for ads or mail directly.
PPC (pay per click)
Search or social ads where you pay per click, usually pointed at a seller landing page. In a CRM: Send contracts back to Google Ads so bidding learns from deals, not form fills. See Google Ads offline conversions .
Seventy percent rule (70% rule)
A flipper's rule of thumb: pay no more than 70% of ARV minus repairs. Markets vary, often 65–80%.
Skip tracing
Finding current phone numbers and emails for property owners from public and commercial data, mostly for cold calling and texting.
Speed to lead
The time from a seller reaching out to a real person on your team responding. In a CRM: Measured from lead created time to first logged call.
Transaction coordinator (TC)
The person who manages a deal from signed contract to closing: title, documents, deadlines and communication. In a CRM: A transactions board with stages and required checklist items.
Underwriting
Checking a deal's numbers (ARV, repairs, MAO, exit strategy) before making or accepting an offer. In a CRM: Underwriting fields and a QC gate on the opportunity.
CRM and Salesforce terms
The technical words that come up when you set up or connect a real estate CRM, each linked to the guide that goes deeper.
A2P 10DLC
US registration system for business texts sent from regular 10-digit numbers. Senders register a brand and a campaign through their texting provider. Texting guide →
API access
Permission for other software to read and write Salesforce data. Included in Enterprise and Unlimited; an add-on for Professional. Many integrations need it. Edition guide →
AppExchange
Salesforce’s marketplace of installable apps and integrations, such as DocuSign or dialer packages. Integrations →
Approval process
A rule that routes a record to a manager before it can move on, for example an offer above MAO. Automation features →
Assignment rule
Ordered rules that set a new lead’s owner automatically, by market, source or rotation. Lead routing →
Buy box
A cash buyer’s criteria: zip codes, price range, property types and condition. Stored on the buyer record so deals can be matched. Cash buyers list →
Custom object
A record type you define yourself in Salesforce, such as Property, Offer or Buyer. Data model →
Dead reason
A required picklist explaining why a lead or deal died, so you can tell bad leads from bad follow-up. Field kit → · Reactivating dead leads →
Duplicate rule
A rule that alerts or blocks when a new record matches an existing one, like the same seller from two lead sources. Data quality →
Express written consent
Documented permission to send marketing texts. CTIA’s messaging guidance calls for it before promotional texts. Texting guide →
Field history tracking
Salesforce’s log of old value, new value, who and when for chosen fields, such as stage or lead source. Data quality →
Flow
Salesforce’s automation tool. Runs when records change, on a schedule, or as guided screens. Automations →
GCLID
Google Click ID. Stored on the lead so Google Ads can learn which clicks became contracts. Lead sources → · Google Ads offline conversions →
Integration user
A dedicated Salesforce login for one integration, with only the permissions it needs. Before you connect →
Junction object
A record linking two others many-to-many, such as which buyers were sent which property. Data model →
Lead source
Where a lead came from: list, mailer, PPC, referral. Should be a picklist set automatically and kept to the closed deal. Lead sources →
Open CTI
The Salesforce framework many dialers use to show inside Salesforce. Salesforce says it reaches end of life on February 28, 2028. Dialer guide →
Opt-out
A seller’s request to stop texts or calls (for example replying STOP). Stored on the record and respected by every tool. Texting guide →
Path
A stage bar on a Salesforce record with key fields and guidance for each stage. Data quality →
Permission set
A bundle of Salesforce permissions added to a user, for example letting VAs create leads without seeing deal financials. Security →
Picklist
A field with fixed choices. Used for lead source, call outcome and dead reason so reports work. Field kit →
Queue
A shared bucket of records that team members claim from, such as hot seller callbacks. Routing →
Reporting snapshot
A saved copy of a report’s results on a schedule, so you can chart trends like weekly pipeline value. Monday 5 →
Roll-up summary field
A field on a parent record that counts or sums its children, such as offers per property. Data model →
Sandbox
A copy of your Salesforce org for testing changes before they reach the team. Integrations →
Validation rule
A rule that blocks saving a record until required data is entered, such as timeline and reason on a warm lead. Handoff checklist →
Web-to-Lead
Salesforce’s built-in way to turn website form submissions into leads, up to 500 a day. Lead sources →

## Wholesaling CRM: What It Must Track, Stage by Stage
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesaling-crm.html

Wholesaling CRM: what it must track, stage by stage.
A wholesaling CRM earns its cost when it shows where deals leak between the marketing dollar and the closing table. Check yours against five stages: spend, answer, follow-up, offer and keep. Each stage needs a few required fields, one or two automations, and one number you review every Monday. Stage rules are in wholesaling pipeline stages , and the seven jobs for a home-buying company are in CRM for a we buy houses company . Turn the checklist into rules your team follows: SOPs inside your CRM .
The checklist
1. Spend: Know what each closed deal cost
☐ Lead source and campaign on every lead, required ☐ Monthly spend per campaign ☐ Source carried through to the closed deal Monday number: Cost per kept deal by campaign
2. Answer: Talk to sellers before another investor does
☐ Missed calls create the lead and a callback task ☐ Routing to the next available rep ☐ Lead created time and first conversation time Monday number: Median speed to lead; missed calls not returned
3. Follow-up: Keep warm sellers from going quiet
☐ Lead temperature and next follow-up date, required ☐ A dated cadence by temperature ☐ Dead reason plus a date to revisit Monday number: Leads with no next step; follow-ups overdue
4. Offer: Same deal, same math, every rep
☐ ARV, repairs, rule %, fee on the deal ☐ MAO as a formula field ☐ Offer amount and date Monday number: Offers made; offers below MAO
5. Keep: Contracts that actually close
☐ Contract and closing dates ☐ Exit type: assignment or double close ☐ Fall-out reason when a deal dies Monday number: Kept deals; fall-out rate and reasons
Every field above, with picklist values and automation rules, is in the free CRM field kit . To score your current setup in two minutes, take the Deal Leak Score .
Wholesaling in Ohio, Connecticut, Louisiana, Missouri or another state with a new law? See what your CRM has to track for the new wholesaling laws . Thinking about Salesforce for all of this? Read Salesforce for real estate investors first; it says plainly when it is overkill.
How to choose: spreadsheet, investor CRM or Salesforce
Spreadsheet
Fine for one person and a handful of deals. It breaks when several people work leads, when missed calls must become tasks on their own, or when you need cost per closed deal without rebuilding it each month.
An investor CRM
Built for wholesaling and quick to start, with dialers, texting and pipelines included. Check it against the checklist above before you buy, especially lead source carried to the closed deal and fall-out reasons.
Salesforce
More setup, but it fits teams with their own process, several markets or custom reporting, and it grows with the business. I build on Salesforce, so weigh that: the checklist matters more than the brand.
Questions
What is a wholesaling CRM?
The system a wholesaler uses to track sellers, properties, offers, contracts and cash buyers from the first call to the closed assignment or double close. A good one also ties every closed deal back to the marketing that produced it.
What is the most important thing a wholesaling CRM tracks?
Lead source, kept all the way to the closed deal. Without it you cannot tell which campaign paid for which deal, so you cannot cut the ones that lose money.
Is a spreadsheet enough?
For one person doing a few deals it can be. It breaks when more than one person works leads, when missed calls need to become tasks automatically, or when you need cost per closed deal by campaign without rebuilding it by hand.
Should I use an investor CRM or Salesforce?
Investor CRMs come set up for wholesaling and are quicker to start. Salesforce takes setup but fits teams that need their own process, several markets, or custom reporting. I build on Salesforce, so weigh my view with that in mind: the checklist on this page matters more than the brand.
How do I check my current CRM?
Go stage by stage through the checklist on this page and mark each line yes or no. The free Deal Leak Score does the same in ten questions and gives a score out of 100.

## Wholesaling Laws 2026: What Your CRM Has to Track
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesaling-laws-crm-tracking.html

New wholesaling laws: what your CRM has to track.
Since 2025, a run of states has put rules on wholesaling homes: a written disclosure before the contract, a window for the seller to cancel, and in some states a registration, a license, a deposit in escrow or a deadline to close. Each rule comes with a date someone has to remember. This page lists what each state asks for in plain words, then the fields, automations and report that let your CRM remember those dates for you.
The short version
Ten states with wholesaling rules that took effect from 2025 on, in date order. "Cancel" means the seller's right to cancel without penalty.
State | In force from | Main rules | Dates your CRM has to hold
Pennsylvania | Jan 4, 2025 | Wholesalers need a real estate license; contract must say it is a wholesale deal; cancel by day 30 | Contract date, day-30 cancel deadline, license number
Tennessee | Mar 25, 2025 | Disclose your equitable interest to the buyer in writing; tell the seller three days before you assign | Seller notice date, planned assignment date
Oregon | Jul 1, 2025 | Register with the Real Estate Agency (unless licensed); disclosure to sellers, buyers and in ads; cancel within 3 business days of the disclosure | Disclosure received date, 3-business-day deadline, registration renewal
North Dakota | 2023, amended 2025 | Written disclosure to all parties that you hold an equitable interest and plan to profit | Disclosure sent and signed dates
Maryland | Oct 1, 2025 | Tell the owner in writing you may assign; tell the assignee you hold an equitable interest | Owner disclosure date, assignee disclosure date
Oklahoma | Nov 1, 2025 | Disclosure before the contract; cancel within 2 business days; earnest money in an Oklahoma FDIC-insured bank | Disclosure date, 2-business-day deadline, where the deposit sits
Ohio | Mar 2, 2026 | Separate signed disclosure in bold 12-point type before the contract; if missing, owner can cancel until closing | Disclosure signed date (must be before contract date)
Connecticut | Jul 1, 2026 | Register with the Department of Consumer Protection; state disclosure report; cancel within 3 business days; closing date no more than 90 days out | Registration, report signed date, 3-business-day deadline, 90-day closing cap
Louisiana | Aug 1, 2026 | Disclosure; cancel for at least 5 calendar days; deposit of at least 1% in escrow; no deed signing until the window ends | Both signature dates, 5-day deadline, deposit amount and holder
Missouri | Aug 28, 2026 | Separate signed disclosure at least 14 calendar days before the contract | Disclosure date, earliest allowed contract date
Several states had wholesaling rules before 2025 (Illinois, Texas, Iowa, Virginia, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Arizona among them; see this state-by-state roundup ). They are not covered below. The same CRM build handles them once you add their rules.
State by state
Pennsylvania In force Jan 4, 2025
What the law says
Act 52 of 2024 treats wholesaling as real estate brokerage, so wholesalers need a license. Every wholesale contract has to say plainly that it is a wholesale deal, that the seller can get an appraisal or talk to a separate licensee or a lawyer, and that the seller can cancel by the 30th day after signing or before the property is conveyed, whichever comes first. Money paid is refunded within 10 business days of a cancellation notice. If the contract leaves this out, the seller can cancel any time before conveyance.
What to track in the CRM
License number and expiry on each user who contracts deals. Contract signed date, a "Cancel by" date set to 30 days later, and a task the day before. A checkbox that the contract version has the required notice, so an old template can't slip through.
Source
Tucker Arensberg: Act 52 takes effect January 4
Tennessee In force Mar 25, 2025
What the law says
Public Chapter 72 allows wholesaling if you disclose your equitable interest in writing to the person you assign to, and notify the seller that you intend to wholesale the property three days before the assignment. The state's newsletter says "three days"; some summaries say business days, so the safer setup counts business days.
What to track in the CRM
Seller notice sent date, planned assignment date, and a validation rule that blocks the "Assigned" stage until three days have passed since the notice. Buyer disclosure signed date on the assignment record.
Source
Tennessee Real Estate Commission newsletter, Spring 2025
Oregon In force Jul 1, 2025
What the law says
HB 4058 requires wholesalers who are not licensed brokers to register with the Oregon Real Estate Agency, renewed each year by June 30. A written disclosure, in at least 10-point bold type, goes to sellers and buyers before the contract, to brokers who help market or buy, and in property ads. Sellers and buyers can cancel by written notice until midnight at the end of the third business day after they get the disclosure. If the seller got no disclosure before the contract, they can end it any time and keep the earnest money.
What to track in the CRM
Registration number and renewal date (with a reminder in May). Disclosure received date for the seller and for the buyer, each with its own 3-business-day deadline. A checkbox on each marketing campaign that the ad carries the disclosure.
Source
Oregon Real Estate Agency: property wholesaling law rule overview
North Dakota In force since 2023, amended 2025
What the law says
Section 43-23-24 of the Century Code requires a wholesaler to tell all parties in writing that they hold an equitable interest, may not be able to convey title, and intend to profit from transferring that interest. If not, the seller can cancel before closing without penalty and keep the wholesaler's earnest money, and the buyer can cancel and get a full refund. The section was amended in 2025 by HB 1125 (signed April 7, 2025). Some summaries say the change widened it beyond homes; ask your attorney how it applies to your deals.
What to track in the CRM
Disclosure sent and signed dates for the seller and for the buyer, with the signed copy attached. A rule that blocks "Under Contract" and "Assigned" until both are filled.
Source
HB 1190 (2023) · HB 1125 enrolled (2025) · HB 1125 actions
Maryland In force Oct 1, 2025
What the law says
Chapter 508 of 2025 (HB 124) covers contracts with owners of owner-occupied homes. Before signing, the wholesale buyer tells the owner in writing that the contract may be assigned. Before assigning, the wholesaler tells the assignee in writing that they hold an equitable interest and may not be able to convey title. If the owner was not told and the contract is assigned, the owner can rescind before closing without penalty. An assignee who was not told can rescind and get the deposit back.
What to track in the CRM
Owner-occupied yes/no on the property. Owner disclosure date (must be on or before the contract date) and assignee disclosure date (must be on or before the assignment date), each with the signed copy.
Source
Chapter 508 (HB 124), Laws of Maryland 2025
Oklahoma In force Nov 1, 2025
What the law says
SB 1075 requires written disclosures before any contract, including your plan to resell for more and the homeowner's right to get a lawyer. Homeowners can cancel within two business days without penalty. Contracts need your contact details, payment terms and a standard cancellation notice from the Oklahoma Real Estate Commission. If a required part is missing, the contract can't be enforced and the homeowner keeps the earnest money. Earnest money has to sit in an Oklahoma FDIC-insured bank.
What to track in the CRM
Disclosure signed date, a 2-business-day "Cancel by" date, the bank holding the deposit, and a checkbox that the commission's cancellation notice is in the contract.
Source
Oklahoma Real Estate Commission press release on SB 1075
Ohio In force Mar 2, 2026
What the law says
SB 155 added section 5301.95 to the Revised Code. For homes with one to four units, a wholesaler buying from the owner has to give a written statement, separate from the purchase contract and in bold type of at least 12 points, saying they act for themselves, may assign the contract without the owner's consent and may charge a fee. The owner and wholesaler both sign and date it before a binding contract. If they don't, the owner can cancel any time before closing without penalty, and earnest money goes to the owner within 30 days. The owner can't waive this.
What to track in the CRM
Disclosure signed date and signed copy. A validation rule: contract date can't be earlier than the disclosure signed date. Property units (1 to 4) so the rule applies only where it should.
Source
Ohio Revised Code 5301.95 · JD Supra: new Ohio law targets wholesaling
Connecticut In force Jul 1, 2026
What the law says
Anyone wholesaling homes in Connecticut has to register with the Department of Consumer Protection, including licensed agents. Registration expires every even year on July 31. Before signing, the wholesaler gives the seller the state's wholesale disclosure report, signed by both. The seller can cancel within three business days for any reason. The contract's closing date can be no more than 90 days after the contract date, and extensions need both sides to agree in writing. When marketing to a buyer, the wholesaler says they are a registered wholesaler who doesn't hold title. No lien may be put on the property.
What to track in the CRM
Registration number and expiry. Disclosure report signed date and copy. A 3-business-day "Cancel by" date. A "Latest allowed closing" date of contract date + 90 days, a rule that the closing date can't be later, and alerts 30 and 14 days before it. Extension signed date if you extend.
Source
Connecticut DCP: real estate wholesaling · DCP news release, June 2026
Louisiana In force Aug 1, 2026
What the law says
Act 807 (HB 468) requires a written, prominent disclosure before each contract: that you intend to assign or sell your rights for more than you offered, that the seller should get legal advice, and that the seller can cancel for any reason for at least five calendar days after the later of the two signatures. The contract carries the notice "You may cancel this contract at any time before 11:59 PM of [date]", and you hand over the Real Estate Commission's cancellation form with each contract. You can't ask the seller to sign a deed or similar document until the window ends. The contract needs a deposit of at least 1% of the price, kept in the seller's account or an in-state escrow account at a federally insured bank. A violation makes the contract voidable by the seller until title transfers, with civil penalties up to $5,000 per violation.
What to track in the CRM
Seller signed date and wholesaler signed date. "Cancel by" = the later of the two + 5 calendar days, shown as the exact date to type into the contract notice. Deposit amount (with a check that it is at least 1% of the contract price) and where it is held. A rule that blocks scheduling the deed signing before the cancel date.
Source
HB 468 enrolled text · Act 807 digest · Louisiana REALTORS
Missouri In force Aug 28, 2026
What the law says
SB 973 added section 407.3600. For homes with one to four units, a wholesaler buying from the owner gives a written disclosure, separate from the contract, in bold 12-point type, at least 14 calendar days before entering the contract. Both sides sign and date it before a binding contract. If not, the owner can cancel any time before closing without penalty, and the escrow agent pays the wholesaler's earnest money to the owner within 30 days.
What to track in the CRM
Disclosure delivered date and signed date. "Earliest contract date" = delivered date + 14 calendar days, with a validation rule on the contract date. This changes your pipeline: Missouri offers need a two-week lead time, so the follow-up cadence has to carry the seller through it.
Source
Anderson & Associates: Missouri rewrote the rules for wholesalers · SB 973 text (perfected version)
The CRM build: one setup for every state
Don't build ten checklists. Put the state on the property, keep each state's rules in one table, and let the CRM work out the dates. Then a new law is a new row, not a rebuild. In Salesforce, the rules table is custom metadata; in other CRMs it can be a simple lookup list.
Fields on the property and deal
Field | Type | Why
Property state | Picklist, required | Picks the rules automatically. Taken from the address, never typed freehand.
Dwelling units / owner-occupied | Number / checkbox | Ohio and Missouri cover 1 to 4 units; Maryland covers owner-occupied homes.
Disclosure sent date | Date | Missouri counts 14 days from here; Oregon's window starts at receipt.
Disclosure signed date + signed copy | Date + file | Most states need it signed before the contract. No file, no stage change.
Contract signed date (seller / you) | Two dates | Louisiana counts from the later one.
Cancel by | Formula | Contract date + the state's window, in calendar or business days.
Latest allowed closing | Formula | Connecticut: contract date + 90 days.
Deposit amount and holder | Currency + text | Louisiana's 1% minimum; Oklahoma's in-state bank rule.
Seller notice of assignment date | Date | Tennessee's three-day notice; Maryland's assignee disclosure.
The state rules table
One row per state: disclosure lead time in days, cancel window length, calendar or business days, closing cap in days, registration or license needed, and the date you last checked the law. Business days need a holiday calendar; in Salesforce, set up business hours and holidays and use them in the formula. How to count weekends, holidays and the signing day is a question for your attorney, so record their answer in the table.
Automations
Stage gate: a validation rule stops a deal moving to "Under Contract" until the disclosure signed date and file are there, in the states that require them.
Cancel window task: when the contract is signed, create a task for the transaction coordinator on the cancel-by date, and keep the deal out of buyer blasts until it has passed.
Missouri lead time: block a contract date earlier than disclosure date + 14 days, and add a follow-up task at day 13.
Closing deadline alerts: alerts at 30, 14 and 7 days before the latest allowed closing date, to the deal owner and their manager.
Registration renewals: a reminder 60 days before each state registration or license expires.
Contract template version: store which template was used, so a law change can be traced to every deal signed on the old one.
The Monday report: compliance exceptions
One report, sorted by state, of open deals where something is missing or close: disclosure not signed, signed after the contract date, cancel window still open on a deal already sent to buyers, closing within 14 days of the state cap, deposit under the minimum, or registration expiring. On a clean week it is empty. That is the point: you review the exceptions, not every file.
The field list above fits next to the rest of a wholesaling setup in the free CRM field kit , and the deal fields come from the wholesaling CRM checklist . For the money side of an assignment, see the assignment fee guide .
Questions
Which states have new wholesaling laws?
From 2025 on: Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Oregon, Maryland and Oklahoma in 2025, a 2025 amendment in North Dakota, then Ohio (March 2, 2026), Connecticut (July 1, 2026), Louisiana (August 1, 2026) and Missouri (August 28, 2026). Other states had rules before 2025. Check with a real estate attorney in your state.
What does my CRM need to track for these laws?
For each deal: the property state, the disclosure sent and signed dates with the signed copy, both contract signature dates, the date the seller's cancel window ends, the latest allowed closing date where there is one, the deposit amount and where it is held, and your registration or license where the state requires it.
How do I calculate the cancellation window end date?
Keep each state's window in a rules table: the number of days and whether they are calendar or business days. A formula adds it to the right start date, such as the later signature in Louisiana or the disclosure receipt in Oregon. Business days need a holiday calendar. Ask your attorney how to count the first day, weekends and holidays.
Do I need a license to wholesale?
It depends on the state. Pennsylvania treats wholesaling as brokerage and requires a license. Oregon and Connecticut require a registration. Ohio, Missouri, Louisiana, Maryland and Oklahoma focus on disclosures and cancellation rights. This is not legal advice; ask a real estate attorney in your state.
Can Salesforce block a contract if the disclosure is missing?
Yes. A validation rule can stop a deal from moving to Under Contract until the disclosure signed date and file are on the record, and only in states whose rule needs it. A flow can then create the cancel-window task and the closing-deadline alerts.
Is this page legal advice?
No. It is a plain-words summary written so you can set up tracking. Laws change and have details this page leaves out. Check with a real estate attorney in each state you work in.

## Wholesaling Pipeline Stages: Entry and Exit Rules
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesaling-pipeline-stages.html

Wholesaling pipeline stages: what must be true to enter and leave each one
Most wholesaling pipelines have the right names and no rules. A deal sits in "Offer made" for five weeks because nobody owns it, another jumps to "Under contract" with no contract on file, and the Monday report shows a pipeline that looks fuller than it is. The stage names aren't the problem. A stage is only useful if there is a rule for getting in, a rule for getting out, a person responsible and a time limit. This guide gives you all four for each stage a home-buying or wholesaling team needs, plus how to build them in Salesforce so the system enforces them instead of memory.
Use eight working stages: New lead, Contacted, Appointment set, Offer made, Under contract, Marketing to buyers, Closed, and Dead. For each one write what must be true to enter it, what must be filled in to leave it, who owns it, and how many days it may sit there. Keep "Not now" out of Dead: a seller with a re-contact date is still a lead. In Salesforce, build this with a Path (up to five key fields and up to 1,000 characters of guidance per stage), validation rules for the must-have fields, and a stage-age alert.
Why do wholesaling pipelines leak?
A pipeline leaks when a stage change is a click instead of a decision. Picture a hypothetical team of six: an acquisitions rep moves a seller to "Offer made" after a phone call, the offer never goes out in writing, and the seller stops answering. Nothing in the CRM says the offer was never sent, so the deal looks alive for a month. Multiply that by forty open deals and your forecast is fiction.
Four things cause most of it:
Stages describe the rep's activity, not the seller's situation. "Working" tells you what someone is doing, not what happens next.
No exit rule. Anyone can move a deal forward with nothing filled in, so the data behind later stages is missing.
No owner for the gaps. The hand-offs (cold caller to acquisitions, acquisitions to dispo) are where deals sit unclaimed.
No clock. A deal can sit in one stage forever without anybody being told.
What are the eight stages of a wholesale or home-buying pipeline?
These are the stages I'd start a 10 to 50 person team on. Rename them to fit your shop, but keep the logic: each stage answers one question about the seller or the deal.
Stage | Enters when | Can't leave until | Owner | Time limit
New lead | Any inquiry creates a record with a source | First contact attempt is logged | Lead queue, then the assigned rep | Minutes, not hours
Contacted | You spoke to the seller or an owner | Reason for selling, timeline, condition and a next follow-up date are filled in | Cold caller or acquisitions | A few days to qualify or park
Appointment set | A call or walkthrough is booked | Date and time, confirmed address, every decision maker named | Acquisitions | Until the appointment date, plus a no-show check
Offer made | An offer has been sent | Offer amount, your maximum allowable offer, offer date and the follow-up date | Acquisitions | Follow-up task due within a day or two
Under contract | The seller has signed | Signed contract on the record, contract price, closing date, title company | Acquisitions, then transaction coordinator | Dispo must start the same day
Marketing to buyers | Dispo has started | Assignment ask, buyers sent, buyer responses logged | Dispositions | Time to a buyer's signature
Closed | A buyer signed or you closed | Buyer, assignment price, fee and exit type | Transaction coordinator | Until funded
Dead | The deal is truly over | Dead reason from a short picklist | Whoever closes it | None
If your pipeline has a lot more stages than this, check whether some are really tasks or statuses. "Waiting on title" is a task. "Seller thinking about it" is a follow-up date. A stage should change what you do with a deal, not describe a to-do on it.
What are the four rules every stage needs?
An entry rule: one sentence a new rep could apply without asking you. "The seller signed" is an entry rule. "Looks good" is not.
An exit rule: the fields that must be filled in before the deal can move on. This is what makes the data usable later. If you need the offer date to measure speed to offer, the exit rule from "Appointment" has to ask for it.
An owner: one name or one queue, never "the team". The hand-offs need the clearest owners of all.
A clock: a maximum number of days before something fires: a task, an alert to the manager, a flag in the report. Choose the number from your own history, not a blog. Look at how long your closed deals took in each stage and flag anything well past that.
Write these four things for each stage on one page and review it with the team once. It takes an hour and it ends most arguments about whose deal something is.
Where do "not now" sellers go?
Not into Dead. A seller who says "call me in March" is a lead with a date, and the biggest source of reactivation deals you have. Give "Not now" its own handling:
A required re-contact date and a reason (timing, price, another buyer, needs repairs done, probate pending).
A task created automatically on that date, assigned to the original owner.
A separate stage or status such as "Nurture", so it never counts in your active pipeline numbers.
Reserve Dead for sellers who bought elsewhere, listed with an agent, or said to stop. Keep the dead reason a short picklist (5 to 8 values), because that is what lets you see why deals die. The playbook for waking up parked sellers is in reactivating dead seller leads , and the cadence is in the follow-up cadence builder .
Should these be Lead statuses or Opportunity stages in Salesforce?
Both, split at the point where an inquiry becomes a real deal. Early stages (New lead, Contacted, and Nurture) usually fit the Lead record. The deal stages (Appointment set through Closed) usually fit the Opportunity. The split matters because an inquiry that never becomes a deal shouldn't clog your opportunity reports, and your forecast should only count deals. Where exactly to convert is covered in Lead, Opportunity or Property: how to model a seller in Salesforce .
How do you build this in Salesforce?
1. Path for the stages that matter
Path shows the stages as a bar at the top of the record. For each step you can pick up to five key fields and write up to 1,000 characters of guidance. Put the exit rule's must-have fields in the key fields, and put the entry rule and a two-line script in the guidance. Reps see what they need at the exact moment they move a deal.
2. Validation rules for the must-haves
Path is guidance, not enforcement. To make a field truly required, add a validation rule that blocks the move to a stage unless the fields are filled. Example: moving to "Under contract" fails with a clear message unless contract price, closing date and a signed contract link are present. Keep the messages specific ("Add the closing date before moving to Under contract") so reps know what to fix.
3. A stage-age alert
Add a date field that stamps whenever the stage changes, then a scheduled flow that finds deals past their time limit and creates a task for the owner, with a notice to the manager when it's past a second limit. A simple flow beats a dashboard nobody opens.
4. Stage history for free
Salesforce keeps a history of opportunity stage changes automatically, which is what lets you report on how long deals spend in each stage. Create a custom report type or use the "Opportunities with History" report type to see stage age and where deals get stuck.
5. Roles and permissions
Decide who can move a deal backward, who can reopen a Dead deal, and who can change a closed deal's price. Fewer people with those rights means cleaner numbers. If VAs work in the CRM, see who sees what .
Which three reports show whether the stages work?
Deals by stage and age: open deals grouped by stage, sorted by days in stage. The oldest rows are your first calls of the week.
Stage-to-stage conversion: of the deals that entered a stage, how many reached the next one, by source and by rep. This shows whether the leak is at the offer or at the contract.
Dead reasons: a count by reason and by source for the last 90 days. If "bought elsewhere" leads the list, the problem is speed or follow-up, not lead quality.
More report recipes are in 20 Salesforce reports for wholesalers and the five numbers I'd put in front of an owner every Monday are in the Monday 5 .
What are the most common mistakes?
Too many stages. Past eight or nine, reps skip stages and the data goes soft.
Required fields on everything. If you require ten fields at stage one, reps will type junk to get past it. Ask for what you need at each step, no more.
Dead as a parking lot. If nothing leaves Dead, you are throwing away your cheapest leads.
Changing stage names without migrating history. Renaming a stage can break reports and any automation or ad-platform feed keyed to it. Plan stage changes like a small project.
No review. Walk through the oldest ten deals in each stage once a week. It takes 15 minutes and it is the cheapest quality control you have.
If you want a second pair of eyes on your stages, this is exactly what the CRM Revenue Audit looks at first.
Questions
What are the stages of a wholesale real estate deal in a CRM?
A workable set is New lead, Contacted, Appointment set, Offer made, Under contract, Marketing to buyers, Closed and Dead. Each stage needs a rule for entering it, the fields required to leave it, an owner and a time limit, so a stage change means something.
How many pipeline stages should a wholesaler have?
Eight or nine is plenty for most teams. More stages usually mean some are really tasks or statuses, and reps start skipping them. If a stage doesn't change what you do with the deal, fold it into a task or a follow-up date.
What is the difference between a lead status and a pipeline stage?
A lead status says how far an inquiry has been worked. A pipeline stage tracks a real deal. In Salesforce, the early steps usually live on the Lead and the deal stages on the Opportunity, split at the point where an inquiry becomes a deal.
Where should sellers who say "not now" go in my pipeline?
Not in Dead. Give them a Nurture status with a required re-contact date and reason, and create a task on that date for the original owner. Keep Dead for sellers who bought elsewhere, listed with an agent or asked you to stop.
How long should a deal stay in each stage?
Set the limit from your own closed deals: look at how long deals spent in each stage and flag anything well past that. The first contact stage should be measured in minutes, offer follow-up in a day or two, and Under contract should hand off to dispo the same day.
How do I set up pipeline stages in Salesforce?
Use a Path on the stage picklist with up to five key fields and up to 1,000 characters of guidance per step, validation rules that block a stage change when must-have fields are empty, and a flow that flags deals past their time limit.
What should a cold caller hand off to acquisitions?
The seller's reason for selling, timeline, condition, price expectation, who else decides, and the next agreed step, all in fields on the record rather than in a note. The checklist is in the cold caller handoff page.

## Wholesaling Systems FAQ: 40 Pain Points Answered
URL: https://amrmagdy.com/wholesaling-systems-faq.html

Wholesaling systems FAQ: 40 pain points, answered from a systems view
These are the questions I hear from owners and ops leads at wholesaling and home-buying companies, in my calls, in investor groups and in the replies to my own posts. They sound different on the surface ("my VA makes 4,500 calls a week and I get nothing", "deals die between the offer and the contract", "my dashboard doesn't match my bank"), but nearly all of them are systems problems: a missing owner, a missing date, a field that isn't required, two records for one seller. Each answer below is short and points to the full guide. For the questions behind Salesforce specifically, there is a separate page with 50 Salesforce answers , and for the very practical "how do I" questions from owners, questions from wholesalers .
Most wholesaling pain points trace back to five system gaps: no owner and no clock on a new lead, no dated next step on an open lead, no rules for moving a deal between stages, more than one record for the same seller, and no source tracked through to the contract. Fix those five and the symptoms (cold leads, stalled offers, wrong numbers, wasted marketing) mostly ease. The answers below take each symptom in turn.
How to use this page: find the symptom that sounds like your week, read the short answer, and follow the link if you want the full version with steps. If your problem isn't here, ask me . Real questions are how this page grows.
Leads and speed
Why do my seller leads go cold before anyone calls them?
Usually because nobody is told to. A new lead lands in a list, and calling it depends on someone checking. Make every new lead create a task for a named person, or for a shared queue with a claim rule, within minutes. Speed to lead has the setup.
How fast should we call a new seller lead?
As fast as you can, measured in minutes. Harvard Business Review's study of online leads found firms that tried to contact a lead within an hour were nearly seven times as likely to qualify it as those that waited longer. Set your own target and report on it by rep. All the sourced statistics .
How do I stop missing seller phone calls?
Treat a missed call as a lead: log it, create a callback task for the owner, and text the number back if you have consent. Then report on missed calls by hour so you can staff the gaps. Missed-call alerts walks through it.
How do I know which lead source is actually working?
Record the source and campaign on every lead at the moment it's created, put the marketing cost on the campaign, and follow each lead through to a signed contract. Then report cost per contract by source, not leads by source. Lead sources in Salesforce .
Why does my lead count look good but my contracts don't?
Because leads are not the same as sellers. Duplicates, junk leads and sources that bring in shoppers inflate the count. Check for duplicate records first, then compare each source's rate of appointment, offer and contract, not just volume. Duplicate seller leads .
What should I do with leads that never answer?
Give them a fixed, finite follow-up plan, then move them to a nurture status with a re-contact date instead of calling them dead. Sellers' circumstances change, and these are your cheapest leads to wake up. Follow-up cadence builder .
Follow-up
How many times should I follow up with a seller?
It depends on the seller's timeline and your lead source, but the rule is consistency over a long period rather than a burst. Build the touch plan into the CRM so it doesn't rely on memory. The cadence builder gives a plan by seller type.
How do I follow up on offers that went quiet?
Make the follow-up date a required field when an offer is sent, and create the task automatically. Quiet offers are usually not rejected offers; they are unattended ones. Offer follow-up covers what to send and when.
How do I stop follow-up depending on my team's memory?
Require a next follow-up date on every open lead and block a stage change without one. Then a scheduled automation creates the task and flags overdue ones to a manager. The system holds the memory, the person does the call.
What is the best way to reactivate old seller leads?
Segment them by why they went quiet and how long ago, approve each segment and message with a person, check consent and opt-outs first, and send in small waves you can measure. Reactivating dead seller leads has the playbook.
Should follow-up be automated or personal?
Both, with a clear split: automation creates the tasks, reminders and the first light touch, while a person has the actual conversation once a seller replies. The AI guide ranks which jobs to hand over first. AI for wholesalers .
Pipeline and handoffs
What stages should my wholesaling pipeline have?
Eight working stages are enough for most teams: New lead, Contacted, Appointment set, Offer made, Under contract, Marketing to buyers, Closed and Dead, plus a Nurture status for "not now". Each needs an entry rule, an exit rule, an owner and a time limit. Pipeline stages .
How do I hand a lead from my cold caller to acquisitions?
Pass the reason for selling, timeline, condition, price expectation, who else decides and the agreed next step, as fields on the record, not a voicemail or a note. Make the handoff a stage with an owner and a clock. Cold caller handoff checklist .
Why do deals stall between the offer and the contract?
Mostly because the offer has no owner and no follow-up date, or the seller's other decision-makers weren't identified at the appointment. Require both before a deal can enter Offer made, and review the oldest offers weekly.
When does a lead become a deal in the CRM?
Usually when an appointment is set. Before that, it's an inquiry on the Lead; after, it's a deal on an Opportunity. Converting too early inflates the pipeline and too late hides the stages you want to measure. Lead, Opportunity or Property .
How should I track a deal after the contract is signed?
Keep the signed contract, closing date, title company and assignment or sale price on the deal, hand it to dispo the same day, and track buyer responses. Dispositions and transaction coordination cover it.
Team and access
What CRM workflow should a new cold caller start with?
A short one: a queue of assigned leads, a few required fields to fill after each conversation, a clear rule for what counts as a handoff, and a daily view of their own numbers. Add rules only when you see a repeated mistake. Team roles and the CRM .
How do I monitor my cold callers' calls and numbers?
Make sure the dialer logs every call to the seller's record, then report calls, conversations, appointments set and handoffs by caller by week. Judge them on appointments and handoff quality, not call volume. Dialers and the CRM .
How much CRM access should my VAs get?
Only what their job needs: usually their own leads and tasks, not exports of the whole database, and a log of what they changed. Set this up before they start, not after something goes missing. Who sees what .
How do I stop an employee from taking my lead list?
Limit who can export, hide phone numbers where the job doesn't need them, turn on field history, and review who exports what. You can't make theft impossible, but you can make it visible and slower. Stopping reps exporting your list .
How do I know if I need another acquisitions rep?
Look at appointments set per rep, the time from appointment to offer, and how many leads wait for a first call at peak hours. If appointments are being missed or delayed, capacity is the issue. The capacity calculator helps, and so does adding reps without losing leads .
What happens to my CRM when the person who built it leaves?
Often, nobody knows how things work, automations fail quietly and changes stop. Keep a short document of what's built, name a backup admin and review automation errors weekly. When your Salesforce admin leaves .
Numbers and reporting
Which five numbers should an owner look at every week?
The ones I'd start with are leads by source, time to first contact, appointments set, offers and contracts, and cost per contract. The Monday 5 sets them out with how to pull each one.
How do I calculate cost per contract?
Divide what you spent on a source in a period by the contracts that source produced, and for the true picture include the cost of people and tools. The cost per deal calculator does the arithmetic by source.
Why doesn't my dashboard match my bank account?
Usually because of dates (created vs closed), the running user's access, double-counted duplicates or deals entered differently by different reps. Ten reasons your numbers are off has a 20-minute check.
How do I send closed deals back to Google Ads?
Capture the Google click ID on every web lead, store it through to the deal, and upload the stages that matter (such as a signed contract) as offline conversions. The setup is in the Google Ads guide.
How do I give credit to the right campaign when a seller comes in twice?
Decide a rule in advance (first touch, last touch or both recorded) and apply it the same way every time, keeping the original source on the record. Which campaign gets credit?
Tools and CRM choice
What is the best CRM for real estate wholesalers?
There isn't one answer: it depends on team size, lead sources and how unusual your process is. Investor CRMs suit teams that want the loop built in, and Salesforce suits teams of about 10 or more that want to control the process. 11 options compared .
Is there a free CRM for wholesaling?
There are spreadsheets and free tiers of general CRMs, but none built around wholesaling. They work for one person with low volume and strain with a second person, big lists and the need for follow-up automation. What free gets you and where it stops .
When should I move off Podio?
When the things you've built around it (automation limits, integrations, reports) cost more than they save. A clean move needs a field map, a pilot and a plan for open deals. Moving off Podio and Podio's automation limit .
Is Salesforce too much for a small team?
For a solo operator or a team of two or three, often yes. It starts to make sense with about 10 people, several lead sources and a process of your own. Salesforce vs investor CRMs and the edition picker help you decide.
Can I run my wholesaling business from a spreadsheet?
At low volume with one person, yes. Add a next follow-up date, an overdue flag and a weekly count by source. Move when a second person needs it or lists get large. Here is a free seller lead tracker .
How do I tag leads without making a mess?
Use fields for what you'll count (source, situation), campaigns for marketing waves, checkboxes for consent, and tags only for short-lived labels from a fixed list. Tags, fields or campaigns .
AI and compliance
Can AI follow up with sellers for me?
For some jobs, yes: summarizing calls, drafting messages and ranking leads are low-risk starts. AI that contacts sellers on its own is higher-risk and needs consent. AI for wholesalers ranks the jobs and the rules.
Do I need consent to text sellers?
Generally yes, and your messaging also needs carrier registration (10DLC) and working opt-outs. This is not legal advice, so check your states. Texting sellers: 10DLC and consent .
How fast do I have to honor a stop text?
Since April 11, 2025, callers must process opt-out requests within a reasonable time not to exceed 10 business days and honor keywords such as STOP, QUIT and UNSUBSCRIBE. Sooner is safer, and one opt-out should cover every duplicate record.
Do wholesaling laws affect what my CRM tracks?
Yes. Several states have rules on wholesaling disclosures, licensing and contract language, and your CRM can hold the fields and checks that prove you followed them. Wholesaling laws and what your CRM has to track .
Fixing or moving your system
How do I know whether my CRM is leaking deals?
Check whether leads have sources and next steps, whether duplicates exist, how long leads wait for a first call and how long deals sit in each stage. The Deal Leak Score turns this into an estimate, and the audit checklist lists the checks.
How do I move to Salesforce from another CRM?
Export everything, map each old field to a new one, move the open pipeline first, run a short planned overlap and keep the old record IDs. How a move works has the plan.
How do I stop duplicate sellers in my CRM?
Match on a cleaned phone, email and property address, alert people instead of blocking integrations, de-duplicate lists before you import, and merge on a schedule. Duplicate seller leads .
